    • Infarcts less than 12 hours old are usually not visible grossly. After 2 to 3 hours they can be shown by triphenyl tetrazolium chloride, which stains normal myocardium brick-red and leaves the infarct pale.
    • Wavy fibres appear in the first 4 to 12 hours. Cardiac muscle cells cannot regenerate, so healing is by scar.
    • After reperfusion the infarct is haemorrhagic and the myocytes show contraction band necrosis.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 12)p. 497p. 499

    Myocardial infarction: complications

    B1

    Complications of MI.

    The main complications of MI are arrhythmias (the commonest, and the cause of early sudden death), contractile dysfunction with heart failure and cardiogenic shock, papillary muscle dysfunction with mitral regurgitation, myocardial rupture, pericarditis, mural thrombosis with embolism, ventricular aneurysm, right ventricular infarction, and progressive heart failure.

    Nearly three-quarters of patients have one or more complications, and their likelihood depends on infarct size, location and the fraction of wall thickness involved.

    1. Arrhythmias occur in up to 90% of patients (ventricular premature beats, ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation, bradyarrhythmias and heart block), are maximal in the first hour, and account for most out-of-hospital deaths.
    2. Left ventricular failure and cardiogenic shock. Pump function falls in proportion to the myocardium lost. Cardiogenic shock occurs in about 10% of transmural infarcts, usually when 40% or more of the left ventricle is damaged.
    3. Myocardial rupture (1–3%), most often 3 to 7 days after infarction when necrotic muscle is softest: free wall rupture causes haemopericardium and tamponade, septal rupture produces an acquired VSD, and papillary muscle rupture causes acute mitral regurgitation.
    4. Papillary muscle dysfunction with mitral regurgitation from ischaemia, later from fibrosis or ventricular dilation.
    5. Pericarditis, a fibrinous or fibrinohaemorrhagic reaction 2–3 days after a transmural infarct, and Dressler syndrome [pericarditis after myocardial infarction] weeks later.
    6. Mural thrombosis with the risk of systemic embolism.
    7. Ventricular aneurysm, a late complication of a large anteroseptal infarct, with thrombi, arrhythmias and heart failure but no rupture.
    8. Right ventricular infarction accompanying posterior septal or inferior infarcts.
    9. Infarct expansion, ventricular remodeling and progressive heart failure (chronic ischaemic heart disease).

    Mention the complications/consequences of myocardial infarction.

    10DU25NDU24MDU22NDU20NDU20JuDU19NovDU14JaDU12JaDU09JuDU03Ja

    Nearly three-quarters of patients have one or more complications.

    1. Contractile dysfunction. Left ventricular failure with hypotension and pulmonary congestion and oedema. Cardiogenic shock occurs in about 10% of transmural MIs, usually when 40% or more of the left ventricle is damaged.
    2. Papillary muscle dysfunction, causing mitral regurgitation.
    3. Right ventricular infarction, with right-sided failure.
    4. Myocardial rupture (1% to 3%): free wall rupture with haemopericardium and cardiac tamponade. Ventricular septal rupture with left-to-right shunt. Papillary muscle rupture with severe mitral regurgitation. Most common 3 to 7 days after infarction, when necrotic muscle is softest.
    5. Arrhythmias. About 90% of patients
      Heart block, bradycardia, tachyarrhythmias, ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation. The risk of ventricular fibrillation is greatest in the first hour.
    6. Pericarditis, fibrinohaemorrhagic, 2 to 3 days after a transmural MI
      Rarely Dressler syndrome [pericarditis after myocardial infarction] weeks later, due to antibodies against damaged pericardium and myocardium.
    7. Chamber dilation from thinning of the infarcted region.
    8. Mural thrombus, with a risk of embolism.
    9. Ventricular aneurysm, a late complication after a large transmural anteroseptal infarct. It causes thrombi, arrhythmias and heart failure but does not rupture.
    10. Progressive heart failure.

    Outlook depends on infarct size, site and thickness of wall involved. About 20% die within the first year, mostly in the first 30 days.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 12)p. 501p. 502

    Myocardial infarction: diagnosis and markers

    B1

    Mention important cardiac biochemical markers. Laboratory diagnosis of acute MI.

    The important cardiac biomarkers are the cardiac-specific troponins T and I (the best markers), CK-MB, myoglobin and, historically, LDH. Acute MI is diagnosed by combining typical symptoms, ECG changes and a rise and fall of troponin above the reference limit.

    The laboratory diagnosis rests on measuring proteins that leak from irreversibly injured myocytes after the sarcolemma loses integrity. Cardiac troponin T or I, regulatory proteins of calcium-mediated contraction, rise within 2–4 hours, peak at 24–48 hours and remain elevated for 7–10 days. With reperfusion they peak earlier and higher because of rapid washout. CK-MB rises in 3–12 hours, peaks at about 24 hours and returns to baseline by 48–72 hours, so it is useful for detecting reinfarction.

    Myoglobin rises within 1–3 hours but is not cardiac-specific. LDH rises at 24–48 hours with a flipped LDH1 greater than LDH2 ratio, peaking at 3–6 days. Low-level troponin elevation ("troponin leak") also occurs in heart failure, pulmonary embolism, renal failure and sepsis, and large acute rises occur in myocarditis and myocardial trauma, so the clinical context and serial values matter. Supporting tests are the ECG (ST elevation in STEMI), echocardiography for regional wall-motion abnormality and coronary angiography.

    Give the laboratory diagnosis of MI.

    DU07Ju

    MI is diagnosed by three things: clinical symptoms, laboratory tests for myocardial proteins in the plasma, and characteristic electrocardiographic changes.

    1. Cardiac troponins T and I (cTnT, cTnI). The most clinically useful biomarkers of myocardial damage. They leak from necrotic myocytes through the damaged sarcolemma. Diagnosis is established when blood levels exceed threshold levels. They begin to rise in 2 to 4 hours, peak at 24 to 48 hours and stay raised for 7 to 10 days.
    2. Electrocardiogram. A transmural infarct shows ST elevation (STEMI) and a subendocardial infarct does not (NSTEMI). Small infarcts may give non-specific changes or none.
    3. Clinical presentation. Chest pain lasting over 30 minutes, crushing or squeezing, with sweating, nausea, vomiting and dyspnoea. Up to 25% of cases are painless.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 12)p. 499p. 500

    What are the cardiac markers/enzymes of MI (with change over time)?

    9DU24MDU22NDU20NDU20JuDU19MDU16JaDU14JuDU13JaDU08Ja

    The clinically useful markers are the cardiac-specific troponins T and I.

    MarkerRisePeakDuration of elevation
    Cardiac troponins T and I2 to 4 hours24 to 48 hours7 to 10 days

    With reperfusion, troponin levels may be higher and peak earlier because of faster washout from the necrotic tissue.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 12)p. 500

    Why is troponin the best indicator for MI?

    DU08JaDU06Ja
    1. Cardiac specific. Troponins T and I are proteins that regulate calcium-mediated contraction of cardiac muscle, so a rise reflects myocardial damage.
    2. Sensitive. They detect irreversible myocyte damage sensitively, because they leak out of necrotic cells once the sarcolemma is disrupted.
    3. Diagnostic threshold. Myocardial injury is established when levels exceed threshold levels.
    4. Long window. They begin to rise at 2 to 4 hours, peak at 24 to 48 hours and remain elevated 7 to 10 days, so late presentation can still be diagnosed.

    Limitation. Acute rises also occur in myocarditis and myocardial trauma, and low-level elevations ("troponin leak") in heart failure, pulmonary embolus, renal failure and sepsis. Serial measurements help, because these do not follow the time course of MI.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 12)p. 500

    Myocardial infarction (case)

    B10

    A 56-year-old male presented to you with sudden severe left-sided chest pain and sweating. The pain was not relieved by taking rest or by sublingual nitroglycerin. What is your probable diagnosis? What investigations should you advise, and what are their expected clinical results?

    My probable diagnosis is acute myocardial infarction, since severe chest pain with sweating that is not relieved by rest or nitroglycerin indicates prolonged ischaemia with myocardial necrosis, usually from plaque rupture with coronary thrombosis. I would order an ECG, serial cardiac troponins, CK-MB, echocardiography and coronary angiography, and I would expect ST-segment elevation and a rising troponin.

    Diagnosis. The pain is severe, lasts more than 30 minutes, is described as crushing and is accompanied by diaphoresis, and, unlike angina, it is unrelieved by rest or nitrates. This indicates acute MI, probably due to occlusive thrombosis over a disrupted atheromatous plaque (an acute coronary syndrome). Aortic dissection must be excluded, since it also causes severe pain.

    Investigations and expected results

    • ECG: ST-segment elevation in the leads overlying the infarct (STEMI) when transmural, with later T-wave inversion and pathologic Q waves. NSTEMI shows ST depression or T-wave changes.
    • Cardiac troponin T or I: raised from 2–4 hours, peaking at 24–48 hours and remaining high for 7–10 days (serial sampling, with a rise and fall).
    • CK-MB: raised at 3–12 hours, peaking at about 24 hours and normalising in 48–72 hours. Myoglobin is raised early.
    • Blood tests: neutrophilic leucocytosis, raised ESR and CRP, possible hyperglycaemia, and a lipid profile.
    • Echocardiography: regional wall-motion abnormality and reduced ejection fraction, and evidence of complications (mitral regurgitation, VSD, effusion, thrombus).
    • Chest radiograph: pulmonary congestion if left ventricular failure. Mediastinal widening if dissection is suspected.
    • Coronary angiography: shows the occluding thrombus and underlying atherosclerotic stenosis, and allows reperfusion by angioplasty and stenting.

    The goal of management is rapid reperfusion ("time is myocardium"), with antiplatelet agents, anticoagulants, beta blockers and nitrates.

    A5

    50-year-old man with severe central chest pain and sweating followed by transient unconsciousness — Likely diagnosis? Laboratory investigations to confirm that diagnosis?

    A5

    Likely diagnosis: acute myocardial infarction. Prolonged crushing central chest pain with sweating is the classic presentation, and syncope may come from an arrhythmia, which complicates about 90% of MIs.

    Investigations to confirm

    1. Cardiac troponin T or I, raised above threshold. Rises in 2 to 4 hours, peaks at 24 to 48 hours, stays up 7 to 10 days. Serial measurement helps distinguish other causes of troponin rise.
    2. Electrocardiogram, with ST elevation (STEMI) in a transmural infarct or no ST elevation (NSTEMI) in a subendocardial one.
    3. The clinical picture itself.

    A patient has severe central chest pain, sweating, ± syncope. What is the probable diagnosis?

    5DU21MDU19MDU17NovDU12JaDU11Ja

    Acute myocardial infarction, caused most often by rupture or erosion of a coronary atheromatous plaque with superimposed thrombosis. The pain is prolonged (more than 30 minutes), crushing or squeezing, with sweating, nausea and dyspnoea. Syncope can be due to an arrhythmia or pump failure.

    Same: what investigations/expected biochemical findings confirm it?

    5DU21MDU19MDU17NovDU12JaDU11Ja
    1. Cardiac troponin T or I raised above the diagnostic threshold, beginning 2 to 4 hours after onset, peaking at 24 to 48 hours and remaining elevated for 7 to 10 days.
    2. ECG: ST elevation (STEMI) or none (NSTEMI).
    3. Serial troponin measurements to separate MI from other causes of mild rise.

    Hypertensive Heart Disease

    A 70y man has long-standing hypertension. What type of adaptive change may occur in his heart?

    DU24N

    Left ventricular hypertrophy (concentric), a pathologic adaptation to the pressure overload of chronic hypertension. It leads to systemic (left-sided) hypertensive heart disease.

    • Myocytes increase in size without new cells.
    • The heart is heavy (may exceed 500 g) with a left ventricular wall over 2.0 cm thick, initially without dilation.
    • Increased interstitial connective tissue makes the wall stiff, impairing diastolic filling and enlarging the left atrium.
    • It is maladaptive in the end: myocardial demand ischaemia, dilation, heart failure and sometimes sudden death.
    • Control of hypertension can prevent hypertrophy and even cause regression.

    Same: mention physiological conditions where this change can occur.

    DU24N

    Hypertrophy is physiologic when it is driven by increased functional demand or by hormones and growth factors.

    1. Uterus in pregnancy. Smooth muscle hypertrophy stimulated by oestrogen.
    2. Skeletal muscle of bodybuilders, from increased demand.

    Valvular Heart Disease

    Rheumatic fever

    B1

    What is the etiopathogenesis of rheumatic fever? Diagnostic criteria of rheumatic fever.

    Rheumatic fever is an acute, immunologically mediated multisystem inflammatory disease that follows group A β-haemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis by 2–3 weeks. Antibodies and CD4⁺ T cells directed against streptococcal M protein cross-react with host cardiac antigens (molecular mimicry). The diagnosis rests on the revised Jones criteria [major and minor criteria for rheumatic fever]: evidence of preceding streptococcal infection plus two major manifestations, or one major and two minor manifestations.

    Aetiopathogenesis. Rheumatic fever (RF) is a hypersensitivity (autoimmune) reaction to group A streptococcal antigens, not an infection of the heart itself. Streptococci are absent from the lesions. Antibodies and CD4⁺ T cells against streptococcal M protein cross-react with pericardial, myocardial and valvular antigens. Antibody binding activates complement and recruits Fc-receptor–bearing cells such as neutrophils and macrophages, and T-cell cytokines activate macrophages (for example within Aschoff bodies [granulomas of rheumatic carditis]).

    The 2–3 week delay (10 days to 6 weeks) reflects the time needed for the immune response. Only 0.3–3% of infected people develop RF, which points to genetic susceptibility. It mostly affects children aged 5–15 years and is favoured by overcrowding and poverty. The chronic valve deformity is the healing and scarring that follows repeated acute inflammation.

    Diagnostic criteria (revised Jones criteria). Evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection (a rising or raised ASO or anti-DNase B titre, positive throat culture or rapid antigen test, or recent scarlet fever), plus:

    Major criteriaMinor criteria
    Migratory polyarthritis of large jointsFever
    Carditis (pancarditis)Arthralgia
    Subcutaneous nodulesRaised acute-phase reactants (ESR, CRP)
    Erythema marginatumProlonged PR interval on ECG
    Sydenham chorea

    The diagnosis requires two major, or one major and two minor, criteria with evidence of preceding streptococcal infection. These criteria are applied differently in low-risk and high-risk populations. In high-risk populations, such as those with a high background incidence of RF, arthralgia may count as a major criterion and lower thresholds for fever and acute-phase reactants apply.

    B1

    Which valve is commonly affected by rheumatic fever? What is an Aschoff body?

    The mitral valve is the valve most commonly affected
    it is involved in virtually all cases of chronic rheumatic heart disease, alone in about two-thirds and together with the aortic valve in another 25%. An Aschoff body [granulomas of rheumatic carditis] is the pathognomonic granulomatous lesion of rheumatic carditis, a focus of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells and plump activated macrophages called Anitschkow cells [caterpillar-nucleus histiocytes of rheumatic carditis] ("caterpillar cells").

    Valve involvement. The mitral valve is virtually always involved in chronic rheumatic heart disease, in isolation in about two-thirds of cases and with the aortic valve in another 25%. The tricuspid valve is infrequently affected and the pulmonary valve rarely. Rheumatic heart disease is virtually the only cause of mitral stenosis, producing "fish-mouth" stenosis with leaflet thickening, commissural fusion, and thickened, fused tendinous cords.

    Aschoff body. The Aschoff body is a distinctive lesion of acute rheumatic carditis, found in the interstitial connective tissue, often perivascular, in any of the three layers of the heart. It consists of an area of fibrinoid necrosis infiltrated by T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells and large macrophages with abundant cytoplasm (Anitschkow cells). In longitudinal section the central chromatin of these cells condenses into a slender wavy ribbon ("caterpillar cells"), and in cross-section appears like an "owl-eye." Some Anitschkow cells fuse to form multinucleated Aschoff giant cells. Aschoff bodies are rarely seen in chronic rheumatic heart disease because of the long interval since the acute illness.

    B1

    Complications of rheumatic fever.

    The complications of rheumatic fever are acute carditis with heart failure, arrhythmias and pericardial effusion (fatal in 1–2%), recurrent attacks, and chronic rheumatic heart disease, whose complications include mitral stenosis, atrial fibrillation, thromboembolism, infective endocarditis and right-sided failure.

    Acute phase. Rheumatic carditis (pancarditis) can cause tachycardia, arrhythmias, cardiac dilation, functional mitral regurgitation and heart failure, and 1–2% of patients die of fulminant cardiac involvement. Fibrinous pericarditis with friction rub and effusion may occur. The arthritis is self-limited and leaves no deformity, and Sydenham chorea and skin lesions resolve. After the first attack, each streptococcal pharyngitis can precipitate a recurrence, and the valve damage is cumulative.

    Chronic rheumatic heart disease (years to decades later). Healing by fibrosis produces leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and shortening, and thickened, fused cords, causing mitral stenosis ("fish-mouth") and/or regurgitation and aortic valve disease. Consequent complications are left atrial dilation with atrial fibrillation and mural thrombi with systemic thromboembolism (stroke), pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular hypertrophy and failure, congestive heart failure, superimposed infective endocarditis, and valve calcification needing surgical repair or replacement.

    B10

    A 6-year-old boy develops fever, joint pain, a diffuse skin rash and a nodule 3 weeks after recovery from a sore throat. His ESR is 70 mm in the first hour, and his ASO titer is 500 IU/mL. What is your probable diagnosis? What are the changes in the heart in this case?

    The probable diagnosis is acute rheumatic fever. The history of a sore throat followed 3 weeks later by fever, migratory joint pain, a rash (erythema marginatum) and a subcutaneous nodule, together with a raised ESR and a raised ASO titre showing preceding streptococcal infection, fulfils the Jones criteria [major and minor criteria for rheumatic fever]. In the heart there is pancarditis with Aschoff bodies [granulomas of rheumatic carditis], fibrinous pericarditis, myocarditis and verrucous endocarditis along the lines of closure of the mitral valve.

    Diagnosis. The child has major criteria (arthritis, erythema marginatum rash and a subcutaneous nodule, with carditis to be sought) and minor criteria (fever, raised ESR), and the ASO titre of 500 IU/mL documents a preceding group A streptococcal infection. The latent period of about 3 weeks is characteristic of an immune-mediated reaction.

    Cardiac changes. During acute rheumatic fever focal inflammatory lesions develop in the heart and the characteristic lesion is the Aschoff body, so that any of the three layers can be involved (pancarditis).

    • Pericarditis: fibrinous or serofibrinous pericarditis ("bread and butter" appearance), with a friction rub, which usually resolves without sequelae.
    • Myocarditis: scattered Aschoff bodies within the interstitial connective tissue, often perivascular, which may cause tachycardia, arrhythmias, cardiac dilation, functional mitral regurgitation and heart failure.
    • Endocarditis (valvulitis): inflammation of the left-sided valves, especially the mitral, with fibrinoid necrosis in the cusps or tendinous cords. Small (1–2 mm), warty vegetations called verrucae form along the lines of closure. Subendocardial lesions exacerbated by regurgitant jets cause irregular thickenings in the left atrium called MacCallum plaques.

    With repeated attacks, healing leads to chronic rheumatic heart disease: leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and shortening, and thickening and fusion of chordae, which produce the "fish-mouth" mitral stenosis.

    What are the criteria for diagnosis of rheumatic fever?

    DU12Ju

    Diagnosis follows the revised Jones criteria [major and minor criteria for rheumatic fever]: evidence of a preceding group A streptococcal infection, plus two major manifestations, or one major and two minor manifestations.

    Major manifestations

    1. Migratory polyarthritis of the large joints.
    2. Pancarditis (myocarditis, pericarditis or endocarditis).
    3. Subcutaneous nodules, typically on extensor surfaces of the limbs.
    4. Erythema marginatum, an irregular circinate skin rash.
    5. Sydenham chorea, a neurological disorder with rapid involuntary movements.

    Minor manifestations are non-specific: fever, arthralgia and raised acute-phase reactants.

    Evidence of preceding infection. Pharyngeal cultures are usually negative by the time of illness, but antibodies to streptococcal enzymes such as streptolysin O and DNase B are found in most patients.

    The criteria are evolving and are applied differently in low-risk and high-risk settings.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 12)p. 511

    Give the pathogenesis of rheumatic fever.

    DU15JaDU12Ja

    Acute rheumatic fever is an immune response to group A streptococcal antigens that cross-react with host proteins.

    1. It follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis (sometimes skin infection) after a delay of 2 to 3 weeks, the time needed to generate an immune response.
    2. Antibodies and CD4⁺ T cells against streptococcal M proteins recognise cardiac antigens in the pericardium, myocardium and valves.
    3. Antibody binding activates complement and recruits neutrophils and macrophages. Cytokines from stimulated T cells activate macrophages, for example within Aschoff bodies [granulomas of rheumatic carditis].
    4. Damage is thus from antibody-mediated and T cell-mediated reactions.
    5. Streptococci are completely absent from the lesions, as expected for an immunological disease.
    6. Only 0.3% to 3% of infected people develop it, so intrinsic genetic susceptibility is likely.
    7. Chronic fibrotic lesions are the result of healing and scarring after the acute inflammation.

    Which valves are commonly involved in rheumatic fever?

    DU15Ja
    • The mitral valve is virtually always involved in chronic rheumatic heart disease. It is affected alone in about two-thirds of cases.
    • The mitral and aortic valves together are affected in another 25%.
    • The tricuspid valve is infrequently involved and the pulmonary valve only rarely.

    In acute rheumatic fever the left-sided valves show fibrinoid necrosis with small (1 to 2 mm) vegetations called verrucae along the lines of closure.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 12)p. 510

    What are the complications of rheumatic fever?

    DU15JaDU11Ju
    1. Acute carditis. Pericarditis with friction rub, myocarditis with arrhythmias and cardiac dilation, which can cause functional mitral regurgitation or heart failure. About 1% to 2% die of fulminant cardiac involvement.
    2. Recurrent attacks. With each streptococcal infection the same manifestations return, and valve damage is cumulative.
    3. Chronic rheumatic heart disease. Mitral leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and shortening, and thickening and fusion of the tendinous cords, giving "fish mouth" mitral stenosis. MacCallum plaques may form in the left atrium.
    4. Late effects. Heart murmurs, cardiac hypertrophy and dilation, heart failure, atrial fibrillation (particularly with mitral stenosis), left atrial mural thrombi with thromboembolism, and infective endocarditis.
    5. Lung changes from long-standing congestion in mitral stenosis.

    Write a short note on Aschoff nodule (myocardial changes, giant cell).

    DU14JuDU06MDU05Ja

    Aschoff bodies [granulomas of rheumatic carditis] are the distinctive lesions of acute rheumatic fever in the heart.

    • Each is a focal inflammatory lesion of T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells and plump activated macrophages called Anitschkow cells [caterpillar-nucleus histiocytes of rheumatic carditis].
    • Anitschkow cells have abundant cytoplasm and a central round-to-ovoid nucleus (occasionally binucleate) in which the chromatin condenses into a central slender wavy ribbon, so they are called "caterpillar cells".
    • They may be found with diffuse inflammation in any of the three layers of the heart, causing pericarditis, myocarditis and endocarditis (pancarditis).
    • They reflect cytokine-driven macrophage activation in an immune-mediated reaction.

    A child has fever, migratory large-joint pain after sore throat. What is your provisional diagnosis?

    DU25NDU14Ju

    Acute rheumatic fever, which follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis after a latent period of 10 days to 6 weeks and occurs most often in children aged 5 to 15 years. Migratory polyarthritis of the large joints, in which one large joint after another becomes painful and swollen for days and then settles without residual disability, is a major manifestation, and fever is a minor one.

    Same: how will you diagnose the case?

    DU25N

    By the revised Jones criteria [major and minor criteria for rheumatic fever]: evidence of a preceding group A streptococcal infection, plus two major or one major and two minor manifestations.

    1. Evidence of streptococcal infection. Raised antibodies to streptolysin O and DNase B (pharyngeal culture is usually negative by then).
    2. Major criteria: migratory polyarthritis, pancarditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea.
    3. Minor criteria: fever, arthralgia, raised acute-phase reactants.
    4. Look for carditis: pericardial friction rub, tachycardia, arrhythmia, murmurs.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 12)p. 511

    Vegetations

    B1

    What is a vegetation? Name the vegetative heart diseases.

    A vegetation is an abnormal mass of thrombotic material, with or without microorganisms and inflammatory cells, attached to a heart valve or the endocardium. The vegetative (verrucous) endocardial diseases are rheumatic heart disease, infective endocarditis, nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis, and Libman-Sacks endocarditis of lupus.

    Robbins identifies four major forms of vegetative endocarditis.

    DiseaseVegetation featuresValve damage / nature
    Rheumatic heart diseaseSmall (1–2 mm), warty, firm vegetations (verrucae) along the lines of closure
    Sterile    		Fibrinoid necrosis of cusps
    Chronic scarring
    Infective endocarditisLarge, bulky, friable, irregular masses on the cusps that may extend onto the chordae
    Contain organisms    		Destructive, with ring abscess and perforation
    Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE)Small (1–5 mm), bland, sterile thrombi loosely attached at the line of closure
    Single or multiple    		Nondestructive, no inflammation
    Libman-Sacks endocarditis (SLE)Small to medium (1–4 mm) sterile vegetations on either or both sides of the leaflets, chordae or mural endocardiumIntense valvulitis and fibrinoid necrosis
    Later scarring

    What is vegetation?

    DU26MDU19M

    A vegetation is a lesion on a heart valve formed of fibrin and thrombotic debris. In infective endocarditis it also contains inflammatory cells and microorganisms and is friable, bulky and destructive.

    Infective endocarditis

    B1

    What is infective endocarditis? Types and causative agents of infective endocarditis.

    Infective endocarditis is a microbial infection of the heart valves or mural endocardium that produces vegetations of thrombotic debris and organisms, often with destruction of the underlying cardiac tissue. It is classified clinically into acute and subacute forms. Acute endocarditis is caused by virulent organisms, chiefly Staphylococcus aureus, and subacute endocarditis is caused by less virulent organisms, chiefly viridans streptococci, on previously damaged valves.

    Infective endocarditis requires a susceptible valve and organisms in the blood. The vegetations are made of platelets, fibrin, inflammatory cells and colonies of organisms, and they may destroy the valve and extend into adjacent myocardium.

    Types.

    • Acute IE: a virulent organism (chiefly Staphylococcus aureus) infects a previously normal valve, with rapid destruction, ring abscess and a stormy course.
    • Subacute IE: a low-virulence organism (chiefly viridans streptococci, 50–60% of native valve cases) infects a previously damaged valve (rheumatic, mitral valve prolapse, calcific stenosis, bicuspid aortic valve, congenital defects), with an insidious course over weeks to months.
    • Special settings: prosthetic valve endocarditis (early: coagulase-negative staphylococci and S. aureus
      Late: streptococci), endocarditis in intravenous drug users (S. aureus, usually right-sided), and culture-negative endocarditis (about 10%).

    Causative agents. S. aureus is the commonest cause overall. Viridans streptococci predominate in subacute disease. Other agents are enterococci, the HACEK group (Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella), gram-negative bacilli and fungi (Candida, Aspergillus), the last two carrying about 50% mortality.

    What is subacute infective endocarditis?

    DU11Ju

    Subacute infective endocarditis is an insidious infection of previously deformed heart valves by organisms of lower virulence, such as viridans streptococci, with less valve destruction than acute endocarditis.

    Write the types/classification of infective endocarditis with infective agents.

    DU26MDU19M

    Traditionally IE is classed on clinical grounds as acute or subacute, based on severity, tempo (microbial virulence) and whether there is underlying valve disease. The two form a spectrum.

    TypeValveOrganismCourse
    AcutePreviously normalHighly virulent, for example Staphylococcus aureusRapid, destructive
    Antibiotics alone often fail and surgery may be needed
    SubacuteDeformed or damagedLow virulence, for example viridans streptococciProtracted over weeks to months
    Often cured by antibiotics alone

    Other agents

    • Viridans streptococci cause 50% to 60% of cases on previously damaged native valves.
    • S. aureus causes most cases overall, including those in intravenous drug users.
    • Enterococci and the HACEK group (Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella).
    • Rarely gram-negative bacilli and fungi.
    • Prosthetic valve endocarditis: within 1 to 2 months of surgery, skin flora (S. aureus, S. epidermidis). a year or more later, streptococci and S. aureus.
    • About 10% are culture negative.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 12)p. 511p. 512

    Give the pathogenesis of infective endocarditis.

    DU19M
    1. Predisposing cardiac lesions. Rheumatic heart disease with valve scarring was historically the main one. It is now replaced by mitral valve prolapse, degenerative calcific stenosis, bicuspid aortic valve, prosthetic valves and congenital defects.
    2. Bacteraemia or fungaemia, the foremost predisposing factor. The source may be an infection elsewhere, a dental or surgical procedure, a contaminated needle in intravenous drug users, or trivial breaks in the epithelial barriers of gut, mouth or skin.
    3. Organisms and valve. Low-virulence viridans streptococci infect damaged valves. Virulent S. aureus infects healthy or damaged valves.
    4. Vegetation formation. The organisms lodge on the valve and form vegetations of fibrin, thrombotic debris, inflammatory cells and organisms, with destruction of the underlying tissue. Organisms deep in the vegetation are hard to release into the blood or reach with antibiotics.
    5. Prevention. Antibiotic prophylaxis lowers risk in patients with valve abnormalities or known bacteraemia.

    Mention the complications of infective endocarditis.

    DU19M

    Complications generally begin within the first few weeks.

    1. Valve destruction and ring abscess, where a vegetation erodes into the myocardium (invasion of the myocardium and conduction system carries a poor outlook).
    2. Embolisation. Fragments with virulent organisms cause abscesses where they lodge, giving septic infarcts and mycotic aneurysms
      Systemic embolisation bodes ill.
    3. Glomerulonephritis from deposition of antigen-antibody complexes.
    4. Sepsis and arrhythmias.
    5. Vascular and immunological signs: splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions [small painless haemorrhagic macules on palms and soles], Osler nodes [tender nodules in the digit pulp], Roth spots [retinal haemorrhages with pale centres]. These are now less common because of earlier treatment.
    6. Outcome. Untreated IE is generally fatal. With 6 weeks or more of antibiotics, or valve replacement, mortality falls. Cure is 98% with low-virulence organisms such as S. viridans, 60% to 90% with enterococci and S. aureus, and half of patients with gram-negative bacilli or fungi die.

    Cardiomyopathies

    B1

    What is cardiomyopathy? Types of cardiomyopathies.

    Cardiomyopathies are diseases of the heart muscle due to intrinsic myocardial dysfunction, excluding dysfunction secondary to coronary artery disease, hypertension, valvular disease and congenital heart disease. They can be primary or secondary to systemic disease, and they are classified into three functional patterns: dilated (the most common, about 90%), hypertrophic and restrictive (the least common).

    FeatureDilated (DCM)Hypertrophic (HCM)Restrictive
    Functional defectImpaired contractility (systolic dysfunction), EF usually under 40%Impaired compliance (diastolic dysfunction), EF 50–80%Impaired compliance, EF 35–55%
    GrossLarge, flabby heart, four-chamber dilation
    Mural thrombi    		Massive hypertrophy without dilation
    Asymmetric septal hypertrophy
    banana-shaped cavity    		Biatrial dilation
    Ventricles of normal size
    Unremarkable myocardium
    MicroscopyNonspecific hypertrophy and fibrosisMyocyte hypertrophy, disarray, interstitial fibrosisInterstitial fibrosis, or deposits (amyloid)
    CausesGenetic (titin TTN, lamin A/C
    up to 50%), alcohol, myocarditis (Coxsackie B), peripartum, anthracyclines, haemochromatosis, catecholamines    		Autosomal dominant sarcomere gene mutations (β-myosin heavy chain, myosin-binding protein C, troponin)Amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, radiation fibrosis, endomyocardial fibrosis, Loeffler endomyocarditis, endocardial fibroelastosis
    ClinicalHeart failure, arrhythmias, embolismExertional dyspnoea, outflow obstruction, atrial fibrillation, sudden death in young athletesHeart failure from impaired filling
    Mimics constrictive pericarditis

    Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (replacement of the right ventricular wall by fat and fibrosis due to desmosomal gene mutations) is sometimes grouped with the dilated type. Myocarditis, Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (stress-induced apical ballooning), cardiotoxic drugs and radiation are other causes of myocardial disease.

    Pericardial Disease

    B1

    What is pericarditis? Important causes of pericarditis.

    Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium, which occurs secondary to cardiac, thoracic or systemic disorders. Important causes are infections (viruses, pyogenic bacteria, tuberculosis), myocardial infarction and Dressler syndrome [pericarditis after myocardial infarction], uraemia, rheumatic fever, SLE and other immunologic disorders, cardiac surgery, neoplasms and radiation.

    Pericarditis is classified by the character of the exudate as serous, fibrinous or serofibrinous, purulent (suppurative), haemorrhagic, and caseous (tuberculous). The causes (Robbins Table 12.13) fall into groups:

    • Infectious: viruses (Coxsackie), pyogenic bacteria (by direct extension from empyema or pneumonia, or from blood), tuberculosis, fungi and parasites.
    • Immunologically mediated: rheumatic fever, SLE, scleroderma, postcardiotomy syndrome, post-MI (Dressler) syndrome and drug hypersensitivity.
    • Miscellaneous: acute myocardial infarction (2–3 days after infarction), uraemia, cardiac surgery, neoplasia (metastasis or direct extension, producing serous or haemorrhagic effusion), trauma and radiation.

    Symptoms of fibrinous pericarditis are pleuritic, positional chest pain and fever, with a loud friction rub that is lost if a large effusion separates the layers. Healing may leave adhesions, or scarring leading to constrictive pericarditis, and rapid accumulation of even 200–300 mL of fluid can cause cardiac tamponade.

    Diseases of White Blood Cells, Lymph Nodes, and Spleen (Haematolymphoid)

    6 questions, in the same order as the NMC viva list.

    B8

    WHO classification of Hodgkin lymphoma.

    The WHO classification recognises five subtypes of Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells]—nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich and lymphocyte-depleted, which are grouped as classic Hodgkin lymphoma, and nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, which is a distinct non-classic type.

    The first four subtypes share a distinctive Reed-Sternberg cell [binucleate owl-eye giant cell] immunophenotype (CD15⁺, CD30⁺, weakly PAX5⁺, usually negative for other B-cell markers, T-cell markers and CD45) and are lumped together as classic Hodgkin lymphoma. In the fifth, lymphocyte predominant type, the neoplastic cells have a B-cell immunophenotype that differs from the classic type. in the International Consensus Classification this entity has been renamed nodular lymphocyte-predominant B-cell lymphoma, dropping the Hodgkin designation.

    Mixed background

    Young adults, both sexes equally
    Lower cervical, supraclavicular and mediastinal nodes

    Excellent prognosis

    Numerous diagnostic RS cells and mononuclear variants in a heterogeneous background

    Systemic symptoms and advanced stage

    B8

    What is an R-S cell? Variants of the R-S cell. Morphology of a classical R-S cell.

    The Reed-Sternberg cell [binucleate owl-eye giant cell] is the neoplastic giant cell of Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells], derived from a germinal centre or post–germinal centre B cell. The classical cell is a large binucleate or multilobed cell with abundant cytoplasm and large, inclusion-like eosinophilic nucleoli, giving an "owl-eye" appearance.

    Definition and origin. The Reed-Sternberg (R-S) cell is the neoplastic cell of Hodgkin lymphoma and is essential for its diagnosis. Single-cell molecular studies show clonal IGH gene rearrangements and somatic hypermutation, establishing origin from a germinal centre or post–germinal centre B cell. Nevertheless, the R-S cells of classic Hodgkin lymphoma fail to express most B-cell–specific genes, including immunoglobulin genes.

    They constitute only a minority of cells (the tumour is more than 90% reactive lymphocytes, macrophages, eosinophils and plasma cells), recruited by cytokines and chemokines secreted by the R-S cells.

    Morphology of the classical (diagnostic) R-S cell. A large cell, 45 µm or more in diameter, with abundant, slightly basophilic or amphophilic cytoplasm. The nucleus is bilobed or multilobed—classically two mirror-image nuclei or lobes lying side by side—each with a thin, sharply defined nuclear membrane, vesicular, open (clear) chromatin, and a large, inclusion-like, eosinophilic or amphophilic nucleolus, about the size of a small lymphocyte (5 to 7 µm), surrounded by a clear halo, giving the "owl-eye" appearance.

    Variants

    1. Mononuclear (Hodgkin) variant: a single nucleus with a large inclusion-like nucleolus.
    2. Lacunar cell: a cell with a delicate, folded or multilobated nucleus and abundant pale cytoplasm that retracts during fixation, leaving the cell in an empty space (lacuna). Characteristic of nodular sclerosis.
    3. Lymphohistiocytic (L&H, "popcorn") variant: polypoid, multilobed nucleus with inconspicuous nucleoli, fine chromatin and moderately abundant cytoplasm. Characteristic of nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma.
    4. Mummified cell: a shrunken, pyknotic cell with condensed eosinophilic cytoplasm, the result of a peculiar form of cell death in classic Hodgkin lymphoma.
    5. Pleomorphic or anaplastic variants: bizarre cells in lymphocyte-depleted (reticular) Hodgkin lymphoma.

    Immunophenotype. In classic Hodgkin lymphoma the R-S cells are CD15⁺, CD30⁺ and weakly PAX5⁺, and negative for CD45 and for most B and T-cell markers
    in nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma the L&H cells are CD20⁺, BCL6⁺, CD45⁺ and negative for CD15 and CD30.

    R-S–like cells may be seen in infectious mononucleosis, solid tumours and some non-Hodgkin lymphomas, so diagnosis depends on identifying R-S cells in the appropriate inflammatory background with a confirmatory immunophenotype.

    B8

    What do you mean by generalized lymphadenopathy? Important causes of generalized lymphadenopathy.

    Generalised lymphadenopathy means enlargement of lymph nodes in two or more non-contiguous regions of the body. The important causes are systemic infections (viral, bacterial, protozoal), lymphoid and haematologic malignancies, autoimmune disorders, drug reactions and storage diseases.

    Meaning. Lymphadenopathy is an abnormality in the size (usually more than 1 cm), number or consistency of lymph nodes. It is called generalised when nodes are enlarged in two or more noncontiguous (non-adjacent) groups, in contrast to localised lymphadenopathy, in which a single region that drains a particular area is involved. The distinction is clinically important, since localised enlargement usually reflects a regional infection or tumour drainage, whereas generalised enlargement implies a systemic process.

    Mechanisms. Nodes enlarge because of (1) reactive hyperplasia of lymphoid follicles and paracortical T-cell zones in response to antigenic stimulation, (2) infiltration by inflammatory cells in lymphadenitis, (3) infiltration by neoplastic lymphoid or metastatic cells, and (4) accumulation of macrophages laden with storage material. In children, systemic viral infections and bacteraemia often produce acute generalised lymphadenopathy.

    Important causes

    • Infections: viral—infectious mononucleosis (EBV), cytomegalovirus, HIV (persistent generalised lymphadenopathy), rubella, measles, hepatitis B. Bacterial—tuberculosis, secondary syphilis, brucellosis, typhoid, plague. Protozoal and others—toxoplasmosis, kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis), filariasis, histoplasmosis.
    • Neoplasms: non-Hodgkin [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells] lymphomas (especially follicular lymphoma and small lymphocytic lymphoma), Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, hairy cell leukaemia, angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma. Widespread metastases are an uncommon cause.
    • Autoimmune and inflammatory disorders: rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, adult Still disease, sarcoidosis, dermatomyositis, Sjögren syndrome [autoimmune dry eyes and dry mouth].
    • Drug reactions and serum sickness: phenytoin, allopurinol, carbamazepine, hydralazine, sulfonamides.
    • Others: lipid storage disorders (Gaucher [glucocerebrosidase deficiency, a lysosomal storage disease] and Niemann-Pick [sphingomyelinase deficiency, a lysosomal storage disease] diseases), hyperthyroidism, Castleman disease, Kikuchi–Fujimoto disease, Rosai–Dorfman disease, amyloidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
    B8

    Differences between Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

    Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells] arises in a single node or axial chain and spreads in an orderly contiguous manner, contains Reed-Sternberg cells [binucleate owl-eye giant cell] in a predominantly reactive background and is mostly curable, whereas non-Hodgkin lymphoma commonly involves multiple peripheral nodes and extranodal sites, spreads noncontiguously and early, and is a monotonous proliferation of neoplastic lymphoid cells.

    FeatureHodgkin lymphomaNon-Hodgkin lymphoma
    Site of originMore often localised to a single axial group of nodes (cervical, mediastinal, para-aortic)More frequent involvement of multiple peripheral nodes
    SpreadOrderly, by contiguity (nodes, then spleen, liver, marrow)Noncontiguous and unpredictable, widely disseminated early
    Mesenteric nodes and Waldeyer ring [ring of pharyngeal lymphoid tissue]Rarely involvedCommonly involved
    Extranodal presentationRareCommon (about one-third)
    Neoplastic cellsReed-Sternberg cells and variants, a minority (<10%) of cellsThe bulk of the tumour is neoplastic B, T or NK cells (monomorphic)
    BackgroundAbundant reactive lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells, macrophagesLittle or no reactive background
    ImmunophenotypeCD15⁺, CD30⁺, PAX5 (weak), CD45⁻ (classic)
    L&H cells CD20⁺    		Lineage-specific markers, CD45⁺
    B-cell (85–90%) or T-cell
    AgeBimodal: young adults and over 55 yearsAll ages, incidence rises with age (children: Burkitt [high-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC translocation], lymphoblastic)
    Systemic (B) symptomsCommon in advanced disease and mixed cellularity and lymphocyte depletionVariable, more in aggressive types
    StagingOf great value for therapy and prognosisLess useful, since disseminated early
    PrognosisCurable in most
    Stage I–IIA cure about 90%    		Varies from indolent to highly aggressive
    B10

    A 60-year-old male presented to you with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. His ESR in the first hour was 100 mm. How will you approach the diagnosis? Important causes of cervical lymphadenopathy.

    In a 60-year-old with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and a very high ESR I think first of lymphoma or a lymphoid leukaemia, then tuberculosis and metastatic carcinoma from the head and neck. I would take a careful history and examine all node groups, do a blood count and smear, chest imaging, and establish the diagnosis by FNAC followed by excision biopsy of an entire node with histology and immunophenotyping.

    Interpretation of the case. A markedly raised ESR (100 mm in the first hour) indicates a significant systemic inflammatory or neoplastic process, since the ESR is raised by acute-phase proteins and by immunoglobulins. In an older adult the leading diagnoses are non-Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells], Hodgkin lymphoma (second incidence peak above 55 years), chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, tuberculous lymphadenitis, and metastatic carcinoma. Other possibilities include multiple myeloma, HIV infection, sarcoidosis, connective tissue disease and chronic infection.

    Approach

    1. History. Duration and rate of growth
      Painless or painful
      Constitutional (B) symptoms—unexplained fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss of more than 10%. Pruritus
      alcohol-induced node pain
      Contact with tuberculosis, cough, haemoptysis
      Sore throat, dental infection, dysphagia, hoarseness, nasal obstruction, epistaxis or deafness (nasopharyngeal and head and neck primary). Smoking and tobacco chewing
      Drug history
      HIV risk
      Bone pain.

FNAC is a useful first step (caseating granuloma with acid-fast bacilli on ZN stain, metastatic carcinoma, or a monomorphic lymphoid population), but it is usually inadequate for diagnosing and subtyping lymphoma because architecture is lost. Excision biopsy of an entire, intact node (not a core or a node from an area of previous scarring) is the investigation of choice, with histology, immunohistochemistry (CD15, CD30, PAX5, CD20, CD3, CD5, CD23, cyclin D1, BCL2, BCL6, Ki-67), flow cytometry, and cytogenetic or molecular studies as required.

    B8

    What are the types of lymphoma?

    Lymphomas are divided into Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells] and non-Hodgkin lymphomas, and the non-Hodgkin group is subdivided according to the cell of origin into B-cell, T-cell and NK-cell lymphomas, many of which are further classified as indolent or aggressive.

    1. Hodgkin lymphoma: classic (nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich, lymphocyte-depleted) and nodular lymphocyte predominant.

    2. Non-Hodgkin lymphomas (WHO classification of lymphoid neoplasms):

    • Precursor B-cell neoplasms: B-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma.
    • Peripheral (mature) B-cell neoplasms: chronic lymphocytic leukaemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma. Splenic and nodal marginal zone lymphoma, extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma. Mantle cell lymphoma
      Follicular lymphoma
      Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
      Burkitt lymphoma [high-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC translocation]
      Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma
      Hairy cell leukaemia
      Plasma cell neoplasms.
    • Precursor T-cell neoplasms: T-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma.
    • Peripheral T-cell and NK-cell neoplasms: T-cell prolymphocytic leukaemia
      Large granular lymphocytic leukaemia
      Mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome [leukaemic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma]
      Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified
      Anaplastic large-cell lymphoma
      Nodal T-follicular helper cell lymphoma (angioimmunoblastic). enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma
      Subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma
      Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma
      Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma
      Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma
      NK-cell leukaemia.

    3. Clinical grouping by behaviour. Indolent (follicular lymphoma, CLL/SLL, marginal zone lymphoma, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, mycosis fungoides). Moderately aggressive (mantle cell lymphoma)
    Aggressive (diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, peripheral T-cell lymphomas, adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma). Highly aggressive (Burkitt lymphoma, lymphoblastic lymphoma). The most common NHL is diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, followed by follicular lymphoma. 85–90% of lymphoid neoplasms are of B-cell origin.

    The Lung (Respiratory System)

    45 questions · viva and written, in Robbins order.

    Obstructive Lung DiseaseRestrictive / Interstitial Lung DiseasePulmonary InfectionsTuberculosisTumors of the Lung

    Obstructive Lung Diseases

    B6

    Define obstructive lung disease. Enumerate the obstructive lung diseases.

    Obstructive lung diseases are disorders characterised by an increase in resistance to airflow due to diffuse airway disease at any level of the respiratory tract. Pulmonary function tests show reduced maximal expiratory flow, with an FEV₁/FVC ratio below 0.7. The obstructive diseases are chronic bronchitis, emphysema, asthma, bronchiectasis and small airways disease (bronchiolitis), with chronic bronchitis and emphysema together forming COPD.

    Obstructive disease contrasts with restrictive disease, in which expansion of the lung parenchyma is reduced and total lung capacity is decreased, with a proportionate fall in both FEV₁ and FVC so that the ratio remains normal.

    Clinical termAnatomic siteMajor pathologic changesAetiology
    Chronic bronchitisBronchusMucous gland hyperplasia and hypersecretionTobacco smoke, air pollutants
    EmphysemaAcinusAirspace enlargement with wall destructionTobacco smoke, α₁-antitrypsin deficiency
    BronchiectasisBronchusAirway dilation and scarringPersistent or severe infections
    AsthmaBronchusSmooth muscle hyperplasia, excess mucus, inflammationImmunologic (atopic) or other causes
    Small airways disease, bronchiolitisBronchioleInflammatory scarring or obliterationTobacco smoke, air pollutants, others

    The distinctions are not absolute, since many patients have overlapping features (for example, asthma with an irreversible component and COPD with a reversible component).

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 15)p. 617p. 618
    B6

    What do you mean by COPD? What are the types and risk factors of COPD?

    COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) is, in the WHO definition, a common, preventable and treatable disease characterised by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities caused by exposure to noxious particles or gases. Its two major clinicopathologic types are emphysema and chronic bronchitis, which usually coexist, and the principal risk factor is cigarette smoking.

    Types. COPD has two major clinicopathologic manifestations, emphysema (airspace enlargement with alveolar wall destruction, typically centriacinar) and chronic bronchitis (persistent productive cough for at least 3 months in at least 2 consecutive years), with small airway inflammation and fibrosis contributing to airflow obstruction. Because they share smoking as the main aetiologic factor, they commonly coexist in the same patient, and the clinical picture ranges from "pink puffers" (emphysema dominant) to "blue bloaters" (chronic bronchitis dominant). Asthma is distinguished by reversible bronchospasm, but some patients have overlap (COPD/asthma).

    Risk factors

    • Cigarette smoking is dominant: about 80% of COPD is attributable to it, and 35–50% of heavy smokers develop COPD.
    • Exposure to environmental and occupational pollutants (dusts, gases, fumes, and also household biomass smoke).
    • Poor lung development early in life.
    • Airway hyperresponsiveness.
    • Genetic factors: α₁-antitrypsin deficiency (panacinar emphysema) and other polymorphisms (for example NRF2 pathway and nicotinic receptor variants).
    • Recurrent respiratory infections, which exacerbate but do not initiate disease.
    B6

    Define emphysema. What are the types of emphysema? Define chronic bronchitis.

    Emphysema is defined by irreversible enlargement of the airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole, accompanied by destruction of the alveolar walls. Its four types are centriacinar (the commonest and the one linked to smoking), panacinar (α₁-antitrypsin deficiency), distal acinar or paraseptal, and irregular. Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically as persistent cough with sputum production for at least 3 months in at least 2 consecutive years in the absence of any other identifiable cause.

    Types of emphysema (classified by the part of the acinus involved):

    TypeDistributionAssociation
    Centriacinar (centrilobular)Central or proximal parts of the acini (respiratory bronchioles) affected, distal alveoli spared
    More than 95% of clinically significant cases
    Upper lobes, apical segments    		Heavy smokers
    Panacinar (panlobular)Uniform enlargement of the acinus from respiratory bronchiole to blind alveoli
    Lower zones, anterior margins, most severe at bases    		α₁-antitrypsin deficiency (worsened by smoking)
    Distal acinar (paraseptal)Distal acinus affected, subpleural and along septa, adjacent to areas of fibrosis
    Multiple enlarged airspaces to over 2 cm    		Spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults
    Irregular (paracicatricial)Irregular acinar involvement associated with scarringUsually clinically insignificant

    Only centriacinar and panacinar types cause clinically significant airflow obstruction.

    Chronic bronchitis is characterised by hypersecretion of mucus, enlargement of the submucosal glands (increased Reid index [ratio of bronchial gland thickness to wall thickness]) and goblet cell hyperplasia, with chronic airway inflammation, mainly caused by smoking (90% of cases).

    B6

    Define bronchial asthma. Name some lung diseases caused by air pollutants.

    Bronchial asthma is a heterogeneous disease characterised by chronic airway inflammation and variable, reversible expiratory airflow obstruction, producing episodic wheezing, dyspnoea, chest tightness and cough. Lung diseases caused by air pollutants include chronic bronchitis, emphysema, the pneumoconioses (coal workers' pneumoconiosis, silicosis, asbestosis, berylliosis), occupational asthma, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and lung cancer.

    Asthma. In its commonest (atopic) form, asthma is a type I hypersensitivity reaction in which a Th2 response with IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 drives IgE production, eosinophilic inflammation, bronchoconstriction, mucus hypersecretion and, with time, airway remodeling. Episodes are triggered by allergens, viral infection, irritants, cold air, exercise and stress. Symptoms tend to be worse at night or early in the morning, and between attacks the patient may be asymptomatic. Nonatopic, drug-induced (aspirin) and occupational forms also occur.

    Lung diseases caused by air pollutants

    • Obstructive diseases: chronic bronchitis and emphysema (tobacco smoke, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, dust), and occupational asthma (fumes, plastics, chemical dusts, formaldehyde).
    • Pneumoconioses: coal workers' pneumoconiosis (coal dust), silicosis (silica), asbestosis and asbestos-related pleural disease and mesothelioma (asbestos), berylliosis (beryllium).
    • Hypersensitivity pneumonitis from organic dusts (e.g., farmer's lung).
    • Lung cancer from asbestos, radon, arsenic, chromium, nickel, uranium and tobacco smoke.
    • Air pollution contributes to lung irritation and inflammation, and exacerbates asthma.

    Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is defined by the World Health Organization as a common, preventable and treatable disease characterised by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway or alveolar abnormalities caused by exposure to noxious particles or gases.

    Write down the pathogenesis of emphysema.

    DU24NDU18M

    Clinically significant emphysema is largely confined to smokers and to patients with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

    1. Toxic injury and inflammation: cigarette smoke and other noxious particles damage the respiratory epithelium and cause inflammation, with parenchymal destruction. Mediators such as leukotriene B4, interleukin-8 and TNF are increased.
    2. Protease-antiprotease imbalance: proteases released from inflammatory and epithelial cells break down connective tissue. There is a relative deficiency of protective antiproteases, in some cases genetic.
    3. Oxidative stress: oxidants from tobacco smoke, alveolar damage and inflammatory cells cause tissue damage, endothelial dysfunction and inflammation.
    4. Infection: not an initiating factor, but may acutely exacerbate existing disease.

    Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency - About 1% of patients with emphysema have this defect. - Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a major inhibitor of proteases, particularly neutrophil elastase. it is encoded by the Pi locus on chromosome 14. - More than 80% of ZZ individuals develop symptomatic panacinar emphysema, earlier and more severely if they smoke. - Injury that increases neutrophil influx releases proteases, which in the absence of alpha-1 antitrypsin digest elastic tissue excessively.

    Airway obstruction. Loss of elastic tissue around respiratory bronchioles reduces radial traction, so they collapse during expiration and cause functional airflow obstruction.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 15)p. 618p. 619p. 620

    Write a short note on COPD.

    DU13Ju

    Definition. A common, preventable and treatable disease characterised by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway or alveolar abnormalities caused by exposure to noxious particles or gases (World Health Organization).

    Aetiology - Heavy cigarette smoking: 35% to 50% of heavy smokers develop COPD, and about 80% of COPD is attributable to smoking. - Poor lung development early in life, environmental and occupational pollutants, airway hyperresponsiveness and certain genetic polymorphisms.

    Pathogenesis. Emphysema and chronic bronchitis often occur together. - Emphysema: tissue destruction by elastases and oxidants released from inflammatory cells, particularly neutrophils, responding to tobacco smoke. protease-antiprotease imbalance. - Chronic bronchitis: mucus hypersecretion with enlargement of mucous glands and goblet cell increase. Chronic inflammation with small airway fibrosis.

    Morphology - Emphysema: voluminous lungs, abnormally large alveoli separated by thin septa, loss of attachments to small airways, decreased capillary bed. - Chronic bronchitis: hyperaemia, swelling and oedema of the mucosa with mucinous or mucopurulent secretions. Chronic inflammation, goblet cell hyperplasia, enlarged mucous glands. Reid index [ratio of bronchial gland thickness to wall thickness] (normally 0.4) increased.

    Clinical features - Usually a smoking history of 40 pack-years or more. Insidious dyspnoea on exertion, chronic cough with sputum. - Spirometry: FEV1 over FVC ratio of less than 0.7. - Pink puffers (emphysema dominant) and blue bloaters (chronic bronchitis dominant, with hypercapnia, hypoxaemia and cyanosis).

    Complications. Pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale and death due to heart failure. Acute respiratory failure from superimposed infection. Pneumothorax from rupture of subpleural blebs.

    Chronic Interstitial (Restrictive) Lung Diseases

    B6

    What is interstitial lung disease? Give some examples.

    Interstitial lung diseases are a heterogeneous group of chronic disorders characterised predominantly by inflammation and fibrosis of the lung interstitium, producing a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function tests with reduced lung volume, compliance and diffusing capacity. Examples include idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, cryptogenic organising pneumonia, pneumoconioses, sarcoidosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

    Affected patients have dyspnoea, tachypnoea, end-inspiratory crackles and eventual cyanosis, without wheezing. Chest radiographs show bilateral small nodules, irregular lines or ground-glass shadows corresponding to interstitial fibrosis. Advanced disease of any type leads to diffuse scarring ("end-stage" or "honeycomb" lung), with secondary pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

    Major categories (Robbins Table 15.5):

    • Fibrosing: usual interstitial pneumonia (idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis), nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, cryptogenic organising pneumonia, connective tissue disease–associated ILD, pneumoconioses, and drug reactions or radiation pneumonitis.
    • Granulomatous: sarcoidosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
    • Eosinophilic: pulmonary eosinophilia.
    • Smoking-related: desquamative interstitial pneumonia, respiratory bronchiolitis–associated ILD, pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
    • Other: pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, lymphoid interstitial pneumonia.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 15)p. 627

    Pulmonary Infections

    Pneumonia

    B6

    What are the common pulmonary infections in Bangladesh? Name the organisms responsible for atypical pneumonia.

    The common pulmonary infections are acute bacterial pneumonia (most often pneumococcal, with Haemophilus influenzae, Klebsiella and Staphylococcus aureus), tuberculosis, viral pneumonias (influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2), lung abscess and fungal infections. "Atypical" pneumonia is caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila species, Coxiella burnetii, Legionella and respiratory viruses.

    The chapter does not give country-specific data, but the common infections in Bangladesh, a resource-limited setting with a heavy burden of respiratory disease, are the following.

    • Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (leading cause of childhood mortality and common in adults): Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest, followed by Haemophilus influenzae, Klebsiella pneumoniae (especially in debilitated and diabetic patients and alcoholics), Staphylococcus aureus (after influenza or measles) and Moraxella catarrhalis.
    • Tuberculosis: Bangladesh is among the high-burden countries.
    • Viral pneumonias: influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, metapneumovirus, adenovirus, and COVID-19.
    • Hospital-acquired pneumonia by gram-negative bacilli, Pseudomonas and MRSA.
    • Lung abscess, bronchiectasis, and fungal infections (e.g., aspergillosis) in compromised lungs.

    Atypical pneumonia is a descriptive term for pneumonia with patchy interstitial inflammation, moderate symptoms and few physical signs relative to the clinical illness, in which the bacterial culture is negative. Causative organisms are Mycoplasma pneumoniae (the commonest, in children and young adults), Chlamydophila pneumoniae and C. psittaci, Coxiella burnetii (Q fever), Legionella pneumophila, and viruses (influenza A and B, RSV, parainfluenza, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus, coronaviruses).

    B6

    Name some viruses that cause pneumonia. What are the morphological stages of acute bacterial pneumonia?

    Viruses that cause pneumonia include influenza A and B, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus, human metapneumovirus, adenovirus, rhinovirus, coronaviruses (including SARS-CoV-2), measles and varicella. The four morphological stages of lobar bacterial pneumonia are congestion, red hepatisation, grey hepatisation and resolution.

    Viruses. Respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus and human metapneumovirus are important in children, influenza A and B in adults, and adenovirus in military recruits. Others are cytomegalovirus and herpesviruses (in the immunocompromised), measles (rubeola), varicella and SARS-CoV-2. Viral pneumonia is characterised by interstitial lymphocytic inflammation rather than the intraalveolar neutrophilic exudate of bacterial pneumonia, and it predisposes to bacterial superinfection ("flu condemns, and additional infection executes").

    Stages of lobar pneumonia.

    1. Congestion: the lung is heavy, boggy and red, with vascular engorgement, intraalveolar oedema fluid, a few neutrophils and numerous bacteria.
    2. Red hepatisation: massive confluent exudation of neutrophils, red cells and fibrin fills the alveoli, and the lobe is red, firm and airless like liver.
    3. Grey hepatisation: red cells disintegrate while the fibrinosuppurative exudate persists, and the lobe becomes greyish-brown.
    4. Resolution: the exudate is enzymatically digested into granular semifluid debris that is resorbed, ingested by macrophages or expectorated, or organised by fibroblasts.
    B6

    Name the etiological agents of pneumonia. What is nosocomial pneumonia?

    Pneumonia is caused by bacteria (most commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae), viruses, mycoplasma and other atypical organisms, fungi and, less commonly, parasites. Nosocomial (hospital-acquired) pneumonia is pneumonia acquired in the course of a hospital stay, most commonly caused by gram-negative rods and Staphylococcus aureus.

    Aetiologic agents (these depend on the clinical setting, and no organism is identified in about 50% of cases):

    • Community-acquired: Streptococcus pneumoniae (the commonest cause), Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Legionella pneumophila, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila species, Coxiella burnetii, and viruses (RSV, parainfluenza, metapneumovirus, influenza A and B, adenovirus, SARS-CoV-2).
    • Hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated: gram-negative rods (Klebsiella, Serratia, E. coli, Pseudomonas) and S. aureus (often MRSA).
    • Aspiration pneumonia: anaerobic oral flora (Bacteroides, Prevotella, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus) mixed with aerobes.
    • Chronic pneumonia: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and atypical mycobacteria, Histoplasma, Coccidioides and Blastomyces.
    • Immunocompromised host: Pneumocystis jirovecii, cytomegalovirus, Aspergillus, Candida, Cryptococcus, Pseudomonas and Legionella.

    Nosocomial pneumonia is a pulmonary infection acquired during a hospital stay (generally developing 48 hours or more after admission). It is common in patients with severe underlying disease, immunosuppression, prolonged antibiotic therapy and invasive devices such as intubation, intravascular catheters and respirators (ventilator-associated pneumonia). Hospital bacteria are often antibiotic-resistant, there are more opportunities for spread, and equipment may be contaminated.

    The commonest isolates are S. aureus and gram-negative rods (Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas). It is serious and often life-threatening and requires broad-spectrum empirical therapy. Healthcare-associated pneumonia (from nursing homes, dialysis clinics and recent hospitalisation) is a related category, caused particularly by MRSA and P. aeruginosa.

    B10

    A 50-year-old male presented with cough, chest pain and hemoptysis. Chest X-ray shows consolidation in the right lung. What is the differential diagnosis? How will you investigate for diagnosis?

    The leading differential diagnoses are acute bacterial (lobar) pneumonia, pulmonary tuberculosis and bronchogenic carcinoma, particularly if the consolidation does not resolve. Other possibilities are lung abscess, pulmonary infarction and (less commonly) fungal infection. I would investigate with sputum Gram stain and culture, sputum for AFB and Xpert MTB/RIF, blood cultures, a complete blood count and inflammatory markers, CT chest, and bronchoscopy with biopsy or CT-guided FNAC if a mass is suspected.

    Differential diagnosis

    1. Lobar or bronchopneumonia: most commonly S. pneumoniae with abrupt fever, rigors, pleuritic chest pain and rusty sputum or haemoptysis, and with lobar consolidation (a radiopaque lobe). Klebsiella pneumonia (in alcoholics and diabetics) gives thick blood-tinged sputum and necrosis.
    2. Pulmonary tuberculosis: subacute or chronic cough, fever, weight loss, haemoptysis, with upper-lobe consolidation or cavitation in secondary TB.
    3. Bronchogenic carcinoma: in a 50-year-old smoker, with obstructive (postobstructive) pneumonia or lobar collapse and haemoptysis. Adenocarcinoma can mimic lobar pneumonia.
    4. Lung abscess (aspiration or necrotising pneumonia, often with foul sputum).
    5. Pulmonary infarction from embolism, with pleuritic pain and haemoptysis.
    6. Others: granulomatosis with polyangiitis, fungal infection, Goodpasture syndrome [anti-glomerular basement membrane disease] and bronchiectasis.

    Investigations

    • Blood: complete blood count (neutrophilic leucocytosis), ESR, CRP, blood cultures (positive in only 20–30% of pneumococcal cases early), blood glucose.
    • Sputum: Gram stain (neutrophils with lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococci in pneumococcal pneumonia) and culture with sensitivity, Ziehl-Neelsen stain and Xpert MTB/RIF or culture, and cytology for malignant cells.
    • Imaging: chest radiograph (lobar versus patchy opacity, cavity, effusion) and CT chest.
    • Bronchoscopy with bronchial washings, brushings and biopsy, or CT-guided FNAC/biopsy for a mass.
    • Others: pleural fluid analysis if there is effusion, urinary Legionella antigen or PCR when indicated, arterial blood gases, and Mantoux [tuberculin skin test] or IGRA if tuberculosis is suspected.
    • Failure of the consolidation to resolve after adequate treatment should prompt exclusion of an underlying carcinoma.

    What is pneumonia?

    4DU25MDU19MDU17NovDU10Ju

    Pneumonia can be very broadly defined as any infection of the lung parenchyma.

    Give the types of pneumonia.

    DU21M

    Classified by the aetiologic agent or, if no pathogen can be isolated (about 50% of cases), by the clinical setting. Pneumonia arises in seven distinct clinical settings.

    TypeCommon pathogens

    Discuss the pathogenesis of lobar pneumonia.

    DU06Ja
    • Pneumonia results when local defence mechanisms are impaired or systemic resistance is lowered.
    • Local defences are compromised by loss of the cough reflex, dysfunction of the mucociliary apparatus (cigarette smoke, viral disease), accumulation of secretions, impaired alveolar macrophage activity (alcohol, tobacco smoke, anoxia) and pulmonary congestion and oedema.
    • Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) is the most common cause, and the inflammation is usually lobar.
    • Often a bacterial infection follows an upper respiratory tract viral infection.
    • Bacterial invasion of the lung parenchyma fills the alveoli with an inflammatory exudate, which causes consolidation of the pulmonary tissue.
    • Predisposing conditions: extremes of age, chronic diseases (congestive heart failure, COPD, diabetes), immune deficiencies, and decreased or absent splenic function, which puts the patient at risk of infection with encapsulated bacteria such as pneumococcus.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 15)p. 643p. 644

    What are the stages of lobar pneumonia?

    5DU25MDU21MDU19MDU17NovDU10Ju
    1. Congestion
    2. Red hepatisation
    3. Grey hepatisation
    4. Resolution

    Discuss the morphology of lobar pneumonia.

    DU06SDU06Ja
    1. Congestion: the lung is heavy, boggy and red
      Vascular engorgement, intra-alveolar oedema fluid with a few neutrophils, and numerous bacteria.
    2. Red hepatisation: massive confluent exudation, with neutrophils, red cells and fibrin filling the alveolar spaces. The lobe is red, firm and airless, with a liver-like consistency.
    3. Grey hepatisation: progressive disintegration of red cells with a persisting fibrinosuppurative exudate. The colour changes to greyish-brown.
    4. Resolution: the exudate is broken down by enzymatic digestion into granular, semifluid debris, which is resorbed, ingested by macrophages, expectorated or organised by fibroblasts.

    The pleural fibrinous reaction (pleuritis) may resolve, but more often is organised, leaving fibrous thickening or permanent adhesions.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 15)p. 645

    Write the complications of pneumonia.

    DU25MDU21M
    1. Tissue destruction and necrosis, causing abscess formation, particularly common with pneumococcal or Klebsiella infections.
    2. Spread of infection to the pleural cavity, causing an intrapleural fibrinosuppurative reaction known as empyema.
    3. Bacteraemic dissemination to the heart valves, pericardium, brain, kidneys, spleen or joints, causing abscesses, endocarditis, meningitis or suppurative arthritis.
    4. Staphylococcal pneumonia has a high incidence of complications such as lung abscess and empyema.
    5. Deaths in treated patients result mostly from a complication such as empyema, meningitis, endocarditis or pericarditis, or from debility or chronic alcoholism.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 15)p. 645p. 646
