    Four stages    : congestion, red hepatisation, grey hepatisation and resolution
    HistologyNeutrophil-rich exudate filling the bronchi, bronchioles and adjacent alveolar spacesAlveoli filled by neutrophils, red cells and fibrin
    RadiologyFocal opacitiesWhole lobe radiopaque
    Common causeNot givenStreptococcus pneumoniae (the inflammation is usually lobar)

    The patterns overlap: patchy involvement may become confluent, and the same organism may produce either pattern.

    Name the etiologic agents of pneumonia.

    DU19M

    Bacteria - Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus): most common cause of community-acquired acute pneumonia. - Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis. - Staphylococcus aureus: secondary to viral respiratory illness. Also hospital-acquired. - Klebsiella pneumoniae: chronic alcoholics and debilitated people. - Pseudomonas aeruginosa: cystic fibrosis, neutropenia, hospital-acquired. - Legionella pneumophila. - Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia species, Coxiella burnetii. - Anaerobic oral flora: aspiration. - Mycobacterium tuberculosis: chronic granulomatous pneumonia.

    Viruses - Respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus and human metapneumovirus in children. Influenza A and B in adults
    Adenovirus in military recruits
    coronavirus.

    Fungi - Histoplasma, Coccidioides and Blastomyces in chronic pneumonia.

    What investigations are done to diagnose a case of pneumonia?

    DU19M
    1. Gram-stained sputum: numerous neutrophils containing gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococci support pneumococcal pneumonia. False positives occur because S. pneumoniae is part of the endogenous flora in 20% of adults.
    2. Blood culture: more specific but less sensitive
      Only 20% to 30% are positive in the early phase of illness.
    3. Culture and other assays: often necessary to establish the diagnosis, since clinical and radiologic features do not clearly distinguish viral from bacterial infection.
    4. Legionella: polymerase chain reaction on sputum or Legionella antigen in the urine. Culture is the gold standard but takes 3 to 5 days.
    5. Chest imaging: the whole lobe is radiopaque in lobar pneumonia and there are focal opacities in bronchopneumonia.
    6. Identification of the organism and its antibiotic sensitivity are the keystones of therapy.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 15)p. 644p. 645p. 646

    Lung abscess

    Write a short note on lung abscess.

    DU19Nov

    Definition. A local suppurative process that produces necrosis of lung tissue.

    Aetiology and pathogenesis - Any bacterial pathogen can produce an abscess
    Most commonly aerobic and anaerobic streptococci, S. aureus and gram-negative organisms. Anaerobic oral organisms (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Peptococcus) are the exclusive isolates in about 60% of cases. 1. Aspiration of infective material (the most frequent cause): suppressed cough reflex (alcohol, opioids, coma, anaesthesia, seizures), severe dysphagia, protracted vomiting, poor dental hygiene. 2. Antecedent primary lung infection: postpneumonic abscess, usually with S. aureus, K. pneumoniae and pneumococcus. 3. Septic embolism: from thrombophlebitis or right-sided infective endocarditis. 4. Neoplasia: postobstructive pneumonia. 5. Miscellaneous: trauma, direct extension from adjacent suppurative infection, haematogenous seeding. Some are primary cryptogenic.

    Morphology - From a few millimetres to cavities of 5 to 6 cm
    Single or multiple. - Aspiration abscesses are more common on the right and usually single. Those from pneumonia or bronchiectasis are multiple and basal. Septic emboli give multiple abscesses. - Suppurative destruction of lung parenchyma around a central cavity. a fibrous wall in chronic cases. - Continued infection gives fetid, green-black, multilocular cavities called gangrene of the lung.

    Clinical features - Cough, fever, and copious foul-smelling purulent or sanguineous sputum. Chest pain, weight loss
    clubbing. - Confirmed radiologically
    in older individuals rule out underlying carcinoma, present in 10% to 15%.

    Complications. Extension into the pleural cavity, haemorrhage, brain abscess or meningitis from septic emboli, and rarely secondary (AA) amyloidosis.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 15)p. 649

    Tuberculosis

    B6

    What are the primary sites of TB? What is Ghon's complex?

    Primary tuberculosis most commonly involves the lung, where the Ghon focus [primary subpleural tuberculous lesion] is a subpleural parenchymal lesion in the lower part of the upper lobe or upper part of the lower lobe, close to the pleura. Less commonly it affects the tonsils and oropharynx or the ileocaecal region of the gut (after ingestion of M. bovis in unpasteurised milk). Ghon's complex consists of the Ghon focus together with the caseating tuberculous lymphangitis and the enlarged, caseous regional (hilar) lymph nodes.

    Primary sites. In primary tuberculosis, after inhalation of droplet nuclei the bacilli lodge in the alveoli of the middle zones of the lung, in the subpleural part of the lower lobe or the lower part of the upper lobe. Other sites of primary infection are the tonsil and pharynx (cervical lymph nodes) and the terminal ileum and caecum (mesenteric nodes), the latter from bovine bacilli.

    Ghon's complex. The Ghon focus is a 1–1.5 cm grey-white area of inflammation with a central caseous necrosis. Bacilli drain through lymphatics to the hilar lymph nodes, which become enlarged and caseous. The combination of the parenchymal Ghon focus, lymphangitis and caseous hilar lymph node lesion is the Ghon complex. With development of cell-mediated immunity after about 3 weeks the lesion usually heals by fibrosis and calcification (Ranke complex when calcified), though viable organisms may persist and cause reactivation later.

    B6

    What is primary and secondary TB? What are the predominant sites in lung for primary and secondary TB?

    Primary tuberculosis is the infection of a previously unexposed, unsensitised person, which forms the Ghon complex [primary subpleural tuberculous lesion], and it is often asymptomatic. Secondary (postprimary or reactivation) tuberculosis arises in a previously sensitised host, from reactivation of dormant bacilli or exogenous reinfection. The predominant site of primary TB in the lung is the subpleural zone of the lower part of the upper lobe or upper part of the lower lobe, and that of secondary TB is the apex of the upper lobes.

    FeaturePrimary TBSecondary (postprimary) TB
    HostPreviously unexposed (unsensitised), mostly childrenPreviously sensitised, adults
    SourceExogenous infectionReactivation of dormant bacilli, or reinfection
    Lung siteSubpleural, lower part of upper lobe or upper part of lower lobeApex of one or both upper lobes (posterior and apical segments)
    Lymph nodeHilar nodes involved with caseationRegional nodes characteristically spared
    LesionGhon focus and Ghon complexSmall apical focus (Assmann focus) that may enlarge with cavitation
    Immune responseDelayed
    Spread and bacteraemia possible before immunity    		Rapid hypersensitivity response, with localisation and tissue destruction
    OutcomeHeals in most (fibrosis, calcification)
    Progressive primary TB in the immunocompromised    		Cavitation, haemoptysis, fibrocaseous disease, spread to other sites, miliary TB
    B6

    Describe the morphology of primary TB. What is miliary TB?

    In primary tuberculosis there is a Ghon focus [primary subpleural tuberculous lesion] of 1–1.5 cm in the subpleural lung with central caseation, and enlarged caseous hilar lymph nodes (Ghon complex), with the characteristic tuberculous granulomas. Miliary tuberculosis is widespread haematogenous dissemination of the organisms, producing numerous tiny (millet-seed size, 2 mm) yellow-white foci in the lungs and many other organs.

    Morphology of primary TB.

    • Ghon focus: a grey-white, firm area, 1–1.5 cm, in the lower part of the upper lobe or upper part of the lower lobe beneath the pleura, with central caseous necrosis. The pleural surface may have a fibrinous reaction.
    • Lymphatic spread to the hilar and peribronchial lymph nodes, which become enlarged with caseation (Ghon complex). In the gut, the corresponding lesion affects Peyer patches and mesenteric nodes.
    • Microscopy: caseating granulomas composed of a central zone of caseous necrosis (amorphous, granular, eosinophilic) surrounded by epithelioid macrophages, Langhans [giant cells with peripheral horseshoe-shaped nuclei]-type multinucleated giant cells, and a rim of lymphocytes and fibroblasts. Acid-fast bacilli can be shown by Ziehl-Neelsen stain.
    • Fate: in most patients cell-mediated immunity develops at about 3 weeks, and the lesions heal by fibrous scarring and calcification (Ranke complex). Rarely, progressive primary TB occurs, with spread to the pleura, bronchi (tuberculous bronchopneumonia), or by haematogenous route.

    Miliary tuberculosis results from erosion of a focus of caseous disease into a blood vessel (or lymphatic channel draining into the venous system), which disseminates the organisms through the blood. It produces innumerable small, yellow-white foci about 2 mm in diameter (like millet seeds) in the lungs (pulmonary vein spread), or in the spleen, liver, kidneys, bone marrow, meninges, adrenals and other organs (systemic arterial spread). It may complicate primary or secondary TB, especially in infants, the elderly and the immunocompromised.

    B6

    Name some sites where TB does not occur. What is granuloma?

    Tuberculosis can involve virtually any organ, but it is rare in tissues such as skeletal muscle, the myocardium, the thyroid and the pancreas, which appear resistant. A granuloma is a focal collection of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), often with multinucleated giant cells and a surrounding rim of lymphocytes, formed in chronic inflammation as a delayed-type hypersensitivity response to a persistent antigen.

    Sites of rare involvement. Tuberculosis characteristically spares skeletal muscle and the heart (myocardium), and the thyroid and pancreas are also rarely involved, probably because of local tissue factors such as the high oxygen environment, motion and lytic enzymes, and the antibacterial milieu. Involvement of these sites is exceptional, even in miliary disease.

    Granuloma. A granuloma is a distinctive pattern of chronic inflammation in which activated macrophages accumulate to form epithelioid cells ("epithelial-like" macrophages with pale pink granular cytoplasm and indistinct borders), which may fuse to form giant cells (Langhans [giant cells with peripheral horseshoe-shaped nuclei] type with nuclei in a horseshoe arrangement at the periphery, or foreign body type with nuclei scattered).

    Lymphocytes (mainly CD4⁺ T cells), and sometimes fibroblasts, surround the aggregate. It is produced by a T-cell–mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity response, when IFN-γ released by Th1 cells activates macrophages, as in tuberculosis. Granulomas may be caseating, with central necrosis (tuberculosis, fungi), or noncaseating (sarcoidosis, Crohn disease [transmural granulomatous inflammatory bowel disease], berylliosis), and may also be caused by foreign bodies.

    B10

    A 25-year-old male with a history of evening rise of temperature, cough and weight loss reported to the OPD. What is the most probable diagnosis? How will you investigate the patient?

    The most probable diagnosis is pulmonary tuberculosis. The evening rise of temperature, chronic cough and weight loss are the classic constitutional and respiratory features. I would investigate with sputum smear for acid-fast bacilli by Ziehl-Neelsen stain, Xpert MTB/RIF and culture, along with a chest radiograph, and I would add Mantoux [tuberculin skin test] or an interferon-gamma release assay and blood tests.

    The history of low-grade evening fever, cough and weight loss in a young adult strongly suggests secondary (reactivation) pulmonary TB. The differential diagnosis includes lung abscess, bronchiectasis, bronchogenic carcinoma, chronic fungal pneumonia, sarcoidosis and HIV-associated infections.

    Investigations

    • Sputum (three early-morning samples): Ziehl-Neelsen (or auramine) smear for AFB
      Xpert MTB/RIF for rapid detection of M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance. Culture on Löwenstein-Jensen or liquid (MGIT) medium for confirmation and drug sensitivity.
    • Chest radiograph: apical or upper-lobe infiltrates, cavitation, fibrosis, calcification, and hilar adenopathy or miliary pattern. CT chest when needed.
    • Tuberculin (Mantoux) test or interferon-gamma release assay (shows sensitisation, not active disease).
    • Blood: raised ESR, mild normocytic anaemia, lymphocytosis
      HIV test.
    • Tissue or fluid sampling if extrapulmonary: FNAC or biopsy (caseating granulomas), pleural fluid analysis (lymphocytic exudate with ADA).
    • Bronchoscopy with lavage when sputum is unobtainable.
    B10

    A 70-year-old male suffering from fever, dry cough, gradual weight loss and occasional hemoptysis for the last four months. Chest X-ray shows irregular opacity in the right apical region. What is the probable diagnosis? How will you confirm the diagnosis?

    The probable diagnosis is secondary (reactivation) pulmonary tuberculosis, since fever, weight loss, cough and haemoptysis with an apical lesion are typical. However, in a 70-year-old (likely smoker) an apical bronchogenic carcinoma, such as a Pancoast tumour, must be excluded. The diagnosis is confirmed by sputum AFB smear, Xpert MTB/RIF and culture, and by tissue diagnosis (bronchoscopic or CT-guided biopsy) if the sputum is negative or malignancy is suspected.

    The apex of the upper lobe is the characteristic site of reactivation TB, which in the elderly may follow waning immunity. The differential includes bronchogenic carcinoma (especially squamous cell carcinoma or an apical Pancoast tumour, which also presents with cough, weight loss and haemoptysis), chronic fungal infection, lung abscess and bronchiectasis.

    Confirmation

    1. Sputum: three AFB smears, Xpert MTB/RIF and culture (LJ or MGIT) with drug sensitivity. Sputum cytology for malignant cells.
    2. Imaging: CT chest to characterise the opacity (cavitation, tree-in-bud, mass, nodal and pleural involvement).
    3. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage, brush cytology and transbronchial biopsy, or CT-guided FNAC or core biopsy. Histology showing caseating granulomas with AFB confirms TB, and malignant cells confirm carcinoma.
    4. Supportive: Mantoux [tuberculin skin test] or IGRA, ESR, and HIV status.

    What are Ghon's focus and Ghon's complex?

    DU17MDU14JaDU13Ja
    • Ghon focus [primary subpleural tuberculous lesion]: a 1 to 1.5 cm area of grey-white inflammation with consolidation, in the lower part of the upper lobe or upper part of the lower lobe close to the pleura, in primary tuberculosis. Its centre usually undergoes caseous necrosis.
    • Ghon complex: the combination of the parenchymal lung lesion (Ghon focus) and caseating involvement of the regional lymph nodes.
    • In about 95% of cases cell-mediated immunity controls the infection, and the Ghon complex undergoes progressive fibrosis, often followed by radiologically detectable calcification.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 8)p. 337

    What are the sites of primary and secondary tuberculosis in lung?

    DU14Ja
    TypeSite
    Primary tuberculosisDistal airspaces of the lower part of the upper lobe or the upper part of the lower lobe, usually close to the pleura
    Secondary tuberculosisApex of the upper lobes of one or both lungs
    The initial lesion is within 1 to 2 cm of the apical pleura

    What are the fates of primary tuberculosis of lung?

    DU14Ja
    1. Healing: in about 95% of cases cell-mediated immunity controls the infection. The Ghon complex [primary subpleural tuberculous lesion] undergoes fibrosis and calcification, and no lesions develop despite seeding of other organs.
    2. Dormancy: viable organisms may remain dormant in the lesion for decades and be reactivated if immune defences are lowered.
    3. Progressive primary tuberculosis: clinically significant disease develops in about 5% of newly infected people
      it resembles acute bacterial pneumonia, with consolidation of the lobe, hilar lymphadenopathy and pleural effusion.
    4. Dissemination: lymphatic and haematogenous spread may cause tuberculous meningitis and miliary tuberculosis.

    Give in short the pathogenesis of pulmonary tuberculosis.

    DU06M
    1. Entry into macrophages: M. tuberculosis is phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages through receptors such as mannose-binding lectin and complement receptor 3.
    2. Replication in macrophages: the bacterium blocks phagosome-lysosome fusion by recruiting coronin to the phagosome membrane, so it replicates unchecked. in the first 3 weeks bacteraemia seeds multiple sites.
    3. Innate immunity: lipoarabinomannan binds TLR2 and unmethylated CpG nucleotides bind TLR9.
    4. Th1 response: about 3 weeks after infection, dendritic cells carry antigen to lymph nodes. interleukin-12 and interleukin-18 drive differentiation of Th1 cells.
    5. Macrophage activation: Th1 cells produce interferon-gamma, which stimulates nitric oxide and reactive oxygen species, antimicrobial peptides and autophagy to kill the bacteria.
    6. Granuloma and caseation: activated macrophages become epithelioid histiocytes that form granulomas, with giant cells. if infection progresses, the immune response causes caseous necrosis. TNF recruits more monocytes.
    7. This response is largely effective, but causes tissue destruction. Loss of T cell immunity is shown by tuberculin negativity in a previously positive person.

    Define miliary tuberculosis.

    DU09Ja

    Miliary pulmonary tuberculosis occurs when organisms draining through lymphatics enter the venous blood and circulate back to the lung. The lesions are microscopic or small visible foci (2 mm) of yellow-white consolidation, resembling millet seeds. Systemic miliary tuberculosis occurs when bacteria disseminate through the systemic arterial system.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 8)p. 338

    Discuss the pathological characteristics of secondary pulmonary TB.

    DU09Ja

    Gross - The initial lesion is a small focus of consolidation, less than 2 cm, within 1 to 2 cm of the apical pleura. - The focus is sharply circumscribed, firm, grey-white to yellow, with central caseation and peripheral fibrosis. - In immunocompetent people it becomes fibrously encapsulated, leaving fibrocalcific scars. - Progressive disease: the apical lesion expands, erodes into bronchi and vessels, and evacuates the caseous centre, leaving a ragged, irregular cavity poorly walled off by fibrous tissue. Erosion of vessels causes haemoptysis. - Cavity erosion into an airway is an important source of spread.

    Microscopy - Coalescent tubercles with central caseation, epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells, within a fibroblastic rim with lymphocytes. - Acid-fast bacilli are found in early exudative and caseous phases, but are usually too few in late fibrocalcific stages.

    Differences from primary disease - Because of preexisting hypersensitivity, the bacilli elicit a prompt tissue response that walls off the focus, so the regional lymph nodes are less prominently involved early. - Cavitation occurs readily if untreated.

    Spread. Along airways, lymphatics and vessels, giving miliary disease, pleural effusion, tuberculous empyema, obliterative fibrous pleuritis, and endobronchial, endotracheal and laryngeal tuberculosis.

    Write a short note on Mantoux test/tuberculin test.

    DU07Ju

    Principle. The tuberculin (purified protein derivative, or Mantoux [tuberculin skin test]) test is performed by intracutaneous injection of purified protein derivative of M. tuberculosis, which induces a visible and palpable induration that peaks in 48 to 72 hours.

    Interpretation - A positive test signifies T cell mediated immunity to mycobacterial antigens, but does not differentiate between infection (current or past) and active disease. - False negative: certain viral infections, sarcoidosis, malnutrition, Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells], immunosuppression and active tuberculous disease. - False positive: infection by atypical mycobacteria, or prior BCG vaccination.

    Interferon-gamma release assays are an in vitro alternative, with uncommon false positives.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 8)p. 337

    A patient has cough, evening rise of temperature, weight loss (± cervical lymphadenopathy, apical opacity). What is your probable diagnosis?

    5DU26MDU24MDU22MDU17JaDU13Ja

    Pulmonary tuberculosis, most likely secondary (postprimary) tuberculosis.

    • Systemic symptoms: malaise, anorexia, weight loss and low grade fever that appears late each afternoon and then subsides, with night sweats.
    • Cough with sputum
      Haemoptysis in about one-half of cases.
    • Secondary pulmonary tuberculosis classically involves the apex of the upper lobes.
    • Cervical lymphadenopathy suggests tuberculous lymphadenitis (scrofula), the most frequent presentation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 8)p. 336p. 337

    Same: what laboratory investigations/tests (incl. on lymph node) confirm it?

    5DU26MDU24MDU22MDU17JaDU13Ja
    1. Acid-fast smears and cultures of sputum: culture on solid media shows growth at 3 to 6 weeks, in liquid media within 2 weeks
      Culture is the gold standard and allows susceptibility testing.
    2. Polymerase chain reaction: rapid diagnosis, and detects rifampin resistance. as sensitive as culture in smear-positive samples.
    3. Tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay: shows T cell immunity, but does not distinguish infection from active disease.
    4. Lymph node biopsy: granulomas with caseation, enclosed within a fibroblastic rim, with multinucleated giant cells. acid-fast stain is indicated whenever granulomas are present, even without caseous necrosis.

    Same (27y with hemoptysis): what microscopic findings do you expect?

    DU13Ja
    • Characteristic granulomatous inflammation with caseating and noncaseating tubercles.
    • Central granular caseation, surrounded by epithelioid cells and multinucleate giant cells.
    • Granulomas usually enclosed within a fibroblastic rim punctuated by lymphocytes.
    • Acid-fast bacilli can often be found in early exudative and caseous phases, but are usually too few in late fibrocalcific stages.
    • Immunocompromised people do not form the characteristic granulomas, and their macrophages contain many bacilli.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 8)p. 337p. 339

    Lung Tumors

    B6

    Classify bronchogenic carcinoma. Which one is most common?

    Bronchogenic carcinoma is broadly classified into small cell carcinoma and non–small cell carcinoma, the latter comprising adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma and large cell carcinoma. Adenocarcinoma is now the most common type, accounting for about 50% of cases.

    Robbins classifies the carcinomas by histologic type, with approximate frequencies:

    TypeFrequencyCharacteristics
    AdenocarcinomaAbout 50% (most common type; commonest in women and nonsmokers)Usually peripheral
    Precursors are atypical adenomatous hyperplasia and adenocarcinoma in situ
    TTF-1 positive
    Squamous cell carcinomaAbout 20%Usually central (hilar)
    Strongly smoking-related
    Keratinisation, intercellular bridges
    p40 positive
    Small cell carcinomaAbout 15%Neuroendocrine
    Central
    Almost always smoking-related
    Very aggressive
    Large cell carcinomaAbout 2%Undifferentiated
    Diagnosis of exclusion
    OtherAbout 13%Adenosquamous, sarcomatoid, salivary gland–type tumours, carcinoid tumours and others

    Combined histologic patterns occur in about 4–5% of cases. Smoking is the most important cause, and about 80% of lung cancers occur in current or recent smokers. Mortality is high, with overall 5-year survival about 18.7%.

    Classify tumours of lung (WHO classification of bronchogenic carcinoma).

    4DU20NDU20JuDU18NovDU16Ju
    CategoryProportion
    Adenocarcinoma (includes adenocarcinoma in situ, minimally invasive adenocarcinoma, and invasive types: lepidic, acinar, papillary, micropapillary, solid, mucinous, colloid, enteric-type, foetal)50%
    Squamous cell carcinoma20%
    Small cell carcinoma15%
    Large cell carcinoma2%
    Other (pleomorphic carcinoma, carcinosarcoma, pulmonary blastoma; salivary gland-type tumours such as adenoid cystic carcinoma, epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma and mucoepidermoid carcinoma)13%

    Lung cancers are broadly classified into small cell and non-small cell types. Combinations of squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma, or small cell and squamous cell carcinoma, occur in about 14% and 5% of patients.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 15)p. 651p. 652p. 654

    Write down briefly the morphology of small cell carcinoma of lung.

    DU08Ja
    • Relatively small cells with scant cytoplasm and ill-defined cell borders.
    • Finely granular nuclear chromatin (salt and pepper pattern), with absent or inconspicuous nucleoli.
    • Cells are round, oval or spindle-shaped, with prominent nuclear moulding.
    • Smaller than three times the diameter of a small resting lymphocyte (about 25 µm).
    • Mitotic count is invariably high.
    • Necrosis is common and often extensive.
    • Basophilic staining of vascular walls from encrustation by DNA of necrotic tumour cells (Azzopardi effect [DNA deposition on vessel walls in necrotic small cell carcinoma]).
    • Electron microscopy: dense-core neurosecretory granules, about 100 nm.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 15)p. 657

    How will you diagnose/investigate a case of bronchogenic carcinoma?

    6DU20NDU20JuDU18NovDU14JuDU12JaDU11Ja
    1. Sputum cytology: keratinised squamous carcinoma cells with prominent hyperchromatic nuclei.
    2. Biopsy: including biopsy of tissues involved by metastatic disease.
    3. Histology with immunohistochemistry: TTF-1 in adenocarcinoma
      p40 for squamous differentiation in poorly differentiated tumours.
    4. Mutation testing in adenocarcinoma: EGFR (about 15% of all cases) and KRAS (about 30% of adenocarcinomas).
    5. Staging by TNM system: by tumour size and involvement of thoracic structures.
    6. Early detection: low-dose computed tomography in high-risk individuals.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 15)p. 659p. 656p. 627

    A smoker has cough, hemoptysis, chest mass/opacity, supraclavicular or cervical node. What is the most likely diagnosis?

    DU14JuDU12JaDU11Ja

    Bronchogenic carcinoma (lung cancer)

    • Cough, haemoptysis and weight loss are common presenting features
      Cough is the commonest (75%).
    • About 80% of lung cancers occur in active smokers.
    • Supraclavicular nodal involvement is N3 disease, and metastases to bronchial, tracheal and mediastinal nodes are found in most cases.
    • Confirm by sputum cytology and biopsy.

    EsophagusCongenital Anomalies of GITStomachIntestines

    Esophagus

    Achalasia and reflux esophagitis

    B2

    What are achalasia and reflux esophagitis?

    Achalasia is a primary oesophageal motility disorder in which the lower oesophageal sphincter fails to relax and the oesophageal body loses peristalsis because the inhibitory, nitric oxide–producing neurons of the myenteric plexus degenerate. it presents with dysphagia and a dilated oesophagus. Reflux oesophagitis is inflammation of the distal oesophageal squamous mucosa caused by repeated reflux of gastric contents through an incompetent lower oesophageal sphincter, and it is the clinical basis of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

    Achalasia. Achalasia is defined by a triad: incomplete relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter (LES) on swallowing, increased resting LES tone, and aperistalsis of the oesophageal body. The sphincter therefore behaves as a functional obstruction, food is retained, and the oesophagus above it dilates progressively.

    Aetiology and pathogenesis. Primary achalasia is rare and idiopathic. It results from degeneration of the nitric oxide–producing inhibitory neurons that normally relax the LES. The extra-oesophageal vagus nerve and the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus may also show degenerative change. Rare familial cases are described, and an immune-mediated destruction of inhibitory neurons is suspected because some cases follow herpes simplex virus 1 infection, show linkage to immunoregulatory gene polymorphisms, or coexist with Sjögren syndrome [autoimmune dry eyes and dry mouth] or autoimmune thyroid disease.

    Secondary achalasia arises when the myenteric plexus is destroyed by another process. The classic example is Chagas disease [Trypanosoma cruzi infection], in which Trypanosoma cruzi infection destroys the myenteric plexus (and may involve the duodenal, colonic, and ureteric plexuses as well). Other causes include diabetic autonomic neuropathy, infiltrative disorders such as malignancy, amyloidosis, and sarcoidosis, systemic sclerosis, lesions of the dorsal motor nucleus (for example after poliomyelitis), and Down syndrome [trisomy 21].

    Morphology and clinical features. The oesophagus above the sphincter is dilated, with hypertrophy of the muscularis in the early stage and thinning later. Histology shows a reduced number or absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus with a variable chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Patients have dysphagia for both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, difficulty in belching, and chest pain, and aspiration pneumonia may follow nocturnal regurgitation.

    A barium swallow shows a dilated oesophagus tapering to a "bird-beak" narrowing, and manometry confirms the diagnosis. Stasis oesophagitis and candidiasis may occur. There is a modestly increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma, but not enough to justify surveillance endoscopy. Treatment is directed at overcoming the obstruction: pneumatic balloon dilation, botulinum toxin injection to inhibit contraction-promoting cholinergic neurons, or surgical myotomy.

    Reflux oesophagitis. Reflux of gastric contents into the lower oesophagus is the commonest cause of oesophagitis and the most frequent outpatient gastrointestinal diagnosis in high-income countries. The stratified squamous epithelium is highly abrasion resistant but is sensitive to gastric acid and pepsin, and bile may add to the injury.

    Pathogenesis. The major mechanism is transient relaxation of the LES, mediated through vagal pathways and triggered by gastric distention. Reflux also follows abrupt rises in intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, straining, bending). Predisposing conditions include alcohol and tobacco use, obesity, central nervous system depressants, pregnancy, hiatal hernia, delayed gastric emptying, increased gastric volume, and drugs or foods that lower LES pressure.

    Morphology. Mild disease may show only hyperaemia, with unremarkable histology. More severe reflux produces erosions, basal zone hyperplasia, elongation of the lamina propria papillae, and infiltration of the squamous mucosa by eosinophils. Neutrophils appear later or when infection or chemical injury is superimposed. Chronic injury leads to ulceration, fibrosis, and stricture.

    Clinical features and complications. Symptoms are heartburn, regurgitation of sour-tasting fluid, and dysphagia, most often after meals, and they may be mistaken for ischaemic heart disease. Symptom severity correlates poorly with the histologic damage. Diagnosis is usually clinical
    Endoscopy is reserved for patients who fail proton pump inhibitor therapy or in whom complications are suspected.

    Proton pump inhibitors relieve symptoms in up to 90% of patients. The complications are erosive oesophagitis with bleeding, ulceration, peptic stricture, Barrett oesophagus [intestinal metaplasia of the lower oesophagus], and, through Barrett oesophagus, oesophageal adenocarcinoma. A sliding hiatal hernia, in which the gastro-oesophageal junction herniates through the diaphragmatic hiatus, may impair LES competence and produce a similar syndrome.

    Esophageal varices

    B2

    What are esophageal varices? Mention their mechanism.

    Oesophageal varices are tortuous, dilated submucosal veins in the lower oesophagus (and proximal stomach) that develop as portosystemic collaterals when portal venous pressure is raised, most commonly because of cirrhosis. They matter because large varices can rupture and cause massive, life-threatening haematemesis.

    Mechanism. Portal hypertension, defined as increased resistance to portal blood flow, may be prehepatic (portal vein thrombosis or narrowing, splenic vein flow increase), intrahepatic (cirrhosis, which accounts for most cases; schistosomiasis, massive fatty change, sarcoidosis, nodular regenerative hyperplasia), or posthepatic (severe right heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, hepatic vein outflow obstruction).

    In cirrhosis, resistance is raised at the level of the sinusoids by scarring and nodule formation, by contraction of sinusoidal smooth muscle cells and myofibroblasts, and by endothelial dysfunction with reduced nitric oxide and increased endothelin-1. At the same time, splanchnic arteriolar vasodilation, driven chiefly by nitric oxide, produces a hyperdynamic circulation that increases portal inflow.

    Because the portal system has no valves, blood seeks alternative pathways to the systemic venous circulation wherever the portal and caval systems communicate. At the gastro-oesophageal junction, blood from the left gastric (coronary) vein is diverted through the subepithelial and submucosal venous plexuses of the distal oesophagus into the azygos system. These thin-walled veins become congested and dilated, forming varices.

    Varices are most common in alcohol-associated cirrhosis but complicate cirrhosis of any cause. non-cirrhotic portal hypertension (presinusoidal as in schistosomiasis, sinusoidal as in amyloidosis, postsinusoidal as in Budd–Chiari syndrome) can also produce them. They are present in about 30% of patients with compensated cirrhosis and about 60% of those with decompensated cirrhosis.

    Morphology. Varices are dilated, tortuous veins within the mucosa and submucosa of the distal oesophagus and proximal stomach that bulge into the lumen under an intact, thinned mucosa. After rupture there may be mucosal ulceration, thrombosis, inflammation, and evidence of prior sclerotherapy or band ligation.

    B2

    What are esophageal varices? Mention their mechanism and complications.

    Oesophageal varices are dilated submucosal veins of the distal oesophagus that form as collateral channels when raised portal pressure, usually from cirrhosis, diverts blood through the left gastric–azygos connections. Their principal complication is variceal rupture with torrential haematemesis, which is a medical emergency with a high mortality.

    Definition and mechanism. Oesophageal varices are tortuous, dilated veins in the lower oesophageal submucosa and mucosa. They are caused by portal hypertension, which most often results from cirrhosis. Increased portal venous pressure opens collateral channels at sites where the portal and systemic venous beds communicate: the oesophagogastric junction, the anorectal junction (haemorrhoids), the falciform ligament (periumbilical veins, giving caput medusae), and the retroperitoneum.

    In the oesophagus the collateral flow passes from the left gastric vein through the oesophageal submucosal plexus to the azygos vein. The plexus has little connective tissue support and dilates under the high pressure. Two factors sustain portal hypertension: increased intrahepatic (sinusoidal) resistance from fibrosis, nodule formation, and vasoconstrictor mediators, and increased portal inflow from splanchnic vasodilation mediated by nitric oxide.

    Complications

    • Variceal haemorrhage is the major complication. Large or tortuous varices, high hepatic venous pressure gradient, red colour signs, previous bleeding, and advanced liver disease increase the risk of rupture. Each episode carries a mortality of roughly 15% to 20%, and more than half of survivors rebleed within one year.
    • Hypovolemic shock and death, directly from exsanguination or from precipitation of hepatic failure, since blood in the gut gives a large nitrogen load that provokes hepatic encephalopathy.
    • Infection (aspiration pneumonia, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis) after a bleed.
    • Renal failure (hepatorenal syndrome) after haemorrhage.
    • Ulceration, thrombosis, and stricture of the oesophageal wall after rupture, banding, or sclerotherapy.

    Management comprises resuscitation, splanchnic vasoconstrictors, endoscopic variceal ligation or sclerotherapy, balloon tamponade, and, for prevention, non-selective beta-blockers and repeated ligation. Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting is used for refractory bleeding.

    Barrett esophagus

    B2

    What is Barrett esophagus? Mention its clinical importance. How will you diagnose?

    Barrett oesophagus [intestinal metaplasia of the lower oesophagus] is a complication of chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux in which the normal squamous epithelium of the lower oesophagus is replaced by metaplastic intestinal-type columnar epithelium containing goblet cells. Its importance is that it is the precursor of oesophageal adenocarcinoma, and it is diagnosed by endoscopy with biopsy showing columnar mucosa with goblet cells above the gastro-oesophageal junction.

    Definition and pathogenesis. Barrett oesophagus is intestinal metaplasia of the oesophageal squamous mucosa arising in the setting of long-standing GERD. Chronic exposure of the squamous epithelium to acid and bile reflux leads to replacement by a more acid-resistant columnar epithelium. It is estimated to occur in up to 10% of persons with symptomatic GERD and in about 2% of the general population
    it is most common in white men between 40 and 60 years of age, and obesity (central) is a recognised risk factor.

    Morphology. Endoscopically, tongues or circumferential bands of red, velvety mucosa extend upward from the gastro-oesophageal junction, alternating with residual pale, smooth squamous mucosa. The segment is classified as long (3 cm or more) or short (less than 3 cm). Histologically, the squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium of intestinal type, with goblet cells (the diagnostic feature) whose distended mucin vacuoles stain pale blue and give the cytoplasm the shape of a wine goblet, along with non-goblet columnar cells.

    Dysplasia, graded as low or high, is characterised by nuclear hyperchromasia, stratification, loss of polarity, irregular budding glands, and gland-within-gland architecture. Invasion into the lamina propria defines intramucosal carcinoma.

    Clinical importance

    1. It is the only recognised precursor of oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Most adenocarcinomas arise in Barrett oesophagus, although most patients with Barrett oesophagus never develop cancer.
    2. The cancer risk is greatest with goblet-cell metaplasia, long-segment disease, increasing age, male sex, and especially the presence and grade of dysplasia.
    3. Because dysplasia is a treatable preinvasive stage, Barrett oesophagus justifies surveillance endoscopy and biopsy, and dysplasia may be treated by radiofrequency ablation or endoscopic mucosal resection.
    4. It also signifies long-standing reflux disease and may be complicated by ulcer and stricture.

    Diagnosis. The diagnosis is made by upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, which demonstrates columnar-lined mucosa extending above the gastro-oesophageal junction, followed by systematic biopsy (four-quadrant biopsies at regular intervals along the segment plus targeted biopsies of any visible lesion). Histology confirms intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells (highlighted by Alcian blue at pH 2.5), and the biopsy must be assessed for dysplasia. a diagnosis of high-grade dysplasia is usually confirmed by a second pathologist. Chromoendoscopy or narrow-band imaging increases the yield of surveillance biopsies.

    Esophageal carcinoma

    B2

    Mention the sites and types of esophageal cancer.

    Nearly all oesophageal cancers are either squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma, the commoner type worldwide, arises mainly in the upper and middle thirds of the oesophagus, whereas adenocarcinoma arises in the distal third on a background of Barrett oesophagus [intestinal metaplasia of the lower oesophagus] and may involve the gastric cardia.

    Spread. The rich lymphatic network promotes longitudinal and circumferential spread with intramural satellite nodules. Upper-third tumours metastasise to cervical nodes, middle-third tumours to mediastinal, paratracheal, and tracheobronchial nodes, and lower-third tumours to gastric and coeliac nodes. Local invasion of the trachea or bronchus (tracheo-oesophageal fistula and pneumonia), aorta (exsanguination), and mediastinum is characteristic.

    Other types. Rare malignancies include undifferentiated carcinoma, neuroendocrine (small cell) carcinoma, melanoma, lymphoma, and sarcomas. Leiomyoma is the commonest benign tumour, arising in the oesophageal wall.

    Clinical features. Progressive dysphagia (first for solids, then liquids), odynophagia, weight loss, and haemorrhage. The 5-year survival is less than 20% overall but about 75% for superficial squamous lesions.

    Stomach

    Gastritis

    B2

    What is gastritis? What are the characteristics of Helicobacter pylori-associated and autoimmune gastritis?

    Gastritis is inflammation of the gastric mucosa, recognised histologically by the presence of neutrophils or chronic inflammatory cells (when inflammatory cells are scanty the lesion is called gastropathy). The commonest cause of chronic gastritis is Helicobacter pylori, which produces an antral-predominant gastritis with increased acid, whereas autoimmune gastritis is a body- and fundus-restricted atrophic gastritis with parietal cell loss, achlorhydria, hypergastrinaemia, and pernicious anaemia.

    Definition and classification. Gastritis is inflammation of the gastric mucosa. Acute gastritis (and gastropathy) results from agents that overwhelm mucosal defences (NSAIDs, alcohol, bile, chemotherapy, radiation, ischaemia, stress, uraemia) and shows oedema, congestion, foveolar hyperplasia, neutrophils, and in severe cases erosion and haemorrhage. In the gastrointestinal tract, "acute" refers to the duration of disease rather than to the pattern of inflammation.

    Chronic gastritis is caused most commonly by H. pylori
    Other causes include NSAIDs, autoimmune gastritis, radiation, chronic bile reflux, mechanical injury, and systemic disease such as Crohn disease [transmural granulomatous inflammatory bowel disease], amyloidosis, and graft-versus-host disease. Symptoms of chronic gastritis are milder but more persistent than in acute disease: nausea, upper abdominal pain, and sometimes vomiting, with haematemesis uncommon.

    Helicobacter pylori–associated gastritis. H. pylori is a spiral, curved bacillus adapted to the gastric mucus niche. Infection is acquired in childhood by the faecal–oral route, is associated with poverty and crowding, and persists for life without treatment. Virulence depends on flagella (motility in mucus), urease (generates ammonia from urea and raises local pH), adhesins (attachment to foveolar cells), and toxins such as CagA and VacA. Host factors such as pro-inflammatory polymorphisms of TNF and IL-1 and reduced IL-10 influence the outcome.

    The infection typically causes a predominantly antral gastritis with normal or increased acid production. Inflammation enhances antral gastrin production, which expands the parietal cell mass and increases acid secretion, predisposing to peptic ulcer. Long-standing infection may extend to the body and fundus (pangastritis), causing patchy atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, and reduced acid secretion, which increases the risk of adenocarcinoma.

    Histologically, organisms lie in the superficial mucus overlying foveolar cells (best seen with special stains or immunostains). The lamina propria contains numerous plasma cells, lymphocytes, and neutrophils, which cross the basement membrane to form pit abscesses. Lymphoid aggregates with germinal centres (induced MALT) are common and may give rise to MALT lymphoma. Diagnosis rests on biopsy, rapid urease test, culture, PCR, urea breath test, stool antigen, or serology
    Treatment is a proton pump inhibitor with antibiotics.

    Autoimmune gastritis. This accounts for less than 10% of chronic gastritis and is the second or third most frequent cause after H. pylori and NSAIDs. It is an autoimmune attack, mediated by CD4⁺ T cells and antibodies, on the parietal cells of the oxyntic mucosa, with antibodies to H⁺,K⁺-ATPase (proton pump) and to intrinsic factor. It affects the body and fundus and characteristically spares the antrum.

    The loss of parietal cells leads to achlorhydria, which stimulates antral G-cell hyperplasia and marked hypergastrinaemia, and to loss of intrinsic factor with defective ileal absorption of vitamin B₁₂, producing megaloblastic (pernicious) anaemia, atrophic glossitis, and neurologic complications such as subacute combined degeneration. Serum pepsinogen I is low. Morphologically, the oxyntic mucosa is thinned with loss of rugae, and there is a deep lymphocytic and plasma-cell infiltrate centred on the glands with lymphoid follicles. Intestinal metaplasia and endocrine cell hyperplasia are common, and the latter may progress to small multicentric neuroendocrine tumours.

    It occurs most often in older women, is associated with other autoimmune diseases (Hashimoto thyroiditis [autoimmune thyroiditis causing hypothyroidism], type 1 diabetes mellitus, Addison disease [primary adrenocortical insufficiency]), and carries an increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

    Antrum spared
    Inflammatory infiltrateNeutrophils, subepithelial plasma cellsLymphocytes, macrophages
    Acid productionIncreased to slightly decreasedDecreased (achlorhydria)
    GastrinNormal to increasedMarkedly increased
    Other lesionsHyperplastic/inflammatory polypsNeuroendocrine hyperplasia
    SerologyAntibodies to H. pyloriAntibodies to parietal cells (H⁺,K⁺-ATPase) and intrinsic factor
    SequelaePeptic ulcer, adenocarcinoma, MALT lymphomaAtrophy, pernicious anaemia, adenocarcinoma, neuroendocrine tumour
    AssociationsLow socioeconomic status, crowdingAutoimmune thyroiditis, diabetes, Graves disease [autoimmune hyperthyroidism]

    Peptic ulcer disease

    B2

    Define ulcer. Mention the ulcers of stomach.

    An ulcer is a local defect or excavation of the surface of an organ or tissue produced by the sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue. In the stomach the principal ulcers are the chronic peptic ulcer, acute stress ulcers and erosions, drug (NSAID)-induced ulcers, and ulcerating malignancies.

    Definition. An ulcer is a break in the continuity of an epithelial surface, in which a defect extending at least into the submucosa results from sloughing of necrotic inflamed tissue. An erosion, by contrast, is a superficial defect confined to the mucosa.

    Ulcers of the stomach

    1. Chronic peptic (gastric) ulcer, usually solitary, on the lesser curvature at the junction of body and antrum, arising on a background of chronic H. pylori gastritis or NSAID injury.
    2. Acute stress-related mucosal ulcers, which are multiple, shallow, and found throughout the stomach in patients with shock, sepsis, severe trauma, or burns (Curling ulcers) or intracranial disease (Cushing ulcers).
    3. Drug-induced ulcers and erosions, notably NSAIDs and aspirin, alcohol, corticosteroids (potentiating NSAIDs), and cytotoxic drugs.
    4. Ulcers of Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma), which are multiple and may involve the stomach, duodenum, and jejunum.
    5. Malignant ulcers, namely ulcerated gastric adenocarcinoma and occasionally lymphoma.
    6. Rarer lesions: ulcers in granulomatous gastritis (Crohn disease [transmural granulomatous inflammatory bowel disease], tuberculosis, sarcoidosis), infectious ulcers (CMV, herpes simplex), ischaemic or radiation ulcers, and bleeding from a Dieulafoy lesion (abnormal submucosal artery eroding the mucosa).
    B2

    List the ulcers in the GIT.

    Ulcers occur throughout the gastrointestinal tract and are classified by site and cause: aphthous and herpetic ulcers in the mouth, reflux, viral, pill, and Barrett [intestinal metaplasia of the lower oesophagus] ulcers in the oesophagus, peptic and stress ulcers in the stomach and duodenum, typhoid, tuberculous, Crohn [transmural granulomatous inflammatory bowel disease], and ischaemic ulcers in the small bowel, and ulcerative colitis, amoebic, bacillary, pseudomembranous, ischaemic, and malignant ulcers in the large bowel.

    SiteUlcers
    MouthAphthous ulcer, herpetic ulcer, Behçet syndrome, traumatic ulcer, ulcerated squamous carcinoma
    OesophagusReflux (peptic) ulcer, Barrett ulcer, pill-induced and corrosive ulcers, herpes simplex virus (punched-out), cytomegalovirus (shallow), candidal ulcer, carcinoma
    StomachChronic peptic ulcer, acute stress ulcer (Curling, Cushing), NSAID-induced ulcer, Zollinger–Ellison ulcers, ulcerated carcinoma and lymphoma
    DuodenumChronic peptic ulcer (first part), Zollinger–Ellison ulcers, Curling ulcer
    Small intestineTyphoid ulcer (longitudinal, over Peyer patches, terminal ileum), tuberculous ulcer (transverse, circumferential), Crohn disease (aphthous, linear, serpentine ulcers), peptic ulcer in Meckel diverticulum, NSAID, ischaemic and radiation ulcers, ulcerated lymphoma
    Large intestineUlcerative colitis, Crohn disease, amoebic (flask-shaped), shigellosis, pseudomembranous colitis, ischaemic colitis, tuberculous and CMV ulcers, solitary rectal ulcer syndrome, stercoral ulcer, ulcerated carcinoma
    B2

    What is PUD? Mention the common sites of peptic ulcer.

    Peptic ulcer disease is chronic mucosal ulceration of the stomach or duodenum caused by an imbalance between mucosal defences and acid–peptic injury, almost always associated with H. pylori infection, NSAID use, or smoking. The commonest site is the first part of the duodenum, followed by the lesser curvature of the stomach near the junction of the body and antrum.

    Definition. Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) is a chronic, usually solitary, mucosal ulceration that arises in areas of the alimentary tract exposed to acid and pepsin. It is almost always associated with H. pylori infection, NSAIDs, or cigarette smoking, and it develops on a background of chronic gastritis. The commonest form arises in the gastric antrum or duodenum in association with H. pylori antral gastritis, which increases acid secretion and reduces duodenal bicarbonate secretion. Patients with gastric mucosal atrophy, who secrete little acid, are protected.

    Common sites

    1. First part (proximal duodenum), within a few centimetres of the pyloric valve, is the most frequent site. Duodenal ulcers outnumber gastric ulcers, and they occur typically on the anterior wall (tendency to perforate) or posterior wall (tendency to bleed).
    2. Stomach, predominantly the lesser curvature near the junction of the body and the antrum (the angularis).
    3. Less common sites: the pyloric channel, the margin of a gastrojejunostomy (marginal ulcer), the lower oesophagus (reflux ulcer and Barrett oesophagus [intestinal metaplasia of the lower oesophagus], or acid secreted by an oesophageal inlet patch), the jejunum in Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, and an ileal Meckel diverticulum containing ectopic gastric mucosa.
    B2

    What is PUD? What are the risk factors for PUD?

    Peptic ulcer disease is chronic, usually solitary ulceration of the duodenum or stomach resulting from an imbalance between mucosal defences and acid–peptic injury. The dominant risk factors are H. pylori infection and NSAID use, with smoking, corticosteroids, and other conditions contributing.

    Definition. PUD is chronic mucosal ulceration affecting the duodenum or stomach, sharply punched out, usually solitary, and developing on a background of chronic gastritis.

    Risk factors

    • *Helicobacter pylori* infection, the most important factor
      Antral gastritis increases acid secretion and gastrin, and reduces duodenal bicarbonate.
    • NSAIDs, including aspirin and selective COX-2 inhibitors, which inhibit prostaglandin E₂ and I₂ synthesis and so reduce mucus, bicarbonate, mucosal blood flow, and epithelial repair. The effect is potentiated by corticosteroids, and amplified in the elderly and in H. pylori–infected individuals.
    • Cigarette smoking, which synergises with H. pylori (particularly for gastric ulcers) and impairs mucosal blood flow and healing.
    • Hypersecretory states: Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma) and endocrine cell hyperplasia, which stimulate parietal cell growth and acid secretion.
    • Associated diseases: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, alcoholic cirrhosis (mainly duodenal ulcers), cardiovascular disease and other conditions with reduced mucosal blood flow, chronic renal failure, and hyperparathyroidism.
    • Drugs and toxins: illicit drugs such as cocaine that reduce mucosal blood flow. alcohol.
    • Other: psychological stress (may increase acid secretion), viral infections (CMV, herpes simplex virus), genetic susceptibility, and blood group O.
    B2

    What are the differences between benign and malignant ulcers?

    A benign (peptic) ulcer is typically small, round or oval, and sharply punched out with a clean smooth base and radiating mucosal folds, whereas a malignant ulcer is large, irregular, and has heaped-up, rolled everted margins, a shaggy necrotic base, and folds that are clubbed, fused, or amputated at the edge.

    Regional nodesNot enlarged (reactive only)Often involved

    Whatever the appearance, every gastric ulcer must be biopsied (multiple biopsies from the margin and base), because some malignant ulcers mimic benign ones and cure after medical therapy does not exclude cancer.

    B2

    How is PUD formed? What are the complications of PUD?

    Peptic ulcer forms when damaging forces (gastric acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) overwhelm the protective mechanisms of the mucosa, on a background of chronic gastritis. The main complications are haemorrhage, perforation, and gastric outlet obstruction, with penetration, intractable pain, and rarely malignant change.

    Formation. The gastric mucosa is protected by a mucus–bicarbonate barrier, tight epithelial junctions that limit back-diffusion of acid, rapid epithelial renewal, prostaglandin synthesis, and a rich mucosal blood supply that removes any acid that has diffused into the lamina propria. A peptic ulcer arises when these defences are impaired or the damaging factors are excessive.

    H. pylori is the principal cause. The organism lives in the gastric mucus and does not invade the tissues
    it injures the mucosa through urease-generated ammonia, CagA and VacA toxins, and the inflammatory response (neutrophils, TNF, IL-1). Antral gastritis increases gastrin and acid secretion and reduces duodenal bicarbonate secretion. The acid load produces gastric metaplasia in the duodenum, which becomes colonised and inflamed and finally ulcerates.

    NSAIDs cause ulceration by inhibiting COX-dependent prostaglandin synthesis. Smoking reduces mucosal blood flow and healing, and Zollinger–Ellison syndrome produces massive acid hypersecretion. Peptic ulcers therefore arise on a background of chronic gastritis.

    Complications

    1. Haemorrhage: the most frequent complication (about 15% to 20% of patients)
      Erosion of a thickened vessel in the scarred base (the gastroduodenal artery in posterior duodenal ulcers) causes haematemesis, melaena, or chronic blood loss with iron deficiency anaemia, and it can be life threatening.
    2. Perforation: about 5% of patients, but it accounts for about two-thirds of ulcer-related deaths and is rarely the first indication of an ulcer
      it is commonest with anterior duodenal ulcers and causes peritonitis, with free air under the diaphragm on an upright abdominal radiograph.
    3. Obstruction (about 2%): from oedema or scarring, mostly with pyloric channel and duodenal ulcers, causing incapacitating pain, repeated vomiting, and rarely complete outlet obstruction with metabolic alkalosis.
    4. Penetration into adjacent organs (pancreas, causing back pain; liver) and fistula formation.
    5. Intractable pain and recurrence.
    6. Malignant transformation: rare, and almost exclusively a concern with gastric (not duodenal) ulcers, most of which were malignant from the outset.
    B2

    Tell the morphological features of PUD.

    A peptic ulcer is usually a solitary, round to oval, sharply punched-out defect with a smooth clean base and radiating folds, and microscopically its base shows four zones: fibrinous debris, neutrophilic exudate, granulation tissue, and fibrous scar.

    Gross. More than 80% of peptic ulcers are solitary. They are round to oval, usually less than 3 to 4 cm, with a sharply punched-out appearance. The mucosal margin is usually level with the surrounding mucosa, though it may overhang the base, particularly proximally. heaped-up margins suggest carcinoma. The base is smooth and clean because of peptic digestion of exudate and may be stained brown or black by altered blood.

    Scarring may involve the full thickness of the wall and draws the surrounding mucosa into folds that radiate outward like spokes of a wheel. The commonest sites are the first part of the duodenum and the lesser curvature of the stomach.

    Microscopic. The ulcer extends through the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa or deeper, and the base has four layers: (1) a thin superficial layer of necrotic fibrinoid debris, often with neutrophils. (2) a zone of active, predominantly neutrophilic inflammation. (3) granulation tissue with immature vessels, neutrophils, and mononuclear cells. and (4) a deep fibrous or collagenous scar that may extend into or through the muscularis propria.

    Vessels within the scar are thickened (endarteritis obliterans) and occasionally thrombosed, and eroded vessels account for bleeding. The adjacent mucosa shows chronic gastritis, and foveolar metaplasia is common in duodenal disease, as a protective response.

    Write in short about the pathogenesis of PUD.

    DU24MDU22N
    • PUD results from imbalance between defence mechanisms and damaging factors that cause chronic gastritis
      it generally develops on a background of chronic gastritis
    • Defences: mucus and phospholipid layer, bicarbonate secretion, epithelial barrier, mucosal blood flow
    • Damaging factors: gastric acid, peptic enzymes, H. pylori, NSAIDs
    • *H. pylori* antral gastritis leads to increased local gastrin production, expansion of gastric body parietal cells and increased acid secretion, with decreased duodenal bicarbonate secretion
    • NSAIDs inhibit COX-dependent synthesis of prostaglandins E2 and I2, which support mucus, bicarbonate and phospholipid secretion, mucosal blood flow and epithelial restitution
    • Individuals with gastric mucosal atrophy (reduced acid secretion) are generally protected from antral and duodenal ulcers

    Explain: H. pylori does not invade the tissues but can cause peptic ulcer.

    DU08Ju
    • H. pylori has adapted to the niche provided by gastric mucus
      it stays in the superficial mucus over surface and neck epithelial cells and does not invade the tissue
    • It causes injury through its virulence factors:
    • Flagella: motility in viscous mucus
    • Urease: generates ammonia from endogenous urea and raises local gastric pH
    • Adhesins: adherence to surface foveolar cells
    • Toxins, such as CagA (injected into the epithelial cytoplasm) and VacA
    • It induces antral gastritis with infiltration by neutrophils and plasma cells. Inflammation enhances local gastrin production, leading to increased acid secretion and decreased duodenal bicarbonate secretion
    • Increased acid with impaired mucosal defence leads to peptic ulcer
    • The outcome depends on host defences, host genetics and immune response, and bacterial virulence

    H. pylori-related diseases

    B2

    Enumerate the H. pylori-related diseases of the stomach.

    Helicobacter pylori causes acute and chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer disease of the stomach and duodenum, gastric adenocarcinoma, and gastric MALT lymphoma, together with polyps and atrophic changes that link them.

    1. Acute gastritis: usually mild and self-limited, with nonspecific dyspeptic symptoms at the time of infection.
    2. Chronic gastritis: initially a superficial antral gastritis with plasma cells, lymphocytes, and neutrophils (pit abscesses), and lymphoid follicles with germinal centres. Later a pangastritis.
    3. Chronic atrophic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia (environmental metaplastic atrophic gastritis): patchy, without autoantibodies, with reduced acid output.
    4. Peptic ulcer disease: gastric ulcer and, through increased antral gastrin and acid, duodenal ulcer.
    5. Hyperplastic and inflammatory gastric polyps, which arise in the setting of chronic gastritis and may show dysplasia.
    6. Dysplasia and intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma, through the sequence of atrophy, metaplasia, dysplasia, and carcinoma. The risk is greatest with CagA-positive strains.
    7. Gastric MALT lymphoma (extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma), arising from induced mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue. Early tumours without translocation may regress after eradication.
    8. Less commonly, associations with hypertrophic gastropathy (Ménétrier disease), eosinophilic and granulomatous gastritis, and extragastric conditions such as iron deficiency anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia.

    Interestingly, H. pylori infection with atrophy lowers the risk of duodenal ulcer and of oesophageal adenocarcinoma, because of reduced acid secretion.

    Gastric carcinoma

    B2

    Tell the role of H. pylori in gastric carcinoma. What is linitis plastica?

    H. pylori is the commonest identifiable cause of gastric adenocarcinoma (intestinal type): chronic infection leads through atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia to dysplasia and carcinoma. Linitis plastica is the "leather bottle" stomach produced by diffuse infiltration of the gastric wall by signet-ring cell (diffuse-type) carcinoma, with a desmoplastic reaction, rigidity, and flattening of the rugae.

    Role of H. pylori. Most gastric cancers are associated with H. pylori infection, and the decline in gastric cancer incidence in high-income countries has been attributed largely to the decline in infection, chiefly of intestinal-type cancers. The mechanism is the long-standing chronic gastritis that causes multifocal mucosal atrophy and intestinal metaplasia, which is the field in which dysplasia and carcinoma arise (the Correa cascade: chronic gastritis, atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia, carcinoma).

    Chronic inflammation exposes the epithelium to free radicals and to regenerative proliferative stimuli, including raised gastrin, which is mitogenic. Achlorhydria permits bacterial overgrowth and production of carcinogenic nitrosamines. Strains carrying the CagA pathogenicity island, present in about 90% of isolates in high-risk populations, colonise the body as well as the antrum and induce cytokine release, atrophy, and metaplasia more effectively.

    Host polymorphisms leading to high TNF and IL-1 and low IL-10 increase the risk. In diffuse gastric cancer the pathogenesis involves loss of E-cadherin (CDH1 mutation or promoter hypermethylation). A minority (about 10%) of gastric cancers are instead associated with Epstein–Barr virus. Eradication of H. pylori reduces the risk, and intestinal metaplasia may regress. Infection is also linked to gastric MALT lymphoma. The inverse relationship between duodenal ulcer (high acid) and gastric cancer (atrophy, low acid) is a notable feature.

    Linitis plastica. In diffuse-type gastric carcinoma, small clusters and individual discohesive signet-ring cells infiltrate the gastric wall. These cells contain large mucin vacuoles that push the nucleus to the periphery, and they provoke an intense desmoplastic reaction. Extensive infiltration produces diffuse thickening and rigidity of the stomach wall with flattening of the rugal folds and a contracted lumen, imparting a "leather bottle" appearance, without a discrete mass and often without an ulcer. It carries a very poor prognosis (5-year survival less than 20% in advanced disease).

    B2

    Mention the macroscopic and microscopic types of gastric carcinoma.

    Gastric adenocarcinoma is classified macroscopically as polypoid (exophytic), ulcerated, or diffusely infiltrative (linitis plastica), and microscopically into the intestinal type, which forms glands, and the diffuse type, composed of signet-ring cells.

    Early versus advanced. Early gastric cancer is limited to the mucosa and submucosa regardless of nodal status and has a 5-year survival exceeding 90% after resection
    Advanced cancer invades the muscularis propria or beyond.

    Macroscopic types (advanced cancer)

    1. Polypoid or fungating (exophytic): bulky, intraluminal mass, typical of intestinal-type tumours.
    2. Ulcerative (malignant ulcer): a crater with heaped-up, irregular margins and a necrotic base.
    3. Diffusely infiltrative: the wall is thickened and rigid
      with extensive involvement, linitis plastica ("leather bottle" stomach).
    4. Superficial spreading (early lesions) may be elevated, flat, or depressed.

    Most distal cancers occur in the antrum, and the lesser curvature is involved more often than the greater curvature.

    Microscopic types

    TypeGrowth and gross patternHistologyEpidemiology and genetics
    IntestinalBulky exophytic or ulcerated mass, cohesive frontsGlandular structures with apical mucin vacuoles
    Mucin lakes may occur    		Predominates in high-risk areas, mean age about 55, male:female 2:1
    Arises from dysplasia and adenomas
    CIN, MSI, and EBV molecular subtypes
    DiffuseInfiltrative thickening of the wall, linitis plasticaDiscohesive signet-ring cells without gland formation
    Desmoplasia    		Uniform incidence worldwide, no precursor
    Loss of E-cadherin (CDH1)
    May be hereditary

    Other recognised histologic patterns are tubular, papillary, mucinous (colloid), and poorly cohesive carcinomas. Extracellular mucin in either type may form mucin lakes.

    Spread. Direct extension to the duodenum, pancreas, and retroperitoneum. Lymph node metastases including the left supraclavicular (Virchow) node and periumbilical (Sister Mary Joseph) nodule. Haematogenous spread to the liver
    Peritoneal seeding with ovarian metastases (Krukenberg tumour) and pouch of Douglas deposits.

    Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST)

    Write a short note on GIST.

    DU20NDU20Ju

    Definition: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) is the most common mesenchymal tumour of the abdomen
    More than half occur in the stomach. It arises from the interstitial cells of Cajal [pacemaker cells of the gut] (pacemaker cells). Peak age is 60 years.

    Pathogenesis - About 75% have gain-of-function mutations in the receptor tyrosine kinase KIT - About 8% have mutations in PDGFRA
    KIT and PDGFRA mutations are mutually exclusive - Tumours without these often have mutations in the succinate dehydrogenase complex genes (SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD) - Associated with Carney triad [gastric GIST, paraganglioma and pulmonary chondroma] (GIST, paraganglioma, pulmonary chondroma) and neurofibromatosis type 1

    Morphology - Solitary, well-circumscribed, fleshy mass, up to 30 cm
    Overlying mucosa frequently ulcerated
    Cut surface whorled - Spindle cell type: bundles of spindle cells
    Epithelioid type: plump epithelial-looking cells
    Mixtures are common
    Nuclear pleomorphism uncommon - KIT (CD117) positive in 95% of gastric GISTs. DOG1 positive in 95%

    Clinical features and complications - Mass effects
    Mucosal ulceration causes blood loss, and about half present with anaemia - Metastasis to serosal nodules in the peritoneal cavity and to the liver. Spread outside the abdomen is uncommon - Prognosis correlates with size, mitotic index and location. Gastric GISTs are less aggressive than small intestinal GISTs - Treatment: complete surgical resection. Imatinib (tyrosine kinase inhibitor) in KIT or PDGFRA mutated tumours that are unresectable, recurrent or metastatic

    Congenital Anomalies

    B2

    What are the congenital anomalies of GIT?

    The principal congenital anomalies of the gastrointestinal tract are atresia, fistulae, and duplications (for example oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula and intestinal atresia), ectopia, Meckel diverticulum, congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, and Hirschsprung disease [congenital aganglionic megacolon].

    1. Atresia, fistulae, and duplications: failure of canalisation or abnormal septation of the foregut, producing oesophageal atresia (usually with a distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula, causing choking, regurgitation, and aspiration at the first feed), intestinal atresia and stenosis (most frequent in the duodenum), and duplications
      Anorectal malformations (imperforate anus) also belong here.
    2. Ectopia: developmental rests of gastric mucosa (the oesophageal inlet patch) or pancreatic tissue in the oesophagus, stomach, or small intestine. They may cause dysphagia, peptic ulceration, or pyloric obstruction.
    3. Meckel diverticulum: the commonest congenital anomaly of the gut, a true ileal diverticulum from failed involution of the vitelline duct.
    4. Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: hyperplasia of the pyloric muscularis presenting at 3 to 6 weeks with projectile nonbilious vomiting and a palpable "olive."
    5. Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon): failure of neural crest migration, causing functional distal obstruction.
    6. Others: malrotation and volvulus, abdominal wall defects (omphalocele, gastroschisis), and diaphragmatic hernia.
    B2

    What is Meckel diverticulum and what is Hirschsprung disease?

    Meckel diverticulum is the commonest congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract, a true diverticulum of the ileum caused by failure of involution of the vitelline duct, whereas Hirschsprung disease [congenital aganglionic megacolon] is a congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel, causing functional obstruction with proximal megacolon.

    Meckel diverticulum. A true diverticulum includes all three layers of the bowel wall. Meckel diverticulum results from persistence of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct, which connects the gut lumen to the yolk sac, and arises from the antimesenteric border of the ileum. The "rule of 2s" applies: it occurs in about 2% of the population, within about 2 feet (60 cm) of the ileocaecal valve, is about 2 inches (5 cm) long, has a male:female ratio of 2:1, and is most often symptomatic by age 2 (although only about 4% ever become symptomatic).

    The lining may resemble normal small intestine, but ectopic gastric (acid-secreting) or pancreatic tissue may be present. The complications are peptic ulceration of the adjacent ileal mucosa with bleeding (occult or massive, particularly in children) and perforation, diverticulitis simulating acute appendicitis, intussusception, volvulus, and obstruction. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan identifies ectopic gastric mucosa.

    Hirschsprung disease. Congenital aganglionic megacolon occurs in about 1 in 5000 live births, with a male predominance, and is associated with Down syndrome [trisomy 21] (about 10%) and other malformations. The enteric neural plexus develops from neural crest cells that migrate into the bowel wall in a craniocaudal direction. When migration is arrested prematurely or ganglion cells die prematurely, the distal segment lacks both Meissner (submucosal) and Auerbach (myenteric) plexuses.

    Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in RET account for most familial and about 15% of sporadic cases, and mutations in EDNRB and EDN3 have also been implicated. The aganglionic segment cannot relax and is hypercontracted, so peristalsis is absent and functional obstruction results, with dilatation of the proximal normally innervated colon (megacolon). The rectum is always involved. short-segment disease (rectosigmoid) is commoner than long-segment disease.

    Diagnosis requires histologic proof of absence of ganglion cells (rectal biopsy; acetylcholinesterase staining highlights hypertrophic nerve fibres). Infants fail to pass meconium in the first 48 hours and develop abdominal distention and bilious vomiting. The major risks are enterocolitis, fluid and electrolyte disturbance, perforation, and peritonitis. Treatment is surgical resection of the aganglionic segment with anastomosis of the normal colon to the rectum.

    List four congenital anomalies of GIT.

    DU17M
    1. Atresia, fistulae and duplications (oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula)
    2. Meckel diverticulum
    3. Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
    4. Hirschsprung disease [congenital aganglionic megacolon] (congenital aganglionic megacolon)

    Write a short note on Hirschsprung disease.

    DU12Ju

    Definition: Hirschsprung disease [congenital aganglionic megacolon] causes functional obstruction of the colon due to failure of ganglion cells to migrate to the wall of the colon. Incidence about 1 in 5000 live births. 10% of cases occur in Down syndrome [trisomy 21].

    Pathogenesis - Arrested migration of neural crest cells from caecum to rectum, or premature death of ganglion cells - Distal segment lacks the Meissner submucosal plexus [enteric nerve plexus of the submucosa] and Auerbach myenteric plexus [enteric nerve plexus between the muscle layers] (aganglionosis). Peristalsis is absent, the aganglionic segment is hypercontracted and the proximal segment dilates - Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations of RET account for most familial and about 15% of sporadic cases. Also EDNRB and EDN3 - Incomplete penetrance

    Morphology - Diagnosis needs histological absence of ganglion cells in the affected segment (acetylcholinesterase staining helps) - Rectum always affected. short-segment (rectosigmoid, more common) or long-segment - Proximal normally innervated colon dilates progressively (megacolon)
    May rupture near the caecum

    Clinical features and complications - Failure to pass meconium, constipation, abdominal distension, bilious vomiting - Life-threatening: enterocolitis, fluid and electrolyte disturbances, perforation, peritonitis - Treatment: surgical resection of the aganglionic segment

    Malabsorption

    List five causes of malabsorption syndrome.

    DU16JaDU14Ju
    1. Pancreatic insufficiency (chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis)
    2. Coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy)
    3. Crohn disease [transmural granulomatous inflammatory bowel disease]
