    5. Whipple disease [Tropheryma whipplei infection causing malabsorption]

    Inflammatory bowel disease

    B2

    Name the inflammatory bowel diseases with macroscopic, microscopic and clinical features.

    Inflammatory bowel disease comprises two chronic relapsing disorders, Crohn disease [transmural granulomatous inflammatory bowel disease] and ulcerative colitis. Crohn disease may involve any part of the gastrointestinal tract, is segmental, transmural, and granulomatous, and causes fistulas and strictures, whereas ulcerative colitis is confined to the colon and rectum, is continuous and limited to the mucosa and superficial submucosa, and presents with bloody diarrhoea.

    Definition and pathogenesis. IBD is a chronic condition composed of Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis (indeterminate colitis, up to 10% of cases, is the term for those that cannot be classified). It results from a combination of abnormal immune regulation (Th1 and Th17 activation), altered host–microbe interactions (dysbiosis), and epithelial barrier dysfunction in genetically susceptible individuals (NOD2 is the strongest association with Crohn disease
    ATG16L1 and IRGM affect autophagy). It most frequently presents in teenage years and the early twenties.

    Crohn disease

    Macroscopic. Any part of the tract may be involved, most commonly the terminal ileum, ileocaecal valve, and caecum
    Small bowel only in about 40%, small bowel and colon in 30%, and colon only in the remainder. The hallmark is skip lesions with sharply delineated diseased segments. Early aphthous ulcers enlarge into deep, linear, serpentine ulcers oriented along the long axis, with oedema, loss of folds, and a cobblestone mucosa.

    The wall is thickened, rubbery, and stenotic from transmural inflammation, oedema, fibrosis, and muscular hypertrophy (strictures). Mesenteric fat extends over the serosa ("creeping fat")
    Deep fissures lead to abscesses, perforation, and fistulas to other loops, bladder, vagina, or skin.

    Microscopic. Transmural inflammation with neutrophilic crypt injury and crypt abscesses, ulceration, crypt distortion, pseudopyloric and Paneth cell metaplasia, and noncaseating granulomas (in about 35% of cases
    a hallmark). Lymphoid aggregates occur throughout the wall.

    Clinical. Intermittent diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and fever, with periods of remission. About 20% present acutely with right iliac fossa pain mimicking appendicitis. Blood loss and iron deficiency anaemia (colonic disease)
    Protein loss, hypoalbuminaemia, and malabsorption of vitamin B₁₂ and bile salts (small bowel disease). Fibrosing strictures, fistulas, perianal disease
    Extraintestinal manifestations (uveitis, migratory polyarthritis, sacroiliitis, ankylosing spondylitis, erythema nodosum, clubbing, primary sclerosing cholangitis). anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies
    Smoking is a risk factor
    Increased risk of colonic carcinoma with long-standing colonic disease.

    Ulcerative colitis

    Macroscopic. The rectum is always involved, and disease extends proximally in a continuous manner to variable extent (proctitis, left-sided colitis, pancolitis). The small bowel is spared, apart from mild backwash ileitis in severe pancolitis. The mucosa is red and granular with broad-based ulcers. Islands of regenerating mucosa form pseudopolyps
    in chronic disease the mucosa is atrophic and smooth. Because it is not transmural, the wall is not thickened, the serosa is normal, and strictures are not a feature. Severe cases may progress to toxic megacolon with perforation.

    Microscopic. Inflammation confined to the mucosa and superficial submucosa, with a lymphoplasmacytic and neutrophilic infiltrate, crypt abscesses, crypt distortion and atrophy, pseudopyloric and Paneth cell metaplasia. Granulomas are absent. Sharp demarcation between diseased and normal mucosa may be seen.

    Clinical. Relapsing attacks of bloody diarrhoea with stringy mucus, lower abdominal pain, and cramps relieved by defecation. Complications include toxic megacolon, perforation, haemorrhage, and colorectal carcinoma (risk increases sharply 8 to 10 years after onset, and is greatest with pancolitis). Extraintestinal manifestations overlap with Crohn disease, with primary sclerosing cholangitis markedly increased (about 5%)
    p-ANCA is positive in about 75%
    Smoking may be protective, and onset can follow smoking cessation.

    What is inflammatory bowel disease?

    DU11Ju

    Polyps

    B2

    Define a polyp. Name the polyps of GIT.

    A polyp is a nodule or mass that projects above the level of the surrounding mucosa into the lumen. Gastrointestinal polyps are classified as nonneoplastic (inflammatory, hyperplastic, hamartomatous) or neoplastic (adenomas and sessile serrated polyps).

    Definition. A polyp is any mass projecting above the surrounding mucosal surface. Those without a stalk are sessile
    as they enlarge, traction and proliferation of adjacent cells may form a stalk, making them pedunculated. A polyp may arise from epithelial or stromal hyperplasia, inflammation, ectopia, or neoplasia, and any mass lesion of the tract, including carcinoma, neuroendocrine tumour, stromal tumour, lymphoma, or a metastasis, may form a polyp.

    What is a polyp and what is a papilloma? What are the differences between them?

    A polyp is any mass that projects above a mucosal surface, irrespective of its nature, which may be hyperplastic, inflammatory, hamartomatous, or neoplastic. A papilloma is a specific benign epithelial neoplasm composed of finger-like (papillary) fronds with a fibrovascular connective tissue core, covered by the epithelium of the surface from which it arises.

    A polyp is a descriptive, gross term, defined by the shape of a lesion, whereas a papilloma is a histogenetic term, indicating a benign neoplasm of surface epithelium. (The definition of papilloma is not in this chapter

    Definition: Colorectal adenomas are epithelial neoplasms characterised by epithelial dysplasia
    They are classified as tubular, tubulovillous or villous by architecture. Villous adenomas are covered by slender villi.

    Aetiology and pathogenesis - Adenomas are precursors to colorectal adenocarcinoma
    Most adenomas do not progress to cancer - Developed in about 30% of adults in the Western world by 60 years

    Polypectomy is diagnostic and therapeutic

    Carcinoid tumor

    B2

    What is carcinoid tumor and what is carcinoid syndrome?

    Carcinoid tumour, now called well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour, is a neoplasm of the diffuse neuroendocrine cells of the gut that most often arises in the small intestine, appendix, and rectum and is composed of uniform cells with "salt and pepper" chromatin. Carcinoid syndrome is the constellation of flushing, diarrhoea, bronchospasm, and right-sided cardiac valvular fibrosis caused by vasoactive substances, mainly serotonin, released into the systemic circulation.

    Carcinoid (neuroendocrine) tumour. Neuroendocrine tumours arise from the diffuse components of the endocrine system. The term carcinoid is still used in the gut. More than 40% occur in the small intestine
    The tracheobronchial tree and lungs are the next commonest site, and the appendix, rectum, and stomach are also important sites. Gastric tumours are associated with endocrine cell hyperplasia, autoimmune atrophic gastritis, MEN1, and Zollinger–Ellison syndrome. They occur most often in the sixth decade.

    Gross. Intramural or submucosal masses forming polypoid nodules with intact or ulcerated overlying mucosa, yellow-tan, and very firm because of intense desmoplasia, which may kink and obstruct the small bowel.

    Microscopic. Islands, trabeculae, strands, glands, and sheets of uniform cells with scant pink granular cytoplasm and round to oval nuclei with "salt and pepper" chromatin
    Positive for synaptophysin and chromogranin A. Grade is determined by mitotic rate and Ki-67 index. Poorly differentiated tumours are neuroendocrine carcinomas (small cell or large cell).

    Behaviour. Prognosis depends on differentiation, mitotic rate, Ki-67, size, and site. Gastric and duodenal tumours rarely metastasise
    Jejunal and ileal tumours are often multiple and aggressive. Appendiceal tumours (usually at the tip, less than 2 cm) are almost always benign. Rectal tumours are usually small and rarely metastasise.

    Carcinoid syndrome. It develops in fewer than 10% of patients, and is caused by vasoactive substances (serotonin, histamine, bradykinin, prostaglandins, tachykinins) secreted by the tumour into the systemic circulation. It occurs when the tumour products bypass the first-pass metabolism by the liver, so it is strongly associated with hepatic metastases (or tumours draining into a nonportal venous bed, such as bronchial carcinoids).

    Its features are cutaneous flushing, sweating, bronchospasm, colicky abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and fibrosis of the right-sided cardiac valves (carcinoid heart disease). Biochemical confirmation is by raised urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), the metabolite of serotonin.

    Write a short note on carcinoid tumour.

    DU03Ja

    Definition: Carcinoid tumour is a neuroendocrine tumour of the gastrointestinal tract. Peak incidence is the sixth decade.

    Morphology - Intramural or submucosal masses forming polypoid lesions. Yellow or tan, very firm because of intense desmoplasia, which may kink and obstruct the small bowel - Islands, trabeculae, strands, glands and sheets of uniform cells with scant pink granular cytoplasm and salt and pepper chromatin - Positive for synaptophysin and chromogranin A

    Clinical features - Symptoms reflect hormones released: gastrin causes Zollinger-Ellison syndrome [gastrin-secreting tumour causing severe peptic ulceration] - Carcinoid syndrome in fewer than 10%: cutaneous flushing, sweating, bronchospasm, colicky abdominal pain, diarrhoea, right-sided cardiac valvular fibrosis - Syndrome is strongly associated with metastasis to the liver, as the liver inactivates the substances on first pass

    Behaviour - Prognosis depends on differentiation, mitotic rate and Ki-67 index - Stomach and duodenum: rarely metastasise - Jejunum and ileum: often multiple and aggressive - Appendix: at the tip, rarely more than 2 cm, almost always benign - Rectum: small, metastasis uncommon

    Malignant tumors of the GIT

    B2

    What are the common malignant tumors of GIT?

    The commonest malignant tumours of the gastrointestinal tract are adenocarcinomas, of which colorectal adenocarcinoma is the most frequent, together with squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus and anus, and, less commonly, lymphomas, neuroendocrine tumours, and gastrointestinal stromal tumours.

    SiteCommon malignant tumours
    OesophagusSquamous cell carcinoma (proximal and middle thirds)
    Adenocarcinoma (distal third, Barrett oesophagus [intestinal metaplasia of the lower oesophagus])
    Rare small cell carcinoma, melanoma, lymphoma, sarcoma
    StomachAdenocarcinoma (more than 90%
    Intestinal and diffuse types)
    MALT lymphoma (about 5%)
    Gastrointestinal stromal tumour
    Neuroendocrine tumour
    Small intestineAdenocarcinoma and neuroendocrine tumours (about equal frequency), lymphoma (including enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma in coeliac disease), sarcoma and GIST
    Colon and rectumAdenocarcinoma (the most common malignancy of the GI tract)
    Neuroendocrine tumours, lymphoma
    AppendixNeuroendocrine tumour (commonest, usually benign), mucinous neoplasms and adenocarcinoma (pseudomyxoma peritonei)
    Anal canalSquamous cell carcinoma (HPV related), adenocarcinoma, basaloid carcinoma

    Colorectal adenocarcinoma. It arises from adenomas and sessile serrated polyps along the chromosomal instability (APC/Wnt), microsatellite instability (mismatch repair deficiency), and CpG island methylator pathways. Right-sided tumours grow as polypoid exophytic masses and present with iron deficiency anaemia. left-sided tumours are annular "napkin-ring" constrictions that cause obstruction and altered bowel habit.

    Microscopically, they are composed of tall columnar cells forming glands with desmoplasia, and some are mucinous or signet ring in type. The most important prognostic factors are depth of invasion and lymph node metastasis. The liver is the commonest site of distant metastasis because of portal drainage.

    Appendix

    B10

    A 15-year-old boy came with acute abdominal pain, vomiting and fever. On examination, rebound tenderness is present in the right iliac fossa. The blood picture shows neutrophilic leukocytosis. What is your clinical diagnosis? How will you confirm it?

    The clinical diagnosis is acute appendicitis. It is confirmed by clinical scoring and imaging (ultrasound or computed tomography), and ultimately by histological examination of the removed appendix, which shows neutrophilic infiltration of the muscularis propria.

    Diagnosis. Acute appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency of adolescents and young adults, with a slight male predominance. The picture here is classic: periumbilical pain that localises to the right iliac fossa (McBurney point), nausea and vomiting, low-grade fever, localised tenderness with rebound (peritoneal irritation), and neutrophilic leucocytosis. It is thought to be initiated by increased intraluminal pressure with compromised venous outflow, most often following luminal obstruction (in 50% to 80% of cases) by a faecalith, or less commonly by a gallstone, tumour, worms (Enterobius), or by lymphoid hyperplasia, with bacterial proliferation, ischaemia, and inflammation.

    Differential diagnosis. Mesenteric lymphadenitis (often secondary to Yersinia or viral enterocolitis), Meckel diverticulitis, acute salpingitis, ectopic pregnancy, mittelschmerz (in females), Crohn disease [transmural granulomatous inflammatory bowel disease], and typhoid.

    Confirmation

    1. Clinical assessment with a scoring system (for example, the Alvarado score), including signs of Rovsing, psoas, and obturator.
    2. Laboratory: complete blood count (neutrophilic leucocytosis, raised C-reactive protein) and urine examination (to exclude urinary tract infection or calculus). Pregnancy test in females.
    3. Imaging: graded-compression ultrasonography (noncompressible, blind-ending tubular structure more than 6 mm in diameter) in children and young patients, and contrast-enhanced computed tomography when needed. Plain abdominal radiography may show a faecalith.
    4. Diagnostic laparoscopy when doubt persists, which can proceed directly to appendectomy.
    5. Definitive confirmation: histopathology of the appendectomy specimen (neutrophils in the muscularis propria).

    A young male has acute abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, RIF tenderness, neutrophilic leukocytosis. What is your diagnosis?

    DU26MDU19NovDU15Ja
    • Acute appendicitis
    • Periumbilical pain that localises to the right lower quadrant, then nausea, vomiting, low-grade fever
    • Deep tenderness at McBurney point (two-thirds of the distance from the umbilicus to the right anterior superior iliac spine)
    • Neutrophilic leucocytosis
    • Most common in adolescents and young adults
      Initiated by increased intraluminal pressure that compromises venous outflow, usually from a faecalith

    Same: write down the possible complications.

    DU26MDU19Nov
    • Perforation and rupture with suppurative peritonitis
    • Focal abscesses in the wall (acute suppurative appendicitis). Gangrenous appendicitis
    • Pylephlebitis
    • Portal venous thrombosis
    • Liver abscess
    • Bacteraemia

    Same: what do you expect in the histopathology after operation?

    DU15Ja
    • Neutrophilic infiltration of the muscularis propria: required for the diagnosis
    • Early: congested subserosal vessels, modest perivascular neutrophilic infiltrate in all layers. Mucosal neutrophils and focal superficial ulceration are not specific
    • More severe: neutrophilic exudate with serosal fibrinopurulent reaction
    • Acute suppurative appendicitis: focal abscesses within the wall
    • Acute gangrenous appendicitis: ischaemia, haemorrhagic ulceration and gangrenous necrosis extending to the serosa, followed by rupture and suppurative peritonitis
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 17)p. 745

    Laboratory Tests of the GIT

    Write a short note on occult blood test.

    DU10JaDU06S

    Definition: Test for hidden (occult) blood in the stool, blood not visible to the eye.

    Principle - Detects haemoglobin or its breakdown products
    The most common method detects haem - Guaiac test: the pseudoperoxidase of haemoglobin converts guaiac to blue - Faecal immunochemical test (FIT): uses antibodies to detect blood

    Indications - Anaemia, suspected gastrointestinal bleeding, colon cancer screening

    Causes of a positive test - Peptic ulcer, carcinoma, diverticulosis, large adenomas, gastric antral vascular ectasia

    Precautions - Any source of blood gives a positive guaiac test, including bleeding haemorrhoids and menstruation - Avoid red meat and vitamin C before a guaiac test - Normal faecal blood loss can approach 1.5 mL per day

    What is pleocytosis?

    DU10Ju
    • Pleocytosis is an increased cell count, particularly an increased white blood cell count, in a body fluid such as cerebrospinal fluid
    • In CSF it means more than 5 white cells per microlitre
    • Lymphocytic pleocytosis: aseptic meningitis
    • Neutrophilic pleocytosis: chemical meningitis

    Jaundice and Hyperbilirubinaemia

    What is jaundice?

    DU17NovDU16JaDU08Ju

    Jaundice is yellow discolouration of the skin (jaundice) and conjunctiva (icterus) due to retention of bilirubin. It becomes evident when serum bilirubin rises above 2 to 2.5 mg/dL (normal 0.3 to 1.2 mg/dL).

    Classify jaundice.

    DU05Ja
    Predominant bilirubinMechanismCauses
    UnconjugatedExcess productionHaemolytic anaemia
    Resorption of blood from internal haemorrhage (alimentary tract bleeding, haematoma)
    Ineffective erythropoiesis (pernicious anaemia, thalassaemia)
    Reduced hepatic uptakeDrug interference with membrane carrier systems
    Some cases of Gilbert syndrome [benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia from reduced UGT1A1 activity] (mild inherited deficiency of UGT1A1, the bilirubin-conjugating enzyme)
    Impaired conjugationPhysiologic jaundice of the newborn (decreased UGT1A1 activity)
    Breast milk jaundice (beta-glucuronidases in milk)
    Genetic UGT1A1 deficiency: Crigler-Najjar syndrome [inherited UGT1A1 deficiency with severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia] types I and II (inherited UGT1A1 deficiency, severe in type I) and some cases of Gilbert syndrome
    ConjugatedDeficiency of canalicular membrane transportersDubin-Johnson syndrome [inherited conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with a black pigmented liver] (MRP2 gene mutation) and Rotor syndrome [inherited conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia without liver pigmentation] (inherited conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia)
    Both autosomal recessive and clinically innocuous
    Hepatocellular diseaseViral or drug-induced hepatitis, cirrhosis
    Impaired bile flowDuct obstruction
    Autoimmune cholangiopathies

    What is physiological jaundice?

    DU14Ja
    • Transient and mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, nearly universal in the first week of life
      it resolves by 2 weeks
    • Cause: levels of UGT1A1 (the enzyme that conjugates bilirubin with glucuronic acid) are low at birth and do not reach adult levels until 3 to 4 months of age
    • Breastfeeding may exacerbate it, possibly because of bilirubin-deconjugating enzymes in breast milk
    • Phototherapy with blue light converts bilirubin to a soluble isomer that is excreted in urine, and is sufficient in most infants
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 18)p. 777

    Mention 2 important causes of obstructive jaundice.

    DU07Ju
    1. Stones in the bile duct (choledocholithiasis)
    2. Malignant neoplasms of the biliary tree or the head of the pancreas, usually adenocarcinoma

    What enzymes are elevated in hepatocellular and obstructive jaundice (AST, ALT, ALP interpretation)?

    DU21MDU13Ja
    TypeEnzymes raisedInterpretation
    Hepatocellular jaundiceAST and ALT (aminotransferases)Above 500 U/L
    Alkaline phosphatase is below 3 times normal. In alcohol-associated liver disease AST is higher than ALT by 2:1 or more
    in other chronic liver diseases ALT tends to be higher than AST
    Obstructive (cholestatic) jaundiceAlkaline phosphatase and GGT (gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase)Both more than 3 times normal
    They are present on the canalicular membranes of hepatocytes and bile duct epithelial cells and are characteristic of cholestatic disease. Aminotransferases are below 200 U/L

    Give the urinary findings of obstructive jaundice.

    DU21MDU16Ja
    • Bilirubin present in the urine, because conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and loosely bound to albumin
    • Dark urine

    What is acholuric jaundice?

    DU10Ja

    Jaundice in which the urine contains no bilirubin because the raised bilirubin is unconjugated. Unconjugated bilirubin is largely insoluble and cannot be excreted in the urine. It is seen in haemolytic anaemia, where the excess serum bilirubin is unconjugated.

    How will you investigate a case of hemolytic jaundice?

    DU08Ju
    1. Serum bilirubin, fractionated: the excess is unconjugated
      Jaundice is rarely severe when the liver is normal
    2. Complete blood count and peripheral blood smear: anaemia, with prominent reticulocytosis
    3. Bone marrow: increased numbers of erythroid precursors (normoblasts)
    4. Evidence of haemolysis: decreased plasma haptoglobin
      Raised lactate dehydrogenase
    5. Direct Coombs test [antiglobulin test for antibody-coated red cells], positive in immune haemolysis
    6. Urine: no bilirubin
      in intravascular haemolysis, haemoglobinuria and haemosiderinuria, with haemoglobinaemia in the blood
    7. Splenomegaly on examination in extravascular haemolysis

    Write a short note on obstructive jaundice.

    DU13Ju

    Definition. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia from impaired bile flow due to obstruction of the large bile ducts. Cholestasis is retention of bilirubin and other solutes normally eliminated in bile.

    Aetiology

    • Adults: stones (choledocholithiasis), malignant neoplasms of the biliary tree or head of pancreas (usually adenocarcinoma), strictures after surgery or ischaemic injury, primary sclerosing cholangitis
    • Children: biliary atresia, cystic fibrosis, choledochal cysts

    Morphology

    • Proximal duct dilatation
    • Liver biopsy: portal expansion by oedema, prominent ductular reaction at the portal-parenchymal interface, neutrophils around ductules (pericholangitis)
    • In ascending cholangitis the neutrophils also involve the bile duct epithelium and lumen
    • Cholestasis: green-brown bile pigment plugs in hepatocytes and dilated canaliculi. Swollen, foamy hepatocytes (feathery degeneration)
    • Persistent obstruction: fibrosis and eventually biliary cirrhosis

    Clinical features

    • Jaundice, pruritus, skin xanthomas
    • Malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins A, D and K
    • Raised alkaline phosphatase and GGT
    • Dark urine and pale stools

    Complications

    • Ascending cholangitis (fever, chills, abdominal pain, jaundice), which can progress to abscess formation, sepsis and death
    • Fibrosis and biliary cirrhosis if obstruction persists. The changes are reversible if the obstruction is corrected early
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 18)p. 752p. 776p. 777

    Write a short note on unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

    DU12Ja

    Definition. Elevation of serum bilirubin that is predominantly unconjugated (indirect).

    Aetiology

    • Excess production: haemolytic anaemia, resorption of blood from internal haemorrhage, ineffective erythropoiesis (pernicious anaemia, thalassaemia)
    • Reduced hepatic uptake: drug interference, some cases of Gilbert syndrome [mild inherited UGT1A1 deficiency]
    • Impaired conjugation: physiologic jaundice of the newborn, breast milk jaundice, genetic UGT1A1 deficiency
    • Crigler-Najjar syndrome [inherited UGT1A1 deficiency with severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia] type I (severe UGT1A1 deficiency) is fatal around birth. in Crigler-Najjar type II and Gilbert syndrome residual UGT1A1 activity gives a milder picture

    Pathogenesis

    • Unconjugated bilirubin is largely insoluble and cannot be excreted in the urine
    • Most is tightly bound to albumin
      at excessive levels the unbound fraction rises and may diffuse into tissues, particularly the brain in infants

    Clinical features and complications

    • Jaundice becomes evident above 2 to 2.5 mg/dL
    • In haemolysis, jaundice is rarely severe when the liver is normal. Excess bilirubin excreted in bile often forms pigment gallstones
    • Neurologic damage in infants: kernicterus
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 18)p. 776p. 777

    Write a short note on kernicterus.

    DU11Ju

    Definition. Damage to the central nervous system caused by unconjugated bilirubin.

    Pathogenesis

    • Haemolysis produces unconjugated bilirubin, which passes through the infant's poorly developed blood-brain barrier
    • Being water-insoluble, bilirubin binds to lipids in the brain and damages the CNS
    • At excessive levels the unbound fraction of unconjugated bilirubin rises and diffuses into the brain
    • Occurs particularly in premature infants and with haemolysis, as in immune hydrops fetalis

    Morphology

    • Brain is enlarged and oedematous, with bright yellow discolouration from bilirubin deposition
    • Most prominent in the basal ganglia, also the thalamus, cerebellum, cerebral grey matter, spinal cord and brainstem

    Clinical features

    • Neural damage usually requires a blood bilirubin above 20 mg/dL in term infants
      The threshold may be considerably lower in premature infants
    • Intense jaundice with signs of neurologic injury

    Treatment

    • Phototherapy converts bilirubin to harmless, water-soluble products that are readily excreted. Total exchange transfusion in severe cases
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 10)p. 420p. 421

    A patient has jaundice, pruritus, bulky pale stool, raised ALP / gallstones with palpable gallbladder. What type of jaundice is this?

    DU25MDU14Ju

    Obstructive (cholestatic) jaundice, due to obstruction of a large bile duct by a stone or a malignant neoplasm.

    • Pruritus and raised alkaline phosphatase are features of cholestasis
    • Pale stools and dark urine occur when bile flow is blocked
    • Malabsorption and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins occur in cholestasis

    Name synthetic liver function tests.

    DU26M
    1. Prothrombin time, which reflects synthesis of the clotting factors (II, V, VII, IX, X, XI, XII and fibrinogen) made by hepatocytes
    2. Serum albumin

    Name two causes of raised prothrombin time.

    DU22MDU17Ja
    1. Liver failure (hepatocellular disease): hepatocytes synthesise clotting factors II, V, VII, IX, X, XI and XII and fibrinogen, so factor deficiency and coagulopathy develop
    2. Vitamin K deficiency, as in cholestasis, where malabsorption causes deficiency of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D and K

    Why is prothrombin time more specific than total protein estimation?

    DU09Ja
    • Prothrombin time tests directly the synthesis of clotting factors by hepatocytes. with liver failure these factors fall and coagulopathy develops
    • Total protein includes globulins, which are raised (hyperglobulinaemia) in chronic hepatitis
    • Albumin is slow to change and nonspecific
      it is also low in poor nutrition, inflammation, and renal or gastrointestinal protein loss

    Viral Hepatitis

    B3

    Name the hepatotrophic viruses. Mention the serological markers of HBV infection.

    The hepatotropic viruses are hepatitis A, B, C, D, and E viruses. The serological markers of hepatitis B virus infection are HBsAg, anti-HBs, HBeAg, anti-HBe, anti-HBc (IgM and IgG), and HBV DNA, and the pattern of their appearance and disappearance defines acute, chronic, resolved, and vaccinated states.

    Hepatotropic viruses

    FeatureHAVHBVHCVHDVHEV
    VirusNonenveloped ssRNA picornavirusPartially double-stranded DNA hepadnavirusEnveloped ssRNA flavivirusDefective circular ssRNA (needs HBsAg)Nonenveloped ssRNA

    Incubation2–6 weeks4–26 weeks4–26 weeks (mean 9)As HBV (superinfection 30–50 days)4–5 weeks

    HCV RNA    		Anti-HDV IgM and IgG

    Nonhepatotropic viruses (Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, adenovirus, yellow fever virus) can also cause hepatitis in association with systemic infection.

    Serological markers of HBV

    MarkerMeaning
    HBsAg (surface antigen)Appears before symptoms and peaks during acute disease
    Its presence indicates active infection (acute or chronic)
    Persistence beyond 6 months defines chronic infection
    Anti-HBsAppears after clearance of HBsAg and signifies recovery and immunity
    Also the only marker after vaccination
    HBeAgAppears soon after HBsAg and signifies active viral replication and high infectivity
    Persistence suggests progression to chronicity
    Anti-HBeSignifies decline of replication and lower infectivity
    Its absence or late appearance in chronic infection
    HBV DNA (and DNA polymerase)Direct marker of viral replication and infectivity
    Used for monitoring therapy
    Anti-HBc IgMEarliest antibody, appearing at onset of symptoms
    Marker of acute infection and the only marker in the "window period," when HBsAg has disappeared and anti-HBs has not yet appeared
    Anti-HBc IgGPersists for life
    Indicates past or chronic infection
    Not protective
    HBcAgNot detectable in serum (found in the hepatocyte nucleus)

    Typical patterns: acute hepatitis (HBsAg, HBeAg, anti-HBc IgM, HBV DNA). Recovery (anti-HBs and anti-HBc IgG, HBsAg negative). Chronic infection (HBsAg persisting with anti-HBc IgG, HBeAg or anti-HBe, HBV DNA). Vaccination (anti-HBs only). The "healthy carrier" has HBsAg and anti-HBe, without HBeAg, with normal transaminases and low or undetectable HBV DNA.

    B3

    Give the possible outcomes of hepatitis B virus infection.

    Hepatitis B infection may end in acute hepatitis with complete recovery, acute liver failure from massive necrosis, chronic hepatitis with or without cirrhosis, or an asymptomatic carrier state, and chronic infection carries a risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.

    1. Acute hepatitis with recovery and viral clearance: the usual outcome in adults (acute infection is subclinical or mild in about two-thirds). HBsAg disappears and anti-HBs appears, conferring immunity.
    2. Acute liver failure (fulminant hepatitis) with massive hepatic necrosis, in about 0.1% to 0.5% of acute infections within 4 to 8 weeks
      The risk is increased by HDV co-infection.
    3. Chronic hepatitis, in 5% to 10% of infected adults, with persistent HBsAg for more than 6 months
      The risk is inversely related to age, being about 90% when infection is transmitted perinatally. It may progress to cirrhosis and its complications.
    4. Asymptomatic (healthy) carrier state: HBsAg positive, with anti-HBe, normal transaminases, low HBV DNA, and little liver injury
      Carriers are a reservoir of infection.
    5. Hepatocellular carcinoma, particularly in those infected perinatally and with chronic infection, even in the absence of cirrhosis.
    6. Superinfection with HDV, causing severe acute hepatitis or exacerbation, and progression to cirrhosis.
    7. Extrahepatic immune-complex disease: glomerulonephritis and polyarteritis nodosa.

    Name the hepatotropic viruses.

    DU26M
    • Hepatitis A virus (single-stranded RNA)
    • Hepatitis B virus (partially double-stranded DNA)
    • Hepatitis C virus (single-stranded RNA)
    • Hepatitis D virus (circular defective single-stranded RNA; needs hepatitis B for replication)
    • Hepatitis E virus (single-stranded RNA)

    Discuss the clinical outcomes of hepatitis B virus infection.

    DU26M

    1. Acute infection with recovery: mild or subclinical in nearly two-thirds of adults. in most cases self-limited and resolves without treatment. anti-HBs appears and persists for life 2. Acute symptomatic hepatitis: anorexia, fever, jaundice, upper right quadrant pain. Immune complex phenomena such as glomerulonephritis and polyarteritis nodosa 3. Acute liver failure: rare, about 0.1% to 0.5% of acutely infected, in 4 to 8 weeks 4. Chronic infection: 5% to 10% of infected individuals. Risk is inversely related to age and about 90% in infants infected at birth - Chronic hepatitis, then cirrhosis - Hepatocellular carcinoma
    Greatest risk in those infected at birth 5. Carrier state: "healthy carrier" has HBsAg and anti-HBe without HBeAg, normal aminotransferases, low or undetectable HBV DNA and no significant liver injury

    Pigmented macrophages scavenge debris    		Interface activity: inflammatory cells cross the limiting plate and injure periportal hepatocytes
    Severe casesConfluent necrosis, panlobular necrosis, bridging necrosis
    Massive necrosis may cause liver failure    		Fibrosis: portal and periportal, then portoportal bridging, then cirrhosis
    Specific featuresNoneHepatitis B: ground-glass hepatocytes (endoplasmic reticulum filled with HBsAg). Hepatitis C: portal lymphoid aggregates or follicles, steatosis, focal bile duct injury
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 18)p. 761

    What alterations occur in liver function tests in acute viral hepatitis / chronic liver disease?

    DU17MDU11Ja

    Acute viral hepatitis - Serum transaminases markedly elevated - Jaundice with raised bilirubin - In liver failure, falling transaminases with worsening jaundice and coagulopathy mean few viable hepatocytes remain

    Chronic hepatitis and chronic liver disease - Persistently elevated transaminases, sometimes the only evidence of chronicity - Prolonged prothrombin time - Hyperglobulinaemia - Hyperbilirubinaemia - Mild elevation of alkaline phosphatase - Decreased serum albumin in impaired synthetic function
    Increased ammonia

    A 30y male with recent blood transfusion has jaundice, weakness. What are the possible fates/outcomes of such a case?

    DU20NDU20JuDU19Nov

    Hepatitis B (parenteral spread, including blood transfusion):

    1. Acute hepatitis followed by recovery and clearance of the virus. Acute infection is mild or subclinical in nearly two-thirds of adults and is self-limited in most cases.
    2. Acute hepatic failure with massive liver necrosis: 0.1% to 0.5% of acutely infected individuals, in 4 to 8 weeks.
    3. Chronic hepatitis, with or without progression to cirrhosis: 5% to 10% of infected individuals. The risk is greatest, about 90%, in infants infected at birth, and these individuals are at greatest risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.
    4. Asymptomatic "healthy" carrier state.

    Hepatitis C (parenteral spread):

    • Acute infection is asymptomatic in about 85% of individuals
    • Chronic hepatitis in 80% to 90% of infected individuals
    • About 20% of these progress to cirrhosis over 20 to 30 years
    • Those who develop cirrhosis are at risk of hepatocellular carcinoma
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 18)p. 756p. 757p. 758

    Same (with anorexia, high SGPT): what is the provisional diagnosis?

    DU19Nov

    Acute viral hepatitis, due to hepatitis B or hepatitis C acquired through the blood transfusion.

    • Both viruses are spread by the parenteral route
    • Anorexia and jaundice are symptoms of acute hepatitis B
    • Serum transaminases (SGPT is alanine aminotransferase) rise in acute infection
    • Hepatitis B is confirmed by HBsAg, which appears before symptoms and peaks in acute disease, and by IgM anti-HBc
    • Hepatitis C is confirmed by HCV RNA, detectable in blood for 1 to 3 weeks in acute infection
      anti-HCV antibodies appear 3 to 6 weeks after infection and can be negative in early infection

    Alcoholic Liver Disease

    Give an outline of the spectrum of liver diseases associated with alcohol abuse.

    DU10Ju

    There are three distinctive, overlapping forms of alcohol-induced liver injury. Injury begins in centrilobular zone 3 and extends outward toward the portal tracts as it becomes more severe.

    FormPathologyClinical features
    Steatosis (fatty change)Lipid droplets accumulate in hepatocytes, small at first and then coalescing
    Mainly macrovesicular. Liver enlarged (4 to 6 kg), soft, yellow and greasy. Completely reversible on abstention    		Hepatomegaly with mild rise of serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase
    Severe dysfunction is unusual
    Alcohol-associated (alcoholic) steatohepatitisBallooned hepatocytes with Mallory hyaline
    Neutrophils around ballooned hepatocytes
    Lobular lymphocytic infiltrate
    Spotty necrosis or apoptosis
    Perivenular and pericellular "chicken wire" fibrosis    		Acute onset after a bout of heavy drinking: malaise, anorexia, weight loss, upper abdominal discomfort, tender hepatomegaly
    Raised bilirubin, aminotransferases (AST higher than ALT by 2:1 or more) and alkaline phosphatase
    Neutrophil leucocytosis. Each episode carries a 10% to 20% risk of death
    Fibrosis leading to cirrhosisProgression from perivenular fibrosis to periportal and bridging fibrosis
    Micronodular cirrhosis (Laennec cirrhosis [micronodular cirrhosis, classically alcoholic], the micronodular cirrhosis of alcohol-associated liver disease) with nodules averaging 3 mm
    Fat no longer seen in the burned-out stage    		Hyperbilirubinaemia, raised aminotransferases, variable alkaline phosphatase, hypoproteinaemia and anaemia
    Cirrhosis develops in about one-third of patients with repeated bouts of hepatitis within a few years
    • Short-term ingestion of about 80 g of alcohol produces mild, reversible steatosis
    • Risk of severe injury becomes significant at 80 g or more of ethanol per day. 160 g or more daily for 10 to 20 years is frequently associated with severe injury
    • Only 10% to 15% of patients with alcohol use disorder develop cirrhosis

    Cirrhosis

    Cirrhosis: types and etiology

    B3

    Define cirrhosis of liver. Mention the types of liver cirrhosis.

    Cirrhosis is a diffuse, irreversible-in-its-established-form process of the liver in which fibrosis and the conversion of normal liver architecture into regenerative parenchymal nodules, surrounded by fibrous bands, is accompanied by vascular remodeling and shunting. It is classified by morphology into micronodular, macronodular, and mixed types, and by aetiology.

    Definition. Cirrhosis is a diffuse remodeling of the entire liver into parenchymal nodules (often regenerative) surrounded by fibrous bands, with a variable degree of vascular (often portosystemic) shunting. It is the end stage of many chronic liver diseases. The three hallmarks are diffuse involvement, bridging fibrous septa, and regenerative nodules, with disruption of the lobular architecture.

    It is not a specific diagnosis, and cirrhosis and liver failure are not synonymous: some cirrhotic patients, such as those whose hepatitis B is suppressed or whose hepatitis C is cured, may never progress to end-stage disease.

    Types

    1. Morphological classification (by nodule size):
      • Micronodular cirrhosis: nodules uniformly less than 3 mm
        Typical of alcohol-associated cirrhosis (Laennec cirrhosis [micronodular cirrhosis, classically alcoholic]), haemochromatosis, biliary obstruction, and hepatic venous outflow obstruction.
      • Macronodular cirrhosis: nodules larger than 3 mm (up to several centimetres), typical of post-necrotic or post-viral hepatitis cirrhosis, Wilson disease [hereditary copper accumulation from ATP7B mutation], and α₁-antitrypsin deficiency.
      • Mixed (micro-macronodular) cirrhosis.
    2. Aetiological classification: alcoholic, post-viral (post-necrotic), biliary (primary and secondary), cardiac (congestive), metabolic and inherited (haemochromatosis, Wilson disease, α₁-antitrypsin deficiency), steatohepatitic (MASH), autoimmune, drug-induced, and cryptogenic (more than 90% of "cryptogenic" cirrhosis is probably burned-out MASH).
    3. Functional classification: compensated and decompensated cirrhosis.
    B3

    Mention the etiology of cirrhosis of liver.

    The leading causes of cirrhosis worldwide are chronic hepatitis B and C, alcohol-associated liver disease, and metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis, with biliary diseases, autoimmune hepatitis, and inherited metabolic disorders as other causes.

    1. Chronic viral hepatitis: hepatitis B (with or without D) and hepatitis C.
    2. Alcohol-associated liver disease (micronodular, Laennec [micronodular cirrhosis, classically alcoholic]).
    3. Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH), the commonest cause in many Western countries, accounting for most "cryptogenic" cirrhosis.
    4. Chronic biliary disease: primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, chronic extrahepatic bile duct obstruction (secondary biliary cirrhosis), biliary atresia, and cystic fibrosis.
    5. Autoimmune hepatitis.
    6. Inherited and metabolic disorders: hereditary haemochromatosis, Wilson disease [hereditary copper accumulation from ATP7B mutation], α₁-antitrypsin deficiency, galactosaemia, tyrosinaemia, glycogen storage diseases.
    7. Vascular causes: chronic hepatic venous outflow obstruction (Budd–Chiari syndrome), chronic right-sided heart failure (cardiac cirrhosis).
    8. Drugs and toxins: methotrexate, amiodarone, isoniazid, and others.
    9. Chronic parasitic disease: schistosomiasis (periportal fibrosis).
    10. Cryptogenic cirrhosis: no cause identified.
    B3

    A 40-year-old male had a history of jaundice, gynecomastia, testicular atrophy and ascites. What is the likely diagnosis? Name the liver function tests that are expected to be altered.

    The likely diagnosis is decompensated cirrhosis of the liver with portal hypertension, most probably alcohol-associated. Gynaecomastia and testicular atrophy reflect hyperoestrogenaemia and hypogonadism from impaired hepatic metabolism of oestrogen, and the liver function tests that are altered are bilirubin, aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, globulins, and prothrombin time.

    Diagnosis. A middle-aged man with jaundice (hepatic failure), gynaecomastia and testicular atrophy (impaired hepatic oestrogen metabolism, leading to hyperoestrogenaemia, and hypogonadism), and ascites (portal hypertension with hypoalbuminaemia) has cirrhosis of the liver in a decompensated stage. Other expected findings are palmar erythema, spider angiomas, loss of body hair, caput medusae, splenomegaly, variceal haemorrhage, and hepatic encephalopathy.

    The commonest cause in such a patient is alcohol, and chronic hepatitis B or C and MASH must be considered. The diagnosis is confirmed by ultrasonography, elastography, endoscopy for varices, and liver biopsy where indicated, and by testing for the cause.

    Liver function tests altered

    • Serum bilirubin raised (mixed hyperbilirubinaemia).
    • AST and ALT mildly to moderately raised (AST > ALT, ratio 2:1 or more in alcoholic cirrhosis).
    • Alkaline phosphatase (and GGT) variably raised.
    • Serum albumin reduced, with raised globulins (reversed A:G ratio).
    • Prothrombin time prolonged (reduced synthesis of clotting factors).
    • Others: raised serum ammonia, anaemia, thrombocytopenia (hypersplenism).

    Define cirrhosis of liver.

    6DU25NDU24NDU22MDU17MDU13JuDU12Ja

    Cirrhosis is a condition marked by diffuse remodelling of the liver into parenchymal nodules (often regenerative) surrounded by fibrous bands and a variable degree of vascular (often portosystemic) shunting.

    Name the etiology of cirrhosis.

    7DU24NDU18MDU16JuDU15JaDU13JuDU10JaDU07Ja
    • Chronic hepatitis B
    • Chronic hepatitis C
    • Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease
    • Alcohol-associated liver disease
    • Metabolic diseases
    • Cryptogenic cirrhosis: cirrhosis arising without any clear cause

    Write the etiopathogenesis of cirrhosis.

    DU25N

    Aetiology: chronic hepatitis B, chronic hepatitis C, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, alcohol-associated liver disease, metabolic diseases. Some cases are cryptogenic.

    Pathogenesis 1. Persistent injury and inflammation activate the hepatic stellate cell, the principal cell of scar deposition
    When quiescent it stores lipid, including vitamin A 2. Stimuli for activation: inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-alpha from Kupffer cells [macrophages lining the hepatic sinusoids] and macrophages. Altered interaction with extracellular matrix
    Toxins and reactive oxygen species 3.

    Activated stellate cells become fibrogenic myofibroblasts, stimulated by platelet-derived growth factor and TGF-beta 4. Extracellular matrix is deposited in the space of Disse [perisinusoidal space of the liver], with loss of sinusoidal endothelial fenestration (sinusoidal capillarisation) 5. Areas of hepatocyte loss are replaced by dense fibrous septa through collapse of the reticulin framework and collagen deposition by myofibroblasts 6.

    Septa encircle surviving hepatocytes, which replicate and form regenerative nodules - If the injury stops (viral clearance, abstinence from alcohol), scarring stops and septa are broken down by metalloproteinases. Vascular remodelling may persist, so portal hypertension may not resolve

    What are the complications of cirrhosis?

    DU25NDU24NDU12Ja
    1. Portal hypertension, with its four major consequences: ascites, portosystemic venous shunts (oesophagogastric varices, haemorrhoids, caput medusae), congestive splenomegaly with hypersplenism, hepatic encephalopathy
    2. Hepatic encephalopathy
    3. Coagulopathy and jaundice
    4. Hepatorenal syndrome
    5. Hepatopulmonary syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension
    6. Bacterial infections (damage to the gut mucosal barrier and Kupffer cell [macrophages lining the hepatic sinusoids] dysfunction)
    7. Hepatocellular carcinoma
    8. Pruritus from persistent cholestasis
    9. Hyperoestrogenaemia: palmar erythema, spider angiomas
      in males hypogonadism and gynaecomastia

    How is ascites formed in cirrhosis of liver?

    5DU22MDU18MDU16JuDU12JaDU09Ja
    • Ascites is accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity. in 85% of cases it is caused by cirrhosis
    • Pathogenesis is complex:
    • Sinusoidal hypertension
    • Hypoalbuminaemia
    • Increased hepatic lymph flow
    • Splanchnic vasodilation and hyperdynamic circulation
    • Fluid is generally serous, with less than 3 g/dL of protein (largely albumin)
      Clinically detectable when at least 500 mL has accumulated
    • Neutrophils in the fluid suggest infection
      Red cells point to possible disseminated intra-abdominal cancer
    • Long-standing ascites may produce right-sided hydrothorax through transdiaphragmatic lymphatics

    Write the mechanism of cirrhotic death.

    DU10Ja

    The common causes of death in cirrhosis are: 1. Hepatic encephalopathy 2. Bleeding from oesophageal varices: varices appear in about 40% of individuals with advanced cirrhosis and cause massive haematemesis and death in about half of those affected 3. Bacterial infections, resulting from damage to the gut mucosal barrier and Kupffer cell [macrophages lining the hepatic sinusoids] dysfunction 4. Hepatocellular carcinoma - Also: hepatorenal syndrome, coagulopathy

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 18)p. 754p. 771

    A male has jaundice, gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy/abdominal distension, ascites. What is the likely diagnosis?

    DU15JaDU12Ja
    • Cirrhosis of the liver (chronic liver failure) with portal hypertension
    • Jaundice and ascites reflect liver failure and portal hypertension
    • Impaired oestrogen metabolism leads to hyperoestrogenaemia, which in males produces hypogonadism (testicular atrophy) and gynaecomastia. Also palmar erythema and spider angiomas

    Same (40y): name the liver function tests expected to be altered.

    DU12Ja
    TestExpected change
    Serum bilirubin, total and direct
    Urine bilirubin    		Increased
    Serum alkaline phosphatase, GGTIncreased
    AST, ALT, LDHIncreased
    Serum albuminDecreased

    Hepatic encephalopathy

    What is hepatic encephalopathy?

    DU18MDU16Ju
    • A spectrum of disturbances in consciousness, ranging from subtle behavioural abnormalities, to marked confusion and stupor, to deep coma and death
    • Fluctuating neurological signs: rigidity, hyperreflexia, asterixis (nonrhythmic, rapid extension and flexion movements of head and extremities, best seen with arms extended and wrists dorsiflexed)
    • Believed to be caused by elevated ammonia, which correlates with impaired neuronal function and cerebral oedema
    • Principal source of ammonia: the gastrointestinal tract, produced by microorganisms and enterocytes during glutamine metabolism
    • Normally ammonia is carried in the portal vein to the liver and metabolised in the urea cycle
      in severe liver disease this fails
    • Neurotoxicity: direct effects on neurons, and conversion to glutamine in astrocytes, which acts as an osmolyte and contributes to oedema
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 18)p. 752

    Portal Hypertension

    B3

    Define ascites. What are the causes of ascites?

    Ascites is the accumulation of excess fluid in the peritoneal cavity. It is a transudate in most hepatic and cardiac causes and an exudate in infective or malignant causes, and the commonest cause overall is cirrhosis of the liver with portal hypertension.

    Definition. Ascites is the pathological accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity, clinically detectable when at least about 500 mL has accumulated (shifting dullness, fluid thrill). In 85% of cases it is caused by cirrhosis. Cirrhotic ascites is serous with a low protein content (less than 3 g/dL) and a serum–ascites albumin gradient of 1.1 g/dL or more
    The fluid may contain scant mesothelial cells and mononuclear cells, neutrophils suggest infection, and red cells suggest disseminated intra-abdominal cancer.

    Causes

    MechanismCauses
    Portal hypertension (high SAAG, transudate)Cirrhosis
    alcohol-associated hepatitis
    Budd–Chiari syndrome
    Portal vein thrombosis
    Schistosomiasis
    right-sided heart failure and constrictive pericarditis
    Hypoalbuminaemia (low SAAG, transudate)Nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy, severe malnutrition
    Exudative (peritoneal disease)Tuberculous peritonitis, secondary bacterial peritonitis, peritoneal carcinomatosis and mesothelioma, pseudomyxoma peritonei, pancreatitis
    OthersMyxoedema, Meigs syndrome and ovarian tumours, chylous ascites (lymphatic obstruction), and bile ascites

    The pathogenesis in cirrhosis is by sinusoidal hypertension, hypoalbuminaemia, increased hepatic lymph flow, and splanchnic vasodilation with renal sodium and water retention.

    Enumerate the important causes of ascites.

    DU21M
    • Cirrhosis of the liver: 85% of cases
    • Other portal hypertension: prehepatic (portal vein thrombosis), intrahepatic (schistosomiasis, massive fatty change, sarcoidosis), posthepatic (right-sided heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, hepatic vein outflow obstruction)
    • Congestive heart failure
    • Hypoalbuminaemia (for example nephrotic syndrome)
    • Disseminated intra-abdominal cancer
    • Infection of the peritoneal fluid
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 18)p. 754

    Tumours of the Liver

    Write down the etiology of hepatocellular carcinoma.

    DU07Ja

    Most hepatocellular carcinomas occur in chronic liver disease with cirrhosis
    15% to 20% arise in noncirrhotic livers. Chronic injury, inflammation and hepatocyte regeneration lead to driver mutations.

    • Chronic viral hepatitis B and C
      More than 85% of cases occur in Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, where chronic hepatitis B infection is common, with peak incidence in young adults who acquired the virus by maternal-foetal transmission
    • Metabolic diseases: hereditary haemochromatosis and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
    • Alcohol-associated liver disease
    • MASLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease), which raises the risk even without cirrhosis
    • Aflatoxin, a mycotoxin of Aspergillus species that contaminates crops. it acts synergistically with alcohol and hepatitis B
    • Cirrhosis from Wilson disease [hereditary copper accumulation from ATP7B mutation] and chronic biliary diseases, where the risk is lower but still above the population average
    • Hepatocellular adenoma, especially with beta-catenin activating mutations, in noncirrhotic liver
    • Dysplastic nodules in cirrhotic liver
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 18)p. 766p. 790

    A 59y male with HBV history has hepatomegaly, SOL in right lobe on USG. How will you proceed to diagnose?

    DU08Ju

    A space-occupying lesion in a man with chronic hepatitis B is hepatocellular carcinoma until proved otherwise.

    1. Clinical assessment for features of underlying chronic liver disease
    2. Serum alpha-fetoprotein: a frequent finding in advanced disease, but not sensitive as a screening test for early tumours and not seen in the fibrolamellar variant
    3. Ultrasonography, used to screen high-risk patients such as those with cirrhosis
    4. Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI: early enhancement of the tumour in the arterial phase, followed by rapid venous washout. These findings are highly characteristic of hepatocellular carcinoma
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 18)p. 781p. 791

    Same: what are your expected findings?

    DU08Ju

    Clinical

    • Abdominal pain, malaise, fatigue, weight loss and hepatomegaly
    • Features of underlying chronic liver disease

    Investigations

    • Raised serum alpha-fetoprotein in advanced disease
    • CT or MRI: early arterial enhancement followed by rapid venous washout

    Morphology

    • Single mass, multiple discrete masses, or diffuse infiltration of the liver, usually in a cirrhotic liver
    • Masses may be pale yellow from fatty change or green from cholestasis
    • Tumours larger than 2 cm are more likely to show vascular invasion and intrahepatic metastases. Veins may be invaded, with extension into the portal vein, inferior vena cava and right side of the heart
    • Cells resemble normal hepatocytes in well and moderately differentiated tumours, growing in thick plates or trabeculae, pseudoglandular structures with bile plugs, or sheets
    • Haematogenous metastases, especially to the lung, occur late. Lymph node metastases occur in less than 5% of cases
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 18)p. 791

    Gallbladder

    Gallstones

    B3

    Mention the etiology, classification and complications of gallstones.

    Gallstones (cholelithiasis) are of two main types, cholesterol stones and pigment stones, formed when bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol or unconjugated bilirubin with gallbladder stasis. Their complications include acute and chronic cholecystitis, obstruction with jaundice and cholangitis, pancreatitis, gallstone ileus, and carcinoma of the gallbladder.

    Classification

    FeatureCholesterol stonesPigment stones
    CompositionMore than 50% crystalline cholesterol monohydrateCalcium salts of unconjugated bilirubin with calcium carbonate and phosphate
    FrequencyAbout 90% in the United States and western EuropeCommon in Asia, haemolytic states
    TypesPure cholesterol stones (pale yellow, round or ovoid, with finely granular surface, radiating crystalline cut surface; solitary or several), and mixed stones (grey-white to black, lamellated, multiple, faceted)Black: small (under 1.5 cm), numerous, friable, spiculated, in sterile gallbladder bile, 50% to 75% radiopaque
    Brown: laminated, soft, greasy, in infected bile ducts, radiolucent
    RadiologyMostly radiolucent (10% to 20% radiopaque)Black often radiopaque

    Mucin glycoproteins form the scaffolding of all stones.

    Aetiology and risk factors

    • Cholesterol stones: age (middle to older), female sex and oestrogen (pregnancy, oral contraceptives), obesity and the metabolic syndrome, rapid weight loss, northern European and Native American ethnicity, ileal disease or resection (Crohn disease [transmural granulomatous inflammatory bowel disease], cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency), gallbladder stasis, hereditary factors (ABCG8 variants), and hypertriglyceridaemia.
    • Pigment stones: chronic haemolysis (sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis, thalassaemia), biliary infection with Escherichia coli, Ascaris lumbricoides, or Clonorchis sinensis liver flukes (β-glucuronidases deconjugate bilirubin), ileal dysfunction or bypass, and cirrhosis.

    Complications. About 70% to 80% of patients remain asymptomatic. Complications are biliary colic. Acute and chronic cholecystitis
    Empyema, gangrene, and perforation of the gallbladder. Obstruction of the cystic or common bile duct with obstructive jaundice and mucocele or hydrops. Ascending cholangitis
    Acute pancreatitis
    Cholecystoenteric fistula with gallstone ileus (Bouveret syndrome)
    and carcinoma of the gallbladder (gallstones are present in 95% of cases, although only 1% to 2% of patients with gallstones develop cancer)
    Porcelain gallbladder and xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis are other sequelae. The smallest stones ("gravel") are most dangerous because they enter the ducts.

    What are the factors that favour stone formation within gallbladder?

    DU09Ja

    Cholesterol stones. Four conditions contribute:

    1. Supersaturation of bile with cholesterol, so that cholesterol nucleates into crystals
    2. Hypomotility of the gallbladder
    3. Accelerated cholesterol crystal nucleation
    4. Hypersecretion of mucus in the gallbladder, which traps the crystals

    Risk factors:

    • Age and sex: prevalence rises through life and is higher in females. Hypersecretion of biliary cholesterol plays the major role. Metabolic syndrome and obesity are associated
    • Oestrogen (oral contraceptives, pregnancy): increases hepatic lipoprotein receptors and HMG-CoA reductase activity, so biliary cholesterol secretion is increased
    • Obesity and rapid weight loss, which increase biliary cholesterol secretion
    • Gallbladder stasis, neurogenic or hormonal
    • Hereditary: ABC transporter genes, particularly a common variant of the sterol transporter gene ABCG8

    Pigment stones. Raised unconjugated bilirubin in bile favours stones:

    • Chronic haemolytic anaemia
    • Severe ileal dysfunction or bypass
    • Bacterial contamination of the biliary tree (Escherichia coli, Ascaris lumbricoides, liver fluke Clonorchis sinensis): microbial beta-glucuronidases hydrolyse bilirubin glucuronides
    • Gallbladder stasis
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 18)p. 794p. 795

    Carcinoma of the gallbladder

    B3

    What type of carcinoma occurs in the gallbladder?

    The overwhelming majority of gallbladder carcinomas are adenocarcinomas, usually arising in the fundus on a background of chronic cholecystitis with gallstones.

    Carcinoma of the gallbladder is the commonest malignancy of the extrahepatic biliary tract. The tumours are mainly adenocarcinomas, growing either as a firm, poorly circumscribed mass or as a diffuse infiltration of the gallbladder wall that simulates chronic cholecystitis. They are most often found in the fundus. Microscopically they consist of glands (of intestinal, biliary, or papillary pattern, and occasionally mucinous or signet-ring) in a desmoplastic stroma. in some, cytologic atypia and stromal response are minimal and perineural and vascular invasion help to establish the diagnosis. Rarely, other primary tumours occur, such as neuroendocrine tumours, squamous cell carcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and sarcomas.

    The precursor lesions are flat dysplasia (carcinoma in situ), intracholecystic papillary-tubular neoplasms, and intestinal metaplasia. Gallstones are present in 95% of cases, with chronic inflammation the common thread. Other risk factors are female sex (at least twice as common), porcelain gallbladder and hyalinising cholecystitis, chronic Salmonella typhi carriage, anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction, and, in high-incidence areas (Chile, Bolivia, northern India, and Native American populations), ethnicity. Molecular changes include TP53 mutations and alterations of the EGFR family (HER2) and RAS.

    The tumour is diagnosed late (preoperative diagnosis in under 20%), spreading by direct extension into the liver and adjacent organs, along the peritoneum and biliary tree, and by metastasis to the liver and portahepatic nodes. The 5-year survival is less than 10%, but incidental carcinoma found early at cholecystectomy can be cured by resection.

    Glomerular Diseases

    Classification of glomerular diseases

    Classify glomerular disease.

    Name the primary glomerular diseases.

    DU19NovDU11Ju
    1. Postinfectious glomerulonephritis
    2. Crescentic (rapidly progressive) glomerulonephritis
    3. Membranous nephropathy
    4. Minimal change disease
    5. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
