    Nephrotic syndrome

    What is nephrotic syndrome?

    4DU26MDU17JaDU12JuDU08Ja

    Nephrotic syndrome, typically caused by severe dysfunction of the glomerular filter, is characterised by heavy proteinuria (more than 3.5 g/day), resulting in hypoalbuminaemia and severe oedema, and hyperlipidaemia and lipiduria (lipids in the urine).

    What are the causes of nephrotic syndrome?

    DU17MDU12Ju

    Nephrotic syndrome is caused by a derangement of the glomerular capillary wall, with increased permeability to plasma proteins. The causes vary with age and geography: in children it is almost always a lesion primary to the kidney, whereas in adults it is often associated with a systemic disease.

    1. Primary glomerular lesions - Minimal change disease, the most common in children in North America - Membranous nephropathy, the most common in older adults - Primary (idiopathic) focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, at all ages 2. Systemic causes, the most frequent being diabetes, amyloidosis and SLE 3. Less common: proliferative glomerulonephritides such as membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and IgA nephropathy 4. Secondary membranous nephropathy: drugs (penicillamine, captopril, gold, NSAIDs) and other systemic diseases. About 75% of membranous nephropathy is primary

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 20)p. 827p. 828p. 833

    Write a short note on nephrotic syndrome.

    DU24NDU15Ja

    Definition. Heavy proteinuria (3.5 g or more per day, less in children), hypoalbuminaemia (plasma albumin below 3 g/dL), generalised oedema, and hyperlipidaemia with lipiduria.

    Aetiology. Minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Systemic causes (diabetes, amyloidosis, SLE).

    Pathogenesis

    1. Increased permeability of the glomerular capillary wall (endothelium, basement membrane and podocytes act as a size and charge barrier) lets proteins escape, causing proteinuria
    2. Heavy proteinuria depletes serum albumin faster than the liver can compensate, and increased renal catabolism of albumin also contributes, causing hypoalbuminaemia
    3. Low plasma albumin lowers intravascular colloid osmotic pressure, causing generalised oedema
      Sodium and water retention aggravates it (aldosterone secretion from renin release, sympathetic stimulation, reduced natriuretic factors)
    4. Hyperlipidaemia follows from increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis, abnormal transport of lipid particles and decreased lipid catabolism. Lipoproteins leak into the urine as free fat or oval fat bodies (lipiduria)

    Clinical features

    • Oedema is soft and pitting, most marked in the periorbital regions and dependent parts. Pleural effusions and ascites if severe
    • Selectivity of proteinuria: highly selective proteinuria is mostly albumin and transferrin, poorly selective proteinuria includes higher-molecular-weight globulins

    Complications

    • Infection, especially staphylococcal and pneumococcal, probably from loss of immunoglobulins in the urine
    • Thrombosis and thromboembolism, partly from loss of antithrombin III in the urine. Renal vein thrombosis is most often a consequence of this hypercoagulable state
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 20)p. 827p. 828p. 830

    What are the urinary/biochemical findings of nephrotic syndrome?

    7DU26MDU18MDU16JuDU14JuDU12JaDU10JuDU06Ja
    • Massive proteinuria: 3.5 g or more per day (less in children)
      The largest proportion is albumin. Highly selective proteinuria is mostly low-molecular-weight proteins (albumin, transferrin). Poorly selective proteinuria also contains higher-molecular-weight globulins
    • Hypoalbuminaemia: plasma albumin below 3 g/dL
    • Hyperlipidaemia: raised cholesterol, triglyceride, very-low-density lipoprotein, low-density lipoprotein, lipoprotein(a) and apoprotein. high-density lipoprotein is decreased in some patients
    • Lipiduria: lipid in the urine as free fat or as oval fat bodies
    • Loss of immunoglobulins and antithrombin III in the urine
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 20)p. 827p. 828

    How will you investigate/diagnose a case of nephrotic syndrome?

    DU04JaDU03Ja

    1. Urine: proteinuria of 3.5 g or more per day
    Selectivity of the proteinuria
    Lipiduria (free fat, oval fat bodies) 2. Blood: plasma albumin below 3 g/dL
    Serum lipids 3. Exclude secondary causes: diabetes, amyloidosis and SLE are the most frequent systemic causes
    Also underlying malignant tumour, infection (hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis) and drugs, because treating the cause can reverse the injury 4. Renal biopsy with light microscopy, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy to identify the lesion: - Minimal change disease: normal glomeruli on light microscopy. Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy, without deposits - Membranous nephropathy: diffuse thickening of the capillary wall. Granular IgG and C3 on immunofluorescence
    Subepithelial deposits on electron microscopy - Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis: sclerosis of part of the capillary tuft in a subset of glomeruli

    Write the laboratory investigations to differentiate AGN from nephrotic syndrome.

    DU17M
    FeatureAcute glomerulonephritis (nephritic)Nephrotic syndrome
    ProteinuriaSubnephrotic, usually less than 1 g/dayMassive, 3.5 g or more per day
    Urine sedimentDysmorphic red cells and red cell castsLipiduria: free fat and oval fat bodies
    BloodRaised BUN and serum creatinine (azotaemia)Plasma albumin below 3 g/dL
    Raised cholesterol and triglyceride
    • In acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, antistreptococcal antibody titres are raised and the serum concentration of C3 and other complement components is low

    Nephritic syndromes and glomerulonephritis

    What is nephritic syndrome (AGN)?

    6DU26NDU22MDU20NDU20JuDU09JaDU08Ja

    Nephritic syndrome is a clinical entity caused by inflammatory glomerular disease and dominated by the acute onset of grossly visible or microscopic haematuria, diminished GFR, mild to moderate proteinuria and hypertension. It is the classic presentation of acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 20)p. 814

    Write down the pathogenesis of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

    8DU25NDU22MDU20NDU20JuDU19NDU17JaDU12JaDU09Ja

    1. Caused by immune complexes containing streptococcal antigens and specific antibodies 2. Only certain strains of group A beta-haemolytic streptococci are nephritogenic
    More than 90% of cases are traced to types 1, 4 and 12, identified by typing of the M protein of the cell wall 3. Streptococcal pyogenic exotoxin B (SpeB) is the principal antigen in most cases and is localised to the "humplike" deposits 4. The inciting antigens are first planted from the circulation in subendothelial locations of the glomerular capillary wall, leading to in situ formation of immune complexes that elicit an inflammatory response 5. The complexes then dissociate, migrate across the GBM, and reform on the subepithelial side
    Deposition of circulating immune complexes may also contribute 6. Leucocyte infiltration and proliferation of glomerular cells injure the capillary walls, allowing blood into the urine. The fall in GFR causes oliguria, fluid retention and azotaemia 7. Evidence for an immunologic basis: - The latent period between infection and nephritis is compatible with the time needed to form antibodies and immune complexes - Antistreptococcal antibody titres are raised in the great majority of patients - Serum complement is low, from activation and consumption - Granular immune deposits are present in the glomeruli

    What are the urinary findings of acute glomerulonephritis?

    19DU25NDU25MDU23NDU22MDU20NDU20JuDU19NovDU18MDU18NovDU17NovDU16JaDU16JuDU14JaDU14JuDU12JaDU11JuDU10JaDU10JuDU06Ja
    • Haematuria: smoky or cola-coloured urine
      Dysmorphic red cells or red cell casts
    • Mild proteinuria, usually less than 1 g/day
    • Oliguria

    Mention the complications of acute glomerulonephritis.

    DU11Ju
    • Acute: oliguria, fluid retention, azotaemia, hypertension
    • Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, in a small minority of children (perhaps less than 1%) who do not improve and become severely oliguric
    • Chronic glomerulonephritis, with or without recurrence of an active nephritic picture, in some of the remaining patients
    • Prolonged and persistent heavy proteinuria and abnormal GFR mark an unfavourable prognosis
    • Adults: only about 60% of sporadic cases recover promptly
      in the rest there is persistent proteinuria, haematuria and hypertension, with progression to chronic glomerulonephritis or rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis in some
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 20)p. 823p. 825

    A child has oliguria, cocoa-coloured urine, periorbital puffiness after sore throat/skin infection. What is the probable diagnosis?

    6DU25MDU23NDU18NovDU17NovDU14JaDU10Ja

    Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (nephritic syndrome).

    • It usually appears 1 to 4 weeks after a streptococcal infection of the pharynx or skin (impetigo), most often in children 6 to 10 years of age
    • The typical child abruptly develops malaise, fever, nausea, oliguria and haematuria (smoky or cola-coloured urine) 1 to 2 weeks after a sore throat
    • Periorbital oedema, mild to moderate hypertension, dysmorphic red cells or red cell casts and mild proteinuria are found
    • Raised antistreptococcal antibody titres and a low serum C3 support the diagnosis
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 20)p. 814p. 823p. 825

    Nephritic and nephrotic syndromes

    B4

    What is nephritic syndrome? Tell 3 microscopic differences between nephritic syndrome and nephrotic syndrome. How can you differentiate between them by serum complement level?

    Nephritic syndrome is a clinical syndrome of glomerular inflammation, characterised by haematuria with red cell casts, oliguria with azotaemia, mild to moderate proteinuria and hypertension, whereas nephrotic syndrome is due to increased glomerular permeability and is characterised by massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia. Microscopically, nephritic syndrome shows red cells and red cell casts in the urine and hypercellular, inflamed glomeruli, while nephrotic syndrome shows oval fat bodies and fatty casts in the urine and normal or only thickened glomeruli with podocyte foot process effacement. Serum complement is usually low in nephritic syndrome of the postinfectious type and normal in the common causes of nephrotic syndrome.

    Complete explanation

    Nephritic syndrome results from proliferative, inflammatory glomerular disease. The cellular proliferation and leucocyte infiltration injure the capillary wall, allowing blood into the urine, and reduce GFR, leading to oliguria, azotaemia, fluid retention and hypertension. The classic example is acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Others are rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy and proliferative lupus nephritis.

    Nephrotic syndrome results from a derangement of the glomerular filter, structural or charge-related, that permits plasma proteins to leak. There is typically little inflammation.

    Microscopic differences

    FeatureNephritic syndromeNephrotic syndrome
    Urine microscopyDysmorphic red cells and red cell castsOval fat bodies, fatty and waxy casts
    Few or no red cells
    Glomerulus by light microscopyEnlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with leucocytic infiltration and endocapillary proliferation (crescents in RPGN)Normal (minimal change disease), diffusely thickened capillary walls (membranous), or focal segmental sclerosis
    Electron microscopy / immunofluorescenceSubepithelial humps and granular IgG and C3 (postinfectious GN)Diffuse foot process effacement without deposits (minimal change)
    Subepithelial deposits (membranous)

    Differentiation by serum complement. In acute postinfectious glomerulonephritis the serum C3 is low (with normal C4) because the alternative pathway is activated and complement consumed, and it returns to normal in about 2 months. Low complement is also found in membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, C3 glomerulopathy and lupus nephritis. In minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy and FSGS — the common causes of nephrotic syndrome — complement levels are normal. IgA nephropathy, a cause of nephritic presentations, also has normal complement.

    B4

    What is glomerulonephritis? Mention five primary glomerular diseases.

    Glomerulonephritis is a group of diseases, mostly immunologically mediated, in which the glomeruli are the primary site of injury, usually with proliferation of glomerular cells and an inflammatory reaction. The five main primary glomerular diseases are acute postinfectious glomerulonephritis, rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, membranous nephropathy, minimal change disease and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and IgA nephropathy complete the list.

    Complete explanation

    Glomerulonephritis denotes inflammatory disease of the glomerulus, most often caused by immunologic mechanisms: deposition or in situ formation of immune complexes, antibodies directed against the glomerular basement membrane, or cell-mediated immunity. Because some of the glomerular diseases have no cellular inflammatory component (minimal change disease and membranous nephropathy, for example), the term glomerulopathy is used for them.

    Diseases in which the kidney is the sole or predominant organ affected are called primary
    Those that are a manifestation of systemic disease, such as lupus, diabetes, amyloidosis or vasculitis, are secondary.

    The primary glomerular diseases are:

    1. Acute postinfectious (poststreptococcal) glomerulonephritis — nephritic syndrome
    2. Rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis — nephritic syndrome with rapid loss of function
    3. Membranous nephropathy — nephrotic syndrome
    4. Minimal change disease — nephrotic syndrome, the commonest cause in children
    5. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis — nephrotic syndrome and progressive disease
    6. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and C3 glomerulopathies — mixed nephritic–nephrotic picture
    7. IgA nephropathy — recurrent haematuria, the commonest glomerulonephritis worldwide
    B4

    What is nephritic syndrome? What are the complications that may arise from nephritic syndrome?

    Nephritic syndrome is the clinical presentation of inflammatory glomerular disease, with haematuria and red cell casts, oliguria and azotaemia, mild to moderate proteinuria and hypertension. Its complications include acute kidney injury with hyperkalaemia and uraemia, hypertensive encephalopathy, acute left ventricular failure with pulmonary oedema, progression to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and eventually chronic kidney disease.

    Complete explanation

    The syndrome arises when proliferative inflammation of the glomeruli injures the capillary walls and reduces the glomerular filtration rate. Because of reduced filtration, salt and water are retained and nitrogenous waste accumulates. Hypertension arises from the volume expansion and from renin release by the ischaemic kidneys.

    Complications in the acute phase follow directly from these disturbances:

    • Acute kidney injury with oliguria or anuria, azotaemia and uraemia, accompanied by hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis, which may be life threatening.
    • Hypertensive encephalopathy, with headache, vomiting, visual disturbance and convulsions.
    • Circulatory overload, with acute left ventricular failure and pulmonary oedema.
    • Heavy proteinuria, occasionally reaching nephrotic range.

    Complications in the later course

    • Rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, with extensive crescent formation and rapid loss of renal function over weeks. This is the most serious sequel and may follow postinfectious glomerulonephritis in a small minority of children and more often in adults.
    • Chronic glomerulonephritis and chronic kidney disease, which may end in end-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis or transplantation. Persistent proteinuria and an abnormal GFR mark patients with an unfavourable prognosis.

    Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

    B4

    Tell the pathogenesis of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. What is AGN? Mention the role of streptococcal infection in the pathogenesis of AGN.

    Acute glomerulonephritis is an acute nephritic syndrome caused by inflammatory proliferation of glomerular cells, of which acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is the prototype. It is an immune complex disease: after a pharyngeal or skin infection with a nephritogenic group A β-haemolytic streptococcus, streptococcal antigen, notably pyogenic exotoxin B, and its antibody form immune complexes in the glomerular capillary wall, activate complement, attract neutrophils and monocytes, and cause proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells, reducing the glomerular filtration rate.

    Complete explanation

    Definition. Acute glomerulonephritis (AGN) is a clinical syndrome of acute onset with haematuria, oliguria, azotaemia, mild proteinuria, hypertension and periorbital oedema, caused by diffuse proliferative inflammation of the glomeruli. In its classic form it appears 1 to 4 weeks after a streptococcal infection, mainly in children aged 6 to 10 years.

    Role of streptococcal infection in pathogenesis

    1. Nephritogenic strains. Only particular strains of group A β-haemolytic streptococci cause nephritis. Over 90% of cases are linked to M types 1, 4 and 12, which are typed by their cell wall M protein.
    2. Antigen–antibody complexes. Streptococcal antigen, most importantly streptococcal pyogenic exotoxin B, is first planted in subendothelial sites in the capillary wall, where it forms immune complexes in situ with antibody. The complexes then dissociate, cross the basement membrane and re-form on the subepithelial side, appearing as humps. Circulating complexes may contribute.
    3. Latent period. The interval of 1 to 4 weeks matches the time required for antibody production and immune complex formation.
    4. Complement activation and inflammation. The complexes activate complement
      C5a and other mediators attract neutrophils and monocytes, and endothelial and mesangial cells proliferate, producing hypercellular glomeruli that obliterate the capillary lumens.
    5. Functional result. GFR falls, causing oliguria, azotaemia, fluid retention, oedema and hypertension. Damage to the capillary wall allows haematuria and mild proteinuria.

    Evidence of an immunological basis. The latent period, elevated antistreptococcal antibody titers, low serum C3 from complement consumption, and granular immunofluorescent deposits of IgG and C3 in the glomeruli, with subepithelial humps on electron microscopy, all point to an immune complex mechanism.

    B10

    A 7-year-old boy developed periorbital edema with high-colored scanty urination, following a history of a sore two weeks earlier. What is your clinical diagnosis? What do you expect in the microscopic findings of his urine?

    The clinical diagnosis is acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis presenting as acute nephritic syndrome. The urine is expected to show red blood cells, many of them dysmorphic, together with red cell casts, along with mild proteinuria, white cells, and granular and hyaline casts.

    Complete explanation

    The age of the child, the periorbital oedema, the high-coloured (smoky) scanty urine and the history of a sore throat about two weeks earlier fit acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. The latent period corresponds to the time needed for antibodies to form against nephritogenic streptococcal antigens and for immune complexes to deposit in the glomeruli, causing inflammation. Oliguria and oedema reflect the reduced glomerular filtration rate and salt and water retention, and the coloured urine reflects haematuria.

    Expected microscopic urine findings

    • Numerous red cells, many dysmorphic (acanthocytes), reflecting passage through damaged glomerular capillaries.
    • Red cell casts, indicating glomerular origin of the bleeding.
    • Granular and hyaline casts, a few white cells and tubular epithelial cells.
    • Mild to moderate proteinuria (usually less than 1 g/day) on chemical testing.

    Supporting tests are a raised antistreptolysin O titer, a low serum C3, and a raised serum urea and creatinine.

    Tubulointerstitial Diseases

    B4

    What is pyelonephritis? What are the predisposing factors for its development?

    Pyelonephritis is inflammation of the kidney caused by infection, affecting the tubules, interstitium and renal pelvis, most often due to ascending bacterial infection from the lower urinary tract. It is predisposed to by urinary tract obstruction and stasis, vesicoureteral reflux, instrumentation or catheterisation, pregnancy, female sex, diabetes mellitus, preexisting renal lesions, and immunosuppression.

    Complete explanation

    Pyelonephritis is one of the commonest diseases of the kidney. Acute pyelonephritis is a suppurative inflammation, usually bacterial, associated with urinary tract infection. Chronic pyelonephritis is chronic tubulointerstitial inflammation and scarring involving the calyces and pelvis, which results from recurrent episodes of infection in the presence of predisposing factors such as reflux and obstruction.

    More than 85% of infections are caused by enteric gram-negative bacilli, above all Escherichia coli, followed by Proteus, Klebsiella and Enterobacter. The kidney is reached either by the ascending route from the bladder (the commoner route) or by the bloodstream (as in infective endocarditis or in debilitated or obstructed patients).

    Predisposing factors

    • Urinary tract obstruction and stasis, whether congenital or acquired (stones, benign prostatic hyperplasia, tumours, neurogenic bladder), because residual urine allows bacteria to multiply unhindered.
    • Vesicoureteral reflux and intrarenal reflux, which carry infected bladder urine into the renal pelvis and parenchyma.
    • Instrumentation of the urinary tract, particularly catheterisation, and cystoscopy.
    • Pregnancy, in which 4% to 6% of women develop bacteriuria and 20% to 40% of these develop symptomatic infection if untreated.
    • Sex and age: infections are much more frequent in females up to about 40 years of age
      in older males the incidence rises because of prostatic enlargement and instrumentation. Congenital anomalies are important in infant boys.
    • Diabetes mellitus, through increased susceptibility to infection, neurogenic bladder and frequent instrumentation.
    • Immunosuppression and immunodeficiency, and preexisting renal lesions with scarring and obstruction.
    B4

    What is UTI? Who are commonly affected and why?

    Urinary tract infection is infection of any part of the urinary tract by microorganisms, usually bacteria, shown by significant bacteriuria and pyuria. it may involve the bladder (cystitis) or the kidney (pyelonephritis). It is most common in females, because of the short urethra and other anatomical and hormonal factors, and also in infants with congenital anomalies, elderly men with prostatic enlargement, pregnant women, diabetics, and patients with obstruction, stones, catheters or immunosuppression.

    Complete explanation

    Urinary tract infection (UTI) is characterised by bacteriuria and pyuria, the presence of bacteria and leucocytes in the urine. It may be symptomatic or asymptomatic and may involve the lower tract (urethritis, cystitis, prostatitis) or the upper tract (pyelonephritis). By convention a count of 10⁵ or more organisms per mL in a properly collected midstream sample is taken as significant. Over 85% of infections are caused by enteric gram-negative bacilli, most commonly E. coli.

    Who is commonly affected, and why

    • Females. After the first year of life and up to about 40 years of age, infection is much commoner in women. The reasons are the shorter female urethra, the close proximity of the urethral meatus to the anus and vagina, the absence of the antibacterial properties of prostatic fluid, hormonal changes that affect bacterial adherence to the mucosa, and urethral trauma during sexual intercourse.
    • Pregnant women, because of ureteric dilatation and stasis, with a risk of progression of asymptomatic bacteriuria to pyelonephritis.
    • Infants and young boys with congenital anomalies, such as obstruction or vesicoureteral reflux.
    • Older men, in whom prostatic hypertrophy causes obstruction and incomplete emptying, and in whom instrumentation is frequent.
    • Diabetics, who have increased susceptibility to infection and neurogenic bladder dysfunction.
    • Patients with obstruction, stones, neurogenic bladder, catheters or instrumentation, and those who are immunosuppressed.
    B10

    A 25-year-old female presented with complaints of dysuria, dribbling of micturition and fever for 5 days. What is your probable diagnosis? How will you investigate the case?

    The probable diagnosis is acute urinary tract infection, most likely acute cystitis with ascending involvement of the kidney, that is acute pyelonephritis, since fever accompanies the dysuria. It is investigated by urine routine examination and microscopy, midstream urine culture and sensitivity, a complete blood count, serum creatinine, and imaging of the urinary tract.

    Complete explanation

    Dysuria and difficulty with micturition indicate irritation of the bladder and urethra (cystitis and urethritis) in a young woman, in whom the shorter urethra predisposes to ascending infection by enteric bacteria, chiefly E. coli. Fever of five days' duration suggests spread to the upper tract and acute pyelonephritis, which is also suggested if there is loin pain and costovertebral angle tenderness.

    Investigations

    1. Urine examination. The urine contains many leucocytes (pyuria) and bacteria. Microscopy may show leucocyte casts, which indicate renal involvement because casts form only in the tubules. A dipstick may show a positive leucocyte esterase and nitrite test, and there may be microscopic haematuria.
    2. Urine culture and sensitivity on a clean-catch midstream specimen, the definitive diagnostic test, showing significant growth (10⁵ or more organisms/mL) of the causative organism and guiding antibiotic therapy.
    3. Blood tests: complete blood count (neutrophil leucocytosis), ESR/CRP, serum urea and creatinine. Blood culture if there is high fever or suspected septicaemia.
    4. Imaging. Ultrasonography of the kidneys and bladder to detect obstruction, stones and residual urine. Further imaging (CT, intravenous urography, voiding cystourethrography) if infection is recurrent or complicated, to look for reflux, obstruction or scarring.
    5. A pregnancy test should be done before imaging or treatment in a woman of this age.

    Why is UTI more common in females?

    DU09Ju

    In the absence of instrumentation, urinary infections are much more common in females because of:

    1. Shorter urethra
    2. Absence of the antibacterial properties of prostatic fluid
    3. Hormonal changes affecting bacterial adherence to the mucosa
    4. Urethral trauma during sexual intercourse

    What is recurrent UTI?

    DU09Ju

    Two episodes of acute bacterial cystitis with symptoms within 6 months, or three episodes within 1 year.

    • Relapse: the same organism returns because it was incompletely eradicated. The interval between the two episodes is less than 2 weeks
    • Reinfection: a new infection after the previous one was wholly eradicated, with a different organism
    • More common in women
      three-quarters are caused by Escherichia coli

    Write the importance of recurrent UTI.

    DU09Ju
    • Recurrent infection is the setting in which chronic pyelonephritis develops: episodes of acute pyelonephritis recur because of predisposing factors such as vesicoureteral reflux and urinary tract obstruction
    • Recurrent episodes leave irregular scars on the cortical surface, with tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis and deformity of the underlying calyx and pelvis
    • Late presentation with gradual renal insufficiency and hypertension
    • Persistent bacteria or infection with new organisms after treatment, and repeated septicaemic episodes when obstruction, diabetes or immunodeficiency is present
    • Papillary necrosis may be superimposed and may lead to acute renal failure
    • Men with recurrent cystitis should be evaluated for prostatitis

    What is pyelonephritis?

    DU11Ja

    Inflammation caused by infection affecting the tubules, interstitium and renal pelvis.

    Describe the pathogenesis of ascending infection in pyelonephritis.

    DU11Ja

    1. Colonisation of the distal urethra and introitus (in the female) by coliform bacteria, by adhesins on the P-fimbriae (pili) of bacteria that bind receptors on urothelial cells 2. Entry into the bladder during urethral catheterisation or other instrumentation. long-term catheterisation carries a particular risk 3. Movement from the bladder to the kidney, favoured by: - Urinary tract obstruction and stasis of urine: residual urine lets bacteria multiply unhindered. Seen with benign prostatic hypertrophy, tumours, calculi and neurogenic bladder (diabetes, spinal cord injury) - Vesicoureteral reflux: an incompetent vesicoureteral valve lets bladder urine and bacteria ascend the ureter into the renal pelvis. Usually due to congenital absence or shortening of the intravesical ureter, and present in about 30% of infants and children with urinary tract infection - Intrarenal reflux: infected urine is propelled through open ducts at the papillary tips deep into the parenchyma, most often at the upper and lower poles where papillae are flat or concave - Without vesicoureteral reflux the infection usually stays in the bladder, causing cystitis and urethritis

    What are the complications of acute pyelonephritis?

    DU11Ja

    1. Papillary necrosis: seen mainly in diabetics, sickle cell disease and urinary tract obstruction. Coagulative necrosis of the tips or distal two-thirds of the pyramids. May lead to acute renal failure 2. Pyonephrosis: total or almost complete obstruction, high in the urinary tract. Pus fills the renal pelvis, calyces and ureter 3. Perinephric abscess: suppurative inflammation extends through the renal capsule into the perinephric tissue - Repeated septicaemic episodes in the presence of unrelieved obstruction, diabetes or immunodeficiency - Healing leaves irregular cortical scars

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 20)p. 816p. 843

    Acute Kidney Injury

    List the causes of acute renal failure.

    DUno yr

    Acute kidney injury can result from glomerular, interstitial, vascular or acute tubular injury.

    1. Acute tubular injury, the most common cause (about 50% of cases in hospitalised patients): - Ischaemic: severe trauma, acute pancreatitis, or any period of inadequate blood flow with hypotension and shock - Nephrotoxic: gentamicin, radiographic contrast agents, heavy metals (mercury), organic solvents (carbon tetrachloride) - Combined: mismatched blood transfusions and other haemolytic crises causing haemoglobinuria. Skeletal muscle injury causing myoglobinuria 2. Interstitial: - Pyelonephritis - Acute drug-induced interstitial nephritis: synthetic penicillins (methicillin, ampicillin), rifampin, thiazide diuretics, NSAIDs, allopurinol, cimetidine, immune checkpoint inhibitors - Acute uric acid nephropathy: precipitation of uric acid crystals in the collecting ducts, as in leukaemias or lymphomas treated with chemotherapy (tumour lysis syndrome) 3. Glomerular: rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis 4. Vascular: thrombotic microangiopathy (haemolytic uraemic syndrome and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura)

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 20)p. 814p. 847p. 853

    A 6y girl has watery stool then cessation of micturition. What is the most likely mechanism?

    DU08Ja

    Typical (diarrhoea-positive) haemolytic uraemic syndrome

    1. Intestinal infection with an E. coli strain (most commonly O157:H7) that produces Shiga-like toxin
    2. The toxin activates endothelial cells, which increase leucocyte adhesion molecules and endothelin and decrease nitric oxide production. with cytokines such as TNF it may cause endothelial apoptosis
    3. Endothelial injury leads to platelet activation, thrombosis and vasoconstriction, producing thrombotic microangiopathy
    4. Thrombi in the glomerular capillaries and arterioles cause ischaemia and renal failure, with red cell haemolysis and consumptive thrombocytopenia

    Cystic Diseases of the Kidney

    B4

    Classify cystic diseases of the kidney.

    Cystic diseases of the kidney are classified into hereditary, developmental and acquired types: autosomal dominant (adult) polycystic kidney disease, autosomal recessive (childhood) polycystic kidney disease, medullary sponge kidney, nephronophthisis (medullary cystic disease complex), multicystic renal dysplasia, acquired (dialysis-associated) cystic disease, and simple cysts.

    Complete explanation

    Cystic diseases of the kidney are a heterogeneous group of hereditary, developmental and acquired disorders. They are important because they are common and pose diagnostic problems for clinicians, radiologists and pathologists, because some, particularly adult polycystic kidney disease, are major causes of chronic kidney disease, and because they may be confused with malignant tumours.

    DiseaseInheritancePathological featuresClinical features / outcome
    Autosomal dominant (adult) polycystic kidney diseaseAutosomal dominant (PKD1, PKD2)Bilaterally enlarged kidneys replaced by multiple cysts
    Liver cysts, berry aneurysms    		Haematuria, flank pain, infection, stones, hypertension
    Chronic renal failure at 40–60 years
    Autosomal recessive (childhood) polycystic kidney diseaseAutosomal recessive (PKHD1)Enlarged smooth kidneys with small radially arranged collecting duct cysts
    Hepatic fibrosis    		Renal failure in infancy or childhood
    Portal hypertension
    Medullary sponge kidneyNoneCystic dilatation of medullary collecting ductsHaematuria, infection, stones
    Usually benign
    Nephronophthisis (familial juvenile)Autosomal recessive (NPHP genes)Small, shrunken kidneys with corticomedullary cysts and tubulointerstitial fibrosisPolyuria, salt wasting, progressive renal failure in childhood
    Multicystic renal dysplasiaNone (sporadic)Irregular cystic kidney with primitive mesenchyme and cartilageRenal failure if bilateral
    Curable by nephrectomy if unilateral
    Acquired (dialysis-associated) cystic diseaseNoneCortical and medullary cysts in end-stage kidneysHaemorrhage, erythrocytosis, renal cell carcinoma
    Simple cystsNoneSingle or multiple cortical cysts in normal-sized kidneysUsually benign and asymptomatic

    The major cystic diseases (polycystic kidney disease and nephronophthisis) are ciliopathies, caused by abnormalities of proteins localised to the primary cilium and basal body of tubular epithelial cells.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 20)p. 856

    Urolithiasis

    B4

    What are common types of renal calculi? Mention a single common test to diagnose renal calculi.

    The four common types of renal calculi are calcium stones (calcium oxalate with or without calcium phosphate), the commonest at about 70%
    Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones, formed after infection by urea-splitting bacteria. Uric acid stones
    and cystine stones. A single common diagnostic test is a plain X-ray of the kidneys, ureters and bladder, which shows radiopaque stones.

    Complete explanation

    Urolithiasis affects 5% to 10% of people during their lifetime, more often males, with peak onset between 20 and 30 years. The most important determinant of stone formation is a raised urinary concentration of the stone constituents that exceeds their solubility (supersaturation). Low urine volume, altered urinary pH, infection, and deficiency of crystal inhibitors (citrate, pyrophosphate, osteopontin, nephrocalcin) contribute.

    1. Calcium stones (about 70%) — calcium oxalate or calcium oxalate mixed with calcium phosphate. Most are associated with hypercalciuria, with or without hypercalcaemia (hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis, bone disease), and some with hyperuricosuria, hyperoxaluria or hypocitraturia. They are radiopaque.
    2. Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones (5–10%) — formed in alkaline urine after infection with urea-splitting bacteria such as Proteus. They can grow into large staghorn calculi that cast the pelvicalyceal system.
    3. Uric acid stones (5–10%) — occur in gout, leukaemia and other hyperuricaemic states, but over half of patients have no hyperuricaemia, only persistently acid urine (pH below 5.5). They are radiolucent.
    4. Cystine stones (1–2%) — caused by inherited defects in tubular reabsorption of amino acids (cystinuria), forming in acid urine.

    An organic mucoprotein matrix, forming 1% to 5% of the stone by weight, is present in all calculi.

    Diagnosis. Plain radiography of the abdomen (KUB) is the commonest single test because most stones (calcium and struvite) are radiopaque. Ultrasonography and non-contrast CT are alternatives, CT being the most sensitive, and uric acid stones, being radiolucent, may be missed on plain films. Urinalysis shows haematuria and crystals.

    Tumors of the Kidney

    Renal cell carcinoma

    B4

    Classify renal cell carcinoma. Tell the genetic association of renal cell carcinoma.

    Renal cell carcinoma is classified into clear cell carcinoma (70–80%), papillary carcinoma (10–15%), chromophobe carcinoma (5%), and rarer types including collecting duct carcinoma and Xp11 translocation carcinoma. Clear cell carcinoma is genetically associated with loss of the VHL tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 3p, and papillary carcinoma with trisomy 7 and 17 and MET mutations.

    Complete explanation

    Renal cell carcinoma accounts for 85% of renal cancers in adults. Classification is based on histological, cytogenetic and genetic features.

    TypeFrequencyCell of originGenetic features
    Clear cell70–80%Proximal tubular epitheliumDeletion of 3p25 containing the VHL gene in 98%
    Second VHL allele inactivated by mutation or hypermethylation in up to 80%
    Papillary10–15%Distal convoluted tubuleNo 3p loss
    Trisomies 7 and 17, loss of Y in males (sporadic)
    gain-of-function MET mutation in the familial form
    Chromophobe5%Intercalated cells of collecting ductsMultiple chromosome losses with extreme hypodiploidy
    Excellent prognosis
    Xp11 translocation (TFE3-rearranged)Uncommon—Translocations of TFE3 at Xp11.2
    Young patients
    Collecting duct carcinoma≤1%Collecting duct, medullaVariable losses
    Poor prognosis (medullary carcinoma is similar, in sickle cell trait)

    Genetic associations (familial syndromes, about 4% of cases)

    • von Hippel–Lindau syndrome: loss-of-function mutations of VHL
      a half to two-thirds of patients develop renal cysts and bilateral, often multiple, clear cell carcinomas.
    • Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma: loss of the FH gene encoding fumarate hydratase
      Aggressive high-grade papillary carcinoma, with cutaneous and uterine leiomyomas.
    • Hereditary papillary carcinoma: activating MET mutations
      Multiple bilateral low-grade papillary tumours.
    • Birt–Hogg–Dubé syndrome: BHD gene, encoding folliculin
      Skin tumours, lung cysts and renal tumours.
    • Tuberous sclerosis also carries an increased risk.

    The VHL protein is part of a ubiquitin ligase complex that degrades hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1) in the presence of oxygen. When VHL is lost, HIF-1 persists even under normoxic conditions and drives the expression of genes such as VEGF (angiogenesis) and IGF-1 (growth).

    Write down the morphology of renal cell carcinoma (short note).

    DU10Ja

    Gross

    • May arise in any part of the kidney, more commonly the poles
    • Clear cell carcinoma: usually a solitary unilateral lesion
      Bright yellow-grey-white spherical mass that distorts the kidney
      The yellow colour is from lipid in tumour cells
    • Large areas of grey-white necrosis and foci of haemorrhage. Margins usually sharply defined and confined within the renal capsule
    • May bulge into the calyces and pelvis and extend into the ureter
    • Strong tendency to invade the renal vein, growing as a solid column that may extend up the inferior vena cava to the right side of the heart

    Microscopy

    • Clear cell: rounded or polygonal cells with abundant clear or granular cytoplasm containing glycogen and lipid, in nested, tubular, solid or pseudopapillary patterns. Delicate branching vasculature
      Cystic areas
      Larger tumours show hyalinisation
      Most are well differentiated, some show bizarre nuclei and giant cells
    • Papillary: may be multifocal and bilateral
      Typically haemorrhagic and cystic
      Cuboidal or low columnar cells in papillae
      Foamy histiocytes in the papillary cores
      Psammoma bodies may be present
    • Chromophobe: pale eosinophilic cells, often with a perinuclear halo, in solid sheets, with the largest cells around blood vessels
    • Collecting duct carcinoma: irregular channels lined by highly atypical epithelium with a hobnail pattern
    • Sarcomatoid change is infrequent in all types and carries a very poor prognosis
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 20)p. 864

    A male has haematuria, loin pain, palpable lumbar mass. What is the likely diagnosis?

    DU18MDU09Ju

    Renal cell carcinoma

    • The classic features are costovertebral pain, a palpable mass and haematuria, but all three are seen in only 10% of cases
    • Haematuria is the most reliable clue, but it is usually intermittent and may be microscopic
    • It occurs most often in the sixth and seventh decades, with a 2:1 male preponderance

    Same: what are the histologic types of this lesion?

    DU18M
    TypeFrequencyFeatures
    Clear cell70% to 80%Clear or granular cytoplasm in variably sized nests
    Deletion of chromosome 3 at band p25.3 (the VHL gene site) in 98%
    Papillary10% to 15%Papillary, tubulopapillary or solid growth
    Trisomies 7 and 17
    MET mutations in the familial form
    Chromophobe5%Prominent cell membranes and pale eosinophilic cytoplasm with a perinuclear halo
    Arises from intercalated cells of collecting ducts
    Excellent prognosis
    Xp11 translocation (TFE3-rearranged)Not givenTranslocations of the TFE3 gene at Xp11.2
    Often in young patients
    Collecting duct carcinomaAbout 1% or lessMalignant cells forming glands in a desmoplastic stroma in the medulla
    Medullary carcinoma is a similar tumour in patients with sickle cell trait
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 20)p. 863p. 864

    Same: how will you confirm it?

    DU09Ju
    • Imaging: computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging detects the renal mass. Many tumours are now found incidentally on these studies
    • Histology: the tumour is typed by its histologic, cytogenetic and genetic features
    • Clear cell (70% to 80%), papillary (10% to 15%), chromophobe (5%), Xp11 translocation and collecting duct carcinoma
    • Spread is looked for: renal vein invasion with a column of tumour towards the inferior vena cava, and metastases to the lungs (more than 50%) and bones (33%)

    Wilms tumour

    Write a short note on Wilms' tumour/nephroblastoma.

    DU06M

    Definition. Wilms tumour [nephroblastoma, a childhood renal tumour] (nephroblastoma) is the most common primary renal tumour of childhood and the fourth most common paediatric malignancy. Peak incidence is 2 to 5 years of age, and 95% occur before 10 years. 5% to 10% involve both kidneys.

    Aetiology and pathogenesis

    SyndromeFeaturesGenetic basisRisk
    WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumour, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, intellectual disability)Aniridia and genitourinary anomaliesGermline deletion of 11p13, with the WT1 geneAbout 33%
    Denys-Drash syndrome [WT1 mutation with nephropathy and Wilms tumour] (gonadal dysgenesis and early-onset nephropathy)Diffuse mesangial sclerosis leading to renal failureDominant-negative missense mutation of WT1About 90%
    Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome [overgrowth syndrome with macroglossia and embryonal tumour risk] (organomegaly, macroglossia, hemihypertrophy, omphalocele, adrenal cytomegaly)Genomic imprinting disorder11p15.5 (WT2 locus)
    Loss of imprinting or paternal disomy with overexpression of IGF2    		Increased
    • Sporadic tumours account for 90%: beta-catenin gain-of-function mutations in about 10%
      Mutations of microRNA processing genes (DROSHA, DGCR8, DICER1) in 15% to 20% of tumours with predominantly blastemal histology
    • TP53 mutation is associated with anaplasia and poor prognosis
    • Nephrogenic rests are precursor lesions

    Morphology

    • Large, solitary, well-circumscribed mass
      Soft, homogeneous and tan-grey on cut section, with foci of haemorrhage, cyst formation and necrosis. About 10% are bilateral or multicentric
    • Classic triphasic pattern: blastemal (sheets of small blue cells), epithelial (abortive tubules or glomeruli) and stromal (fibroblastic or myxoid, sometimes skeletal muscle) components
    • About 5% are anaplastic: large hyperchromatic pleomorphic nuclei and abnormal mitoses
    • Nephrogenic rests are found next to 25% to 40% of unilateral tumours and nearly 100% of bilateral tumours

    Clinical features and complications

    • Large abdominal mass, unilateral or extending across the midline into the pelvis. Haematuria, abdominal pain, intestinal obstruction and hypertension. Pulmonary metastases may be present at diagnosis
    • Cure rate is about 90%
      Anaplastic histology is the most critical adverse factor
    • Increased risk of second primary tumours (sarcomas, leukaemia, lymphoma, breast cancer), some from radiation therapy
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 10)p. 437p. 438p. 439

    Clinical Manifestations of Renal Disease

    Hematuria

    B4

    What is hematuria? Tell 4 renal causes and 4 post-renal causes of hematuria.

    Haematuria is the presence of red blood cells in the urine, either grossly visible or detected only on microscopy. Renal causes include glomerulonephritis, pyelonephritis, renal calculi and renal tumours such as renal cell carcinoma. post-renal causes include ureteric or bladder stones, cystitis, bladder carcinoma and benign prostatic hyperplasia or prostate carcinoma.

    Complete explanation

    Haematuria is the presence of red blood cells in the urine in excess of the normal, conventionally three or more red cells per high-power field in a centrifuged specimen. It is gross (macroscopic) when the urine is visibly red, smoky or cola-coloured, and microscopic when blood is detected only by dipstick or microscopy. It is one of the commonest manifestations of renal and urinary tract disease and, when painless, must always be investigated to exclude a neoplasm.

    Renal causes (any four of the following)

    1. Glomerulonephritis — acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, crescentic glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis, Alport syndrome [inherited type IV collagen defect with nephritis, deafness and eye changes]
    2. Acute pyelonephritis, and renal tuberculosis
    3. Renal calculi
    4. Renal tumours — renal cell carcinoma, Wilms tumour [nephroblastoma, a childhood renal tumour], urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis
    5. Polycystic kidney disease and medullary sponge kidney
    6. Renal trauma, papillary necrosis (diabetes, sickle cell disease, analgesic abuse), renal infarction, and vascular malformations

    Post-renal causes (any four of the following)

    1. Ureteric calculi
    2. Bladder calculi
    3. Cystitis, including schistosomal and haemorrhagic (cyclophosphamide, radiation, adenoviral) cystitis
    4. Bladder tumours — urothelial carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma
    5. Benign prostatic hyperplasia and carcinoma of the prostate. Prostatitis
    6. Urethritis, urethral trauma, and instrumentation or catheterisation

    Coagulation disorders and anticoagulant therapy can cause or unmask haematuria from any of these sources.

    Write a short note on haematuria.

    DU19NovDU08Ju

    Definition. Haematuria is the abnormal presence of blood in the urine. It is gross (visible blood) or microscopic (red blood cells found only on microscopic urinalysis, with normal-looking urine).

    Causes. Glomerular or nonglomerular (see the causes of haematuria).

    Features

    • Gross: red, pink or tea-coloured urine
    • Microscopic haematuria: 3 or more red blood cells per high-power field on microscopy of the urine
    • Glomerular bleeding shows proteinuria, dysmorphic red cells or red cell casts
    • Nonglomerular bleeding shows normal red cells, without proteinuria or casts

    Investigation

    • Urinalysis is the first test
      a positive dipstick must be confirmed by microscopy of the urine sediment
    • Absence of red cells in a strongly dipstick-positive sample suggests myoglobinuria or haemoglobinuria
    • Cystoscopy and CT urogram are used to exclude urothelial or renal malignancy
    • A renal biopsy is needed when a glomerular source is likely

    Importance. Haematuria is the presenting symptom in most bladder cancers and is often the earliest sign of a renal neoplasm, so malignancy must always be excluded.

    Enumerate the important causes of haematuria.

    4DU24MDU16JuDU13JuDU08Ju

    Glomerular

    • Alport syndrome [inherited type IV collagen defect with nephritis, deafness and eye changes]
    • IgA nephropathy (Berger disease [IgA nephropathy])
    • Poststreptococcal (postinfectious) glomerulonephritis
    • Crescentic and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
    • Lupus nephritis
    • Goodpasture syndrome [anti-glomerular basement membrane disease]
    • Thin basement membrane disease
    • Polycystic kidney disease

    Nonglomerular

    • Urinary tract infection (cystitis, urethritis, prostatitis)
    • Urolithiasis and nephrolithiasis
    • Bladder and urothelial cancer, renal cell carcinoma, prostate cancer
    • Benign prostatic hyperplasia
    • Trauma and instrumentation of the urinary tract
    • Haemorrhagic cystitis and radiation cystitis
    • Sickle cell disease (papillary necrosis), thrombocytopenia and coagulopathies
    • Drugs such as cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide
    • Schistosomiasis in endemic regions
    • Strenuous exercise

    Write a short note on microscopic haematuria.

    DU12Ju

    Definition. Microscopic haematuria is the detection of 3 or more red blood cells per high-power field on microscopic urinalysis, without an apparent cause, while the urine looks normal.

    Types

    TypeMeaning
    Asymptomatic, no proteinuriaNormal red cells
    Possible urothelial malignancy
    Asymptomatic with proteinuriaDysmorphic red cells
    Glomerular disease
    SymptomaticInfection, prostatitis or benign prostatic hyperplasia

    Investigation

    • A dipstick alone does not make the diagnosis
      Microscopy of the urine sediment must confirm it
    • Blood from recent urological procedures, infection, or rectal or vaginal bleeding must be excluded
    • Patients are placed in low, intermediate or high risk groups for urothelial cancer by age, smoking history and the number of red cells per high-power field
    • Higher risk patients need cystoscopy and a CT urogram
      a renal biopsy may be needed in glomerular haematuria

    Proteinuria

    What do you mean by massive proteinuria?

    5DU25MDU24MDU14JaDU11JaDU06S

    Daily loss of 3.5 g or more of protein in the urine (less in children), the feature of nephrotic syndrome.

    What are the causes of massive proteinuria?

    5DU22NDU13JaDU11JuDU09JaDU07Ju

    Massive proteinuria is caused by derangement of the glomerular capillary wall, which increases permeability to plasma proteins, as in nephrotic syndrome.

    • Primary glomerular lesions: minimal change disease (most common in children), membranous nephropathy (most common in older adults), primary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (all ages)
    • Systemic causes: diabetes, amyloidosis and systemic lupus erythematosus are the most frequent
    • Less common: membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and IgA nephropathy
    • Secondary membranous nephropathy: drugs (penicillamine, captopril, gold, NSAIDs), carcinomas of lung and colon and melanoma, systemic lupus erythematosus, infections (chronic hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis, schistosomiasis, malaria) and thyroiditis
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 20)p. 827p. 830p. 833

    Name the tests we do for proteinuria.

    DU09Ju
    1. Urine dipstick for protein
    2. 24-hour urine protein collection
    3. Random urine protein to creatinine ratio
      an early morning sample is preferred as it represents the 24-hour sample
    4. Urine albumin, in a 24-hour collection or as an early morning or random albumin to creatinine ratio

    What are the causes of proteinuria?

    DUno yr
    • Glomerular proteinuria: defect in permselectivity of the glomerular filtration barrier, as in glomerulonephritis and nephrotic syndrome
    • Tubular proteinuria: incomplete tubular reabsorption of protein, as in interstitial nephritis
    • Overflow proteinuria: increased plasma concentration of protein, as in multiple myeloma (Bence Jones protein [free monoclonal light chains in the urine]) and myoglobinuria
    • Urinary tract inflammation or tumour
    • Conditions not related to renal disease: posture, fever, exercise, and urinary tract infection

    How do you perform the heat coagulation test of urine?

    DU05MDU03M

    Principle. Heat in an acid medium denatures and precipitates the proteins of the urine, which appear as turbidity.

    Procedure

    1. Fill about three-fourths of a test tube with clear urine
    2. Heat the upper part of the urine over a flame, keeping the lower part unheated as a control
    3. Add 3 to 5 drops of dilute (3%) acetic acid

    Interpretation

    • Turbidity that persists or increases: protein is present (positive)
    • Turbidity that disappears: it was due to phosphates and carbonates, which acetic acid dissolves (negative)

    What is microalbumin? Write its importance.

    DU09Ju
    • Microalbumin is an obsolete term, as there is no such biochemical molecule. it is now called urine albumin
    • Marker for the detection of incipient nephropathy in diabetics
    • Independent marker for cardiovascular disease, since it indicates increased endothelial permeability
    • Marker of chronic renal impairment
    • Measured in a 24-hour urine or as an early morning or random albumin to creatinine ratio
    • Albuminuria on two occasions, with urinary tract infection excluded, indicates glomerular dysfunction. Albuminuria for 3 months or more indicates chronic kidney disease

    Renal function tests

    B4

    Tell the important renal function tests. Why is serum creatinine a more specific renal function test?

    The important renal function tests are those of glomerular function — serum creatinine, blood urea, creatinine clearance and estimated GFR — and of tubular function, such as urine concentration, together with urinalysis for protein and sediment. Serum creatinine is more specific than blood urea because creatinine is produced at a constant rate from muscle, is freely filtered and not reabsorbed, and is largely unaffected by diet, hydration or liver function, whereas urea varies with all of these.

    Complete explanation

    Important renal function tests

    1. Glomerular filtration: serum creatinine and blood urea (BUN)
      Creatinine clearance
      Estimated GFR (derived from serum creatinine, age and sex). Cystatin C
      Inulin clearance (the reference method, used for research).
    2. Tubular function: urine specific gravity and osmolality, the concentration test after water deprivation, urinary acidification, and tests for specific tubular transport defects.
    3. Urinalysis: protein, albumin–creatinine ratio, and microscopy for red cells, casts and crystals.
    4. Serum electrolytes (sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate) and acid–base status. and imaging.

    Why serum creatinine is more specific than blood urea

    • Creatinine is produced from muscle creatine at a steady rate proportional to muscle mass, so its plasma level is stable. it is freely filtered at the glomerulus and not reabsorbed, with only slight tubular secretion. Its level therefore reflects GFR.
    • Urea production varies widely: it increases with high protein intake, gastrointestinal bleeding, catabolic states, tissue breakdown, fever and corticosteroids, and falls in liver disease and low protein intake. A large fraction of filtered urea is passively reabsorbed in the tubules, and this increases in dehydration and reduced flow, so blood urea rises in prerenal states without any parenchymal damage.
    • Creatinine is thus a more reliable index of GFR, although it is insensitive in early disease, since it rises above normal only after GFR has fallen by about half.

    Give the normal serum concentration of uric acid.

    DU03Ja
    • Adult men and postmenopausal women: 3.5 to 7.2 mg/dL
    • Premenopausal women: 2.6 to 6.0 mg/dL

    Give the normal serum albumin value.

    DU11Ja

    3.5 to 5.0 g/dL

    Give the normal serum urea value.

    DU11Ja

    Blood urea nitrogen: 8 to 20 mg/dL, with levels up to 23 mg/dL regarded as normal in those over 60 years.

    Give the normal serum creatinine value.

    DU11Ja
    • Males: 0.6 to 1.2 mg/dL
    • Females: 0.4 to 1.0 mg/dL

    What do you mean by renal clearance test?

    DU07Ju
    • The rate in mL per minute at which a substance is removed from the plasma by the kidney
    • Clearance equals urinary concentration multiplied by urinary flow rate (volume per time), divided by plasma concentration
    • The glomerular filtration rate is the clearance of a substance that is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the tubule
    • Inulin clearance is the reference method
      Radioisotopes and iohexol are other exogenous markers
    • Creatinine clearance is the most commonly used endogenous marker
      it needs a 24-hour urine collection, or preferably an accurately timed collection of 5 to 8 hours, and is corrected for body surface area
    • Normal GFR in an adult male is 90 to 120 mL per minute

    Write about the causes of uremia.

    DU15Ja

    Uraemia is azotaemia that has led to clinical signs and symptoms, so it arises from renal failure.

    • Acute kidney injury: rapid decline in GFR over hours to days, from glomerular, interstitial, vascular or acute tubular injury
    • Pre-renal causes: reduced blood flow to the kidneys, as in hypotensive and cardiogenic shock, dehydration and major blood loss
    • Renal causes: nephrotoxic drugs and toxins, sepsis, myeloma, autoimmune and inflammatory disease, tubular damage
    • Post-renal causes: blockage of the urinary tract by bladder, prostate or cervical cancer, large stones and blood clots
    • Chronic kidney disease: GFR persistently less than 60 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres for at least 3 months and/or persistent albuminuria
      Hypertension and diabetes are the most common causes worldwide
    • End-stage kidney disease: GFR less than 5% of normal, the terminal stage of uraemia

    Why is serum creatinine more specific than blood urea?

    4DU14JaDU12JuDU08JaDU07Ju
    • Creatinine is the by-product of creatine phosphate in muscle and is produced at a constant rate
    • It is cleared from the blood almost entirely by the kidney
    • Urea is formed in the liver from protein metabolism and only about 85% is eliminated by the kidneys
    • Urea also rises in upper gastrointestinal bleeding, dehydration, catabolic states and high protein diet, and falls in starvation, low protein diet and severe liver disease
    • Serum creatinine is therefore the more accurate assessment of renal function, although urea rises earlier in renal disease

    Give the clinical importance of serum creatinine.

    DU11JaDU10JaDU10Ju
    • Raised when there is a significant reduction in GFR or when urine elimination is obstructed
    • A late marker: about 50% of kidney function is lost before the level rises
    • Used in the estimating equations for GFR (MDRD and CKD-EPI), which are superior to serum creatinine alone as they include age, gender and race
    • Used to stage chronic kidney disease and to define acute kidney injury
    • Used with BUN to give the BUN to creatinine ratio, which separates pre-renal from renal causes
    • Limitations: raised by high protein intake and increased muscle bulk. Unreliable in the elderly, amputees and muscular dystrophy. Falls in pregnancy

    State the clinical significance of raised serum uric acid.

    4DU10JuDU10JaDU08JaDU03Ja
    • Most people with hyperuricaemia are asymptomatic (85% to 90%)
    • Raised uric acid in the blood or urine can lead to gout, which is its most common manifestation
    • It can lead to nephrolithiasis (uric acid stones)
    • It can cause acute uric acid nephropathy, from precipitation of uric acid crystals in the renal tubules
    • Uric acid levels can be raised 10 to 15 years before the clinical onset of gout

    Name the causes of hyperuricaemia.

    DU08Ja

    Overproduction (about 10% of cases)

    • Increased breakdown of purines
    • Fructose, whose hepatic metabolism produces uric acid

    Underexcretion (about 90% of cases)

    • Decreased glomerular filtration, as in chronic kidney disease
    • Reduced tubular secretion and increased tubular reabsorption of urate
    • Drugs: thiazide and loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin, ciclosporin
    • Alcohol, which increases production and decreases excretion
    • Lead poisoning

    What is renal glycosuria?

    DU26MDU24NDU11Ja

    Glycosuria is the presence of reducing sugars in the urine. Renal glycosuria is glucose in the urine with a normal blood glucose level, because of an isolated defect of glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule of the nephron.

    • It is often found as an incidental finding on routine urine testing in otherwise healthy people
    • Familial renal glucosuria is caused by mutation of the SLC5A2 gene, which codes for the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2)

    Why is sugar present in renal glycosuria?

    DU23N
    • Glucose is filtered at the glomerulus and is normally reabsorbed completely in the proximal tubule
    • In renal glycosuria the tubule cannot reabsorb the filtered glucose, so glucose appears in the urine although the blood glucose is normal
    • The usual cause is a mutation of the SLC5A2 gene, which codes for the SGLT2 transporter
    • Tubular absorption of glucose is also impaired in Fanconi syndrome [generalised proximal tubular reabsorption defect], where phosphate and amino acids are lost as well

    Urine examination

    Name the routine tests/investigations done on urine.

    DU26MDU24NDU13Ja

    1. Physical examination: colour and clarity - Normal urine is straw-coloured. Dark in dehydration
    Red in haematuria, porphyria or after beetroot
    Cloudy in pyuria - Specific gravity, 1.003 to 1.030 2. Chemical examination by dipstick: protein, glucose, blood, ketones, bilirubin, urobilinogen, nitrite and leucocyte esterase 3. Microscopic examination: cells, casts, crystals and micro-organisms - A freshly voided midstream sample is best, as it is less likely to be contaminated by epithelial cells and commensal bacteria

    Mention the chemical examinations done in urine with their principles.

    DU16JuDU13JuDU08Ju

    The urine dipstick uses dry chemistry: reagents impregnated on the paper change colour on contact with urine, and the colour is compared with a chart.

    AnalyteInterpretation
    ProteinNot detectable in healthy urine
    GlucoseNot detected in health
    Seen in diabetes mellitus, pregnancy and renal glycosuria, when the renal threshold of 180 mg/dL is lowered
    BloodDetects the globin portion of haemoglobin, so cannot separate haemoglobin from myoglobin
    Ascorbic acid causes a falsely negative result
    KetonesPresent in fasting, severe vomiting and diabetic ketoacidosis
    Detects acetoacetate and acetone only

    UrobilinogenMay be present normally

    What are the reducing substances/agents found in urine?

    DU22NDU14JuDU05Ja

    Reducing substances reduce cupric ions in an alkaline solution to cuprous ions (cuprous oxide), as in Benedict's test [copper-reduction test for reducing sugars].

    • Reducing sugars: glucose, fructose, galactose and lactose
    • Reducing non-sugars: ascorbic acid, uric acid and urates, glucuronides, creatinine, salicylates, streptomycin, homogentisic acid, formaldehyde
    • Sucrose is a nonreducing sugar and gives a negative result

    How do you perform Benedict's test and interpret it?

    DU23NDU21MDU03S

    Principle. Reducing sugars reduce the blue cupric ions of Benedict's [copper-reduction test for reducing sugars] reagent, in alkaline medium and on heating, to red cuprous oxide.

    Procedure

    1. Take 5 mL of Benedict's qualitative reagent in a test tube
    2. Add 8 drops (0.5 mL) of urine
    3. Boil for 2 minutes over a flame or in a boiling water bath
    4. Let it cool and note the colour

    Interpretation

    ColourGradeSugar
    Blue, no changeNegativeNone
    Green solutionTraceLess than 0.5 g/dL
    Green precipitate1 plus0.5 to 1 g/dL
    Yellow precipitate2 plus1 to 1.5 g/dL
    Orange precipitate3 plus1.5 to 2 g/dL
    Brick-red precipitate4 plusMore than 2 g/dL
    • The test detects any reducing substance, so it is not specific for glucose
    • Creatinine, ascorbic acid and urate in concentrated urine can interfere with the reaction

    Define oliguria.

    DU18MDU14Ju

    Urine output of less than 400 mL per day.

    Mention the causes of oliguria.

    DU18MDU14Ju
    • Pre-renal: reduced renal blood flow, as in hypotensive and cardiogenic shock, dehydration and major blood loss
    • Renal: acute tubular injury, nephrotoxic drugs, sepsis, myeloma, autoimmune disease. Nephritic syndrome and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
    • Post-renal: blockage of the urinary tract
      Complete bilateral obstruction of rapid onset leads to oliguria or anuria

    Bence Jones protein

    B4

    What is Bence Jones protein? What are the conditions in which it is found? How can you detect it in the laboratory?

    Bence Jones protein [free monoclonal light chains in the urine] is free monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (kappa or lambda) excreted in the urine. Because the light chains are small, they are filtered by the glomerulus. It is found chiefly in multiple myeloma, and also in Waldenström macroglobulinaemia [lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with IgM paraprotein], light-chain amyloidosis, light-chain deposition disease and other plasma cell disorders. It is detected by urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, and classically by the heat test.

    Complete explanation

    What it is. Bence Jones protein consists of free monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains, produced in excess by a neoplastic clone of plasma cells, which are small enough to be filtered at the glomerulus and appear in the urine. The reagent strip, which detects mainly albumin, may be negative, though the sulfosalicylic acid test is positive.

    Conditions in which it is found

    1. Multiple myeloma (the commonest), with Bence Jones proteinuria detectable in a large proportion of patients
    2. Waldenström macroglobulinaemia and other lymphoplasmacytic disorders
    3. AL amyloidosis (primary amyloidosis), in which the light chains form amyloid, and light-chain deposition disease
    4. Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, and occasionally chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and lymphomas

    Renal significance. In myeloma, Bence Jones proteins injure the kidney in two ways: some light chains are directly toxic to tubular epithelial cells, and others combine with Tamm–Horsfall protein under acidic conditions to form large tubular casts that obstruct the tubules and provoke a giant cell reaction (light-chain cast nephropathy, "myeloma kidney"). This is the main cause of renal dysfunction in myeloma, which develops in about half the patients. Light chains also cause AL amyloidosis and light-chain deposition disease.

    Laboratory detection

    1. Heat test (classic). On slow heating of acidified urine (pH about 5), the protein precipitates at 40–60 °C, redissolves partially or completely on boiling at about 100 °C, and reappears on cooling. The test is now of historical interest because it is insensitive and unreliable.
    2. Urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation. The definitive method, performed on a concentrated 24-hour urine specimen, which shows a monoclonal band and identifies its type (kappa or lambda).
    3. Serum free light-chain assay and serum protein electrophoresis, which are more sensitive.
    4. Bone marrow examination for clonal plasma cells.

    Urinary Bladder

    B4

    Classify malignant tumors of the urinary bladder. Mention the risk factors for urothelial carcinoma of the urinary bladder.

    Malignant tumours of the urinary bladder are overwhelmingly epithelial (more than 95%), the commonest being urothelial carcinoma, with squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma and small cell carcinoma as less common types. Mesenchymal tumours such as rhabdomyosarcoma and leiomyosarcoma are rare. The main risk factors for urothelial carcinoma are cigarette smoking, occupational exposure to aryl amines such as 2-naphthylamine, chronic infection with Schistosoma haematobium (mainly squamous carcinoma), long-term analgesic use, cyclophosphamide therapy, and pelvic irradiation.

    Complete explanation

    Classification of malignant bladder tumours

    1. Epithelial (over 95%)
      • Urothelial carcinoma (about 90% of bladder tumours): noninvasive papillary urothelial carcinoma, low grade and high grade. Flat carcinoma in situ
        and invasive urothelial carcinoma, with its histological variants (nested, micropapillary, plasmacytoid, sarcomatoid and others)
      • Squamous cell carcinoma (3–7% in the United States, much commoner where schistosomiasis is endemic)
      • Adenocarcinoma (rare)
      • Small cell (neuroendocrine) carcinoma (rare, very aggressive)
    2. Mesenchymal — embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (sarcoma botryoides) in children and leiomyosarcoma in adults
    3. Secondary — direct extension from the cervix, uterus, prostate or rectum. Lymphoma
      and rarely metastases

    Urothelial carcinoma develops by two routes: from noninvasive papillary tumours, which arise from papillary urothelial hyperplasia, and from flat carcinoma in situ. Non–muscle-invasive papillary cancers often have activating alterations in growth factor signalling (FGFR3, RAS, PI3-kinase), recur frequently, but progress to muscle invasion in only about 20%
    Most muscle-invasive cancers arise from carcinoma in situ with inactivation of TP53 and RB.

    Risk factors for urothelial carcinoma

    • Cigarette smoking, the most important, which increases the risk three- to seven-fold, and accounts for 50–80% of bladder cancers in men
    • Industrial exposure to aryl amines, especially 2-naphthylamine, with a latent period of 15 to 40 years
    • *Schistosoma haematobium* infection (Egypt, Sudan), which causes squamous metaplasia, dysplasia and carcinoma, mostly squamous
    • Long-term analgesic abuse (phenacetin)
    • Cyclophosphamide therapy (haemorrhagic cystitis) and pelvic irradiation
    • Male sex (male-to-female ratio 3:1), age (80% between 50 and 80 years), and urban residence
      The disease is rarely familial
    B4

    Mention 3 differences between low- and high-grade urothelial carcinoma of the urinary bladder.

    Low-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma shows an orderly architecture, cohesive cells and only slight nuclear variation, recurs often but rarely progresses
    high-grade carcinoma shows architectural disarray with loss of polarity, large pleomorphic hyperchromatic nuclei, frequent atypical mitoses and dyscohesive cells, and has a much higher incidence of progression to muscle invasion.

    Complete explanation

    FeatureLow-grade papillary urothelial carcinomaHigh-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma
    ArchitectureOrderly, with polarity maintained
    Evenly spaced cells    		Disorganised, with loss of polarity
    CohesionCohesiveDyscohesive, shedding into urine
    NucleiScattered hyperchromatic nuclei
    Slight variation in size and shape    		Large, markedly hyperchromatic nuclei with irregular chromatin and prominent nucleoli
    Some cells highly anaplastic
    MitosesInfrequent, mainly toward the baseFrequent, including atypical forms, at all levels
    BehaviourRecurs
    Rarely progresses in grade or stage
    Rarely threatens life    		Much higher progression to muscle-invasive disease
    Death in about 25%
    Molecular profileActivating FGFR3, RAS and PI3-kinase alterationsTP53 and RB inactivation
    B4

    Mention the staging of bladder cancer.

    Bladder cancer is staged by the pathological TNM system, based chiefly on the depth of invasion of the bladder wall: Ta is noninvasive papillary carcinoma, Tis is flat carcinoma in situ, T1 invades the lamina propria, T2 the muscularis propria, T3 the perivesical tissue, and T4 adjacent organs, with N for regional lymph nodes and M for distant metastasis.

    Complete explanation

    The extent of spread (stage), determined mainly by the depth of invasion of the bladder wall at initial diagnosis, is the most important prognostic factor and it determines treatment. The key point is whether the tumour invades the muscularis propria (detrusor muscle).

    CategoryDefinition
    pTaNoninvasive papillary carcinoma
    pTisUrothelial carcinoma in situ (flat carcinoma)
    pT1Invades lamina propria (subepithelial connective tissue)
    pT2Invades muscularis propria (T2a, inner half; T2b, outer half)
    pT3Invades perivesical soft tissue (T3a, microscopically; T3b, macroscopically)
    pT4Extravesical tumour invading prostatic stroma, seminal vesicles, uterus or vagina (T4a), or pelvic or abdominal wall (T4b)
    N0 – N3No nodes
    Single regional node in the true pelvis (N1)
    Multiple regional pelvic nodes (N2)
    Common iliac nodes (N3)
    M1a / M1bDistant metastasis limited to nodes beyond the common iliac arteries (M1a)
    Other distant metastasis (M1b)

    Ta, Tis and T1 are non–muscle-invasive tumours, which constitute 70–80% of urothelial neoplasms and are managed by transurethral resection with intravesical BCG for high-risk lesions. Muscle-invasive tumours (T2 and above) carry a significant risk of metastasis and are treated by radical cystectomy or radiotherapy with chemotherapy.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 21)p. 873p. 877

    The Male Genital Tract

    25 questions · viva and written, in Robbins order.

    Testis

    Classify testicular (germ cell) tumours.

    10DU25NDU24MDU22NDU21MDU19MDU17MDU17JaDU15JaDU09JaDU08Ja

    Germ cell tumours (95% of testicular neoplasms) are in two groups, with the other main category being sex cord–stromal tumours.

    1. Derived from germ cell neoplasia in situ - Pure forms: seminoma, embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumour, choriocarcinoma, teratoma (postpubertal) - Mixed germ cell tumours (more than one histologic type; 30% to 40% of germ cell tumours) 2. Unrelated to germ cell neoplasia in situ - Spermatocytic tumour - Prepubertal-type teratoma and yolk sac tumour, and mixed teratoma with yolk sac tumour of prepubertal type - Clinically they are divided into seminomas and nonseminomatous germ cell tumours

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 21)p. 882

    Name the testicular tumour markers.

    4DU16JuDU14JaDU13JuDU12Ju
    • Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP): raised by yolk sac tumour elements
    • Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG): raised by syncytiotrophoblastic elements

    Mention the uses of testicular tumour markers.

    DU13Ju
    1. Initial evaluation of testicular masses
    2. Staging: after orchiectomy, persistent elevation of hCG or AFP indicates metastatic spread
    3. Assessing tumour burden: markers are incorporated into the TNM stage for prognostic stage grouping
    4. Monitoring the response to therapy

    Name the tumour associated with increased beta-hCG.

    DU14Ja
    • Choriocarcinoma (syncytiotrophoblasts contain hCG)
    • Also seminoma with syncytiotrophoblasts (about 15%), where the rise is minimal
    • Raised hCG or AFP in more than 80% of nonseminomatous germ cell tumours at diagnosis

    Write down the morphology of seminoma (short note).

    5DU25MDU22NDU12JaDU11JaDU09Ju

    Gross - Bulky masses, sometimes 10 times the size of the normal testis - Homogeneous, grey-white, lobulated cut surface, usually without haemorrhage or necrosis - Tunica albuginea generally not penetrated. Occasional extension to the epididymis, spermatic cord or scrotal sac

    Microscopy - Sheets of uniform cells divided into poorly demarcated lobules by delicate fibrous septa containing a lymphocytic infiltrate. ill-defined granulomas in some - Classic seminoma cell: round to polyhedral, distinct cell membrane, clear or watery cytoplasm containing glycogen, large central nucleus with one or two prominent nucleoli - About 15% contain syncytiotrophoblasts, with a mild rise in serum hCG - Immunohistochemistry: positive for KIT, OCT3/4 and podoplanin. Negative for cytokeratin

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 21)p. 883

    How does seminoma differ from non-seminomatous germ cell tumour?

    5DU19MDU17JaDU15JaDU13JuDU12Ju

    CellsResemble primordial germ cells or early gonocytesUndifferentiated cells resembling embryonic stem cells (embryonal carcinoma), or differentiation into yolk sac tumour, choriocarcinoma and teratoma
    Cut surfaceHomogeneous, grey-white, usually no haemorrhage or necrosisVariegated, with haemorrhage or necrosis (embryonal carcinoma)
    Local spreadTunica albuginea generally not penetratedEmbryonal carcinoma often extends through the tunica albuginea into the epididymis or spermatic cord
