    How will you investigate a case of testicular mass/tumour in the laboratory?

    4DU24MDU21MDU16JuDU10Ju

    1. Serum tumour markers: AFP and hCG, in the initial evaluation - Marked rise of AFP indicates yolk sac tumour. of hCG indicates syncytiotrophoblastic elements 2. Histology of the radical orchiectomy specimen - Any solid testicular mass is considered neoplastic until proven otherwise - Biopsy is avoided because of the risk of tumour spillage - Intraoperative frozen section may be done when a benign lesion is suspected and partial orchiectomy is possible 3. Markers after orchiectomy: persistent elevation indicates metastatic spread

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 21)p. 885p. 886

    A 30y man has painless testicular swelling. What is your provisional diagnosis?

    DU10Ju

    Germ cell tumour of the testis, most likely seminoma.

    • Germ cell tumours are the most common cancer in males between 15 and 45 years of age
    • Painless enlargement of the testis is the characteristic feature
    • Seminoma is the most common germ cell tumour (about 50%), with peak incidence in the fourth decade
    • Any solid testicular mass is considered neoplastic until proven otherwise
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 21)p. 883p. 885

    What is cryptorchidism?

    DU25NDU19MDU11Ju

    Complete or partial failure of the intra-abdominal testes (one or both) to descend into the scrotal sac.

    • Found in about 1% of 1-year-old boys
      Bilateral in 25%
    • Most common arrest site is the inguinal canal
      Arrest within the abdomen accounts for 5% to 10%
    • Associated with testicular dysfunction and an increased risk of testicular cancer (four- to 10-fold, not removed by orchiopexy)
    • Other associations: hypospadias, Prader-Willi syndrome [imprinting disorder from loss of paternal 15q11-13 with hypotonia and obesity], Noonan syndrome [RAS-pathway disorder with webbed neck and pulmonary stenosis]
    • Morphology: small, firm testis
      Thickened tubular basement membrane, loss of spermatogonia leaving only Sertoli cells [supporting cell of the seminiferous tubule], hyalinised scarred tubules, prominent Leydig cells [testosterone-secreting interstitial cell of the testis]. Germ cell neoplasia in situ may be present
    • Clinical features: empty scrotal sac
      Sterility
      Inguinal hernia (10% to 20%)
      Crushing injury
    • Most inguinal testes descend spontaneously in the first year. Otherwise orchiopexy at 6 to 12 months of age

    Prostate

    Prostate diseases and PSA

    B7

    Tell the diseases of the prostate. How will you differentiate nodular hyperplasia of prostate and prostatic adenocarcinoma by microscopic examination?

    The diseases of the prostate are prostatitis (acute and chronic bacterial, chronic abacterial and granulomatous), benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostatic carcinoma. Microscopically, nodular hyperplasia shows large, branching glands with papillary infoldings lined by two layers of cells, including basal cells, whereas adenocarcinoma shows small, crowded glands without branching or papillary infolding, lined by a single layer of cells with prominent nucleoli and without a basal cell layer.

    Complete explanation

    Diseases of the prostate

    1. Inflammation (prostatitis): acute bacterial prostatitis (usually E. coli)
      Chronic bacterial prostatitis
      Chronic abacterial prostatitis (chronic pelvic pain syndrome, the commonest form). and granulomatous prostatitis (most often after BCG instillation).
    2. Benign prostatic hyperplasia (nodular hyperplasia), arising in the transition zone.
    3. Neoplasms: adenocarcinoma (acinar, ductal), usually arising in the peripheral zone from high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia, as well as small cell carcinoma and secondary tumours (most often urothelial carcinoma).

    Microscopic differentiation of nodular hyperplasia from adenocarcinoma

    FeatureBenign prostatic hyperplasiaAdenocarcinoma
    GlandsLarge, irregular, often cystically dilated
    Papillary infoldings and branching    		Smaller, crowded, uniform glands
    Lack branching and papillary infolding
    EpitheliumTwo layers: inner columnar secretory cells and outer basal cellsSingle layer of cuboidal or low columnar cells
    Basal layer absent (highlighted by basal cell markers)
    NucleiSmall and regularEnlarged, with one or more large (prominent) nucleoli
    Limited pleomorphism
    Stroma and patternNodules of glands with a stromal component
    The lobular architecture is preserved    		Infiltrative growth between benign glands
    Perineural invasion is specific
    OtherCorpora amylacea, infarcts with squamous metaplasiaAMACR positive in most cases
    Graded by the Gleason system
    B7

    What is PSA? What is the clinical importance of PSA?

    PSA, prostate-specific antigen, is a serine protease produced by the prostatic epithelium and normally secreted in semen, where it liquefies the seminal coagulum. Only minute amounts circulate in normal serum. Its clinical importance is in the detection, staging and especially the follow-up of prostate cancer, although it is organ specific rather than cancer specific, and is also raised in benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis, infarction, and after instrumentation.

    Complete explanation

    PSA is an androgen-regulated serine protease secreted by prostatic epithelium whose function is to cleave and liquefy the seminal coagulum formed after ejaculation. In healthy men only minute amounts are found in the serum.

    Clinical importance

    1. Detection and diagnosis. Elevated blood levels occur in both localised and advanced prostate cancer, and PSA is widely used with digital rectal examination to select patients for biopsy.
    2. Monitoring after treatment. Once the diagnosis has been established, serial measurement after therapy is of clear value in monitoring recurrence and disease progression.
    3. Prognosis and staging, in combination with grade and stage.

    Limitations. PSA is organ specific, but not cancer specific. Serum levels are on average lower in benign prostatic hyperplasia than in cancer, but the two overlap considerably. Prostatitis, prostatic infarction, instrumentation of the prostate and ejaculation also increase PSA. Its sensitivity and specificity as a screening test are suboptimal: false-negative results occur, and many cancers are indolent, so that screening leads to overdiagnosis and overtreatment, for which reason some countries do not recommend its use for screening.

    Benign prostatic hyperplasia

    Write a short note on benign prostatic hyperplasia (70y male with prostatism: likely diagnosis).

    DU18MDU04M

    Benign prostatic hyperplasia (nodular hyperplasia) is the most common benign prostatic disease in males older than 50 years
    Histologic evidence is found in up to 90% of males by age 80 years. It is not a premalignant lesion. The likely diagnosis in a 70-year-old male with urinary obstructive symptoms is benign prostatic hyperplasia.

    Aetiology and pathogenesis - Dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is the main androgen in the prostate, formed from testosterone by type 2 5-alpha-reductase in stromal cells - DHT binds androgen receptors and switches on androgen-dependent genes for growth factors, chiefly fibroblast growth factor family members and transforming growth factor beta - The ultimate cause is unknown

    Morphology - Prostate weight rises three- to five-fold (60 to 100 g) or more - Affects the transition zone and compresses the urethra to a slit-like orifice - Nodules rich in glands are yellow-pink, soft and exude milky prostatic fluid. Nodules of fibromuscular stroma are pale grey and firm - Microscopy: small to large to cystically dilated glands separated by bland spindle-shaped stromal cells. Glands lined by an inner columnar secretory layer and an outer cuboidal or flattened basal layer - Prostatic infarcts may occur, with adjacent squamous metaplasia

    Clinical features - Urinary frequency, nocturia, difficulty in starting and stopping the stream, overflow dribbling and dysuria - Sudden acute urinary retention may need emergency catheterisation

    Complications - Bladder muscular wall hypertrophy and distension, with trabeculation - Residual urine, a common site of infection. Increased risk of bacterial infection of the bladder and kidney

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 21)p. 888p. 868

    Mention the important diagnostic workup for BPH.

    DU18M
    1. History with the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)
    2. Physical examination: abdominal examination for bladder enlargement
      Digital rectal examination for prostate size, consistency and tenderness
    3. Urinalysis for glucosuria, proteinuria, haematuria and infection
    4. Serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA): not required routinely
      Used after shared decision-making
    5. Post-void residual urine and ultrasound for prostate volume and residual urine, when needed

    Male Infertility

    Investigation of male infertility

    What are the common hormones done in male and female to evaluate infertility?

    DU13Ju

    In the male

    • Serum total testosterone (8 AM to 10 AM) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) are the first tests
    • If testosterone is low, repeat total and free testosterone and add luteinising hormone (LH) and prolactin
    • Other pituitary hormones are checked when the picture suggests hypogonadotropic hypogonadism: free T4, morning cortisol and prolactin
    PatternMeaning
    Low testosterone, high FSH, high LHPrimary testicular failure
    Normal testosterone, normal LH, high FSHSeminiferous tubule damage without Leydig cell [testosterone-secreting interstitial cell of the testis] dysfunction
    Low testosterone, low or normal FSH and LHHypogonadotropic hypogonadism
    High prolactin suggests a prolactin-secreting tumour
    High testosterone, high LH, normal FSHPartial androgen insensitivity

    How will you investigate a case of male infertility in the laboratory?

    DU17M
    1. Semen analysis: volume, pH, liquefaction, viscosity, sperm number, motility, vitality and morphology
    2. Post-ejaculation urine for sperm when semen volume is low, to confirm retrograde ejaculation
    3. Tests for sperm antibodies when sperm agglutination is seen: mixed antiglobulin reaction test and immunobead test
    4. Seminal markers: fructose, zinc and neutral glucosidase
    5. Peroxidase staining and leucocyte markers on round cells
      More than 1 million leucocytes per mL (pyospermia) needs a search for genital tract infection
    6. Hormones: serum total testosterone, FSH, LH and prolactin
    7. Genetic tests: karyotyping for Klinefelter syndrome [47,XXY] and Y chromosome microdeletion
      CFTR gene testing in congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens

    Semen analysis

    B4

    What are the indications for semen analysis? Mention the microscopic findings of semen analysis.

    The indications for semen analysis are the evaluation of infertility in a couple, confirmation of the success of a vasectomy and the monitoring of vasectomy reversal, assessment of testicular disease or hormonal and treatment effects, screening of sperm donors and before assisted reproduction, and medicolegal purposes. The microscopic findings assessed are sperm concentration, motility, morphology and vitality, along with agglutination and the presence of white cells, red cells and immature germ cells.

    Complete explanation

    Indications

    1. Evaluation of male infertility, in couples unable to conceive after 12 months of unprotected intercourse.
    2. Follow-up after vasectomy to establish azoospermia, and after vasectomy reversal or other surgery (for example varicocele repair) to assess recovery.
    3. Evaluation of testicular and hormonal disorders and follow-up of effects of chemotherapy, radiation or drugs on spermatogenesis.
    4. Selection of donors for artificial insemination and assessment before assisted reproductive procedures (IUI, IVF, ICSI), and semen cryopreservation.
    5. Medicolegal indications (rape, paternity disputes).

    Microscopic findings in a semen analysis

    • Sperm concentration and total sperm number.
    • Motility (progressive, non-progressive and immotile), assessed on a fresh preparation within an hour.
    • Vitality (live sperm by eosin–nigrosin stain), important when motility is low.
    • Morphology on a stained smear (Papanicolaou stain [cervical cytology screening]), assessed by strict criteria: the proportion of normal forms, and abnormalities of head, midpiece and tail.
    • Agglutination or aggregation of sperm, suggesting antisperm antibodies.
    • Round cells: leucocytes (more than 1 million per mL suggests infection, leucocytospermia) and immature germ cells. Red cells, crystals and debris.
    B4

    What instructions do you need to give a patient for semen analysis?

    The patient should abstain from ejaculation for 2 to 7 days, collect the entire ejaculate by masturbation into a clean, sterile, wide-mouthed container without lubricants or ordinary condoms, label it with his name, the date and time and the period of abstinence, and deliver it to the laboratory within one hour while keeping it at body temperature.

    Complete explanation

    The reliability of semen analysis depends on proper collection, so the patient must be instructed as follows.

    1. Abstinence from ejaculation for a minimum of 2 days and a maximum of 7 days before collection, the period being the same for repeated samples.
    2. Collect the specimen by masturbation into a clean, sterile, wide-mouthed container provided by the laboratory, which is non-toxic to sperm. A lubricant, saliva or soap must not be used, and ordinary condoms, which contain spermicides, must not be used.
    3. The entire ejaculate must be collected
      The first portion is the sperm-rich fraction, and the patient must report any loss of any part of the specimen.
    4. Label the container with the patient's name, the date and time of collection, the period of abstinence, and any difficulties with collection.
    5. Deliver the specimen to the laboratory within one hour of collection, protected from temperature extremes (kept at body temperature, not cooled or heated).
    6. The patient should record recent illness (fever), medication, and alcohol or drug use. and two or three samples are examined at intervals of at least a week or two.
    B4

    What is oligospermia? Give 3 causes of oligospermia.

    Oligospermia (oligozoospermia) is a sperm concentration below the lower reference limit, that is, below 16 million per mL (15 million per mL in the earlier WHO reference). Causes include varicocele, cryptorchidism or testicular atrophy, and endocrine disorders such as hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

    Complete explanation

    Oligospermia is a reduction in the number of spermatozoa in the ejaculate, defined as a sperm concentration below the lower reference limit (below 16 × 10⁶/mL by the WHO 2021 reference values; below 15 × 10⁶/mL in the 2010 edition). It is a common cause of male infertility, and the severity ranges from mild to severe.

    Causes

    1. Varicocele, the commonest correctable cause.
    2. Cryptorchidism and other testicular atrophy (after mumps orchitis, torsion, trauma, irradiation), reflecting loss of spermatogenic tissue.
    3. Endocrine disorders: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease and androgen or anabolic steroid use.
    4. Genetic causes: Klinefelter syndrome [47,XXY] and Y chromosome microdeletions.
    5. Drugs, toxins and heat exposure: cytotoxic drugs, alcohol, smoking, sulfasalazine, radiation, and prolonged testicular heating.
    6. Infection of the genital tract, partial obstruction of the ducts, antisperm antibodies, and systemic illness. Many cases remain idiopathic.

    Mention the indications of semen analysis.

    9DU24NDU21MDU19MDU18NovDU17JaDU16JaDU15JaDU14JaDU12Ja
    • Assessment of male factor infertility
    • Planning of assisted fertilisation

    How is semen collected?

    DU19MDU18NovDU15Ja
    1. Collected by the man by masturbation, at home or near the laboratory, after a minimum of 3 days and a maximum of 7 days of abstinence
    2. The whole ejaculate must be collected
      Any loss of the sample is reported to the laboratory
    3. Collected into a clean, wide-mouthed container that is nontoxic to spermatozoa and kept at 20 to 37 °C
    4. If masturbation is not possible, semen can be collected in a nontoxic condom during intercourse
      Latex condoms are not used because they affect sperm viability and motility
    5. Delivered to the laboratory within 1 hour of collection
    6. Two or three samples are advisable, because semen composition varies

    What is oligospermia?

    DU24NDU16JaDU14Ja

    Oligospermia (oligozoospermia) is semen with a reduced sperm concentration: less than 15 million per mL, or a total sperm count of less than 39 million.

    What is azoospermia?

    DU24N

    Azoospermia is semen without spermatozoa. It is diagnosed only after the ejaculate has been centrifuged and the sperm pellet examined under the microscope.

    Write down the causes of azoospermia.

    5DU24NDU19MDU18NovDU17JaDU15Ja

    1. Hypothalamic-pituitary failure (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism): other pituitary hormone deficiencies, prolactin-secreting tumour 2. Primary testicular failure: Klinefelter syndrome [47,XXY], Y chromosome microdeletion, radiation or chemotherapy, testicular trauma, torsion of the testes, mumps 3. Obstruction of the genital tract: - Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, often with CFTR mutations (cystic fibrosis) - Ejaculatory duct obstruction from chlamydia, gonorrhoea, tuberculosis or vasectomy 4. Transient azoospermia can follow toxic, environmental, infectious or iatrogenic insults

    Write a short note on semen analysis.

    6DU13JaDU10JuDU09JuDU09JaDU08JaDU07Ja

    Semen analysis is the laboratory test used to evaluate male fertility. Semen is a mixture of spermatozoa from the testes, processed in the epididymides and mixed with secretions of the prostate, seminal vesicles and bulbourethral glands.

    Procedure

    1. Liquefaction at 37 °C, which may take up to 60 minutes
    2. Measurement of volume, then pH
    3. Wet preparation for appearance, motility and agglutination. Motility is tested within 1 hour of collection
    4. Vitality test, especially when sperm number is low
    5. Dilution and counting of sperm
    6. Smears for morphology

    Interpretation

    • Low volume (less than 1.5 mL): incomplete collection, retrograde ejaculation, testosterone deficiency, ejaculatory duct obstruction or absent vas deferens and seminal vesicles
    • Agglutination: test for anti-sperm antibodies
    • Many immotile and nonviable sperm: epididymal pathology
      Immotile but viable sperm suggest a flagellar defect
    • Abnormal morphology: a problem of spermatogenesis
    • Abnormal results are repeated after 3 months, one full cycle of spermatogenesis

    The Female Genital Tract

    35 questions · viva and written, in Robbins order.

    Infections (Pelvic Inflammatory Disease)

    B4

    What is PID? Mention 4 complications of PID. Mention 5 causes of pelvic inflammatory disease. How does PID affect sterility?

    Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an ascending infection from the vulva and vagina involving much of the genital tract, most often due to gonococcus, chlamydia, puerperal or IUCD-related infection, and it causes sterility by scarring and obstructing the fallopian tubes.

    • PID: ascending infection from vulva/vagina involving most of the genital tract. It causes pelvic pain, adnexal tenderness, fever and discharge.
    • Causes (5): N. gonorrhoeae
      Chlamydia
      puerperal/post-abortal infections (polymicrobial: staphylococci, streptococci, coliforms, Clostridium perfringens). IUCD-associated chronic endometritis
      TB (rare in high-resource countries).
    • Complications (4 or more): peritonitis, bacteraemia (endocarditis, meningitis, suppurative arthritis), tubo-ovarian abscess, pyosalpinx. Chronic: infertility, ectopic pregnancy, pelvic pain, intestinal obstruction from adhesions.
    • Sterility: acute salpingitis strips the tubal epithelium. The denuded plicae fuse and scar (chronic salpingitis), with tubal obstruction, fimbrial fusion and hydrosalpinx. The tube cannot pick up or pass oocytes.

    Cervix

    B7

    What are the diseases of the uterine cervix?

    The diseases of the uterine cervix are cervicitis, endocervical polyp, condyloma, squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL/HSIL) and invasive carcinoma.

    Cervicitis (acute/chronic: gonococcus, chlamydia, mycoplasma, HSV), endocervical polyp, condyloma, squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL/HSIL), and invasive carcinoma (squamous ~80%, adenocarcinoma ~15%, adenosquamous/neuroendocrine ~5%). Gartner duct cysts are a developmental remnant.

    B7

    Define and classify CIN. What are the risk factors for cervical cancer?

    Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is a precancerous squamous lesion at the transformation zone, with nuclear atypia and loss of maturation, caused by high-risk HPV and graded CIN 1 to CIN 3 (LSIL/HSIL)
    Persistent high-risk HPV is the main risk factor for cervical cancer.

    • CIN: a precancerous squamous lesion at the transformation zone with nuclear atypia and loss of maturation, caused by high-risk HPV.
    Old termCINBethesdaImmature cells
    Mild dysplasiaCIN 1LSILLower third
    Moderate dysplasiaCIN 2HSILBeyond lower third (text: upper two-thirds)
    Severe dysplasia/CISCIN 3HSILFull thickness
    • Risk factors: persistent high-risk HPV (16, 18)
      Early first intercourse
      Multiple partners (or partner with multiple partners). Immunosuppression
      no screening. Smoking and parity are co-factors.
    B7

    How will you diagnose a case of cervical carcinoma?

    Cervical carcinoma is diagnosed by Pap smear [cervical cytology screening] with HPV testing, colposcopy-directed biopsy and histology, with cone biopsy where needed.

    1. Pap smear from the transformation zone, with HPV DNA testing from age 30.
    2. Colposcopy with acetic acid (aceto-white areas), then directed biopsy.
    3. Cone biopsy if needed
      Histology plus clinical/imaging staging.
    4. p16 and Ki-67 IHC for equivocal cases.

    Write down the risk factors for carcinoma of cervix.

    DUno yr
    • Persistent infection with high-risk HPV, the most important factor
      HPV-16 accounts for almost 60% of cases and HPV-18 for another 10%
    • Young age at first intercourse
    • Multiple sexual partners
    • Male partner with multiple sexual partners
    • Co-carcinogens and host immune status, which decide whether an HPV infection regresses or persists
    • Lack of participation in regular screening: more than one-half of invasive cancers occur in females who were not screened
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 22)p. 901p. 905p. 906

    Describe briefly the pathogenesis of carcinoma cervix.

    DU07Ju
    1. High-risk HPV infection of immature basal squamous cells, at sites of squamous trauma and repair and in the immature metaplastic cells of the transformation zone
    2. Most infections are transient (50% cleared within 8 months, 90% within 2 years)
      Persistent infection leads to precursor lesions
    3. Viral E6 binds p53 and promotes its degradation
      E6 also upregulates telomerase, which leads to immortalisation
    4. Viral E7 promotes degradation of RB and inhibits p21 and p27, so cells progress through the cell cycle and cannot repair DNA damage
    5. Integration of viral DNA into the host genome increases expression of E6 and E7 and may dysregulate nearby oncogenes such as MYC
    6. Additional mutations accumulate
      low-grade lesion progresses to high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion and then invasive carcinoma, over decades

    State the role of HPV in causing carcinoma of cervix.

    DU25NDU19M
    • High-risk HPVs are by far the most important factor
      15 high-risk types are known
    • HPV-16 accounts for almost 60% of cases, HPV-18 for another 10%
    • More than 80% of low-grade and 100% of high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions are associated with high-risk HPV
    • Carcinogenic action depends on viral E6 (binds and degrades p53; upregulates telomerase) and E7 (degrades RB. Inhibits p21 and p27)
    • Viral DNA is integrated into the host genome in most cancers, increasing E6 and E7 expression
    • Only a few infected females develop cancer, so co-carcinogens and host immune status also matter
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 22)p. 905p. 906p. 907

    What is CIN?

    DU25NDU19MDU08Ja

    Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, the precursor lesion of cervical squamous carcinoma, graded by dysplasia:

    CIN gradeDysplasiaCurrent term
    CIN 1MildLow-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL)
    CIN 2ModerateHigh-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL)
    CIN 3Severe, carcinoma in situHigh-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL)
    • Grading depends on how far immature cells expand from the basal layer: lower one-third in LSIL. Upper two-thirds in HSIL
    • Nuclear atypia with perinuclear halos (koilocytic atypia)
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 22)p. 906p. 907

    Mention the diagnostic tools of cervical cancer.

    DU19M
    1. Pap test [cervical cytology screening] (cervical cytology) from the transformation zone
    2. HPV DNA testing of the cervical scrape: higher sensitivity but lower specificity than the Pap test
    3. Colposcopy after acetic acid, which shows abnormal epithelium as aceto-white areas
    4. Biopsy of abnormal areas for histology
      Ki-67 and p16 immunohistochemistry confirm equivocal squamous intraepithelial lesions
    5. Cervical conisation treats high-grade lesions and superficially invasive carcinoma

    Write a short note on Pap smear.

    DU18Nov
    • Cytologic screening for cervical precursor lesions and low-stage cancer
      Credited with a 75% fall in cervical cancer death rate
    • Technique: the transformation zone of the cervix is circumferentially scraped with a spatula or brush, and the cells are smeared or spun down onto a slide. The smear is fixed and stained by the Papanicolaou method [cervical cytology screening], then screened microscopically or by automated image analysis
    • Findings: the spectrum from low-grade to high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion
    • Schedule: first smear at 21 years or within 3 years of onset of sexual activity, then every 3 years
      After 30 years with normal cytology and negative HPV, every 5 years by HPV testing alone or with a Pap test [cervical cytology screening]
    • An abnormal result is followed by colposcopy and biopsy
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 22)p. 906p. 909

    A female has PV bleeding/discharge, contact bleeding, an ulcerated/friable/fungating cervical growth. What is the likely diagnosis?

    10DU26MDU24NDU23NDU22NDU21MDU20NDU20JuDU19NovDU13JuDU11Ja

    Invasive carcinoma of the cervix, most likely squamous cell carcinoma.

    • The average age is 45 to 50 years
    • Squamous cell carcinoma accounts for about 80% of cases
      Adenocarcinoma for about 15%
    • All are caused by high-risk HPV
    • It appears as a fungating (exophytic) or infiltrative mass
    • More than one-half of cases are found in females who did not attend regular screening
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 22)p. 907p. 908p. 910

    Same: what do you expect in histopathology?

    DU22NDU21MDU13Ju
    • Squamous cell carcinoma (about 80%): nests and tongues of malignant squamous epithelium, keratinising or nonkeratinising, invading the cervical stroma
    • Adenocarcinoma (about 15%): proliferating malignant endocervical glands with large hyperchromatic nuclei and mucin-depleted cytoplasm
    • Adenosquamous and neuroendocrine carcinomas (remaining 5%)
    • Preceding high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion shows nuclear atypia and koilocytes
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 22)p. 907p. 908

    Same: name the microbial agent/oncogenic virus associated with it.

    4DU26MDU22NDU21MDU13Ju

    High-risk human papillomavirus, mainly HPV-16 (almost 60%) and HPV-18 (about 10%).

    Same: how will you confirm it / which investigations are needed?

    6DU24NDU23NDU20NDU20JuDU19NovDU11Ja
    1. Biopsy of the lesion, with histology: the diagnosis is made on tissue
    2. Pap test [cervical cytology screening] and HPV DNA testing of the cervical scrape
    3. Colposcopy with acetic acid, then biopsy of abnormal areas
    4. Staging: stage 0 carcinoma in situ
      Stage I confined to the cervix
      Stage II beyond the cervix but not the pelvic wall, and not the lower third of the vagina. Stage III lower third of vagina, pelvic wall, hydronephrosis or nodes. Stage IV beyond the true pelvis or bladder or rectal mucosa

    Body of Uterus

    Endometrium and myometrium

    B7

    What are the diseases of the body of the uterus?

    The diseases of the uterine body are functional (dysfunctional bleeding), inflammatory (endometritis), misplaced endometrium (endometriosis, adenomyosis), polyps and hyperplasia, and neoplasms (carcinoma, leiomyoma and others).

    • Functional: dysfunctional uterine bleeding, anovulatory cycle.
    • Inflammatory: acute and chronic endometritis.
    • Misplaced endometrium: endometriosis, adenomyosis.
    • Polyps and hyperplasia: endometrial polyp, endometrial hyperplasia (without/with atypia).
    • Neoplasms: endometrioid and serous carcinoma, carcinosarcoma, adenosarcoma, stromal tumours, leiomyoma, leiomyosarcoma.
    B7

    What is dysfunctional uterine bleeding? Mention the causes of abnormal uterine bleeding.

    Dysfunctional uterine bleeding is abnormal uterine bleeding without a structural lesion, usually from hormonal disturbance and most commonly from an anovulatory cycle.

    • DUB: abnormal uterine bleeding without a structural lesion, usually from hormonal disturbance.
    • Commonest cause: anovulatory cycle (menarche, perimenopause). Unopposed oestrogen with no corpus luteum gives proliferative or disordered endometrium without secretory change.
    • Other causes of anovulation: thyroid, adrenal and pituitary disease
      PCOS or functioning ovarian tumours
      Obesity, malnutrition, chronic disease.
    AgeCauses (Table 22.2)
    PrepubertyPrecocious puberty
    AdolescenceAnovulatory cycle, coagulation disorders
    ReproductivePregnancy complications (abortion, trophoblastic disease, ectopic), leiomyoma, adenomyosis, polyps, hyperplasia, carcinoma, DUB
    PerimenopauseDUB, carcinoma, hyperplasia, polyps
    PostmenopauseEndometrial atrophy, carcinoma, hyperplasia, polyps
    B7

    What is endometriosis and adenomyosis? Describe the pathogenesis of endometriosis.

    Endometriosis is endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus, whereas adenomyosis is endometrial tissue within the myometrium
    Endometriosis is explained by the regurgitation, benign metastasis, metaplastic and stem-cell theories.

    • Endometriosis: endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus. Sites in descending frequency: ovary, uterine ligaments, rectovaginal septum, cul-de-sac, pelvic peritoneum, bowel serosa, others. It affects ~10% of women.
    • Adenomyosis: endometrial tissue within the myometrium, in continuity with the endometrium (down-growth). Present in up to 20% of uteri.
    • Pathogenesis (four theories):
    • Regurgitation: retrograde menstrual flow.
    • Benign metastasis: vascular or lymphatic spread.
    • Metaplastic: from coelomic epithelium or mesonephric remnants.
    • Extrauterine stem/progenitor cells (bone marrow).
    • Molecular support:
    • Inflammatory and angiogenic mediators (PGE₂, IL-1, TNF, IL-6, VEGF, MMPs).
    • Aromatase in endometriotic stroma gives local oestrogen. PGE₂ feeds this loop.
    • Epigenetic oestrogen hyper-responsiveness and progesterone resistance.
    • Mutations in KRAS, PIK3CA, ARID1A, PPP2R1A.
    B7

    What is endometrial hyperplasia? What are the conditions associated with this disease?

    Endometrial hyperplasia is an increased gland-to-stroma ratio caused by prolonged oestrogen stimulation unopposed by progesterone, and atypical hyperplasia is a precursor of endometrial carcinoma.

    • Definition: increased gland-to-stroma ratio from prolonged oestrogen stimulation, unopposed by progesterone.
    • Associated conditions: obesity (peripheral androgen-to-oestrogen conversion), menopause, anovulation, PCOS, functioning granulosa cell tumours, cortical stromal hyperplasia, oestrogen replacement therapy.
    • Types (WHO): hyperplasia without atypia (carcinoma risk ~1-3%) and atypical hyperplasia (endometrioid intraepithelial neoplasia: complex back-to-back glands with nuclear atypia; up to 40% have carcinoma at hysterectomy).
    • PTEN mutation is common in both.
    B7

    What is endometrial carcinoma? How can you diagnose a case of endometrial carcinoma?

    Endometrial carcinoma is the most common malignancy of the female genital tract
    it is diagnosed by endometrial biopsy or curettage in a woman with irregular or postmenopausal bleeding.

    • Definition: the commonest invasive cancer of the female genital tract in the US. Types: endometrioid (80-85%) and serous (~15%).
    • Diagnosis: presents with irregular or postmenopausal bleeding. There is no screening test. Diagnosis is by endometrial biopsy or curettage (histology). Ultrasound for endometrial thickness. Test endometrioid tumours for mismatch repair defects to detect Lynch syndrome.
    B7

    Tell the morphology and complications of leiomyoma.

    Leiomyoma is a sharply circumscribed, firm, whorled, grey-white benign smooth muscle tumour of the myometrium. Its complications are abnormal bleeding, pain, infertility and pregnancy complications, and malignant change is extremely rare.

    • Gross: sharply circumscribed, round, firm, grey-white tumours with a whorled cut surface. Single or multiple
      Intramural, submucosal or subserosal. Large ones may show yellow-brown or red softening.
    • Micro: bundles of smooth muscle with uniform oval nuclei and scant mitoses. Variants: bizarre-nuclei (FH mutation), cellular, intravenous leiomyomatosis, disseminated peritoneal leiomyomatosis.
    • Genetics: MED12 mutation in ~70%
      HMGIC/HMGIY rearrangements
      FH (HLRCC).
    • Complications: abnormal bleeding, urinary frequency, pain from infarction, infertility. In pregnancy: abortion, malpresentation, uterine inertia, postpartum haemorrhage. Malignant change is extremely rare.

    Endometriosis

    Write a short note on endometriosis.

    DU07JaDU06Ja

    Definition: endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus. The ectopic tissue may bleed cyclically.

    Pathogenesis 1. Regurgitation theory: retrograde flow of menstrual endometrium 2. Benign metastasis theory: spread through blood vessels and lymphatics to distant sites such as bone, lung and brain 3. Metaplastic theory: from coelomic epithelium, or from mesonephric remnants 4. Extrauterine stem or progenitor cell theory: from bone marrow cells - Implants release proinflammatory and angiogenic factors, and stromal cells produce aromatase, so oestrogen enhances their survival

    Morphology - Red-blue to yellow-brown nodules on or beneath mucosal or serosal surfaces - Organising haemorrhage causes fibrous adhesions between tubes and ovaries and obliterates the pouch of Douglas - Ovarian chocolate cysts (endometriomas), 3 to 5 cm, filled with brown fluid - Microscopy: endometrial glands and stroma, with or without haemosiderin

    Clinical features and complications - Severe dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia and pelvic pain. Menstrual irregularity - Infertility in 30% to 40% - Malignancy (endometrioid and clear cell carcinoma) may arise in endometriotic cysts

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 22)p. 913p. 914

    Endometrial carcinoma

    A 60y woman has postmenopausal bleeding with thick endometrium on USG. What is the provisional diagnosis?

    DU17MDU16Ju

    Endometrial carcinoma, most likely endometrioid type
    Endometrial hyperplasia is the other important cause.

    • Peak incidence in postmenopausal females 55 to 65 years of age
    • Usually produces irregular or postmenopausal vaginal bleeding
    • Endometrial hyperplasia, an important cause of abnormal bleeding, is a frequent precursor and follows prolonged oestrogenic stimulation (obesity, polycystic ovarian syndrome, granulosa cell tumour, oestrogen therapy)

    Same: how can you confirm it?

    DU17MDU16Ju

    The diagnosis must be established by histologic examination of tissue obtained by biopsy or curettage.

    • Endometrioid carcinomas are then analysed for DNA mismatch repair deficiency
    • Atypical hyperplasia cannot always be distinguished from cancer without hysterectomy. up to 40% of those diagnosed with it have carcinoma at hysterectomy

    B7

    What are the hormone-producing tumors of the ovary? Describe the morphology of a dermoid cyst.

    The hormone-producing ovarian tumours are granulosa cell tumour and thecoma (oestrogen), Sertoli [supporting cell of the seminiferous tubule]-Leydig [testosterone-secreting interstitial cell of the testis] and Leydig cell tumours (androgen), struma ovarii (thyroid hormone), carcinoid (serotonin) and choriocarcinoma (hCG).

    • Oestrogen: granulosa cell tumour, thecoma. Effects: precocious puberty in children. Endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma and proliferative breast disease in adults.
    • Androgen: Sertoli-Leydig and Leydig cell tumours
      Pregnancy luteoma may virilise.
    • Thyroid hormone: struma ovarii (hyperthyroidism).
    • Serotonin: carcinoid (carcinoid syndrome without liver metastases if large).
    • hCG: choriocarcinoma
      Some dysgerminomas.
    • Dermoid morphology: see Q1284.
    B7

    Name the germ cell tumors of the ovary. What is a Krukenberg tumor?

    The germ cell tumours of the ovary are teratoma, dysgerminoma, yolk sac tumour, choriocarcinoma, embryonal carcinoma, polyembryoma and mixed tumours. a Krukenberg tumour is a bilateral ovarian metastasis of mucin-secreting signet-ring cell carcinoma, most often from the stomach.

    • Germ cell tumours (15-20% of ovarian tumours): teratoma (mature, immature, monodermal), dysgerminoma, yolk sac tumour, choriocarcinoma, embryonal carcinoma, polyembryoma, mixed.
    • Krukenberg tumour: bilateral ovarian metastases of mucin-secreting signet-ring cell carcinoma, most often gastric (also colon, breast).
    B7

    Define and classify teratoma. What is Meigs syndrome?

    Teratoma is a germ cell tumour showing differentiation into elements of two or more germ layers, classified as mature, immature and monodermal. Meigs syndrome is ovarian fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion.

    • Teratoma: a germ cell tumour with differentiation into elements of two or more germ layers.
    • Classification: (1) mature (benign), mostly cystic (dermoid)
      (2) immature (malignant), with primitive neuroepithelium. (3) monodermal/specialised (struma ovarii, carcinoid).
    • Meigs syndrome: ovarian fibroma (usually >6 cm) with ascites and pleural effusion (usually right-sided). Mechanism unknown.

    What is dermoid cyst of ovary? Describe its morphology.

    7DU26MDU25MDU24MDU22MDU11JuDU10JaDU06Ja

    A mature (benign) cystic teratoma, called a dermoid cyst because it is almost always lined by skin-like structures. Found usually in young adult females.

    Gross - Bilateral in 10% to 15% - Unilocular cyst containing hair and sebaceous material - Wall lined by opaque, grey-white, wrinkled epidermis, often with protruding hair shafts - Teeth and areas of calcification in the wall

    Microscopy - Stratified squamous epithelium with sebaceous glands, hair shafts and other skin adnexal structures - Tissues of other germ layers: cartilage, bone, thyroid and neural tissue

    Other points - Karyotype 46,XX - About 1% undergo malignant transformation, most commonly to squamous cell carcinoma

    2. Germ cell tumours: teratoma, dysgerminoma, yolk sac tumour, choriocarcinoma, embryonal carcinoma, polyembryoma, mixed germ cell tumours

    Gestational and Placental Disorders

    B7

    What are the gestational trophoblastic diseases? How can you diagnose hydatidiform mole in the laboratory?

    The gestational trophoblastic diseases are hydatidiform mole (complete and partial), invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumour and epithelioid trophoblastic tumour. a mole is diagnosed by markedly raised hCG, ultrasound and histology showing swollen hydropic villi with trophoblastic hyperplasia.

    • GTD spectrum: hydatidiform mole (complete, partial), invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumour, epithelioid trophoblastic tumour.
    FeatureComplete molePartial mole
    OriginEmpty egg with paternal genome: 90% one sperm duplicating (46,XX), 10% dispermicEgg fertilised by two sperm
    Karyotype46,XX or 46,XYTriploid (69,XXY) or tetraploid
    EmbryoNoneMay be present, growth-restricted
    VilliAll or most enlarged, smooth, with cisternsOnly some enlarged, scalloped
    TrophoblastCircumferential cyto- and syncytiotrophoblastFocal, syncytiotrophoblast only
    Risk2.5% choriocarcinoma
    15% invasive/persistent mole    		Persistent disease
    Not typically choriocarcinoma
    • Laboratory diagnosis:
    • hCG markedly higher than in a normal pregnancy of the same gestational age. Followed for 6-12 months until non-pregnant levels.
    • Pelvic ultrasound.
    • Histology of curettage: swollen hydropic villi with trophoblastic hyperplasia.
    • Cytogenetics/ploidy and p57 IHC to separate complete from partial mole.
    B7

    What is ectopic pregnancy? Which site is most common? How can you confirm such a case?

    Ectopic pregnancy refers to implantation of the gestation in a site other than the normal intrauterine location. The most common site is the fallopian tube (approximately 90% of cases). It is confirmed by an inappropriately rising hCG, pelvic sonography, endometrial biopsy and laparoscopy.

    • Definition: implantation outside the uterine cavity. Fallopian tube is the commonest site (~90%)
      Others are ovary, abdomen, caesarean scar and cornual region.
    • Predisposing factors: chronic salpingitis from PID (35-50%), peritubal adhesions (appendicitis, endometriosis, surgery), IUCD (two-fold).
    • Clinical: abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding at 6-8 weeks. Rupture causes haemorrhagic shock, a medical emergency. It causes 4-10% of pregnancy-related deaths.
    • Confirmation: inappropriately rising hCG, pelvic sonography, endometrial biopsy (decidua without villi or trophoblast), laparoscopy.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 22)p. 935p. 936
    B7

    What is choriocarcinoma? How can you diagnose such a case? Mention the common sites of its metastasis.

    Choriocarcinoma is a malignant neoplasm of trophoblast, diagnosed by markedly raised hCG and histology showing sheets of cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts without villi, and it metastasises mainly to the lungs and vagina.

    • Definition: malignant neoplasm of trophoblast, arising in 1 in 20,000-30,000 pregnancies. Preceded by complete mole (50%), spontaneous abortion (25%), normal pregnancy (~22%), or ectopic pregnancy. Non-gestational choriocarcinoma (germ cell) lacks paternal DNA.
    • Morphology: soft, fleshy, yellow-white haemorrhagic and necrotic mass. Micro: sheets of malignant cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts without chorionic villi, with frequent vascular invasion.
    • Diagnosis: irregular bloody spotting, markedly raised hCG, histology, and imaging for metastases.
    • Metastatic sites: lungs (50%), vagina (30-40%), then brain, liver, bone, kidney.
    • Treatment: chemotherapy gives nearly 100% remission
      Gestational type is curable.

    The Endocrine System

    49 questions · viva and written, in Robbins order.

    Thyroid GlandPituitary GlandPancreas / Diabetes Mellitus

    Pituitary Gland

    B8

    Name two pituitary tumors. Mention their significance.

    Two important pituitary tumours are the prolactin-secreting lactotroph tumour (prolactinoma) and the growth hormone-secreting somatotroph tumour. Both are pituitary neuroendocrine tumours (PitNETs, formerly pituitary adenomas) arising from the anterior lobe. Their significance lies in the hormone-excess syndromes they cause and in the local mass effects of an expanding sellar tumour.

    Complete explanation: PitNETs are the commonest cause of hyperpituitarism. They are classified by the hormone and lineage-specific transcription factor expressed by the tumour cells (POU1F1 for somatotroph, lactotroph and thyrotroph tumours. TBX19 for corticotroph tumours
    SF-1 for gonadotroph tumours). Histologically they are soft, circumscribed, composed of monotonous polygonal cells in sheets or cords with a sparse reticulin network, which distinguishes them from the mixed cell population and rich reticulin of normal anterior pituitary.

    The lactotroph tumour is the most common functioning PitNET. Hyperprolactinaemia produces amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, loss of libido and infertility, and is detected earlier in females than in males. Serum prolactin tends to rise in proportion to tumour size. Hyperprolactinaemia is not always due to a tumour: it also occurs in pregnancy, with dopamine-blocking drugs, with hypothyroidism and renal failure, and when any suprasellar mass interrupts the dopaminergic inhibition travelling down the pituitary stalk. Treatment is usually with dopamine agonists (bromocriptine or cabergoline).

    The somatotroph tumour secretes growth hormone, which stimulates hepatic IGF-1. In children before epiphyseal closure it causes gigantism. in adults it causes acromegaly, with enlargement of the jaw, hands, feet and viscera, together with glucose intolerance, hypertension and cardiomyopathy. These tumours are often large at diagnosis because the clinical changes are insidious.

    Any PitNET may cause mass effects: erosion of the sella turcica, compression of the optic chiasm (bitemporal hemianopia), headache, hypopituitarism through destruction of normal gland, and pituitary apoplexy after haemorrhage into the tumour. A corticotroph tumour causes Cushing disease [ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma].

    Thyroid Gland

    Hypothyroidism and goitre

    Mention four important causes of hypothyroidism.

    DU25N
    1. Hashimoto thyroiditis [autoimmune thyroiditis causing hypothyroidism]: the commonest cause in iodine-sufficient areas
    2. Postablative: surgery, radioiodine therapy or external irradiation
    3. Drugs: lithium, amiodarone, iodides, p-aminosalicylic acid, thionamides
    4. Congenital: endemic iodine deficiency (the commonest worldwide) and dyshormonogenetic goitre

    What is goitre?

    DU17Nov

    Goitre is enlargement of the thyroid gland. It can be associated with hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism or euthyroidism.

    What are the causes of goitre?

    DU18MDU17Nov

    1. Endemic goitre: low iodine in soil, water and food, as in the Andes and Himalayas 2. Sporadic goitre: - Ingestion of substances that interfere with thyroid hormone synthesis - Hereditary enzymatic defects (dyshormonogenetic goitre), autosomal recessive - No apparent cause in most cases 3. Multinodular goitre 4. Hashimoto thyroiditis [autoimmune thyroiditis causing hypothyroidism] 5. Graves disease [autoimmune hyperthyroidism]

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 24)p. 981p. 985

    Give the etiopathogenesis of multinodular goitre.

    DU18M
    • Recurrent episodes of hyperplasia and involution of a simple goitre produce irregular enlargement
    • Follicular cells vary in their response to external stimuli such as trophic hormones
    • Cells with a growth advantage, perhaps from acquired genetic abnormalities like those in adenomas, proliferate autonomously and form a nodule
    • Polyclonal and monoclonal nodules coexist in the same gland
    • It occurs in sporadic and endemic forms, in older individuals, as a late complication of simple goitre
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 24)p. 985p. 986

    Thyroiditis

    Write in short the pathogenesis of Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

    DU25NDU18NovDU11Ja

    1. A breakdown in self-tolerance to thyroid autoantigens, shown by autoantibodies against thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase 2. The inciting events are unknown
    Possibilities are abnormal regulatory T cells or exposure of sequestered thyroid antigens 3. Strong genetic component 4. Progressive depletion of thyroid epithelial cells, replaced by lymphocytic infiltrates and fibrosis, by: - CD8 positive cytotoxic T cell killing of follicular cells - Cytokine-mediated damage: CD4 positive Th1 cells produce interferon gamma, which activates macrophages - Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity and complement-dependent damage by antithyroid antibodies, though it is unclear if the antibodies are cause or consequence

    What are the expected laboratory findings in Hashimoto's thyroiditis?

    DU06Ja
    • Autoantibodies against thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase in the vast majority of patients
    • As hypothyroidism develops, T4 and T3 fall and TSH rises
    • Serum TSH is the most sensitive screening test for primary hypothyroidism
    • Early on there may be transient thyrotoxicosis (hashitoxicosis) from release of thyroid hormones

    Write a short note on papillary carcinoma of thyroid (microscopic morphology).

    DU17NovDU12Ja

    • Nuclei with finely dispersed chromatin and an optically clear appearance: ground-glass (Orphan Annie eye) nuclei

    Thyroid disease and tumors

    B8

    Tell two benign and four malignant tumors of the thyroid gland. Which malignancy is common in the thyroid gland? Mention its prognosis.

    Two benign thyroid tumours are follicular adenoma and oncocytic (Hürthle cell) adenoma. The four main malignant tumours are papillary carcinoma, follicular carcinoma, medullary carcinoma and anaplastic carcinoma. Papillary carcinoma is the most common, accounting for about 85% of thyroid cancers, and has an excellent prognosis with a 10-year survival above 95%.

    Complete explanation: Follicular adenoma is a solitary, encapsulated nodule of well-differentiated follicles that compresses adjacent gland. it is diagnosed only after the capsule has been examined and found to lack invasion. A minority are functioning (toxic adenoma).

    Among the malignant tumours, papillary carcinoma arises in young and middle-aged adults and spreads by lymphatics to cervical nodes. Follicular carcinoma spreads by blood. Medullary carcinoma arises from calcitonin-secreting C cells, about 70% sporadic and the rest in MEN-2 with germline RET mutations. Anaplastic carcinoma arises in the elderly, often from a pre-existing differentiated tumour, and is almost uniformly fatal within a year.

    Prognosis of papillary carcinoma is influenced by age (worse above 55), extrathyroidal extension and distant metastasis. Local recurrence occurs in 5–20% and distant spread in 10–15%.

    B8

    What is follicular adenoma and follicular carcinoma of thyroid gland? How will you differentiate them by FNAC?

    Follicular adenoma is a benign, encapsulated thyroid tumour of well-differentiated follicular cells, whereas follicular carcinoma is the malignant counterpart that shows capsular and/or vascular invasion. FNAC cannot separate them, because the cytology is identical. The distinction needs histological examination of the entire capsule.

    Complete explanation: Both tumours are composed of uniform follicles containing colloid, and both commonly harbour RAS mutations. Cytologically, an aspirate from either shows cellular smears of follicular cells in microfollicles without the nuclear features of papillary carcinoma. The decisive feature of carcinoma is invasion: penetration of the tumour capsule, invasion of vessels within or beyond the capsule (usually veins), or invasion of adjacent thyroid.

    Because this can be assessed only by extensive sampling of the capsule in the resected specimen, FNAC results are reported as "follicular neoplasm" and the nodule is surgically excised (lobectomy), with molecular testing sometimes helping to stratify indeterminate nodules. Adenomas do not recur or metastasise
    Follicular carcinoma spreads haematogenously to bone, lung and liver.

    B8

    What is hyperthyroidism? What are the types of hyperthyroidism?

    Hyperthyroidism is a hypermetabolic state caused by excess circulating thyroid hormone due to overactivity of the thyroid gland. Strictly, thyrotoxicosis is the broader term and includes causes in which hormone excess does not arise from gland hyperfunction. The commonest cause is Graves disease [autoimmune hyperthyroidism].

    Complete explanation: Types are as follows.

    Associated with increased gland function (true hyperthyroidism):

    • Primary: Graves disease (diffuse hyperplasia, about 85% of cases), toxic multinodular goitre (Plummer disease), toxic (hyperfunctioning) adenoma, iodine-induced hyperthyroidism, and neonatal thyrotoxicosis from maternal Graves disease.
    • Secondary: TSH-secreting pituitary tumour (rare)
      Here TSH is normal or raised.

    Thyrotoxicosis without increased gland function: granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis, painless thyroiditis, struma ovarii and factitious thyrotoxicosis from exogenous thyroxine.

    In all except the pituitary type, TSH is suppressed. The clinical effects are heat intolerance, weight loss with increased appetite, tachycardia and atrial fibrillation, tremor, anxiety, proximal myopathy, diarrhoea and osteoporosis, with a staring gaze and lid lag from sympathetic overactivity. Radioiodine uptake distinguishes diffuse increased uptake (Graves), a hot nodule (toxic adenoma) and low uptake (thyroiditis).

    B10

    A 30-year-old lady presented with diffuse enlargement of the thyroid gland with exophthalmos. What is your clinical diagnosis? What will be the status of the thyroid hormone level in this case? What is hypothyroidism? Tell some common causes of hypothyroidism.

    A young woman with a diffusely enlarged thyroid and exophthalmos has Graves disease [autoimmune hyperthyroidism], an autoimmune hyperthyroidism. Her thyroid hormone status will show raised free T₄ and T₃ with suppressed TSH. Hypothyroidism is the opposite state of thyroid hormone deficiency, caused most often by Hashimoto thyroiditis [autoimmune thyroiditis causing hypothyroidism], iodine deficiency and iatrogenic ablation.

    Complete explanation: Graves disease is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins that stimulate the TSH receptor. Free T₄ and T₃ are elevated and TSH is suppressed. Radioiodine uptake is diffusely increased and TSI/TRAb are present. The gland shows diffuse hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the epithelium with lymphoid infiltrates.

    Hypothyroidism is a state of structural or functional derangement that interferes with thyroid hormone production. It is classified as primary (intrinsic thyroid disease), secondary (pituitary) or tertiary (hypothalamic). Common causes are Hashimoto thyroiditis (most common in iodine-sufficient regions), endemic iodine deficiency, surgical or radioiodine ablation, drugs (lithium, amiodarone, thionamides), congenital biosynthetic defects and thyroid dysgenesis.

    Serum TSH is raised in primary disease and is the most sensitive screening test. In infancy, deficiency produces cretinism with intellectual disability. in adults it causes myxoedema with slowing of mental and physical activity, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, non-pitting oedema from glycosaminoglycan accumulation, and hypercholesterolaemia.

    B8

    Define and classify goiter.

    Goitre is enlargement of the thyroid gland. It is classified by pattern into diffuse and multinodular, and by function into non-toxic (euthyroid or hypothyroid) and toxic (hyperthyroid).

    Complete explanation

    1. Diffuse non-toxic (simple) goitre: the whole gland is enlarged without nodules. It is endemic (iodine deficiency, goitrogens) or sporadic (goitrogenic drugs, dyshormonogenesis, usually unknown cause). It evolves from a hyperplastic phase to a colloid involution phase.
    2. Multinodular goitre: irregular nodular enlargement resulting from recurrent hyperplasia and involution. Usually euthyroid, but occasionally toxic (Plummer disease).
    3. Diffuse toxic goitre: Graves disease [autoimmune hyperthyroidism].
    4. Goitrous thyroiditis: Hashimoto thyroiditis [autoimmune thyroiditis causing hypothyroidism] with goitre.
    5. Neoplastic enlargement from a tumour.

    The common mechanism is raised TSH from reduced hormone output, producing hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the follicular epithelium. in most patients the enlarged functional mass restores euthyroidism, and only when the defect is severe does goitrous hypothyroidism result. Clinical features arise mainly from mass effect.

    Diabetes Mellitus (Endocrine Pancreas)

    Diabetes mellitus

    B8

    What is hypoglycemia? Which one is more dangerous: hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia? Explain.

    Hypoglycaemia is a fall in blood glucose to a level low enough to cause symptoms of neuroglycopenia and adrenergic activation, generally below about 3.0 mmol/L (50–54 mg/dL). In the acute situation hypoglycaemia is the more immediately dangerous, because the brain depends on a continuous glucose supply and prolonged hypoglycaemia causes irreversible neuronal injury and death within hours. Hyperglycaemia is dangerous mainly through chronic complications, although severe acute hyperglycaemia (ketoacidosis, hyperosmolar state) is also life-threatening.

    Complete explanation: The brain accounts for about 20% of the body's oxygen consumption and is strictly dependent on aerobic glucose metabolism, so the cellular effects of glucose deprivation resemble those of hypoxia. The cortical pyramidal neurons, the CA1 (Sommer) sector of the hippocampus and the cerebellar Purkinje cells are especially vulnerable. Clinically, hypoglycaemia presents with dizziness, confusion, sweating, palpitations and tachycardia, progressing to loss of consciousness and coma.

    It most often complicates insulin or sulfonylurea therapy (missed meals, excess exercise, over-dosage), and also occurs with insulinoma, adrenal insufficiency and severe liver disease. Patients with long-standing frequent episodes may lose warning symptoms ("hypoglycaemia unawareness"), so that neurological impairment is the first sign. Rapid correction with oral or intravenous glucose prevents permanent damage.

    Chronic hyperglycaemia, by contrast, damages vessels and nerves slowly over 15 to 20 years, causing nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy and accelerated atherosclerosis.

    B8

    What is glycosylated hemoglobin? Tell its importance.

    Glycosylated haemoglobin (HbA1c) is haemoglobin A to which glucose has become non-enzymatically attached. Its level reflects the average blood glucose over the preceding two to three months, so it is the standard measure of long-term glycaemic control and is also used to diagnose diabetes.

    Complete explanation: Glucose combines non-enzymatically and irreversibly with the amino terminal valine of the β-chain of HbA, and the amount formed is proportional to the prevailing glucose concentration over the life span of the red cell (about 120 days), weighted towards the most recent weeks. It is not affected by day-to-day fluctuations or by fasting. A value of 6.5% or more is diagnostic of diabetes, 5.7–6.4% indicates prediabetes, and in most diabetic patients the treatment target is below 7%.

    Higher values correlate with a greater risk of microvascular complications. Results are unreliable in conditions altering red cell survival or haemoglobin structure (haemolytic anaemia, recent haemorrhage or transfusion, haemoglobinopathies, iron deficiency, chronic renal failure).

    B10

    A 50-year-old diabetic patient becomes unconscious following a chest infection. He did not take any antidiabetic drugs. He also developed a musty odor in the breath. What is the diagnosis? What may be the likely findings in urine analysis?

    A diabetic who becomes unconscious after a chest infection, omits insulin or antidiabetic treatment and has a fruity or musty odour on the breath has diabetic ketoacidosis. Urine analysis will show marked glycosuria and ketonuria.

    Complete explanation: Infection raises counter-regulatory hormones (epinephrine, glucagon, cortisol) that block insulin action while insulin is absent or insufficient. The combination of insulin deficiency and glucagon excess increases gluconeogenesis and lipolysis. Free fatty acids reach the liver and are converted to ketone bodies (acetoacetic acid and β-hydroxybutyric acid, with acetone, which causes the odour).

    Hyperglycaemia (usually 250–600 mg/dL) causes osmotic diuresis and dehydration
    Ketone accumulation causes metabolic acidosis with deep, laboured (Kussmaul) breathing, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain, and eventually coma. In the urine one finds heavy glycosuria, positive ketones on nitroprusside testing, an acid reaction and a high specific gravity. Protein and pus cells may be present if there is renal involvement or infection.

    Blood shows high glucose, ketonaemia, low bicarbonate and pH, raised anion gap, and a total body potassium deficit even though serum potassium may be initially raised.

    B8

    What is OGTT? Discuss its procedure. Name the indications for OGTT. What are renal and alimentary glycosuria?

    The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) measures the body's ability to dispose of a standard oral glucose load. After a 75 g glucose load in an adult, a two-hour plasma glucose of 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or more establishes diabetes, whereas 7.8–11.0 mmol/L defines impaired glucose tolerance. Renal glycosuria is glucose in urine despite normal blood glucose because of a low renal threshold, and alimentary glycosuria is transient glycosuria after a meal due to rapid absorption.

    Complete explanation

    Procedure. The patient eats an unrestricted, carbohydrate-adequate diet (at least 150 g daily) for three days and remains physically active, and fasts for 8–14 hours overnight with no smoking or exercise. A fasting blood sample is taken. The patient drinks 75 g anhydrous glucose dissolved in about 250–300 mL water within five minutes (1.75 g/kg up to 75 g in children). A further sample is taken at two hours, with additional samples at 30-minute intervals when a curve is wanted. Urine may be tested at each interval.

    Indications. Borderline fasting glucose (impaired fasting glucose)
    Suspected diabetes with a normal fasting value
    Screening for gestational diabetes at 24–28 weeks
    Unexplained glycosuria
    Unexplained neuropathy, retinopathy or nephropathy. and assessment of high-risk individuals such as the obese and those with a family history.

    Interpretation.

    CategoryFasting2-h plasma glucose
    Normalbelow 5.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL)below 7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL)
    Impaired fasting glucose / IGT5.6–6.9 / —— / 7.8–11.0
    Diabetes7.0 or more11.1 or more

    Renal glycosuria: the renal tubular threshold (about 10 mmol/L or 180 mg/dL) is abnormally low (familial, pregnancy, tubular disease), so glucose appears in urine although the OGTT curve is normal.

    Alimentary (lag-storage) glycosuria: rapid absorption after gastrectomy, gastroenterostomy or thyrotoxicosis produces a high early peak above the renal threshold with glycosuria, but fasting and 2-hour values are normal.

    B8

    Classify diabetes mellitus. What is gestational diabetes mellitus?

    Diabetes mellitus is classified by pathogenesis into type 1, type 2, other specific types and gestational diabetes. Gestational diabetes is glucose intolerance first recognised during pregnancy.

    Complete explanation

    1. Type 1 diabetes: autoimmune β-cell destruction leading to absolute insulin deficiency (5–10% of cases).
    2. Type 2 diabetes: insulin resistance with inadequate β-cell compensation (90–95%).
    3. Other specific types:
      • Monogenic β-cell defects: maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY, HNF1A, HNF4A, GCK and others), neonatal diabetes (KCNJ11, ABCC8), maternally inherited diabetes and deafness (mitochondrial DNA), insulin gene mutations.
      • Genetic defects of insulin action (insulin receptor mutations, type A insulin resistance).
      • Exocrine pancreatic disease ("type 3c"): chronic pancreatitis, pancreatectomy or trauma, pancreatic cancer, cystic fibrosis, haemochromatosis.
      • Endocrinopathies: Cushing syndrome [glucocorticoid excess], acromegaly, phaeochromocytoma, glucagonoma, hyperthyroidism.
      • Drug- or chemical-induced: glucocorticoids, thiazides, nicotinic acid, phenytoin, β-adrenergic agonists.
      • Infections (congenital rubella, cytomegalovirus) and genetic syndromes (Down, Turner [45,X monosomy], Klinefelter [47,XXY]).
    4. Gestational diabetes mellitus: glucose intolerance first detected in pregnancy, which occurs because pregnancy is a diabetogenic state. it usually resolves after delivery but most affected women develop overt diabetes within 10 to 20 years.
    B8

    Name the ketone bodies. What are the causes of ketonuria?

    The ketone bodies are acetoacetic acid, β-hydroxybutyric acid and acetone. Ketonuria occurs whenever fat is being oxidised faster than the tissues can use the ketones formed, most importantly in uncontrolled diabetes, but also in starvation and prolonged vomiting.

    Complete explanation: Ketone bodies are produced in hepatic mitochondria from acetyl coenzyme A derived from fatty acids. β-hydroxybutyrate is quantitatively the main one in ketoacidosis, whereas the routine nitroprusside (Rothera) test detects acetoacetate and acetone only. They are normally used as fuel by muscle, heart and brain, and when production outstrips use they appear in blood (ketonaemia) and urine (ketonuria).

    Causes of ketonuria:

    • Diabetic ketoacidosis (insulin deficiency).
    • Starvation, prolonged fasting, very low carbohydrate diet.
    • Persistent vomiting (hyperemesis of pregnancy, pyloric stenosis) and severe diarrhoea.
    • Alcoholic ketoacidosis
      Febrile illness in children
      thyrotoxicosis.
    • Glycogen storage diseases, and treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors.
    B8

    What is diabetic ketoacidosis? How does diabetic ketoacidosis develop in a case of uncontrolled diabetes?

    Diabetic ketoacidosis develops when a profound deficiency of insulin, together with excess glucagon and other stress hormones, causes unrestrained lipolysis and hepatic ketone production, together with severe hyperglycaemia and osmotic dehydration. It is mainly a complication of type 1 diabetes.

    Complete explanation: The usual precipitant is omission of insulin, or infection, trauma or other stress. Epinephrine and other stress hormones antagonise residual insulin and stimulate glucagon secretion. The glucagon-to-insulin imbalance reduces peripheral glucose utilisation and increases hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, so that plasma glucose rises to 250–600 mg/dL. Glucose exceeds the renal threshold, causing osmotic diuresis, loss of water and electrolytes and dehydration.

    Insulin deficiency also activates hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue, which releases free fatty acids. In the liver these are converted to fatty acyl coenzyme A and oxidised to acetoacetic acid and β-hydroxybutyric acid. The rate of formation exceeds peripheral use, causing ketonaemia and ketonuria. When dehydration limits renal excretion of ketones, systemic metabolic acidosis results. Protein catabolism supplies ketogenic amino acids and aggravates the process.

    Patients present with fatigue, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fruity breath and Kussmaul respiration, and become drowsy and comatose if untreated. Ketoacidosis is less frequent in type 2 diabetes because the higher portal insulin level restrains hepatic fatty acid oxidation. Type 2 patients are more liable to a hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state. Treatment consists of insulin, fluid and electrolyte replacement and correction of the precipitating cause.

    B8

    Tell the pathogenesis of type-2 diabetes mellitus.

    Type 2 diabetes results from the combination of insulin resistance in peripheral tissues and a failure of the pancreatic β cells to compensate, producing relative insulin deficiency. Genetic susceptibility and obesity, especially visceral obesity, are the main determinants.

    Complete explanation: There is no autoimmune basis.

    Genetic factors. Concordance in monozygotic twins exceeds 90%, and first-degree relatives have a 5- to 10-fold increased risk. Genome-wide studies have identified more than 30 loci (such as TCF7L2) of modest effect, many involved in β-cell function, adipose tissue function and obesity.

    Insulin resistance. Insulin resistance usually precedes hyperglycaemia. Its consequences are failure to suppress hepatic gluconeogenesis (high fasting glucose), reduced glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis in skeletal muscle after meals (high postprandial glucose), and uncontrolled lipolysis in adipose tissue (high free fatty acids). Defects include reduced tyrosine phosphorylation of the insulin receptor and IRS proteins and decreased GLUT-4 translocation.

    Obesity contributes through several mechanisms: excess free fatty acids that generate toxic lipid intermediates (diacylglycerol, ceramides) and impair insulin signalling. Altered adipokines with lowered adiponectin
    Chronic inflammation, in which fatty acids activate the inflammasome and release IL-1β and other cytokines. and hepatic steatosis (MASLD).

    β-cell dysfunction. Initially the β cells hypersecrete and hyperinsulinaemia maintains euglycaemia. Eventually they fail, through lipotoxicity from excess fatty acids, glucotoxicity, a blunted incretin effect (reduced GIP and GLP-1 action), and islet amyloid deposition (found in over 90% of long-standing cases), together with genetic effects on insulin secretion.

    Other risk factors are a sedentary lifestyle, sleep disorders and circadian disruption. The combination of obesity, hyperglycaemia, dyslipidaemia and hypertension is the metabolic syndrome.

    B8

    What are the macroscopic complications of diabetes mellitus? What is hypoglycemic coma?

    The macroscopic (macrovascular) complications of diabetes result from accelerated atherosclerosis of the aorta and large and medium-sized arteries, causing myocardial infarction, stroke and peripheral vascular disease with gangrene. Hypoglycaemic coma is unconsciousness from a fall in blood glucose, usually due to excessive insulin or sulfonylurea dosage.

    Complete explanation: Persistent hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance cause widespread endothelial dysfunction, which predisposes to atherosclerosis that is histologically identical to that in non-diabetics but occurs earlier and more severely. Hypertension and dyslipidaemia (high triglycerides and LDL, low HDL) potentiate it. Myocardial infarction is the most common cause of death in diabetes and is almost as common in diabetic women as in men. Cerebrovascular disease and renal artery atherosclerosis follow, and gangrene of the lower limbs is about 100 times more frequent than in the general population.

    Gross renal changes include diffuse granular, contracted kidneys from arteriolosclerosis and nephrosclerosis, and pyelonephritis with papillary necrosis.

    The microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) are due to diffuse basement-membrane thickening and increased capillary permeability.

    Hypoglycaemic coma follows missed meals, exertion or inappropriate dosing. The patient is cold, pale and sweating with tachycardia and hunger, then confused and unconscious. It requires immediate oral or intravenous glucose, since prolonged hypoglycaemia causes permanent neuronal damage, especially of the cortex and hippocampus.

    B8

    Define diabetes mellitus. Give the WHO diagnostic criteria of diabetes mellitus.

    Diabetes mellitus is a group of metabolic disorders sharing the feature of hyperglycaemia caused by defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or most commonly both. By WHO and ADA criteria it is diagnosed by a fasting plasma glucose of 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or more, a two-hour OGTT value or random glucose of 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or more with classic symptoms, or an HbA1c of 6.5% or more.

    Complete explanation: The chronic hyperglycaemia causes secondary damage in the kidneys, eyes, nerves and blood vessels, and diabetes is a leading cause of end-stage renal disease, blindness and non-traumatic amputation. Diagnostic criteria (any one; all except a symptomatic random glucose must be confirmed on a separate day, and if two tests disagree the more abnormal result is accepted):

    1. Fasting plasma glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L).
    2. Random plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) in a patient with classic symptoms.
    3. Two-hour plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL during a 75 g OGTT.
    4. HbA1c ≥ 6.5%.

    Acute stresses such as infection, burns or trauma can cause transient hyperglycaemia, so persistence after recovery is required.
