    OGTT and glucose tolerance

    What is OGTT? Write its procedure, indications and interpretation.

    8DU24MDU22NDU21MDU18NovDU17MDU15JaDU13JuDU11Ja

    OGTT is the oral glucose tolerance test, in which plasma glucose is measured 2 hours after a loading dose of 75 g of glucose.

    Interpretation

    2-hour plasma glucoseMeaning
    200 mg/dL or moreDiabetes
    140 to 199 mg/dLImpaired glucose tolerance
    • As many as one-quarter of individuals with impaired glucose tolerance develop overt diabetes over 5 years
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 24)p. 998p. 999

    What is the normal fasting blood glucose level?

    DU15Ja
    • Blood glucose is normally maintained in a narrow range of 70 to 120 mg/dL
    • A fasting plasma glucose of 100 to 125 mg/dL is impaired fasting glucose
    • A fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or more is diabetes
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 24)p. 998p. 999

    What is impaired glucose tolerance (IGT)?

    DU15JaDU12Ja

    Impaired glucose tolerance is a 2-hour plasma glucose between 140 and 199 mg/dL following a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test.

    • It is one of the criteria of prediabetes, a state of dysglycaemia that often precedes type 2 diabetes
    • The others are impaired fasting glucose (fasting plasma glucose 100 to 125 mg/dL) and an HbA1c of 5.7% to 6.4%
    • Individuals with prediabetes are also at significant risk of cardiovascular complications
    • A fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or more, or a 2-hour value of 200 mg/dL or more, is diabetes rather than prediabetes
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 24)p. 999

    Draw different types of diabetic curves.

    DU09Ja
    Glucose tolerance curveFasting plasma glucose2-hour plasma glucose after 75 g
    Diabetic126 mg/dL or more200 mg/dL or more
    Impaired glucose toleranceMay be 100 to 125 mg/dL140 to 199 mg/dL
    NormalWithin 70 to 120 mg/dLBelow 140 mg/dL

    HbA1c

    A6

    What is HbA1c (glycosylated haemoglobin)?

    6A6DU25NDU20NDU20JuDU16JuDU04M

    Also asked as: What is HbA1c?

    • HbA1c is haemoglobin in the red cell that has become bound to glucose by a nonenzymatic process during its circulating life span of about 120 days
    • The amount formed is proportional to the average blood glucose
    • It therefore reflects the average blood glucose of the previous 2 to 3 months
    • A fasting sample is not needed
    A6

    Importance of HbA1c.

    A6
    1. Diagnosis of diabetes: a level of 6.5% or more
    2. Diagnosis of prediabetes: a level of 5.7% to 6.4%
    3. Monitoring long-term glycaemic control in type 1 and type 2 diabetes
    4. It is not affected by the daily fluctuations seen with single glucose readings
    5. Used to judge the effect of treatment, usually every 3 months

    Hyperglycaemia

    What is hyperglycaemia?

    DU12Ju

    Hyperglycaemia is a raised blood glucose level.

    • It is the common feature of all forms of diabetes mellitus
    • Persistent hyperglycaemia (glucotoxicity) is responsible for many of the long-term complications of diabetes

    Mention the important causes of hyperglycaemia.

    DU05M
    1. Diabetes mellitus: type 1, type 2, monogenic forms, gestational
    2. Acute stress: severe infections, burns or trauma cause transient hyperglycaemia through catecholamines and cortisol, which oppose insulin
    3. Exocrine pancreatic disease: chronic pancreatitis, pancreatectomy, pancreatic cancer, cystic fibrosis
    4. Drugs: thiazides, nicotinic acid, phenytoin, β-adrenergic agonists
    5. Pregnancy, which favours insulin resistance

    What is hyperglycaemia sine glycosuria? Why is sugar absent in urine?

    4DU22NDU21MDU09JuDU08Ju
    • In diabetes the filtered glucose exceeds the renal tubular threshold for reabsorption, so glucose appears in the urine
    • Sugar is therefore absent from the urine when the filtered glucose does not exceed the tubular threshold for reabsorption

    Complications and ketoacidosis

    Write the complications of diabetes mellitus (macro- and microvascular).

    14DU26MDU25MDU22MDU20NDU20JuDU19NovDU18NovDU18MDU17NovDU17MDU17JaDU15JaDU13JuDU12Ju

    Macrovascular (damage to large and medium-sized muscular arteries)

    • Accelerated atherosclerosis
    • Myocardial infarction, stroke and lower extremity ischaemia
    • Hypertension in about 75% of those with type 2 diabetes
    • Two to four times greater incidence of coronary artery disease

    Microvascular (damage to small vessels)

    • Diabetic retinopathy: 60% to 80% develop it
      Leading cause of adult blindness
      Neovascularisation from hypoxia-induced VEGF
      Also cataract and glaucoma
    • Diabetic nephropathy: 30% to 40% develop it
      First sign is moderately increased albuminuria (30 to 300 mg per day)
    • Diabetic neuropathy: distal symmetric polyneuropathy in a glove-and-stocking pattern, autonomic neuropathy and mononeuropathy

    Other

    • Infections of the skin, tuberculosis, pneumonia and pyelonephritis
    • Acute: diabetic ketoacidosis, hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state and hypoglycaemia
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 24)p. 1006p. 1010

    What are ketone bodies (ketonuria)?

    DU16JuDU11JuDU10Ja
    • Ketone bodies are acetoacetic acid and β-hydroxybutyric acid
    • They are produced in the liver mitochondria by oxidation of fatty acyl coenzyme A, when insulin deficiency raises free fatty acids
    • When their formation exceeds their use by peripheral tissues, ketonaemia and ketonuria result

    Write a short note on ketoacidosis / discuss the pathogenesis of DKA.

    7DU26MDU24NDU23NDU19MDU17JaDU11JuDU12Ju

    Definition. Diabetic ketoacidosis is a severe acute metabolic complication mainly seen in type 1 diabetes.

    Pathogenesis

    1. A precipitating factor, most often failure to take insulin, or infection, illness, trauma or drugs
    2. These release epinephrine, which blocks residual insulin action and stimulates glucagon
    3. Insulin deficiency with glucagon excess decreases peripheral glucose use and increases gluconeogenesis, so plasma glucose reaches 250 to 600 mg/dL
    4. Hyperglycaemia causes osmotic diuresis and dehydration
    5. Insulin deficiency stimulates hormone-sensitive lipase, so fat breakdown raises free fatty acids
    6. In the liver these form ketone bodies faster than they can be used, leading to ketonaemia and ketonuria
    7. Dehydration compromises urinary excretion of ketones, giving metabolic ketoacidosis

    Clinical features. Fatigue, nausea and vomiting, severe abdominal pain, a characteristic fruity odour, and deep laboured (Kussmaul) breathing. Persistence leads to depressed consciousness and coma.

    Treatment. Insulin, correction of metabolic acidosis, and treatment of the precipitating factor.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 24)p. 1005

    A 48y diabetic became unconscious after chest infection with musty odour in breath. What may be the likely urine finding?

    DU12Ju

    Diabetic ketoacidosis

    • Infection is a recognised precipitating factor
    • Insulin deficiency and raised ketone bodies cause metabolic ketoacidosis, with a characteristic fruity odour of the breath
    • Persistence of the ketotic state leads to depressed consciousness and coma
    • Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state is the alternative in type 2 diabetes, but it has no ketoacidosis symptoms

    Diabetes cases

    A 58y obese male has weight loss, FBS 6.6, RBS 10.0 mmol/L, raised lipids. What is the diagnosis?

    DU11Ju

    Type 2 diabetes mellitus, or prediabetes progressing to it, in an obese patient. The values do not yet confirm diabetes.

    • The fasting glucose of 6.6 mmol/L and the random glucose of 10.0 mmol/L are below the diagnostic cut-offs of 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) fasting and 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) random
    • They fall in the range of impaired fasting glucose
    • Type 2 diabetes is typically seen in obese patients older than 40 years, and dyslipidaemia is a frequent accompanying risk
    • Weight loss with hyperglycaemia should raise suspicion of diabetes

    Same: how will you investigate the case?

    DU11Ju
    1. Repeat fasting plasma glucose on a separate day
    2. Oral glucose tolerance test with 75 g glucose: 2-hour value of 200 mg/dL or more confirms diabetes
      140 to 199 mg/dL is impaired glucose tolerance
    3. HbA1c: 6.5% or more confirms diabetes
      5.7% to 6.4% is prediabetes
    4. Test for complications: urinary albumin (first sign of nephropathy), eye examination for retinopathy, assessment of neuropathy

    The Skin

    16 questions · viva and written, in Robbins order.

    Terminology and Normal Skin

    B9

    Common terminology of skin: papule, pustule, vesicles, bulla, blister, wheal, macule, patch.

    These are the descriptive terms used for primary skin lesions. Macules and patches are flat lesions distinguished only by colour, the macule being less than 5 mm and the patch larger. Papules are solid elevations less than 5 mm. Vesicles and bullae are fluid-filled blisters, smaller and larger than 5 mm respectively. A pustule is a pus-filled elevation, and a wheal is a transient, oedematous, pale-pink raised plaque.

    Complete explanation: Dermatopathology begins with a precise clinical vocabulary, because the distribution and character of a lesion often point to the diagnosis before any tissue is examined.

    TermDefinition
    MaculeFlat, circumscribed area of colour change, less than 5 mm in diameter.
    PatchA flat lesion of altered colour larger than 5 mm.
    PapuleSolid, elevated, dome-shaped or flat-topped lesion less than 5 mm in diameter.
    VesicleFluid-filled, raised lesion less than 5 mm in diameter, lying within or just beneath the epidermis.
    BullaA fluid-filled, raised lesion larger than 5 mm.
    BlisterGeneral term for a fluid-filled lesion, covering both vesicle and bulla.
    PustuleDiscrete, raised lesion filled with pus, i.e. neutrophils and debris.
    WhealFirm, oedematous, pale-pink, transient plaque produced by dermal oedema and typically itchy, as in urticaria
    it resolves within hours without leaving a mark.

    A plaque is the larger counterpart of the papule: an elevated, flat-topped lesion greater than 5 mm in diameter, usually produced by confluent papules. The size limit of 5 mm is the conventional dividing line between each small and large pair.

    B9

    Structure of the skin. What are parakeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis and spongiosis?

    The skin consists of the epidermis, the dermis and the subcutis, with appendages such as hair follicles and sweat and sebaceous glands. The epidermis is a keratinising stratified squamous epithelium of basal, spinous, granular and cornified layers. Parakeratosis is retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum, hypergranulosis is thickening of the granular layer, acanthosis is thickening of the epidermis from hyperplasia of the spinous layer, and spongiosis is intercellular oedema of the epidermis.

    Complete explanation

    Structure of the skin. The epidermis is a stratified squamous epithelium whose principal cell, the keratinocyte, matures as it moves upward from the basal layer. The deepest layer, the stratum basale, is a single row of cuboidal cells attached to the basement membrane by hemidesmosomes. it contains the proliferating stem cells. Above it lies the stratum spinosum, whose cells are joined by desmosomes, giving the spiny appearance on fixation.

    Next is the stratum granulosum, with coarse basophilic keratohyalin granules that contribute to the cornified envelope. The outermost layer, the stratum corneum, consists of flattened, anucleate, keratin-filled squames that form the barrier. on the palms and soles a clear stratum lucidum may be identified. Interspersed among the keratinocytes are melanocytes in the basal layer, which transfer melanin to neighbouring keratinocytes and protect the nuclei from ultraviolet radiation, Langerhans cells, which are antigen-presenting dendritic cells in the spinous layer, and Merkel cells [neuroendocrine touch-receptor cell of the epidermis], which are touch-related neuroendocrine cells.

    The epidermis is separated from the dermis by the basement membrane zone, which anchors it and whose components (hemidesmosomal proteins, laminin, type VII collagen) are targeted in several blistering diseases. The dermis has a superficial papillary layer of loose connective tissue containing capillary loops, and a deeper, denser reticular layer of thick collagen bundles and elastic fibres, with blood vessels, lymphatics, nerves and sensory receptors.

    The subcutis is composed of lobules of fat separated by fibrous septa. The appendages (pilosebaceous units, eccrine and apocrine sweat glands, and nails) arise from the epidermis and extend into the dermis.

    Descriptive terms

    • Parakeratosis is the retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum. It indicates rapid epidermal turnover with incomplete maturation of keratinocytes, and it is accompanied by a thin or absent granular layer, as in psoriasis.
    • Hypergranulosis is an increase in the thickness of the stratum granulosum, usually a response to chronic rubbing or scratching, and a prominent feature of lichen planus.
    • Acanthosis is diffuse epithelial hyperplasia, with thickening of the stratum spinosum, and is a common response to chronic irritation or growth factors.
    • Spongiosis is intercellular oedema of the epidermis. The oedema stretches the intercellular bridges so that the keratinocytes are pulled apart. it is the hallmark of eczematous dermatitis, and when severe it forms intraepidermal vesicles.

    Related terms that complete the group are hyperkeratosis (thickening of the stratum corneum), acantholysis (loss of intercellular cohesion between keratinocytes, as in pemphigus), and dyskeratosis (premature, abnormal keratinisation of individual cells).

    Blistering (Vesiculobullous) Diseases

    B9

    What are the blistering diseases of the skin?

    The blistering diseases of the skin are classified by the level at which the blister forms. Pemphigus vulgaris and pemphigus foliaceus form intraepidermal blisters through acantholysis. Bullous pemphigoid, dermatitis herpetiformis, epidermolysis bullosa and porphyria cutanea tarda form subepidermal blisters. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and impetigo produce subcorneal blisters.

    Complete explanation: In vesiculobullous disease, a blister arises either within the epidermis, from damage to desmosomes and keratinocyte cohesion, or beneath it, from damage to the basement membrane zone. The distinction is clinically important because intraepidermal blisters have a thin roof and rupture easily, producing erosions, whereas subepidermal blisters have a full-thickness roof and remain tense and intact.

    DiseaseLevel of splitMechanismCharacteristic findings
    Pemphigus vulgarisSuprabasal (intraepidermal)Type II hypersensitivity

    Nikolsky sign positive
    "row of tombstones" basal cells
    Fishnet intercellular IgG on immunofluorescence

    Mucosa spared
    Bullous pemphigoidSubepidermalIgG to BP180 and BP230 (hemidesmosomal proteins) with complement activation and eosinophilsTense bullae in the elderly on flexures
    Linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane
    Dermatitis herpetiformisSubepidermal at papillary tipsIgA against epidermal/tissue transglutaminase, associated with coeliac diseaseIntensely itchy grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces

    Erythema multiforme, Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are acute inflammatory dermatoses that may also produce blisters through keratinocyte necrosis at the dermoepidermal junction, and viral infections such as herpes simplex and varicella produce intraepidermal vesicles through ballooning degeneration.

    Tumors of the Epidermis

    Premalignant and malignant skin tumors

    B9

    Name some pre-malignant conditions of the skin.

    The important premalignant conditions of the skin are actinic (solar) keratosis, Bowen disease, arsenical and radiation keratoses, xeroderma pigmentosum, leukoplakia of mucosal surfaces, long-standing scars and chronic ulcers, and the dysplastic naevus.

    Complete explanation: Many cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas, and a proportion of melanomas, arise from recognisable precursor lesions in which cumulative DNA damage has already produced cytological atypia.

    • Actinic keratosis is the commonest premalignant lesion. It appears on sun-exposed skin of fair-skinned older people as a small, rough, scaly erythematous or brown patch. Microscopically there is atypia of the basal keratinocytes with parakeratosis and solar elastosis in the dermis. Malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma is uncommon for any single lesion but cumulatively significant.
    • Bowen disease is squamous cell carcinoma in situ, with full-thickness epidermal atypia but an intact basement membrane.
    • Arsenical keratosis and radiation dermatitis result from chemical or ionising carcinogen exposure and are followed by squamous carcinoma after a long latent interval.
    • Xeroderma pigmentosum is an autosomal recessive defect of nucleotide excision repair, producing multiple cancers at a young age on exposure to sunlight.
    • Leukoplakia and lichen sclerosus of the oral or genital mucosa carry a risk of squamous carcinoma.
    • Chronic scars, burn scars, sinus tracts and non-healing ulcers may give rise to squamous carcinoma (Marjolin ulcer).
    • Dysplastic naevus, particularly in the familial dysplastic naevus syndrome, is both a marker of increased risk and a precursor of melanoma.
    B9

    Name some important tumors of the skin. Mention the locally malignant tumor of the skin.

    The important tumours of the skin include benign tumours such as seborrhoeic keratosis, naevi, adnexal tumours and dermatofibroma, and malignant tumours such as squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma and malignant melanoma, together with Kaposi sarcoma [HHV-8-associated vascular tumour] and cutaneous lymphoma. The locally malignant tumour of the skin is basal cell carcinoma.

    Complete explanation: Skin tumours may be grouped according to the cell of origin.

    OriginBenignMalignant (or premalignant)
    Epidermal keratinocytesSeborrhoeic keratosis, acanthosis nigricans, keratoacanthoma, epidermal cystActinic keratosis (premalignant), squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma
    MelanocytesMelanocytic naeviMalignant melanoma
    AppendagesTrichoepithelioma, pilomatricoma, sweat gland adenomasSebaceous, sweat gland carcinomas
    Dermal connective tissueDermatofibroma, haemangioma, neurofibromaDermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, Kaposi sarcoma, angiosarcoma
    Lymphoid and neuroendocrine cells—Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides), Merkel cell [neuroendocrine touch-receptor cell of the epidermis] carcinoma

    Basal cell carcinoma is the locally malignant tumour of the skin. It invades and destroys adjacent tissue (rodent ulcer) and recurs after inadequate excision, but it very rarely metastasises.

    Basal cell carcinoma

    B9

    What do you mean by basal cell carcinoma? Sites of basal cell carcinoma. Mention the morphology of basal cell carcinoma.

    Basal cell carcinoma is a distinctive, locally aggressive cutaneous tumour associated with mutations that activate the Hedgehog signalling pathway. It is the commonest cancer in humans and is locally invasive but rarely metastasises. It occurs mainly on sun-exposed skin of the face, especially the nose, cheeks, forehead and inner canthus. Grossly it is a pearly papule with telangiectasia that may ulcerate, and microscopically it shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading.

    Complete explanation: Basal cell carcinoma arises from the basal cells of the epidermis and follicular epithelium, and in the great majority of cases it is associated with cumulative exposure to ultraviolet light. It is more frequent in fair-skinned people, in those with xeroderma pigmentosum, in chronic arsenic exposure and in immunosuppression. Most cases carry mutations in the Hedgehog signalling pathway, usually inactivating PTCH1
    Germline PTCH1 mutations underlie the basal cell naevus syndrome (Gorlin syndrome [basal cell naevus syndrome from PTCH1 mutation]), characterised by multiple basal cell carcinomas appearing early, jaw keratocysts and skeletal abnormalities. TP53 mutations arising from UV damage are also frequent.

    Sites. Tumours occur on hair-bearing, sun-exposed skin, particularly the face (nose, inner canthus, cheeks, forehead and upper lip), the ears and the scalp. The palms, soles and mucosal surfaces are only rarely involved.

    Morphology. Grossly, the lesion begins as a small, pearly, dome-shaped papule with prominent overlying telangiectatic vessels. It enlarges slowly and may ulcerate centrally, leaving a crusted ulcer with a raised, rolled, pearly edge (rodent ulcer). Some tumours contain melanin and appear brown or black, and a sclerosing form resembles a scar.

    Microscopically, the tumour consists of nests, cords and islands of basaloid cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and scanty cytoplasm, resembling the cells of the normal basal layer, within a stroma. The cells at the periphery of each nest are arranged in a regular, palisading fashion, while those in the centre are haphazardly arranged. A characteristic retraction space (cleft) separates the tumour nests from the surrounding mucinous stroma.

    Mitoses and apoptotic cells are usually numerous. The tumour often grows in the superficial, nodular, infiltrative or sclerosing (morpheaform) patterns, the last two being more aggressive and more likely to recur.

    Behaviour. The tumour grows slowly, destroying the skin, cartilage and even bone, notably around the eye and nose, but metastasis is extremely rare. Complete excision, Mohs surgery or radiotherapy is curative in most cases.

    Write a short note on basal cell carcinoma.

    DU10JuDU08Ju

    Definition. Basal cell carcinoma is a distinctive locally aggressive cutaneous tumour associated with mutations that activate the Hedgehog signalling pathway. It is the most common invasive cancer in humans. It is slow growing and rarely metastasises.

    Aetiology and pathogenesis

    • Occurs at sun-exposed sites in lightly pigmented older adults
    • Incidence is increased in immunosuppression and in disorders of DNA repair such as xeroderma pigmentosum
    • Nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome [basal cell naevus syndrome from PTCH1 mutation], basal cell naevus syndrome): autosomal dominant
      Multiple basal cell carcinomas often before age 20 years, with medulloblastomas, ovarian fibromas, odontogenic keratocysts and pits of the palms and soles
    • Gene is PTCH (9q22), a tumour-suppressor gene: germline loss-of-function mutation in one allele, with the second allele inactivated in tumours
    • PTCH is the receptor for sonic hedgehog (SHH)
      it normally blocks SMO. Loss of PTCH function causes constitutive activation of SMO and the transcription factor GLI1
    • Hedgehog-activating mutations are also common in sporadic tumours
      About one-third of PTCH mutations are C to T transitions, the hallmark of UV damage

    Morphology

    • Pearly papules with prominent dilated subepidermal blood vessels (telangiectasias)
      These may be less prominent in darker skin
    • Some tumours contain melanin and resemble naevi or melanomas
    • Advanced lesions may ulcerate, and extensive local invasion of bone or facial sinuses may follow years of neglect, hence the name rodent ulcers
    • Superficial basal cell carcinoma is an erythematous, occasionally pigmented plaque that may mimic melanoma
    • Tumour cells resemble the basal cell layer of the epidermis. They arise from the epidermis or follicular epithelium and do not occur on mucosal surfaces
    • Two patterns: multifocal superficial growth from the epidermis, and nodular growth into the dermis as cords and islands of basophilic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei in a mucinous matrix
    • Palisading of the peripheral cells of the islands, with retraction clefts between tumour and stroma
      The clefts help to separate it from appendage tumours such as trichoepithelioma

    Clinical features and complications

    • Metastasis is very rare
      Fewer than 0.5% are locally aggressive and disfiguring
    • Most are cured by local excision
    • Locally advanced or metastatic disease often responds to Hedgehog pathway inhibitors or immune checkpoint inhibitors
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 25)p. 1041p. 1043

    Squamous cell carcinoma

    B9

    Most common malignant tumor of the skin. Morphology of squamous cell carcinoma.

    Basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignant tumour of the skin, and squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common. Squamous cell carcinoma is a malignant tumour of keratinocytes. Grossly it is a crusted, scaly, ulcerated nodule on sun-exposed skin, and microscopically it shows invasive nests of atypical squamous cells with intercellular bridges and keratin pearls.

    Complete explanation: Basal cell carcinoma is the commonest skin malignancy overall. Squamous cell carcinoma is the second commonest, although in people with darker skin pigmentation it is often the more frequent skin cancer.

    Squamous cell carcinoma occurs mainly in older people on sun-exposed skin: the face, ears, scalp, lower lip, dorsum of the hands and forearms. Other causes are chronic arsenic ingestion, ionising radiation, tar and oil exposure, chronic ulcers, burn scars and draining sinus tracts, immunosuppression (especially after organ transplantation) and human papillomavirus infection in the anogenital region. UV light is the principal factor, producing characteristic mutations in TP53 and others.

    Morphology. The earliest lesion is the in situ carcinoma (Bowen disease or its precursor actinic keratosis), presenting grossly as a sharply defined, red, scaly plaque, and microscopically as full-thickness atypia of the epidermal cells with an intact basement membrane. When the tumour becomes invasive, the gross appearance is of a firm, keratotic, crusted, nodular lesion which tends to ulcerate, forming an ulcer with an indurated, raised, everted edge.

    Microscopically, the invasive tumour consists of irregular nests, cords and sheets of atypical squamous epithelial cells, which infiltrate the dermis and sometimes deeper tissues. Well-differentiated tumours form keratin pearls and show prominent intercellular bridges, with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Poorly differentiated tumours show greater nuclear pleomorphism, numerous mitoses including atypical forms, little keratinisation, and sometimes a spindled pattern.

    Behaviour. Metastasis, chiefly to regional lymph nodes, is much more likely than for basal cell carcinoma, but still uncommon for tumours arising in sun-damaged skin. The risk is greater for tumours that arise on the lip, ear, or in scars, burns, irradiated skin or the immunosuppressed, and for large, deep and poorly differentiated tumours or those with perineural invasion.

    B10

    A 72-year-old male has developed an ulcerative lesion in his right great toe for the last 6 months. It has been gradually spreading for the last month. He also noticed a swelling in his right inguinal region. What are the probable diagnoses? How will you investigate the patient?

    The most probable diagnosis is a squamous cell carcinoma of the great toe with metastasis to the right inguinal lymph nodes. The main alternative is a malignant melanoma, particularly the acral or subungual type, and a chronic ulcer with reactive lymphadenitis must be excluded. I would confirm the diagnosis by biopsy of the ulcer edge and FNAC or biopsy of the inguinal node, followed by staging investigations.

    Complete explanation: An elderly man with a six-month non-healing ulcer on the toe that has recently begun to spread, together with an enlarging swelling in the ipsilateral groin, which is the first-station nodal group for the lower limb, has a cutaneous malignancy with nodal metastasis until proven otherwise.

    Probable diagnoses

    1. Squamous cell carcinoma of the toe, possibly arising in a chronic ulcer, a scar or a site of trauma (Marjolin ulcer), with inguinal nodal metastasis.
    2. Malignant melanoma (acral lentiginous or ulcerated nodular type), which can also be ulcerated and spreads to inguinal nodes.
    3. Less likely: Kaposi sarcoma [HHV-8-associated vascular tumour], a chronic diabetic, venous, arterial or trophic ulcer with reactive lymphadenitis, a tuberculous or fungal ulcer, and a pigmented or ulcerated basal cell carcinoma, which is unusual at this site.

    Investigations

    • Biopsy of the edge of the ulcer, including adjacent normal skin, for histology. Immunohistochemistry (cytokeratin, p63 or p40 for squamous carcinoma; S100, HMB-45, Melan-A or SOX10 for melanoma) to settle the diagnosis.
    • FNAC or excision biopsy of the inguinal lymph node to confirm metastasis.
    • Imaging: X-ray of the foot to detect bone invasion
      Ultrasonography, CT or MRI of the groin and pelvis for deep (iliac) nodes. Chest X-ray or CT, and abdominal imaging or PET-CT, for distant metastases.
    • Laboratory tests: complete blood count, ESR, blood glucose (to exclude diabetes), liver and renal function tests, and serum LDH if melanoma is confirmed.
    • Bacteriological culture of the ulcer if infection is suspected.

    Melanocytic Tumors

    Nevus

    B9

    What is a nevus? Types of nevus.

    A naevus is a benign, localised proliferation of melanocytes, commonly called a mole. The principal types are the acquired melanocytic naevi (junctional, compound and intradermal), congenital naevus, blue naevus, Spitz naevus and the dysplastic naevus.

    Complete explanation: The term naevus denotes any congenital or acquired benign localised proliferation of melanocytes (naevus cells) in the skin. Acquired melanocytic naevi are extremely common, appearing in childhood and early adulthood. Most carry the activating BRAF V600E mutation. Proliferation is limited by oncogene-induced senescence, and so most naevi remain small and stable and later involute.

    Types

    1. Common acquired naevus. This is a small (usually less than 6 mm), symmetric, uniformly tan to dark-brown, sharply circumscribed macule or papule. It evolves through three histological stages.
      • Junctional naevus: nests of naevus cells at the dermoepidermal junction. a flat, brown macule.
      • Compound naevus: nests at the junction and in the dermis
        a raised papule.
      • Intradermal naevus: nests and cords only in the dermis
        a dome-shaped, often skin-coloured papule. The cells become smaller with increasing depth ("maturation").
    2. Congenital naevus: present at birth, often larger, with naevus cells extending deep around adnexa. Giant forms carry a small risk of melanoma.
    3. Blue naevus: a dark blue papule of heavily pigmented dermal spindle melanocytes.
    4. Spitz naevus: a pink, dome-shaped nodule in children, with large epithelioid and spindle cells. it can be mistaken for melanoma.
    5. Dysplastic naevus: larger than common naevi (generally more than 5 mm), with irregular borders and variegated colour
      it shows architectural disorder, cytological atypia and lamellar fibroplasia. It is a marker of, and a precursor to, melanoma, especially in the familial dysplastic naevus syndrome (CDKN2A mutations).

    Write a short note on nevus.

    DU03S

    Definition. Melanocytic naevi (moles) are common benign neoplasms strongly associated with acquired activating mutations in components of the RAS signalling pathway. Acquired melanocytic naevi are the most common type and are found in virtually all individuals.

    Pathogenesis

    • Many have acquired mutations causing constitutive activation of RAS or of BRAF, which lies immediately downstream of RAS
    • Naevi rarely give rise to melanoma because of oncogene-induced senescence: activated RAS or BRAF causes only limited proliferation, followed by permanent growth arrest through accumulation of p16, an inhibitor of CDK4 and CDK6
    • This protective response is disrupted in melanoma

    Morphology

    • Common acquired naevi are tan to brown, uniformly pigmented, small (usually less than 6 mm), flat macules or elevated papules with well-defined, rounded borders
    • Junctional naevus: the earliest lesion
      Nests of round cells along the dermoepidermal junction, with uniform rounded nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli and little or no mitotic activity
    • Compound naevus: growth into the dermis as nests or cords of cells, so epidermal and dermal components are both present. Raised and dome shaped
    • Intradermal naevus: in older lesions the epidermal nests are lost entirely
    • Superficial naevus cells are larger, produce melanin and grow in nests
      Deeper cells are smaller, produce little or no pigment and appear as cords and single cells
    • At the deepest extent the cells become fusiform and grow in fascicles resembling neural tissue (neurotisation), with progressive loss of tyrosinase activity
      This helps to distinguish naevi from melanomas

    Variants

    VariantFeaturesClinical significance
    Congenital naevusDeep dermal and sometimes subcutaneous growth around adnexa, neurovascular bundles and vessel wallsPresent at birth
    Large variants have increased melanoma risk
    Blue naevusNon-nested dermal infiltration
    Highly dendritic, heavily pigmented cells    		Black-blue nodule
    Often confused with melanoma clinically
    Spitz naevus (spindle and epithelioid cell naevus)Fascicular growth
    Large plump cells with pink-blue cytoplasm    		Common in children
    red-pink nodule
    Often confused with haemangioma
    Halo naevusLymphocytic infiltration around naevus cellsHost immune response against naevus cells and surrounding normal melanocytes
    Dysplastic naevusCoalescent intraepidermal nests
    Cytological atypia    		Potential marker or precursor of melanoma

    Clinical features and complications

    • May become more prominent during pregnancy, indicating hormone sensitivity
    • Dysplastic naevi are larger than most acquired naevi (often more than 5 mm), with variable pigmentation and irregular borders, and occur on sun-exposed and protected surfaces
    • Dysplastic naevi are best regarded as markers of increased melanoma risk. Most never progress
    • In dysplastic naevus syndrome (autosomal dominant), the probability of melanoma is over 50% by age 60 years
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 25)p. 1031p. 1036

    Malignant melanoma

    B9

    Morphology of malignant melanoma.

    Malignant melanoma is a malignant tumour of melanocytes. Grossly it is an asymmetrical pigmented lesion with irregular borders, variegated colour and a diameter often greater than 6 mm. Microscopically it consists of large atypical melanocytes with prominent nucleoli, growing as nests and single cells at all levels of the epidermis and invading the dermis. It passes from a radial to a vertical growth phase, and the depth of invasion determines prognosis.

    Complete explanation: Melanoma arises from epidermal melanocytes, chiefly in the skin, and is related to intense intermittent sun exposure, fair skin, numerous naevi, a family history, and inherited mutations in CDKN2A. Acquired mutations of BRAF, NRAS and KIT drive many tumours, and acral and mucosal melanomas are more often KIT-mutant.

    Gross morphology. Melanomas are recognised by the "ABCDE" features: Asymmetry, Border irregularity (notched and scalloped), Colour variegation (shades of brown, black, red, blue and white where there is regression), Diameter greater than 6 mm, and Evolution or enlargement. The surface may be elevated, and ulceration occurs in advanced lesions.

    Microscopic morphology. There are two phases of growth. In the radial growth phase, malignant cells spread horizontally within the epidermis and superficial papillary dermis. The cells are usually large, with abundant cytoplasm containing fine melanin dust, large, pleomorphic, irregular nuclei, and prominent, eosinophilic ("cherry-red") nucleoli. They form nests of varying size and spread as single cells upward through all epidermal levels (pagetoid spread).

    Cells in this phase generally do not have metastatic potential. In the vertical growth phase, the tumour cells invade the deeper dermis as an expansile nodule or as sheets, with mitotic figures, and acquire the capacity to metastasise.

    Clinical subtypes. Superficial spreading melanoma is the commonest. Lentigo maligna melanoma occurs on the sun-damaged face of the elderly. Nodular melanoma has a vertical growth phase from the start and is aggressive. Acral lentiginous melanoma occurs on the palms, soles and under the nails, and is the commonest type in dark-skinned populations.

    Prognosis. The single most important prognostic factor is the Breslow thickness (depth of invasion in millimetres), followed by ulceration, mitotic rate and regional lymph node status. Melanoma metastasises to regional lymph nodes and then to the lungs, liver, brain and bone. Tumour cells are positive for S100, HMB-45, Melan-A and SOX10.

    B10

    A 70-year-old man develops a blackish, pigmented and ulcerated lesion on the sole of the right foot for the last 3 months. Recently, a right inguinal swelling has been noted. What is the probable diagnosis?

    The probable diagnosis is malignant melanoma of the acral lentiginous type, arising on the sole of the foot, with metastasis to the right inguinal lymph nodes.

    Complete explanation: An elderly man with a rapidly changing, blackish pigmented and ulcerated lesion on the sole, which is a classical site of acral lentiginous melanoma, and a new swelling in the ipsilateral groin, the first-order nodal station for the foot, most probably has a malignant melanoma with regional lymph node metastasis. Pigmentation (the black colour from melanin), rapid growth and ulceration, which means vertical growth phase and a thick tumour, all support this diagnosis.

    Acral melanoma is not related to sun exposure and is the commonest type in dark-skinned populations
    The delay in diagnosis, because the lesion is hidden on the sole, explains why such cases usually present late with nodal spread.

    Differential diagnoses include squamous cell carcinoma of the sole, Kaposi sarcoma [HHV-8-associated vascular tumour], pigmented basal cell carcinoma (very rare at this site), a plantar wart or pyogenic granuloma with haemorrhage, a subcutaneous haematoma, and a chronic trophic ulcer with a pigmented margin. Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy with immunohistochemistry (S100, HMB-45, Melan-A, SOX10), and the inguinal swelling by FNAC or biopsy
    Breslow thickness and the nodal status stage the disease.

    B9

    How will you differentiate between a benign mole and a malignant melanoma grossly and microscopically?

    A benign mole is small, symmetrical, evenly pigmented and sharply circumscribed, and microscopically shows bland naevus cells in nests that become smaller with depth. A malignant melanoma is larger and asymmetrical, with an irregular border and variegated colour, and microscopically shows atypical melanocytes with prominent nucleoli, mitoses and invasion, without maturation.

    Complete explanation

    FeatureBenign mole (naevus)Malignant melanoma
    SizeUsually less than 6 mmUsually greater than 6 mm
    SymmetrySymmetrical, round or ovalAsymmetrical
    BorderRegular, sharply definedIrregular, notched, scalloped
    ColourUniform tan or brownVariegated: black, brown, red, white, blue
    SurfaceSmooth, flat or dome-shapedMay be elevated, nodular, ulcerated or bleeding
    EvolutionStableEnlarges, changes, itches or bleeds
    Distribution of cellsNests confined to junction and dermis
    Symmetric and well circumscribed    		Nests and single cells at all levels of epidermis (pagetoid spread)
    Asymmetric, poorly circumscribed
    CytologySmall, uniform cells with round, bland nucleiLarge, pleomorphic cells with irregular nuclei and prominent eosinophilic nucleoli
    MitosesAbsent or rareFrequent, often atypical, including in deep tumour cells
    Maturation with depthPresent: cells become smaller and spindled deeper in the dermisAbsent: cells remain large and atypical
    Invasion and dermal reactionNoneInvasion of dermis and deeper tissue
    Lymphocytic infiltrate, regression

    A 70y male has a black ulcerated lesion of right great toe for 6 months, spreading rapidly. What is the differential diagnosis?

    DU17Ja

    Malignant melanoma is the most likely diagnosis: it shows striking variation in colour, with shades of black, brown, red, dark blue and grey, irregular and often notched borders, and a vertical growth phase heralded by a nodule.

    The lesions that it must be distinguished from are:

    • Acral lentiginous melanoma: the melanoma type that arises on non-sun-exposed sites
    • Pigmented basal cell carcinoma: some tumours contain melanin and superficially resemble naevi or melanomas. Advanced lesions ulcerate
    • Blue naevus: a black-blue nodule often confused with melanoma clinically
    • Seborrhoeic keratosis: a pigmented lesion
      Small pore-like keratin-filled openings seen with a hand lens help to tell it from melanoma

    Same: how will you confirm the disease?

    DU17Ja

    Excision biopsy with histological examination

    • Cells are larger than normal melanocytes, with enlarged irregular nuclei, chromatin clumped at the nuclear membrane and prominent eosinophilic nucleoli
    • Neurotisation (maturation) is absent in the deep invasive part, unlike a naevus
    • Atypical lesions in the histological grey zone need complete excision and close follow-up

    The prognosis is assessed from:

    1. Breslow thickness (depth of invasion)
    2. Number of mitoses
    3. Tumour regression
    4. Ulceration of the overlying skin
    5. Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes
    6. Site (central body or extremity)
      • Sentinel lymph node biopsy: most melanomas first metastasise to regional nodes. Micrometastasis, which can be shown with the melanocytic marker HMB-45, confers a worse prognosis
      • Metastatic melanomas are tested for BRAF mutation

    OsteomyelitisBone TumorsSoft Tissue Tumors

    Osteomyelitis

    Osteomyelitis

    B9

    Define osteomyelitis. What are the causes of osteomyelitis? What is the route of entry of bacteria to the bone? Define and classify osteomyelitis. Describe the morphology of chronic osteomyelitis. Define and classify osteomyelitis. What are sequestrum, involucrum and Brodie's abscess?

    Osteomyelitis is inflammation of the bone and marrow, almost always due to infection. The commonest cause is Staphylococcus aureus, and bacteria reach bone by haematogenous spread, by extension from a contiguous focus, or by direct implantation after trauma or surgery. It is classified as acute or chronic, and by aetiology as pyogenic or tuberculous. In chronic osteomyelitis, a sequestrum is a fragment of dead bone, an involucrum is the new bone formed around it, and Brodie abscess is a small walled-off intraosseous abscess.

    Complete explanation

    Definition. Osteomyelitis is an inflammatory process of bone and bone marrow caused by infection. It is a clinical and pathological term for infection, usually bacterial, that may be acute or chronic.

    Causes. The causative organism is usually a pyogenic bacterium. Staphylococcus aureus accounts for most cases, and is the commonest agent at all ages. Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas and Klebsiella are associated with genitourinary tract infection and intravenous drug use. Haemophilus influenzae and group B streptococci cause neonatal infection, and Salmonella is a classic cause in patients with sickle cell disease. Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes tuberculous osteomyelitis, and fungi and other organisms may be responsible in the immunocompromised.

    Routes of entry. (1) Haematogenous spread from a distant focus (the most common route, especially in children), (2) direct extension from an adjacent focus of infection, such as a diabetic foot ulcer, a sinus or an infected joint, and (3) direct implantation through compound fractures or surgery.

    Classification. By duration, it is acute or chronic. By cause, it is pyogenic (bacterial), tuberculous, or due to other organisms such as fungi and syphilis. By route, it is haematogenous, contiguous or post-traumatic.

    Morphology of chronic osteomyelitis. Chronic osteomyelitis follows incompletely treated acute infection, or arises as a primary chronic infection. The central feature is necrotic bone, which is the persistent focus of infection because it cannot be penetrated by inflammatory cells and antibiotics. Around the dead bone is chronic inflammatory tissue (lymphocytes, plasma cells and macrophages) with fibrosis and granulation tissue, and new reactive bone is laid down by the periosteum.

    A sinus tract (cloaca) may discharge pus through the involucrum and the skin. Radiologically, the sequestrum appears as a dense fragment surrounded by a radiolucent zone with thickened sclerotic bone.

    Sequestrum, involucrum and Brodie abscess. The sequestrum is a segment of necrotic bone, separated from the living bone by granulation tissue and suppuration. The involucrum is a sleeve of new bone formed by the periosteum around the infected, necrotic bone. it may have openings (cloacae) through which pus drains. Brodie abscess is a small (usually 1–4 cm) intraosseous abscess walled off by reactive sclerotic bone, usually in the metaphysis of the tibia, representing a subacute or chronic infection with a low-virulence organism.

    What is osteomyelitis?

    6DU25NDU20NDU20JuDU19MDU18MDU10Ju

    Osteomyelitis is bone and marrow inflammation, virtually always secondary to infection.

    Name the different types of osteomyelitis.

    DU25NDU20NDU20Ju

    Organisms of all types can cause it, including viruses, parasites, fungi and bacteria, but certain pyogenic bacteria and mycobacteria are the most common.

    1. Pyogenic osteomyelitis, almost always bacterial
    2. Mycobacterial osteomyelitis, including tuberculous osteomyelitis of the spine (Pott disease [tuberculosis of the spine])
    3. Skeletal syphilis, congenital or acquired

    By stage, the changes are acute, subacute and chronic.

    What are its predisposing factors, etiologic agents and causes?

    DU19MDU18M

    Routes of infection

    1. Haematogenous spread
    2. Extension from a contiguous site
    3. Direct implantation after compound fracture or orthopaedic procedures

    Predisposing factors

    • In otherwise healthy children, most osteomyelitis is haematogenous, from trivial mucosal injuries or minor skin infections
    • In adults: open fractures, surgical procedures and diabetes (infections of the feet)
    • Sickle cell anaemia: osteonecrosis acts as a nidus, and loss of splenic function impairs immunity
    • Infants: epiphyseal infection can spread to the joint
    • Delayed diagnosis, extensive bone necrosis, inadequate antibiotic treatment or debridement, and weakened host immunity favour failure to resolve

    Aetiological agents

    SettingOrganism
    Most culture-positive pyogenic casesStaphylococcus aureus, 80% to 90%
    NeonatesGroup B streptococci and E. coli
    Older childrenGram-positive organisms such as S. aureus
    Direct spread, surgery or open fracturesMixed bacterial infections
    Sickle cell anaemiaSalmonella and other gram-negative organisms
    Mycobacterial osteomyelitisMycobacterium tuberculosis
    RareTreponema pallidum and yaws
    • Specific organisms are identified in only about 50% of patients
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 26)p. 1076p. 1077

    Give the morphology of pyogenic osteomyelitis.

    4DU21MDU19MDU18MDU16Ju
    • The changes depend on the stage (acute, subacute and chronic) and the site of infection
    • In neonates the metaphysis, epiphysis or both are infected. in older children the metaphysis
      in adults after growth plate closure the epiphysis and subchondral regions

    Acute phase

    1. Bacteria proliferate and induce a neutrophilic reaction
    2. Necrosis of bone cells and marrow within 48 hours
    3. Spread through the Haversian canals to the periosteum
    4. Subperiosteal abscesses dissect along the bone surface in children, because the periosteum is loosely attached. Lifting of the periosteum further impairs blood supply
    5. Soft tissue abscesses after periosteal rupture, which may drain through sinuses to the skin

    Subacute and chronic phase

    • During the first week, chronic inflammatory cells release cytokines that stimulate bone resorption, fibrous tissue ingrowth and deposition of reactive bone at the periphery
    • Dead bone is the sequestrum
    • Reactive bone forms a living shell, the involucrum, around the dead infected bone
    • Histology: marrow fibrosis, sequestrum, and a chronic inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 26)p. 1076

    Write the pathogenesis (aetiopathogenesis) of (chronic) osteomyelitis.

    DU25MDU10Ju

    - Staphylococcal cell wall proteins bind to bone matrix components such as collagen, which helps bacteria to adhere to bone - Bacteria proliferate and induce a neutrophilic reaction, and bone cells and marrow become necrotic - Chronic inflammatory cells release cytokines that stimulate bone resorption, fibrous tissue ingrowth and reactive bone deposition - Dead bone persists as sequestrum within an involucrum of new bone - In 5% to 25% of cases acute osteomyelitis fails to resolve, which leads to chronic infection. This is likely with: 1. delayed diagnosis 2. extensive bone necrosis 3. inadequate antibiotic treatment or surgical debridement 4. weakened host immunity - Chronic infection may flare spontaneously after years of dormancy

    Write a short note on chronic osteomyelitis.

    4DU22NDU14JuDU13JuDU10Ju

    Definition. Bone and marrow inflammation, virtually always secondary to infection, that has failed to resolve. 5% to 25% of acute osteomyelitis does not resolve.

    Aetiology and pathogenesis

    • Delayed diagnosis, extensive bone necrosis, inadequate antibiotic treatment or surgical debridement, and weakened host immunity
    • Chronic inflammatory cells release cytokines that stimulate bone resorption, fibrous tissue ingrowth and reactive bone formation

    Morphology

    • Sequestrum (dead bone) surrounded by involucrum (shell of living new bone)
      a drainage tract in the involucrum reveals the necrotic cortex
    • Marrow fibrosis, sequestrum, and a chronic inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells

    Clinical features and complications

    • Course punctuated by spontaneous flares after years of dormancy
    • Complications: pathological fracture, secondary (reactive) amyloidosis, endocarditis, sepsis, squamous cell carcinoma in draining sinus tracts, and sarcoma in the infected bone
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 26)p. 1076p. 1077

    Write the complications of (chronic) osteomyelitis.

    DU25MDU20NDU20Ju
    1. Pathological fracture
    2. Secondary (reactive) amyloidosis
    3. Endocarditis
    4. Sepsis
    5. Squamous cell carcinoma in draining sinus tracts
    6. Sarcoma in the infected bone
    7. Spontaneous flares after years of dormancy
      • In infants, epiphyseal infection can spread to a joint and cause septic (suppurative) arthritis, articular cartilage destruction and permanent disability
      • Soft tissue abscesses may channel to the skin as draining sinuses

    A 16y boy has severe left tibial pain, high fever, TLC 18000, periosteal thickening on X-ray. What is your clinical diagnosis?

    DU18Nov

    Acute (haematogenous) pyogenic osteomyelitis of the tibia

    • In otherwise healthy children, most osteomyelitis is haematogenous and more common in long bones
    • It presents acutely as a systemic illness with malaise, fever, chills, leucocytosis and intense throbbing pain over the affected region
    • The commonest organism is Staphylococcus aureus, responsible for 80% to 90% of culture-positive cases
    • Infection lifts the periosteum, and reactive bone is deposited at the periphery of the infection

    Differential diagnosis: Ewing sarcoma [small round blue cell bone tumour with t(11;22)] also presents in children with a painful, tender, warm, swollen mass and systemic findings that mimic infection (fever, raised sedimentation rate, anaemia, leucocytosis), with a periosteal reaction.

    Same: how would you confirm it?

    DU18Nov
    • Plain radiograph: a lytic focus of bone destruction with associated reactive bone
    • MRI: more sensitive and specific for the changes of osteomyelitis
    • Biopsy and microbial culture: required to identify the pathogen in most instances. The organism is identified in only about 50% of patients
    • Histology of the biopsy: neutrophilic reaction and necrosis of bone and marrow in the acute phase
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 26)p. 1076p. 1077

    Tuberculosis of bone (Pott disease)

    Write a short note on Pott's disease.

    DU19Nov

    Definition. Pott disease [tuberculosis of the spine] is mycobacterial (tuberculous) osteomyelitis of the spine. The spine is involved in 40% of mycobacterial osteomyelitis cases.

    Aetiology and pathogenesis

    • Usually bloodborne, from a focus of active visceral disease elsewhere
    • Direct extension may occur, for example from tracheobronchial nodes into adjacent vertebrae
    • About 1% to 3% of individuals with tuberculosis develop osseous infection

    Morphology

    • Caseating granulomas, as in other sites
    • Infection tracks through the intervertebral discs to involve multiple vertebrae and the surrounding soft tissues
    • More destructive and resistant to control than pyogenic osteomyelitis

    Clinical features and complications

    • Localised pain, low-grade fever, chills or weight loss
    • Disc and vertebral destruction lead to permanent compression fractures, which produce scoliosis, kyphosis and neurological deficits from compression of the spinal cord and nerves
    • Sinus tract formation, abscesses, tuberculous arthritis and amyloidosis
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 26)p. 1077

    Bone Tumors

    Bone tumors

    B9

    Classify bone tumors. What is Pott's disease?

    Bone tumours are classified according to the tissue they produce into bone-forming, cartilage-forming, fibrous, vascular, haematopoietic and tumours of unknown origin, each with benign and malignant examples. Pott disease [tuberculosis of the spine] is tuberculosis of the spine, with vertebral destruction, kyphosis and a cold abscess.

    Complete explanation

    Line of differentiationBenignMalignant
    Bone-formingOsteoma, osteoid osteoma, osteoblastomaOsteosarcoma
    Cartilage-formingOsteochondroma, chondroma (enchondroma), chondroblastoma, chondromyxoid fibromaChondrosarcoma
    FibrousFibrous cortical defect and non-ossifying fibroma, fibrous dysplasia (tumour-like lesions)Fibrosarcoma
    Unknown originGiant cell tumour (benign but locally aggressive)Ewing sarcoma [small round blue cell bone tumour with t(11;22)], malignant giant cell tumour
    NotochordalBenign notochordal tumourChordoma
    VascularHaemangiomaAngiosarcoma
    Haematopoietic—Multiple myeloma, lymphoma
    Metastatic—Metastases from carcinomas of the breast, prostate, lung, kidney and thyroid

    Metastases are the commonest malignant tumours of bone overall. Among primary bone tumours, myeloma is the commonest, followed by osteosarcoma.

    Pott disease is tuberculous osteomyelitis of the vertebral column. Haematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to the lower thoracic and upper lumbar vertebrae causes caseating granulomatous destruction of the vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs. Vertebral collapse causes kyphosis (gibbus), a cold abscess may track along the psoas sheath to the groin, and cord compression may cause paraplegia.

    B9

    Name the bone-forming tumors. Describe the morphology of osteosarcoma. What is the common site of origin of osteosarcoma? Describe the morphology of osteosarcoma. What are the radiological findings?

    The bone-forming tumours are osteoma, osteoid osteoma, osteoblastoma and osteosarcoma. Osteosarcoma is the commonest primary malignant bone tumour apart from myeloma. It most often arises in the metaphysis of long bones around the knee, particularly the lower end of the femur and the upper end of the tibia. It is a bulky gritty tumour that microscopically produces neoplastic osteoid and bone, and radiologically shows Codman triangle [periosteal elevation in aggressive bone tumours] and a sunburst pattern.

    Complete explanation

    Bone-forming tumours. These are osteoma, osteoid osteoma and osteoblastoma, which are benign, and osteosarcoma, which is malignant.

    Osteosarcoma. It is a malignant mesenchymal tumour in which the neoplastic cells produce osteoid and bone. It has a peak incidence in adolescents and young adults between 10 and 20 years, and a second smaller peak in the elderly, in whom it is associated with Paget disease [disordered bone remodelling] of bone, bone infarcts and prior irradiation. It is more frequent in males. Predisposing genetic factors are inactivating mutations of RB1 (hereditary retinoblastoma) and TP53 (Li–Fraumeni syndrome)
    CDK4 and MDM2 amplification also occurs.

    Site. The tumour typically arises in the metaphysis of long bones, with about 60% of tumours around the knee, in the distal femur and proximal tibia. The proximal humerus is the next commonest site.

    Gross morphology. A large, gritty, grey-white, often haemorrhagic and necrotic tumour that arises in the metaphysis and frequently destroys the cortex, lifts the periosteum and forms a soft tissue mass. It extends through the marrow cavity but usually spares the epiphyseal cartilage, although it may extend into the epiphysis and sometimes the joint.

    Microscopic morphology. The tumour is composed of pleomorphic, malignant cells, often with hyperchromatic, bizarre nuclei, atypical mitoses and giant cells. The essential diagnostic feature is the formation of neoplastic osteoid (and bone) directly by the tumour cells, which appears as lace-like, eosinophilic matrix. Matrix may be mineralised and appear as a fine, lace-like deposit around tumour cells. Variants include osteoblastic, chondroblastic, fibroblastic, telangiectatic and small cell patterns.

    Radiology. The radiograph shows a destructive, mixed lytic and sclerotic lesion in the metaphysis, with an ill-defined margin, soft tissue extension, elevation of the periosteum that appears as Codman triangle, and radiating bone spicules, giving a "sunburst" appearance.

    Clinical features. Painful progressive swelling, and sometimes a pathological fracture, with raised serum alkaline phosphatase. It metastasises early by the blood stream, mainly to the lungs. Treatment is neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by limb-sparing surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy. The 5-year survival is about 60–70% in the absence of metastasis at presentation.

    B9

    Classify bone tumors. Describe the morphology of giant cell tumor of bone.

    Bone tumours are classified as bone-forming, cartilage-forming, fibrous, vascular, haematopoietic, and those of unknown origin, such as giant cell tumour and Ewing sarcoma [small round blue cell bone tumour with t(11;22)]. Giant cell tumour of bone typically occurs in the epiphysis of long bones in adults aged 20 to 40. Microscopically it consists of mononuclear stromal cells with scattered multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells, and it is locally aggressive.

    Complete explanation

    Classification. Bone tumours are grouped by the type of tissue they differentiate towards. Bone-forming tumours include osteoma, osteoid osteoma, osteoblastoma and osteosarcoma. Cartilage-forming tumours include osteochondroma, enchondroma, chondroblastoma, chondromyxoid fibroma and chondrosarcoma. Fibrous and fibro-osseous lesions include fibrous cortical defect, non-ossifying fibroma and fibrous dysplasia. The tumours of uncertain origin are giant cell tumour and Ewing sarcoma. Others include chordoma, vascular tumours, myeloma and lymphoma, and metastatic tumours.

    Giant cell tumour of bone. It is a locally aggressive tumour that occurs in young adults between 20 and 40 years of age, slightly more often in women. The tumour arises in the epiphysis (extending into the metaphysis) of long bones, most commonly at the lower end of the femur, upper end of the tibia and lower end of the radius.

    Gross. The tumour is large, soft, red-brown and haemorrhagic, often with cystic degeneration and areas of necrosis. It expands the end of the bone, thins and erodes the cortex, and may extend into the soft tissue and, rarely, into the joint.

    Microscopic. The tumour consists of sheets of uniform, round to oval mononuclear stromal cells, which are the neoplastic element, among which are numerous evenly distributed multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells with many nuclei that resemble the nuclei of the stromal cells. The mononuclear cells show little pleomorphism and moderate mitotic activity. The giant cells are recruited by RANKL expressed by the stromal cells. Haemorrhage, haemosiderin deposition, foamy macrophages and reactive woven bone are frequent. The tumour cells carry mutations of H3F3A (G34W).

    Radiology and behaviour. A purely lytic, eccentric, expansile "soap-bubble" lesion extending to the subchondral bone. Recurrence after curettage occurs in 40–60%, and a few tumours metastasise to the lungs. Treatment is curettage or excision, and denosumab, an antibody to RANKL, is used for unresectable tumours.

    B9

    Classify bone tumors. What is Ewing sarcoma?

    Bone tumours are classified into bone-forming, cartilage-forming, fibrous, vascular, haematopoietic and tumours of uncertain origin, and each includes benign and malignant tumours. Ewing sarcoma [small round blue cell bone tumour with t(11;22)] is a highly malignant small round blue cell tumour of bone, occurring in children and adolescents, characterised by the t(11;22) translocation producing the EWSR1–FLI1 fusion gene.

    Complete explanation

    Classification. Bone tumours are classified as bone-forming (osteoma, osteoid osteoma, osteoblastoma, osteosarcoma), cartilage-forming (osteochondroma, enchondroma, chondroblastoma, chondromyxoid fibroma, chondrosarcoma), fibrous (fibrous cortical defect, non-ossifying fibroma, fibrosarcoma), tumours of uncertain origin (giant cell tumour, Ewing sarcoma), vascular (haemangioma, angiosarcoma), haematopoietic (myeloma, lymphoma), notochordal (chordoma) and metastatic tumours.

    Ewing sarcoma. This is a primitive malignant tumour of small round cells showing neuroectodermal differentiation, and it is the second most common bone sarcoma of childhood. It occurs mainly in the first two decades (peak around 10–15 years) and more often in boys. It arises in the diaphysis of long bones such as the femur, tibia and humerus, and also in the pelvis and ribs. More than 90% carry the translocation t(11;22)(q24;q12), creating the EWSR1–FLI1 fusion gene, which acts as an aberrant transcription factor.

    Gross. A soft, tan-white tumour arising in the medullary cavity, with haemorrhage and necrosis, which invades the cortex and extends into the soft tissue.

    Microscopic. Sheets of uniform small round cells, slightly larger than lymphocytes, with scanty, clear to pale cytoplasm that is rich in glycogen (PAS-positive) and round nuclei with fine chromatin, with few mitoses. Homer Wright rosettes are found in some cases. The tumour cells express CD99 (MIC2) strongly.

    Clinical. Local pain and swelling, which may be accompanied by fever, leucocytosis and raised ESR, mimicking osteomyelitis. Radiography shows a destructive, permeative lytic lesion with lamellated "onion-skin" periosteal reaction. The tumour is chemosensitive, and treatment with chemotherapy, surgery and radiotherapy gives 5-year survival of about 70–75% for localised disease.

    Name the bone-forming tumours / classify bone tumours.

    DU25NDU09Ju

    Bone tumours are classified according to the normal cell type they recapitulate or the matrix they produce. Lesions without a normal tissue counterpart are grouped by clinicopathological features.

    CategoryBenignMalignant
    Bone formingOsteoid osteoma, osteoblastomaOsteosarcoma
    Cartilage formingOsteochondroma, chondroma, chondroblastoma, chondromyxoid fibromaChondrosarcoma
    Unknown originGiant cell tumour, aneurysmal bone cystEwing sarcoma [small round blue cell bone tumour with t(11;22)], adamantinoma
    NotochordalNoneChordoma
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 26)p. 1078p. 1079

    Osteosarcoma

    Write in brief about the morphology of osteosarcoma.

    4DU25NDU09JuDU09JaDU07Ju
    • Large, gritty, grey-white tumours that often contain haemorrhage and cystic degeneration
    • Frequently destroy the surrounding cortices to produce a soft tissue mass, spread extensively in the medullary canal and replace the haematopoietic marrow
    • Infrequently penetrate the epiphyseal plate or enter the joint
    • Pleomorphism, large hyperchromatic nuclei, bizarre tumour giant cells and abundant mitoses, including abnormal (tripolar) forms
    • Extensive necrosis and intravascular invasion are common
    • Diagnosis requires malignant cells producing unmineralised osteoid or mineralised bone, typically fine and lacelike, but sometimes broad sheets or primitive trabeculae
    • If the cells also produce abundant cartilage, the tumour is a chondroblastic osteosarcoma
    • Radiologically: destructive mixed lytic and sclerotic mass
      Lifting of the periosteum produces Codman triangle [periosteal elevation in aggressive bone tumours]
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 26)p. 1079

    Ewing sarcoma

    Write a short note on Ewing's sarcoma.

    DU17JaDU05Ja

    Definition. Ewing sarcoma [small round blue cell bone tumour with t(11;22)] is a malignant bone tumour strongly associated with oncogenic fusion genes composed of portions of the EWSR1 gene and genes encoding ETS family transcription factors. It accounts for about 10% of primary malignant bone tumours and is the second most common bone sarcoma in children after osteosarcoma.

    Aetiology and pathogenesis

    • More than 90% contain a balanced translocation involving EWSR1 on chromosome 22 and FLI1 on chromosome 11
    • The fusion gene encodes a chimeric EWSR1/FLI1 protein that binds chromatin and dysregulates transcription
    • Fewer than 10% have fusion genes involving other members of the FET or ETS gene families
    • The cell of origin is not certain: mesenchymal stem cells and primitive neuroectodermal cells are possible sources

    Morphology

    • Arises in the medullary cavity and invades the cortex, periosteum and soft tissue
    • Grossly soft, tan-white, with areas of haemorrhage and necrosis
    • Sheets of uniform small round cells, more cohesive than lymphocytes, with scant cytoplasm that may be clear because of glycogen
    • Homer-Wright rosettes (circular groups of cells with a central fibrillary core) may be present
    • Tumour cells do not produce bone or cartilage

    Clinical features and complications

    • About 80% of patients are younger than 20 years
      Boys are affected slightly more often
    • Usually in the diaphysis of long bones, especially the femur, and the flat bones of the pelvis. About 20% are extraskeletal
    • Painful, enlarging mass
      The site is tender, warm and swollen, with systemic findings that mimic infection: fever, raised red cell sedimentation rate, anaemia and leucocytosis
    • Radiograph: destructive lytic tumour with permeative or moth-eaten margins and an onion-skin periosteal reaction
    • With neoadjuvant chemotherapy, surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy, 5-year survival is 75% and long-term cure 50%
      chemotherapy-induced necrosis is a positive prognostic indicator
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 26)p. 1083

    Giant cell tumour of bone

    Write a short note on giant cell tumour of bone.

    DU24MDU23N

    Definition. Giant cell tumour is a neoplasm composed of monotonous mononuclear stromal cells, macrophages and osteoclast-type giant cells. While benign, it can be locally aggressive.

    Aetiology and pathogenesis

    • Most cells are non-neoplastic osteoclasts and their precursors
    • The neoplastic cells are primitive osteoblast precursors that express high levels of RANKL, which promotes proliferation of osteoclast precursors and their differentiation into mature osteoclasts
    • Absent feedback between osteoblasts and osteoclasts leads to localised but highly destructive bone resorption
    • The neoplastic cells have mutations in the H3-3A gene encoding histone 3.3

    Morphology

    • Large, red-brown masses that frequently undergo cystic degeneration
    • Often destroy the overlying cortex, giving a bulging soft tissue mass delineated by a thin shell of reactive bone
    • Uniform oval mononuclear tumour cells and abundant osteoclast-type giant cells with 100 or more nuclei. Necrosis and mitotic activity may be prominent

    Clinical features and complications

    • Usually arises in the third to fifth decades, in the epiphysis of long bones, and may extend into the metaphysis. Most are near the knee, in the distal femur or proximal tibia
    • Arthritis-like symptoms, because it arises near joints
      Pathological fracture
    • Treated by curettage
      40% to 60% recur locally
    • Up to 4% metastasise to the lungs, but these regress spontaneously or can be cured by excision
    • The RANKL inhibitor denosumab is an alternative to surgery when resection would cause significant morbidity
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 26)p. 1064p. 1084

    Joint Diseases

    Name 2 systemic diseases that affect joints.

    DU09Ja
    1. Rheumatoid arthritis: a chronic autoimmune disorder that principally attacks the joints, producing a non-suppurative, proliferative, inflammatory synovitis. extra-articular lesions may also occur
    2. Gout: transient attacks of acute arthritis initiated by monosodium urate crystals deposited within and around joints, with excessive uric acid in the tissues and body fluids
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 26)p. 1089p. 1091

    Soft Tissue Tumors

    B9

    What do you mean by soft tissue? Give some examples of soft tissue tumor.

    Soft tissue refers to all non-epithelial extraskeletal tissues of the body, excluding the viscera, the coverings of the brain, and the haematopoietic and lymphoid tissues. Examples of soft tissue tumours are lipoma and liposarcoma, fibroma and fibrosarcoma, leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, haemangioma, neurofibroma and synovial sarcoma.

    Complete explanation: Soft tissue comprises fat, fibrous tissue, skeletal and smooth muscle, blood vessels, peripheral nerve sheaths and synovium, which are mesenchymal in origin, and it excludes the viscera, the meninges, the haematopoietic and lymphoid tissues, and the skeleton. Tumours are named after the tissue to which they show differentiation, and are divided into benign tumours, whose suffix is "-oma", and malignant tumours, called sarcomas.

    Tissue of differentiationBenignMalignant
    FatLipomaLiposarcoma
    Fibrous tissueFibroma, nodular fasciitis (reactive), fibromatosis (locally aggressive)Fibrosarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma
    Skeletal muscleRhabdomyomaRhabdomyosarcoma
    Smooth muscleLeiomyomaLeiomyosarcoma
    Blood vesselsHaemangiomaAngiosarcoma, Kaposi sarcoma [HHV-8-associated vascular tumour]
    Peripheral nerve sheathNeurofibroma, schwannomaMalignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour
    Synovium / uncertainGiant cell tumour of tendon sheathSynovial sarcoma

    Soft tissue sarcomas are rare compared with carcinomas, and typically arise in the deep tissues of the limbs and retroperitoneum. They tend to grow as expansile masses with a pseudocapsule, and they spread mainly by the blood stream, to the lungs, rather than through lymphatics. Their grade, depth, size and resectability determine prognosis.

    The Central Nervous System

    15 questions · viva and written, in Robbins order.

    Infections

    Meningitis

    B9

    What is meningitis? Causes of meningitis.

    Meningitis is inflammation of the leptomeninges, the pia and arachnoid, with an inflammatory exudate in the cerebrospinal fluid of the subarachnoid space. It may be acute pyogenic (bacterial), aseptic (usually viral) or chronic (tuberculous or fungal). The causative organisms depend on the age of the patient: Escherichia coli and group B streptococci in neonates, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae in infants and children, and N. meningitidis and S. pneumoniae in adolescents, adults and the elderly.

    Complete explanation: Meningitis is defined as inflammation of the leptomeninges and of the subarachnoid CSF. Microorganisms reach the meninges mostly by the haematogenous route, from an infected focus such as the nasopharynx or lung, and less often by direct spread from otitis media, mastoiditis or sinusitis, by direct implantation through a skull fracture or neurosurgery, or by a congenital neural tube defect. Because the CSF has little immune defence, bacteria that enter it multiply freely, and the inflammatory response, rather than the organism alone, produces much of the damage.

    Causes

    TypeOrganisms
    Acute pyogenic (bacterial) meningitisNeonates: Escherichia coli, group B streptococci (Streptococcus agalactiae), Listeria monocytogenes. Infants and children: Haemophilus influenzae type b (now much less frequent after vaccination), Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae. Adolescents and young adults: N. meningitidis. Elderly: S. pneumoniae, Listeria, gram-negative bacilli.
    Acute lymphocytic (aseptic) meningitisViruses: enteroviruses (coxsackie, echovirus), mumps, herpes simplex virus 2, HIV, arboviruses.
    Chronic meningitisMycobacterium tuberculosis, Cryptococcus neoformans and other fungi, Treponema pallidum, and Borrelia burgdorferi.

    Grossly in acute pyogenic meningitis, a creamy-yellow exudate lies within the subarachnoid space over the brain surface, especially around the sulci and the base. Microscopically there are neutrophils in the subarachnoid space, and in severe cases the exudate extends along the perivascular spaces and causes ventriculitis, vasculitis, thrombophlebitis and cerebral oedema. Complications include hydrocephalus, cerebral infarction, and cranial nerve palsies. Clinically there is fever, headache, photophobia, irritability, neck stiffness and altered consciousness.

    What is meningitis? What are the types?

    DU26MDU20NDU20Ju

    Definition. Meningitis is an inflammatory process involving the leptomeninges and CSF within the subarachnoid space, usually caused by infection. Meningoencephalitis is inflammation of the meninges and brain parenchyma, most commonly viral.

    Types (by aetiology and clinical evolution of infectious meningitis)

    1. Acute pyogenic meningitis, usually bacterial
    2. Aseptic meningitis, usually acute or subacute viral
    3. Chronic meningitis, usually tuberculous, spirochaetal or cryptococcal
      • Chemical meningitis may follow an irritant introduced into the subarachnoid space
      • Meningitis may also occur in a systemic autoimmune disease
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 28)p. 1147

    What are the causes of neonatal meningitis?

    DU23N
    • Escherichia coli
    • Group B streptococci

    Mention the CSF findings of different types of meningitis.

    DU26MDU10Ju
    TypeCellsProteinGlucoseOther
    Acute pyogenicNumerous neutrophilsIncreasedMarkedly reducedCloudy or frankly purulent
    Increased pressure
    Aseptic (viral)Lymphocytic pleocytosisOnly moderately increasedNearly always normalClear

    Give the differences in CSF findings between pyogenic, tubercular and viral meningitis.

    10DU23NDU22MDU20NDU20JuDU19NovDU18MDU16JuDU14JuDU13JuDU12Ja
    FeaturePyogenic meningitisTuberculous meningitisViral meningitis
    AppearanceCloudy or frankly purulentCloudy or yellowClear
    PressureIncreasedIncreasedNormal or mildly increased
