    Acid–base & electrolytes

    Give the normal serum levels of Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻ and HCO₃⁻.

    4DU16JaDU15JaDU05JaDU03S
    ElectrolyteNormal serum level
    Sodium (Na⁺)136 to 146 mmol/L
    Potassium (K⁺)3.5 to 5.0 mmol/L
    Chloride (Cl⁻)95 to 105 mmol/L
    Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻)22 to 28 mmol/L

    What is the normal pH of blood and urine?

    DU12Ju
    FluidNormal pH
    Blood7.35 to 7.45
    Urine4.5 to 8.0
    • Blood pH below 7.35 is acidaemia and above 7.45 is alkalaemia
    • Normal urine is slightly acidic
      it varies with diet and with acid-base disturbances

    What do you mean by metabolic acidosis?

    4DU22NDU22MDU18NovDU11Ja

    Metabolic acidosis is an acid-base disturbance with an increase in hydrogen ion concentration in the systemic circulation, shown as a fall in serum bicarbonate (below 24 mEq/L) and a blood pH below 7.35.

    • It signifies an underlying disorder that needs correction
    • The respiratory system compensates by hyperventilation, which lowers the arterial PCO2
      Compensation never fully corrects the pH

    What are the causes of metabolic acidosis?

    5DU18NovDU17MDU16JaDU12JuDU11Ja

    Mechanisms: increased production of acid, decreased excretion of acid, acid ingestion, and renal or gastrointestinal loss of bicarbonate.

    The causes are classified by the anion gap (sodium minus the sum of chloride and bicarbonate; normal about 12):

    TypeCauses
    High anion gapLactic acidosis from anaerobic metabolism
    Diabetic ketoacidosis
    Uraemia (renal failure)
    Salicylates
    Methanol and ethylene glycol
    Paraldehyde
    Iron and isoniazid
    Cyanide and carbon monoxide
    Arsenic
    Toluene
    Metformin
    Normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic)Diarrhoea (gastrointestinal loss of bicarbonate)
    Renal tubular acidosis
    Addison disease [primary adrenocortical insufficiency]
    Ureterosigmoid or pancreatic fistulae
    Acetazolamide
    Total parenteral nutrition
    Large volumes of normal saline
    • A positive urine anion gap points to renal loss of bicarbonate such as renal tubular acidosis. a negative value points to non-renal loss such as diarrhoea

    What is metabolic alkalosis?

    DU18NovDU09JaDU07Ju

    Metabolic alkalosis is a state in which the pH is elevated to greater than 7.45 because of a metabolic process, with an increase in serum bicarbonate.

    What conditions may lead to metabolic alkalosis? Give the biochemical changes.

    DU04M

    Conditions

    1. Loss of gastric acid: prolonged vomiting or nasogastric suction
    2. Diuretics: thiazide and loop diuretics
    3. Volume depletion (hypovolaemia) and chloride depletion
    4. Hypokalaemia, which shifts hydrogen ions into cells and increases renal bicarbonate reabsorption
    5. Mineralocorticoid excess: Conn syndrome [primary hyperaldosteronism], Cushing syndrome [glucocorticoid excess], Bartter [inherited loop of Henle salt wasting causing hypokalaemic alkalosis] and Gitelman [inherited distal tubular salt wasting causing hypokalaemic alkalosis] syndromes, Liddle syndrome [inherited renal sodium-channel overactivity causing hypertension with hypokalaemia]
    6. Alkali (bicarbonate) administration
    7. Recovery after prolonged hypercapnia

    Biochemical changes

    • Primary increase in serum bicarbonate
    • Raised blood pH, though it may be nearly normal
    • Hypokalaemia and hypochloraemia
    • Compensatory hypoventilation, with a rise in arterial PCO2
    • Urine chloride below 10 mEq/L in chloride-responsive causes (vomiting, diuretics) and above 20 mEq/L in chloride-resistant causes

    Write a short note on respiratory acidosis.

    DU20NDU20Ju

    Definition. Respiratory acidosis is an acid-base disturbance due to alveolar hypoventilation, with a primary rise in arterial PCO2, a fall in the bicarbonate to PCO2 ratio and a fall in blood pH.

    Causes

    • Impaired respiratory drive from drugs or CNS disease
    • Airflow obstruction: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma, sleep apnoea, airway oedema
    • Obesity hypoventilation syndrome, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and severe thoracic skeletal defects

    Biochemical changes

    • Arterial blood gas: PCO2 above 45 mmHg, pH below 7.35
    • Acute: bicarbonate rises by 1 mEq/L for each 10 mmHg rise in PCO2
    • Chronic: renal compensation over days
      Bicarbonate rises by 4 mEq/L for each 10 mmHg rise in PCO2 and exceeds 30 mEq/L. pH is normal or near normal

    Clinical features

    • Acute: headache, confusion, drowsiness
      with severe prolonged hypoventilation, altered mental status, myoclonus and seizures
    • Chronic form is often asymptomatic

    A 10y boy has severe diarrhoea. What changes do you expect in his electrolyte and acid-base status?

    DU18NovDU10Ja

    Normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis

    • Diarrhoea causes loss of bicarbonate from the gut, so serum bicarbonate and blood pH fall
    • Chloride rises to balance the fall in bicarbonate, so the anion gap stays normal
    • The urine anion gap is negative, since the loss is non-renal
    • Hypokalaemia accompanies the acidosis of diarrhoea
    • The respiratory compensation is hyperventilation, which lowers the arterial PCO2

    A 25y man in shock after RTA passed 40 ml urine in 24 h. What will be his acid-base and electrolyte status?

    DU09Ja

    High anion gap metabolic acidosis

    • Oliguria of 40 mL in 24 hours after shock indicates acute kidney injury, so acid excretion falls (uraemia)
    • Shock causes anaerobic metabolism and lactic acid accumulation
    • Unmeasured anions increase, so the anion gap is raised
      Serum bicarbonate and blood pH are low
    • The respiratory compensation is hyperventilation, which lowers the arterial PCO2

    Write the clinical importance of serum calcium.

    DU10Ja

    Normal total serum calcium is 2.12 to 2.62 mmol/L (8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL)
    Ionised calcium is 1.16 to 1.31 mmol/L. About 40% is protein-bound (mainly to albumin and globulin), about 9% is chelated, and about 51% is free (ionised) and physiologically active. Over 99% of body calcium is in bone as hydroxyapatite. Total calcium is corrected for albumin by adding about 0.8 mg/dL for each 1 g/dL that albumin falls below 4 g/dL.

    Hypercalcaemia

    • Causes: PTH-mediated (hyperparathyroidism)
      non-PTH-mediated: malignancy (the most common cause of rapidly progressive hypercalcaemia), granulomatous disorders, drugs, endocrinopathies and genetic causes
    • Clinical features: mild (below 11.5 mg/dL) is usually asymptomatic
      Above 11.5 mg/dL there is nausea, vomiting, confusion, headache, abdominal or flank pain, constipation, depression, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, polyuria, polydipsia and nocturia. Coma in severe cases
    • Signs: hypertension, bradycardia, hyperreflexia, tongue fasciculations
    • ECG: shortened QT interval, flattened or inverted T waves, J waves, prolonged PR and QRS intervals

    Hypocalcaemia

    • Causes: hypoparathyroidism (most often after thyroid, parathyroid or neck surgery; about 75% of cases), hungry bone syndrome after parathyroidectomy, vitamin D deficiency, chronic kidney disease, pseudohypoparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia, acute pancreatitis, sepsis, massive blood transfusion (citrate binds calcium), drugs (bisphosphonates, denosumab, cinacalcet, cisplatin, foscarnet)
    • Clinical features: tetany, paraesthesia (perioral and distal), seizures, laryngospasm, QT prolongation with risk of arrhythmia, heart failure
    • Signs: Chvostek sign [facial twitching on tapping the facial nerve in hypocalcaemia] (facial twitch on tapping the facial nerve) and Trousseau sign [migratory thrombophlebitis associated with cancer] (carpopedal spasm on inflating a cuff)
    • Chronic: dry skin, coarse hair, brittle nails, poor dentition, cataracts

    Approach

    • Hypocalcaemia: check albumin first to exclude factitious hypocalcaemia, then PTH, magnesium, vitamin D, phosphate, renal and liver function, and an ECG
    • Hypercalcaemia: confirm with albumin and ionised calcium, then PTH, renal function, TSH and electrolytes
      if malignancy is suspected, look for lung, breast or kidney masses and for myeloma, lymphoma or leukaemia

    Enzymes

    What are the indications of enzymes of clinical importance?

    DU24NDU23NDU21M

    Serum enzymes are measured:

    1. To detect tissue damage, because intracellular enzymes leak into the blood from damaged cells
    2. To localise the site of damage, showing which parts of the body are involved
    3. To quantify the extent of damage
    4. For diagnosis, differential diagnosis, prognosis and early detection, for example alanine aminotransferase (ALT) rises in viral hepatitis before jaundice appears
    5. To follow the course of liver disease and to check the hepatic origin of a raised alkaline phosphatase
    6. To evaluate pancreatic and salivary gland disease
    7. To monitor organophosphate poisoning and hepatic synthetic capacity (cholinesterase)

    Results are interpreted together with the history and clinical findings.

    Give the clinical importance of ALT.

    DU10JuDU10JaDU08Ja

    Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) is largely cytosolic and more liver-specific than aspartate aminotransferase (AST), so it is more specific for hepatocellular injury in most settings. Reference range is typically 4 to 36 IU/L. Each laboratory sets its own.

    Degree of rise above upper limit of normalCauses
    Borderline (less than 2 times)Non-specific
    Mild (2 to 5 times)MASLD and MASH (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and steatohepatitis), chronic alcohol use, chronic hepatitis B or C, drugs (statins, NSAIDs, antiepileptics), early haemochromatosis, extrahepatic causes (muscle disorders, thyroid disease)
    Moderate (5 to 15 times)Acute viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury
    Severe (more than 15 times)Acute hepatitis A, B or E, severe drug-induced injury, toxins (Amanita phalloides), ischaemic hepatitis
    Massive (more than 10,000 IU/L)Paracetamol toxicity, profound ischaemic injury
    Rarely herpes simplex hepatitis
    • ALT-predominant pattern: viral hepatitis, steatohepatitis, acute Budd-Chiari syndrome [hepatic vein thrombosis], ischaemic hepatitis, autoimmune conditions, haemochromatosis, drugs and toxins, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, Wilson disease [hereditary copper accumulation from ATP7B mutation], coeliac disease
    • The pattern and trend matter more than a single value
    • Mild elevations are often transient: up to 30% of asymptomatic elevations resolve within 3 weeks, so repeat testing is advised before an extensive work-up
    • The size of the rise does not reliably track histological severity or prognosis. in acute liver failure the aminotransferases can improve while synthetic function worsens
    • A normal ALT does not exclude MASLD or fibrosis

    Give the clinical importance of AST.

    DU10JuDU10JaDU08Ja

    Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) is found in liver, skeletal muscle, myocardium, kidney, brain, leucocytes and erythrocytes. It exists in cytosolic and mitochondrial forms, which explains its extrahepatic elevations. Reference range is typically 5 to 30 IU/L
    Each laboratory sets its own.

    • AST-predominant pattern: alcohol-related liver disease, steatohepatitis, cirrhosis
    • Non-hepatic causes of a raised AST: haemolysis, myopathy, thyroid disease, exercise
    • An AST to ALT ratio of 2 to 1 or greater suggests chronic alcohol use
    • Degree of rise above the upper limit of normal: borderline, less than 2 times
      Mild, 2 to 5 times
      Moderate, 5 to 15 times
      Severe, more than 15 times
      Massive, more than 10,000 IU/L (paracetamol toxicity, profound ischaemic injury)
    • Alcoholic hepatitis usually causes a mild to moderate rise, rarely above 300 to 500 IU/L
    • The pattern and trend matter more than a single value
      Mild elevations are often transient
    • Haemolysis falsely raises AST
      a persistent isolated rise may be macro-AST, which is benign

    Give the clinical importance of LDH.

    DU10Ju

    Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is an enzyme present in almost all body tissues. Its five isozymes, LDH-1 to LDH-5, are expressed differently in different tissues, which is the basis of its use as a diagnostic marker.

    • Myocardial infarction: LDH-1 exceeds LDH-2 (a flipped ratio above 1)
      LDH-1 stays raised from the second to the fourth day. It has been replaced by troponin as the marker of myocardial infarction
    • Liver injury: LDH-5 is raised
    • Raised in tissue destruction because of cell death and loss of cytoplasm. The level can remain raised for up to 7 days
    • Common causes of a raised level: cardiorespiratory disease, malignancy, fracture or trauma, infection, inflammation and hepatitis
    • Limitations: it is non-specific, so alternative assays are preferred (creatine kinase for muscle, ALT for liver, troponin for heart)
      Haemolysis falsely raises the result because red cells contain LDH

    Give the clinical importance of PSA.

    DU10JuDU10JaDU08Ja

    Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is an enzyme made by prostatic epithelial cells. It is released as an inactive precursor, becomes active in the prostatic ducts and then enters the blood. In semen it breaks down the proteins that keep semen gel-like.

    • Normal: a single upper limit of 4 ng/mL is commonly used. age-specific limits are 2.5 ng/mL (40 to 49 years), 3.5 ng/mL (50 to 59), 4.5 ng/mL (60 to 69) and 6.5 ng/mL (70 to 79)
    • A value of 4.0 ng/mL or more is the consensus threshold for further evaluation
    • Causes of a raised PSA: prostate cancer, benign prostatic hyperplasia (up to 86% of cases), prostatitis, infection, inflammation, trauma, digital rectal examination, urological instrumentation, recent ejaculation, constipation
    • Lowered by: 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (by about 50% over 6 to 12 months), and possibly statins, NSAIDs, paracetamol and thiazides. Obesity lowers PSA by dilution
    • Free PSA: the free to total ratio falls in malignancy
      Most useful when total PSA is 4 to 10 ng/mL
      Free PSA below 10% carries about a 50% cancer risk and above 25% carries below 10% risk
    • PSA density (total PSA divided by prostate volume): 0.15 or more is suspicious
    • PSA velocity: a rise above 0.75 ng/mL per year or 25% per year is suspicious. Shorter doubling time is linked to higher mortality
    • Screening: by shared decision after discussing risks and benefits, with a digital rectal examination for an abnormal result
    • Monitoring: after radical prostatectomy any detectable PSA suggests remaining prostate tissue, and biochemical recurrence is two consecutive values above 0.2 ng/mL. After radiotherapy, biochemical recurrence is two values more than 2 ng/mL above the nadir
    • Limitations: highly sensitive but non-specific, because benign and malignant conditions both raise it. up to 91% of elevated results are not due to cancer
      no value rules cancer in or out
      it leads to overdiagnosis, overtreatment and unnecessary biopsies. Very poorly differentiated, high-Gleason cancers may produce little or none

    Give the clinical importance of serum amylase.

    5DU11JaDU11JuDU10JaDU08JuDU08Ja

    Amylase is made mainly by the pancreas (acinar cells, P-type) and the salivary glands (S-type). Pancreatic amylase forms about 40 to 50% of total serum amylase in healthy adults. No international reference range exists. Reported intervals run from about 20 to 300 U/L, and each laboratory sets its own.

    Acute pancreatitis

    • Diagnosis needs at least 2 of 3: abdominal pain, amylase or lipase above 3 times the upper reference limit, and characteristic imaging
    • Amylase above 3 times the upper limit strongly suggests acute pancreatitis. at this cut-off P-type amylase is over 90% specific
    • It often returns to normal within 3 to 5 days
    • The level does not predict severity and does not track the course of the disease
    • Lipase is preferred because it is more specific and stays raised longer
    • A raised amylase with normal lipase suggests an extrapancreatic source or macroamylasaemia
    • Hypertriglyceridaemia can falsely lower amylase

    Other causes of a raised amylase

    • Pancreatic: chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic trauma
    • Salivary: gland trauma, surgery or radiation, alcoholism, vomiting in anorexia and bulimia
    • Abdominal: bowel obstruction, perforation, mesenteric infarction, appendicitis, peritonitis, cholecystitis, ruptured ectopic pregnancy
    • Reduced clearance: renal insufficiency, macroamylasaemia
    • Others: liver disease, diabetic ketoacidosis, pneumonia, cardiac surgery, burns, cerebral trauma, phaeochromocytoma, drugs
    • Amylase-producing tumours (lung, ovary, multiple myeloma)

    Macroamylasaemia: amylase binds to immunoglobulins (mainly IgA or IgG) to form large complexes that are poorly filtered by the kidney. An amylase to creatinine clearance ratio below 1% suggests it, and above 5% supports acute pancreatitis. It is usually benign.

    Low amylase: cystic fibrosis, chronic pancreatitis, diabetes, obesity, metabolic syndrome, chronic tobacco use. Falsely low in tubes containing oxalate, citrate or EDTA.

    Give the clinical importance of acid phosphatase.

    DU11JuDU05M

    Acid phosphatase is secreted by prostate tissue (prostatic form), expressed by osteoclasts (bone form) and released in seminal fluid. Normal serum level is about 2 ng/mL or less.

    • Prostatic acid phosphatase is inhibited by tartrate (tartrate-sensitive)
    • Bone acid phosphatase is tartrate-resistant (TRAP), also called purple acid phosphatase

    Raised in

    • Prostate cancer: about 95% of patients, especially with bone metastasis, because cancerous prostate tissue overexpresses the enzyme
    • Bone resorption: osteoporosis
      Bone metastases from several cancers raise TRAP
    • Hairy cell leukaemia: the leukaemic cells contain TRAP, which is sensitive and specific for this disease
    • Gaucher disease [glucocerebrosidase deficiency, a lysosomal storage disease]: TRAP is a marker when chitotriosidase is normal

    Clinical significance

    • It comes from several tissues, so it is non-specific
      it is more useful for monitoring therapy and prognosis than for diagnosis
    • It was once the main serum marker for prostate cancer but has largely been replaced by PSA
    • It remains useful in forensic work to identify seminal fluid
    • TRAP is a candidate marker for bone resorption and for monitoring osteoporosis treatment

    Give the clinical importance of CK-MB.

    DU11Ju

    Creatine kinase (CK) has three isoenzymes built from M (muscle) and B (brain) subunits: MM (skeletal muscle), MB (heart) and BB (brain). Skeletal muscle is almost entirely MM
    Cardiac muscle has about 20 to 30% MB. In healthy people serum CK is mostly MM with small amounts of MB.

    • CK-MB is a more specific indicator of myocardial damage than total CK
    • Raised in: myocardial infarction, myocarditis, some cardiac procedures
    • A CK-MB (CK-2) above about 6% of total CK is significant in myocardial infarction
    • Total CK in myocardial infarction rises within about 12 hours, peaks at 24 to 36 hours and returns to normal after 48 to 72 hours
    • The CK-MB2 to CK-MB1 isoform ratio helps separate cardiac from non-cardiac sources: above 1.7 is diagnostic and 1.5 or more strongly suggests infarction. Sampling is most useful 8 to 36 hours after onset of symptoms
    • Troponin is increasingly used instead, because CK is not heart-specific

    Give the clinical importance of alpha-fetoprotein.

    DU20NDU20JuDU11Ju

    Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a foetal glycoprotein of about 70 kDa made in the yolk sac, foetal liver and gastrointestinal tract. Some adult tumours re-express it. Its half-life is about 4 to 5 days. Normal level in men and non-pregnant women is typically 0 to 40 ng/mL.

    Hepatocellular carcinoma

    • Used for screening in high-risk groups: chronic hepatitis B or C, cirrhosis
    • In cirrhosis, a level above 200 ng/mL strongly suggests hepatocellular carcinoma
    • AFP-L3% (cut-off 10%) has a sensitivity of 75 to 96.9% and a specificity of 90 to 92%
      L3 is specific to malignancy, whereas L1 is linked to non-cancerous liver inflammation
    • A high AFP or AFP-L3% with a raised bilirubin (above 2 mg/dL) is linked to a poorer prognosis

    Germ cell tumours

    • Yolk sac tumour raises AFP
      Choriocarcinoma raises hCG
      Embryonal carcinoma raises both
    • Seminoma does not raise AFP
      Teratoma raises neither
    • About 90% of non-seminomatous testicular tumours have one or both markers raised

    Prenatal screening: maternal serum AFP is part of the triple and quadruple tests.

    • Raised: neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly), abdominal wall defects (omphalocele, gastroschisis), sacrococcygeal teratoma, cystic hygroma, renal abnormalities, osteogenesis imperfecta, threatened abortion
    • Low: Down syndrome [trisomy 21], trisomy 18, foetal demise, hydatidiform mole

    Other causes of a raised AFP in adults: metastatic liver cancer, cirrhosis, hepatitis, ataxia-telangiectasia.

    Monitoring

    • A persistently raised level after surgery suggests incomplete removal or metastasis
    • Falling levels suggest response to treatment
      Rising levels suggest failure or recurrence
    • In germ cell tumours, response is judged from the fall in AFP (half-life about 5 days) and hCG (12 to 20 hours)

    Give the clinical importance of creatine kinase.

    DU05S

    Creatine kinase (CK, creatine phosphokinase) regenerates ATP in tissues with high energy demand: heart, skeletal muscle and brain. Its isoenzymes are MM (skeletal muscle), MB (heart) and BB (brain). Skeletal muscle is almost entirely MM
    Cardiac muscle has about 20 to 30% MB. In healthy people serum CK is mostly MM.

    Causes of a raised CK

    • Muscle injury or breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) after crush injury, drugs, viral infection or strenuous exercise
    • Chronic muscle disease: muscular dystrophy (in Duchenne dystrophy [X-linked dystrophin deficiency] the level can rise before symptoms and in many female carriers), myositis, burns
    • Prolonged or intense exercise, with greater rises in untrained people
    • Heart disease: myocardial infarction, myocarditis, some cardiac procedures
    • Hypothyroidism
    • Statins, particularly simvastatin, with higher risk when drugs inhibiting CYP3A4 are taken together
    • Non-specific rises in kidney disease and arrhythmias

    Myocardial infarction: total CK rises within about 12 hours, peaks at 24 to 36 hours and returns to normal after 48 to 72 hours. Because CK is not heart-specific, CK-MB and, increasingly, troponin are used instead.

    Rhabdomyolysis

    • Muscle pain, weakness and dark urine caused by myoglobin
    • CK above 1,000 IU/L indicates rhabdomyolysis
      Above 5,000 IU/L indicates severe disease
    • Acute kidney injury is the most common complication, so prompt intravenous fluids are given

    Low CK: seen in connective tissue diseases and reduced physical activity, and linked to higher mortality in chronic kidney disease.

    CK is a useful but non-specific marker
    Interpretation depends on sex, age, muscle mass, activity and clinical context.

    Lipid profile

    What is lipid profile? What are its components and normal range?

    11DU25MDU23NDU22NDU21MDU18NovDU17MDU17JaDU14JaDU13JaDU11JaDU07Ja

    The lipid profile (lipid panel) is a fasting blood test (after a 9 to 12 hour fast) that includes total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol (HDL-C), LDL cholesterol (LDL-C) and triglycerides
    non-HDL cholesterol is also reported in a routine panel.

    ComponentHow obtainedClassification (mg/dL)
    Total cholesterolMeasured directlyBelow 200 desirable
    200 to 239 borderline high
    240 and above high
    LDL cholesterolUsually calculatedBelow 100 optimal
    100 to 129 near optimal or above optimal
    130 to 159 borderline high
    160 to 189 high
    190 and above very high
    HDL cholesterolMeasured directlyBelow 40 low
    60 and above high
    TriglyceridesMeasured directlyBelow 150 normal
    150 to 199 borderline high
    200 to 499 high
    500 and above very high
    • Friedewald equation: LDL-C is total cholesterol minus HDL-C minus triglycerides divided by 5 (in mg/dL)
    • It becomes inaccurate when triglycerides are high
      LDL-C is then measured directly (when fasting triglycerides are above about 200 to 400 mg/dL)
    • Total cholesterol to HDL ratio: 5 to 1 desirable, 3.5 to 1 optimum
    • Without fasting, only total cholesterol and HDL-C are usable
    • Abnormal results prompt a search for secondary causes: diabetes, hypothyroidism, liver or kidney disease, and drugs

    What are the fractions of lipid?

    DU07Ja

    Fractions measured in the lipid profile

    1. Total cholesterol
    2. HDL cholesterol
    3. LDL cholesterol (usually calculated)
    4. Triglycerides

    Lipoprotein fractions that carry plasma lipids

    1. Chylomicrons: made in the intestine
      Carry dietary triglycerides
    2. VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein): made in the liver. Carries endogenous triglycerides and some cholesterol
    3. IDL (intermediate-density lipoprotein): remnant of VLDL. Carries cholesterol esters and triglycerides
    4. LDL (low-density lipoprotein): carries cholesterol esters
    5. HDL (high-density lipoprotein): carries cholesterol esters. Moves excess cholesterol from tissues to the liver

    Write a short note on lipoprotein.

    DU12Ju

    Lipoproteins carry lipids through the watery blood, which lipids cannot do alone. Their metabolism determines the serum lipid levels.

    LipoproteinOrigin and main lipidApolipoproteinsRole
    ChylomicronIntestine
    Dietary triglycerides    		A-I, A-II, A-IV, B-48, C-I, C-II, C-III, EDelivers triglycerides to tissues
    Remnants are cleared by the liver
    VLDLLiver
    Endogenous triglycerides and some cholesterol    		B-100, C-I, C-II, C-III, ETriglycerides are hydrolysed by lipoprotein lipase in muscle and fat
    IDLRemnant of VLDL
    Cholesterol esters and triglycerides    		B-100, C-III, EFurther depleted of triglycerides and converted toward LDL
    LDLCholesterol estersB-100Delivers cholesterol to tissues
    Cleared by the LDL receptor
    HDLCholesterol estersA-I, A-II, C-I, C-II, C-III, D, EReverse cholesterol transport: moves excess cholesterol from tissues to the liver

    Functions of apolipoproteins

    • A-I: main structural protein of HDL
      Activates LCAT (lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase)
    • C-II: activates lipoprotein lipase
    • C-III: inhibits lipoprotein lipase
    • E: ligand for the LDL receptor

    Clinical importance

    • Raised LDL cholesterol is strongly associated with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease
    • Apo B-100 correlates with LDL particle number, so higher levels raise the risk of atherosclerosis
    • Familial hypercholesterolaemia is caused mainly by mutations of the LDL receptor gene
    • Severe lipoprotein lipase deficiency causes chylomicronaemia, with triglycerides above 2000 mg/dL and a risk of pancreatitis

    Why is HDL good cholesterol and LDL harmful (which fraction is better)?

    4DU23NDU22NDU08JaDU07Ja
    FeatureHDLLDL
    Cholesterol transportFrom peripheral tissues to the liver (reverse cholesterol transport)Delivers cholesterol to tissues
    Effect on the artery wallAntiatherogenic and anti-inflammatory
    Removes cholesterol from foam cells in plaques, which can reduce plaque size and inflammation    		Oxidised LDL is deposited in the arterial wall and forms foam cells
    Main apolipoproteinA-IB-100 (correlates with LDL particle number)
    Association with riskLow HDL is linked to higher cardiovascular riskRaised LDL cholesterol is strongly associated with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease
    LevelBelow 40 mg/dL is low
    60 mg/dL and above is high    		Below 100 mg/dL is optimal
    • A high HDL and a low LDL are the favourable fractions
    • In treatment, lowering LDL cholesterol is paramount
    • Raising HDL has not been shown to help: HDL-raising therapies have given no clinical benefit, and CETP inhibitors raised HDL by up to 100% yet cardiovascular events rose
    • Very high HDL due to CETP deficiency, primary familial hyperalphalipoproteinaemia or endothelial lipase deficiency may not be protective

    How will you diagnose a case of dyslipidaemia?

    DU22NDU11Ju

    1. Define the abnormality: raised LDL-C, triglycerides, non-HDL-C or lipoprotein(a), or low HDL-C
    More than one is often present 2. History - Diet: saturated and trans fats, simple sugars, alcohol - Drugs that raise LDL-C, triglycerides or lipoprotein(a), or lower HDL-C - Comorbidities: hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, obesity, HIV, inflammatory disease, liver disease - A new or suddenly worsening abnormality suggests a secondary cause - Anabolic steroid use in young, fit males with very low HDL-C 3. Family history: premature cardiovascular disease, lipid disorders, use of lipid-lowering drugs. Pancreatitis if triglycerides are markedly raised. a marked abnormality or onset at a young age suggests a genetic disorder 4. Examination: look for xanthomas, xanthelasma and corneal arcus 5. Fasting lipid profile (after 9 to 12 hours): total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL-C, calculated LDL-C and non-HDL-C - Direct LDL-C is measured if fasting triglycerides are high (above about 200 to 400 mg/dL) - LDL-C of 130 to 159 mg/dL is borderline high, 160 to 189 high and 190 or more very high. Triglycerides of 150 to 499 mg/dL indicate hypertriglyceridaemia and 500 or more very high. HDL-C below 40 mg/dL is low 6. Exclude secondary causes: TSH for raised LDL-C
    Glycaemic control for raised triglycerides with diabetes. Also liver and kidney disease and drugs 7. Further tests - Lipoprotein(a): premature coronary heart disease, strong family history, familial hypercholesterolaemia, statin resistance, aortic stenosis of uncertain cause, unexplained ischaemic stroke - Apo B: above 130 mg/dL is a risk enhancer - Genetic testing if monogenic hypercholesterolaemia is suspected, with screening of family members - Coronary calcium scan when the decision to start a statin is uncertain

    Body fluids

    Name the body fluids usually examined in clinical pathology.

    8DU24MDU21MDU16JuDU14JuDU13JuDU12JaDU10JuDU09Ja
    1. Cerebrospinal fluid: white cell count, protein, glucose, red cells (haemorrhage). For meningitis, tumours and demyelinating diseases
    2. Pleural fluid: appearance, protein and LDH (transudate or exudate), leucocytes, pH, triglycerides and cholesterol, adenosine deaminase, amylase
    3. Pericardial fluid: appearance, total white cell count with differential, cytology, bacteriological smears and cultures
    4. Peritoneal (ascitic) fluid: appearance, serum-ascites albumin gradient, total protein, polymorphonuclear count, glucose, amylase, triglycerides, urea and creatinine, adenosine deaminase
    5. Amniotic fluid: appearance and bilirubin (an indirect measure of foetal anaemia). Amniocentesis assesses chromosomal anomalies, foetal lung maturity and alloimmunisation
    6. Synovial fluid: volume, viscosity, clarity, colour, Gram stain, cell count and differential, crystals, culture
    7. Saliva: antibodies (for example to Helicobacter pylori, Lyme disease [tick-borne Borrelia infection], mumps, measles, HIV-1), hormones (cortisol, testosterone), drugs

    Diseases of White Blood Cells, Lymph Nodes, Spleen, and Thymus

    16 questions · viva and written, in Robbins order.

    Reactive Leukocyte Disorders

    Granulopoiesis

    A8

    What is granulopoiesis?

    A8Q1

    Granulopoiesis is the stepwise development of neutrophils in the bone marrow, in which granulocyte-monocyte progenitor cells pass through successive stages to become mature neutrophils.

    A8

    Stages of the granulocytic series.

    A8Q1
    1. Myeloblast: the earliest precursor recognisable by morphology
      Delicate nuclear chromatin, two to four nucleoli, and fine azurophilic granules in the cytoplasm.
    2. Promyelocyte: larger cell with more basophilic cytoplasm and coarse primary (azurophilic) granules
      Round or oval nucleus with one or two nucleoli.
    3. Myelocyte: specific (secondary) granules start to form
      This is the stage at which the cell becomes a neutrophilic, eosinophilic or basophilic myelocyte.
    4. Metamyelocyte: specific granules are fully present
      The nucleus is indented.
    5. Band form: the last stage before the mature cell
      The nucleus is band shaped.
    6. Segmented neutrophil: mature cell
      The nucleus has three to five lobes.

    As the cell matures, the nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio falls, granule production increases and the nucleus becomes more segmented. Eosinophils and basophils pass through the same stages, named eosinophilic or basophilic before the stage, for example eosinophilic metamyelocyte.

    Leukocytosis and leukopenia

    Define neutrophilia.

    DU26M

    Neutrophilia (neutrophilic leucocytosis) is an increase in the number of neutrophils in the blood. The adult reference range for neutrophils is 1,400 to 6,500 per microlitre.

    Name four important causes of neutrophilic leukocytosis.

    DU26M

    Causes of neutrophilic leucocytosis

    • Acute bacterial infections, especially those caused by pyogenic organisms.
    • Sterile inflammation caused by tissue necrosis, for example myocardial infarction and burns.
    • Chronic infection or inflammation.
    • Paraneoplastic, for example Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells].
    • Myeloproliferative neoplasms, for example chronic myeloid leukaemia.

    Mechanisms

    • Increased release from marrow stores: in acute inflammation, such as infection, there is a rapid increase in the egress of mature granulocytes from the bone marrow pool, mediated through tumour necrosis factor (TNF) and interleukin-1 (IL-1).
    • Increased marrow production: in prolonged infection or inflammation, IL-1, TNF and other mediators stimulate macrophages, marrow stromal cells and T cells to produce more haematopoietic growth factors. These increase proliferation and differentiation of committed granulocytic progenitors and sustain neutrophil production over several days. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) induces neutrophilia.
    • Chronic infection or inflammation and paraneoplastic causes are growth factor dependent
      Myeloproliferative neoplasms are growth factor independent.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 532p. 534

    Write a short note on eosinophilia.

    DU10JaDU06Ja

    Definition: eosinophilic leucocytosis, an increase in the number of eosinophils in the blood. The adult reference range is 0 to 500 per microlitre.

    Aetiology

    • Allergic disorders, such as asthma and hay fever.
    • Parasitic infestations.
    • Drug reactions.
    • Certain malignancies, for example Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells] and some non-Hodgkin lymphomas.
    • Autoimmune disorders, for example pemphigus and dermatitis herpetiformis.

    Pathogenesis: growth factors preferentially stimulate single leucocyte types. interleukin-5 mainly stimulates eosinophil production.

    Leukocyte disorders and leukaemoid reaction

    A8

    What do you mean by leucocytosis?

    A8Q2

    Leucocytosis refers to an increase in the number of white cells in the blood. It is a common reaction to a variety of inflammatory states.

    A8

    Causes of neutrophilia.

    A8Q2

    Causes of neutrophilic leucocytosis

    • Acute bacterial infections, especially those caused by pyogenic organisms.
    • Sterile inflammation caused by tissue necrosis, for example myocardial infarction and burns.
    • Chronic infection or inflammation.
    • Paraneoplastic, for example Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells].
    • Myeloproliferative neoplasms, for example chronic myeloid leukaemia.

    Mechanisms

    • Increased release from marrow stores: in acute inflammation, such as infection, there is a rapid increase in the egress of mature granulocytes from the bone marrow pool, mediated through tumour necrosis factor (TNF) and interleukin-1 (IL-1).
    • Increased marrow production: in prolonged infection or inflammation, IL-1, TNF and other mediators stimulate macrophages, marrow stromal cells and T cells to produce more haematopoietic growth factors. These increase proliferation and differentiation of committed granulocytic progenitors and sustain neutrophil production over several days. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) induces neutrophilia.
    • Chronic infection or inflammation and paraneoplastic causes are growth factor dependent
      Myeloproliferative neoplasms are growth factor independent.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 532p. 534
    A8

    Causes of eosinophilia.

    A8Q3
    • Allergic disorders, such as asthma and hay fever.
    • Parasitic infestations.
    • Drug reactions.
    • Certain malignancies, for example Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells] and some non-Hodgkin lymphomas.
    • Autoimmune disorders, for example pemphigus and dermatitis herpetiformis, and some vasculitides.
    • Atheroembolic disease (transient).
    A8

    What is Loeffler syndrome?

    A8Q3

    Löffler syndrome (a self-limited eosinophilic pneumonitis) is a form of secondary eosinophilia caused by invasive infection of the alveoli by the larvae of Ascaris, hookworm or Strongyloides helminth species. It presents with dry cough, dyspnoea and fever.

    A8

    Define lymphocytosis.

    A8Q4DU07Ja

    Also asked as: What do you mean by lymphocytosis?

    Lymphocytosis is an increase in the number of lymphocytes in the blood, one of the five principal types of leucocytosis.

    A8

    What are the causes of lymphocytosis?

    A8Q4DU07Ja

    Also asked as: Causes of lymphocytosis.

    Reactive

    • Disorders associated with chronic immunologic stimulation, where it accompanies monocytosis, for example tuberculosis and brucellosis.
    • Viral infections, for example hepatitis A, cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus [herpesvirus that causes infectious mononucleosis].
    • Bordetella pertussis infection.
    • Acute viral infections, particularly in children, which cause large numbers of activated lymphocytes that resemble neoplastic lymphoid cells.

    Neoplastic

    • Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, in which the absolute lymphocyte count is more than 5000 per cubic millimetre.
    • Monoclonal lymphocytosis of uncertain significance, a precursor lesion with about a 1% risk per year of progressing to chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.
    • T-cell and NK-cell large granular lymphocytic leukaemia, which usually presents with mild-to-moderate lymphocytosis and splenomegaly.
    A8

    Write a short note on leukopenia.

    A8Q5DU07Ju

    Also asked as: What is leucopenia?

    Definition: leucopenia is a decrease in the number of circulating white cells.

    Aetiology and pathogenesis

    • A low white cell count most commonly results from reduced numbers of neutrophils (neutropenia, granulocytopenia).
    • Lymphopenia is less common. Causes are congenital immunodeficiency diseases, advanced HIV infection, therapy with glucocorticoids or cytotoxic drugs, autoimmune disorders, malnutrition and certain acute viral infections.
    • In acute viral infections, lymphopenia stems from lymphocyte redistribution rather than a decrease in the number of lymphocytes in the body. Type I interferons activate T lymphocytes and change the surface proteins that regulate T-cell migration, so activated T cells are sequestered in lymph nodes and adhere more to vascular endothelium.
    • An enlarged spleen may trap white cells and induce leucopenia.

    Clinical features and complications

    • Granulocytopenia is more common and is often associated with diminished granulocyte function.
    • Its consequences are the infections of neutropenia and agranulocytosis.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 533p. 572
    A8

    Write a short note on neutropenia.

    A8Q5DU09Ja

    Also asked as: What is neutropenia?

    Definition: neutropenia is a reduction in the number of neutrophils in the blood. Agranulocytosis is a marked reduction in neutrophils, usually less than 100 per microlitre.

    Aetiology and pathogenesis

    1. Inadequate or ineffective granulopoiesis - Suppression of haematopoietic stem cells, as in aplastic anaemia and infiltrative marrow disorders (tumours, granulomatous disease). Granulocytopenia is then accompanied by anaemia and thrombocytopenia. - Suppression of committed granulocytic precursors by certain drugs. - Ineffective haematopoiesis, as in megaloblastic anaemia and myelodysplastic neoplasms, in which defective precursors die in the marrow. - Rare congenital conditions, such as severe congenital neutropenia (Kostmann syndrome [severe congenital neutropenia]), in which inherited gene defects impair granulocytic differentiation. 2. Increased destruction or sequestration of neutrophils - Immune mediated injury, which can be idiopathic, associated with a defined immunologic disorder such as systemic lupus erythematosus, or caused by drugs. - Splenomegaly, with sequestration and destruction of neutrophils by increased numbers of splenic macrophages. - Increased peripheral utilisation, in overwhelming bacterial, fungal or rickettsial infections.

    Morphology

    • Marrow is hypercellular when neutrophils are destroyed in the periphery or granulopoiesis is ineffective, because of a compensatory increase in granulocytic precursors.
    • Marrow is hypocellular when agranulocytosis is caused by agents that suppress or destroy granulocyte precursors.
    • Infection is a common consequence. Necrotising ulcerative lesions of the gingiva, floor of the mouth, buccal mucosa, pharynx or elsewhere in the oral cavity are characteristic. They are deep, undermined and covered by grey to green-black necrotic membranes from which bacteria or fungi can be isolated.
    • Similar ulcers occur less often in the skin, vagina, anus or gastrointestinal tract.
    • Life-threatening invasive bacterial or fungal infections may occur in the lungs, urinary tract and kidneys. Deep fungal infections by Candida and Aspergillus are a particular risk.
    • Sites of infection often show massive growth of organisms with little leucocytic response.

    Clinical features and complications

    • Malaise, chills and fever, often followed by marked weakness and fatigability.
    • In agranulocytosis, infections are often overwhelming and may cause death within hours to days.
    • Serious infections are most likely when the neutrophil count falls below 500 per cubic millimetre.
    • Broad-spectrum antibiotics must be given promptly when signs or symptoms appear. After myelosuppressive chemotherapy, neutropenia is treated with G-CSF.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 533
    A8

    What is agranulocytosis?

    A8Q5

    Agranulocytosis is a marked reduction in neutrophils (usually less than 100 per microlitre), which has the serious consequence of making individuals susceptible to bacterial and fungal infections.

    A8

    Important causes of leucopenia, neutropenia and agranulocytosis.

    A8Q5

    Leucopenia

    • Neutropenia, the most common cause of a low white cell count.
    • Lymphopenia: congenital immunodeficiency, advanced HIV infection, glucocorticoid or cytotoxic drug therapy, autoimmune disorders, malnutrition, certain acute viral infections.
    • Splenomegaly, which may trap white cells.

    Neutropenia

    • Suppression of haematopoietic stem cells: aplastic anaemia, infiltrative marrow disorders.
    • Suppression of committed granulocytic precursors by certain drugs.
    • Ineffective haematopoiesis: megaloblastic anaemia, myelodysplastic neoplasms.
    • Congenital: severe congenital neutropenia (Kostmann syndrome [severe congenital neutropenia]).
    • Immune mediated injury: idiopathic, systemic lupus erythematosus, drugs
      Acquired idiopathic neutropenia from autoantibodies against neutrophil-specific antigens.
    • Splenomegaly.
    • Increased peripheral utilisation in overwhelming bacterial, fungal or rickettsial infections.
    • Monoclonal proliferations of large granular lymphocytes (LGL leukaemia), probably through suppression of granulocytic progenitors by products of the neoplastic cell.

    Agranulocytosis

    • Drug toxicity is the most common cause.
    • Alkylating agents and antimetabolites used in cancer treatment cause it in a predictable, dose-related fashion, through generalised suppression of haematopoiesis.
    • Idiosyncratic reaction to a large variety of agents, including certain antibiotics, anticonvulsants, anti-inflammatory drugs, antipsychotic drugs and diuretics.
    • Antipsychotic agents such as chlorpromazine and related phenothiazines act through a toxic effect on granulocytic precursors in the marrow.
    • Sulfonamides and some other drugs probably act through antibody-mediated destruction of neutrophils.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 533p. 572
    A8

    Define leukaemoid reaction / write a short note (incl. blood picture).

    13A8Q13DU25NDU25MDU23NDU22MDU16JuDU13JaDU12JaDU11JaDU09JuDU09JaDU08JaDU06Ja

    Also asked as: What is leukaemoid reaction?

    Definition: a leukaemoid reaction is a marked increase in white cells (more than 50,000 per microlitre), typically neutrophils, as an acute inflammatory reaction that can mimic leukaemia. In severe infections many immature granulocytes appear in the blood, mimicking myeloid leukaemia.

    Aetiology and pathogenesis

    • Severe infection.
    • Intoxication.
    • Other malignancies.
    • Severe haemorrhage.
    • Acute haemolysis.
    • It often results from accelerated release of cells from the bone marrow. In acute infection, release of mature granulocytes from the marrow is mediated by TNF and IL-1.

    Blood picture

    • Persistent reactive neutrophilic leucocytosis, with a white cell count of more than 50,000 per microlitre.
    • A mixture of early mature neutrophil precursors: myelocytes and metamyelocytes, with promyelocytes and rarely myeloblasts. There is no leukaemic hiatus (the gap between blasts and mature cells seen in acute leukaemia).
    • Toxic granulation, cytoplasmic vacuolation and Döhle bodies [sky-blue patches of dilated endoplasmic reticulum].
    • A high neutrophil alkaline phosphatase score.
    • Normal eosinophil and basophil counts
      no monocytosis.
    • No Philadelphia chromosome [t(9;22) producing the BCR-ABL1 fusion] or BCR::ABL1 translocation.
    • Marrow is hypercellular but otherwise normal.
    A8

    What is subleukaemic leukaemia?

    A8Q13

    Subleukaemic leukaemia is a leukaemia with abnormal white cells in the peripheral blood in which the total white cell count is normal.

    In aleukaemic leukaemia blasts are entirely absent from the blood, so a bone marrow examination is essential to exclude acute leukaemia in pancytopenic patients.

    A8

    Write a short note on leukoerythroblastic blood picture.

    A8Q18DU19MDU12Ju

    Also asked as: What is a leukoerythroblastic blood picture?

    Definition: leukoerythroblastosis is the premature release into the blood of nucleated erythroid and early granulocyte progenitors (immature precursors).

    Aetiology and pathogenesis

    • Processes that distort the marrow architecture, such as deposits of metastatic cancer or granulomatous disorders.
    • Fibrosis of the marrow, as in primary myelofibrosis.
    • Immature cells also enter the circulation from sites of extramedullary haematopoiesis.

    Blood picture

    • Nucleated red cells and immature granulocytes in the blood.
    • Teardrop-shaped red cells (dacryocytes), which are probably damaged during the birthing process in the fibrotic marrow.
    • In myelofibrosis, moderate to severe normochromic normocytic anaemia. Large platelets and basophilia are common but nonspecific.

    Clinical significance

    • It is characteristic of primary myelofibrosis but is seen in other infiltrative disorders of the marrow, including granulomatous diseases and metastatic tumours.
    • The blood findings are not specific
      Bone marrow biopsy is essential for diagnosis.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 532p. 569p. 570
    A8

    Causes of leukoerythroblastic blood picture.

    A8Q18
    • Primary myelofibrosis, and the spent phase of other myeloproliferative neoplasms.
    • Metastatic tumours in the marrow.
    • Granulomatous diseases of the marrow.
    • Other infiltrative disorders of the marrow.
    • Marrow infiltration by lymphoid tumour, for example chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, together with premature release of progenitors in the face of severe anaemia.

    Lymph Node Disorders

    A8

    What do you mean by lymphadenopathy?

    A8Q36

    Lymphadenopathy is enlargement of lymph nodes. It occurs in 2 patterns:

    • Localised: nodes in a contiguous grouping, in one body area.
    • Generalised: nodes in 2 or more non-contiguous regions.
    A8

    Common causes of lymphadenopathy.

    A8Q36
    • Infections: bacterial and viral infections of the drained area. Tuberculosis and Mycobacterium avium intracellulare. Fungal (coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis, Candida). Parasitic (toxoplasmosis, Chagas disease [Trypanosoma cruzi infection]). cat-scratch disease.
    • Reactive hyperplasia: acute and chronic nonspecific lymphadenitis
      Follicular hyperplasia in rheumatoid arthritis, toxoplasmosis and early HIV infection. Paracortical hyperplasia in infectious mononucleosis.
    • Autoimmune disease.
    • Malignancy: lymphoma, leukaemia, metastatic cancer and head and neck cancers.
    A8

    Common causes of lymphadenitis.

    A8Q38

    Acute nonspecific lymphadenitis

    • Cervical nodes: infections of the teeth or tonsils.
    • Axillary or inguinal nodes: infections of the extremities.
    • Mesenteric nodes: acute appendicitis and other inflammatory conditions of the gut, including self-limiting viral infections.
    • Generalised: systemic viral infections, particularly in children, and bacteraemia.

    Chronic nonspecific lymphadenitis

    • Many chronic immunological stimuli
      Common in inguinal and axillary nodes, which are stimulated by immune reactions to trivial injuries and infections of the extremities.
    • Follicular hyperplasia: rheumatoid arthritis, toxoplasmosis and early HIV infection.
    • Paracortical hyperplasia: acute viral infections, for example infectious mononucleosis.
    • Sinus histiocytosis: nodes draining cancers, for example carcinoma of the breast.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 535p. 536
    A8

    Morphological features of chronic non-specific lymphadenitis / reactive hyperplasia.

    A8Q40

    Several patterns are often seen within the same node. The nodes are nontender because enlargement is slow and there is no acute inflammation.

    1. Follicular hyperplasia: large oblong germinal centres (secondary follicles) surrounded by a collar of small resting naive B cells, the mantle zone. - Germinal centres have a dark zone of proliferating blast-like B cells (centroblasts) and a light zone of B cells with irregular or cleaved nuclei (centrocytes). - Follicular dendritic cells and tingible body macrophages containing nuclear debris of apoptotic B cells lie among them. - Features favouring reactive over neoplastic follicles: preserved node architecture, including interfollicular T-cell zones and sinusoids. Marked variation in follicle shape and size
    Frequent mitotic figures, phagocytic macrophages, and recognisable light and dark zones. 2. Paracortical hyperplasia: expanded T-cell zones with immunoblasts (three to four times the size of resting lymphocytes, with round nuclei, open chromatin and prominent nucleoli). Hypertrophy of sinusoidal and vascular endothelial cells, sometimes with macrophages and eosinophils.

    Exuberant reactions may efface the B-cell follicles. 3. Sinus histiocytosis (reticular hyperplasia): increased number and size of endothelial cells lining the sinuses, and increased intrasinusoidal macrophages that expand and distort the sinuses.

    Write down the causes of generalized lymphadenopathy.

    7DU25NDU22NDU18NovDU17NovDU16JuDU12JaDU07Ja
    • Systemic viral infections, particularly in children, and bacteraemia.
    • Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma, in 50% to 60% of symptomatic patients.
    • Follicular lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma and peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified.
    • Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, from neoplastic infiltration.
    • Tuberculosis and other mycobacterial, fungal and parasitic infections (for example toxoplasmosis).
    • Autoimmune disease.
    • Generalised lymphadenopathy means nodes in 2 or more non-contiguous regions.

    What are the causes of cervical lymphadenopathy?

    DU05M
    • Acute nonspecific lymphadenitis from infections of the teeth or tonsils.
    • Posterior cervical nodes: localised bacterial and viral infections, and lymphoma.
    • Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells] and other lymphomas.
    • Metastatic cancer, including head and neck cancers.

    Leukaemias

    Leukaemia: definition and classification

    What is the etiology of leukaemia?

    DU24MDU22N
    • Genetic alterations in cancer genes: nonrandom chromosomal abnormalities, most commonly translocations, are present in most white cell neoplasms, with driver mutations that block differentiation, drive growth or prevent apoptosis.
    • Inherited factors: diseases with genomic instability (Bloom syndrome [inherited DNA-helicase defect with sun-sensitive rash and cancer predisposition], Fanconi anaemia [inherited DNA-repair defect causing marrow failure], ataxia telangiectasia) raise the risk of acute leukaemia. Down syndrome [trisomy 21] (trisomy 21) and type I neurofibromatosis are associated with childhood leukaemia.
    • Viruses: HTLV-1 with adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma
      EBV with a subset of Burkitt lymphoma [high-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC translocation] and other lymphomas
      HHV8 with an unusual B-cell lymphoma presenting as an effusion.
    • Chronic inflammation: for example Helicobacter pylori with gastric B-cell lymphomas, and gluten-sensitive enteropathy with intestinal T-cell lymphomas.
    • Treatment: chemotherapy with alkylating agents has been followed by a high incidence of acute myeloid leukaemia.

    Acute leukaemias

    A8

    Define leukaemia.

    8A8Q6DU26MDU25MDU22NDU20NDU20JuDU19MDU18M

    Leukaemias are neoplasms that present with widespread involvement of the bone marrow and (usually, but not always) the peripheral blood.

    A8

    Clinical presentation of acute leukaemia.

    A8Q7
    • Abrupt, stormy onset within days to a few weeks of the first symptoms.
    • Marrow failure: fatigue from anaemia
      Fever from infections secondary to neutropenia
      Bleeding from thrombocytopenia.
    • Bleeding: cutaneous petechiae and ecchymoses, serosal haemorrhages, and mucosal haemorrhages into the gingivae and urinary tract. Procoagulants and fibrinolytic factors released by leukaemic cells, especially in AML with t(15;17), make bleeding worse.
    • Infections, frequent in the oral cavity, skin, lungs, kidneys, urinary bladder and colon, often caused by opportunists such as fungi, Pseudomonas and commensal organisms.
    • Mass effects from neoplastic infiltration, more common in ALL: bone pain, generalised lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, testicular enlargement, and in T-ALL compression of large vessels and airways in the mediastinum.
    • Central nervous system manifestations, more common in ALL: headache, vomiting and nerve palsies from meningeal spread.
    • In AML, tumours with monocytic differentiation often infiltrate the skin (leukaemia cutis) and gingiva. AML occasionally presents as a localised soft tissue mass, a myeloid sarcoma.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 542p. 563p. 564
    A8

    How will you diagnose a case of acute leukaemia in the laboratory?

    8A8Q9DU24MDU22NDU17MDU11JuDU10JaDU09JaDU07Ju

    Also asked as: Laboratory diagnosis of acute leukaemia.

    1. Peripheral blood: blast count is highly variable
      in AML blasts may be more than 100,000 per microlitre but are under 10,000 in about 50% of patients, and occasionally blasts are absent from the blood (aleukaemic leukaemia).
    2. Bone marrow examination is essential. The marrow is hypercellular and packed with blasts, generally 20% or more of marrow cells.
    3. Morphology of blasts: lymphoblasts have condensed chromatin, small nucleoli and scant agranular cytoplasm. Myeloblasts have delicate chromatin, two to four nucleoli and more cytoplasm with fine azurophilic granules and often Auer rods [needle-shaped azurophilic inclusions in myeloblasts].
    4. Cytochemistry: myeloperoxidase positive in myeloblasts
      Lymphoblasts are myeloperoxidase negative and often contain periodic acid–Schiff positive cytoplasmic material. Monoblasts are nonspecific esterase positive.
    5. Immunophenotyping by flow cytometry, which confirms the lineage. Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is positive in more than 95% of ALL. B-ALL: CD19, CD10, PAX5
      T-ALL: CD1, CD2, CD5, CD7. Myeloid blasts: CD34, CD33, CD15 and CD64.
    6. Cytogenetics and molecular tests: chromosomal aberrations in 50% to 70% of AML by standard techniques
      Approximately 90% of ALL have numerical or structural chromosomal changes.

    A8

    Laboratory diagnosis of AML.

    A8Q10
    1. Peripheral blood: blast count highly variable
      May be more than 100,000 per microlitre but under 10,000 in about 50%. Occasionally absent (aleukaemic leukaemia). Anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia are present.
    2. Bone marrow examination is essential to exclude acute leukaemia in pancytopenic patients. Generally 20% or more myeloid blasts
      The WHO permits the diagnosis with fewer than 20% if a defining genetic aberration is present.
    3. Blast morphology: myeloblasts have delicate nuclear chromatin, two to four nucleoli and more cytoplasm than lymphoblasts, with fine peroxidase positive azurophilic granules. Auer rods [needle-shaped azurophilic inclusions in myeloblasts] (needle-like azurophilic granules) are present in many cases, particularly numerous in t(15;17). Monoblasts have folded or lobulated nuclei, lack Auer rods and are nonspecific esterase positive.
    4. Immunophenotyping: stains for myeloid-specific antigens confirm the diagnosis, since myeloblasts and lymphoblasts are hard to tell apart by morphology. Blasts express CD34, CD33 and in part CD15, but not CD64. Megakaryocytic blasts are detected with antibodies such as GPIIb/IIIa.
    5. Cytogenetics: abnormalities are detected in 50% to 70% of cases with standard techniques and about 90% with high-resolution banding. Balanced translocations t(8;21), inv(16) and t(15;17) are typical of de novo AML in younger adults. Deletions or monosomies of chromosomes 5 and 7 and p53 mutations follow DNA-damaging agents.
    6. DNA sequencing detects mutations such as NPM1.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 563
    A8

    Why is infection common in acute leukaemia?

    A8Q15
    • Accumulation of neoplastic blasts in the bone marrow suppresses normal haematopoiesis by physical crowding, competition for growth factors and other poorly understood mechanisms.
    • This depresses marrow function, so neutropenia develops
      Fever reflects infections secondary to neutropenia.
    • Neutropenia leads to infections, which are often fulminant.
    • Infections are frequent in the oral cavity, skin, lungs, kidneys, urinary bladder and colon.
    • They are often caused by opportunists such as fungi, Pseudomonas and commensal organisms.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 542p. 563

      Fever from infections secondary to neutropenia
      Bleeding from thrombocytopenia.
    • Bleeding: cutaneous petechiae and ecchymoses, serosal haemorrhages, and mucosal haemorrhages into the gingivae and urinary tract. Procoagulants and fibrinolytic factors released by leukaemic cells, especially in AML with t(15;17), make bleeding worse.
    • Infections, frequent in the oral cavity, skin, lungs, kidneys, urinary bladder and colon, often caused by opportunists such as fungi, Pseudomonas and commensal organisms.
    • Mass effects from neoplastic infiltration, more common in ALL: bone pain, generalised lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, testicular enlargement, and in T-ALL compression of large vessels and airways in the mediastinum.
    • Central nervous system manifestations, more common in ALL: headache, vomiting and nerve palsies from meningeal spread.
    • In AML, tumours with monocytic differentiation often infiltrate the skin (leukaemia cutis) and gingiva. AML occasionally presents as a localised soft tissue mass, a myeloid sarcoma.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 542p. 563p. 564

    Give the laboratory diagnosis/bone marrow findings of ALL.

    4DU25NDU25MDU15JaDU08Ju
    1. Peripheral blood: blast count is highly variable
      in AML blasts may be more than 100,000 per microlitre but are under 10,000 in about 50% of patients, and occasionally blasts are absent from the blood (aleukaemic leukaemia).
    2. Bone marrow examination is essential. The marrow is hypercellular and packed with blasts, generally 20% or more of marrow cells.
    3. Morphology of blasts: lymphoblasts have condensed chromatin, small nucleoli and scant agranular cytoplasm. Myeloblasts have delicate chromatin, two to four nucleoli and more cytoplasm with fine azurophilic granules and often Auer rods [needle-shaped azurophilic inclusions in myeloblasts].
    4. Cytochemistry: myeloperoxidase positive in myeloblasts
      Lymphoblasts are myeloperoxidase negative and often contain periodic acid–Schiff positive cytoplasmic material. Monoblasts are nonspecific esterase positive.
    5. Immunophenotyping by flow cytometry, which confirms the lineage. Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is positive in more than 95% of ALL. B-ALL: CD19, CD10, PAX5
      T-ALL: CD1, CD2, CD5, CD7. Myeloid blasts: CD34, CD33, CD15 and CD64.
    6. Cytogenetics and molecular tests: chromosomal aberrations in 50% to 70% of AML by standard techniques
      Approximately 90% of ALL have numerical or structural chromosomal changes.

    Write a short note on blast crisis.

    7DU24NDU22MDU17MDU17JaDU16JaDU15JaDU13Ju
    • Blast crisis is the terminal event in CML, a picture resembling acute leukaemia.
    • About 50% of patients first enter an accelerated phase after a variable period averaging 3 years, with increasing anaemia and thrombocytopenia, sometimes a rise in basophils, and new cytogenetic abnormalities such as trisomy 8, isochromosome 17q or duplication of the Ph chromosome. Within 6 to 12 months this ends in blast crisis.
    • In the other 50%, blast crisis occurs abruptly without an accelerated phase.
    • In 70% of crises the blasts are myeloid (myeloid blast crisis)
      in most of the remainder they are of pre-B cell origin (lymphoid blast crisis). This is evidence that CML originates from a pluripotent stem cell with both myeloid and lymphoid potential.
    • In lymphoid blast crisis, 85% of cases have mutations that interfere with Ikaros, a transcription factor encoded by IKZF1.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 560p. 567

    A8

    What is Philadelphia chromosome?

    6A8Q8DU26MDU20NDU20JuDU18MDU05Ja

    Also asked as: What is the Philadelphia chromosome?

    The Philadelphia chromosome [t(9;22) producing the BCR-ABL1 fusion] (Ph) is the reciprocal (9;22)(q34;q11) translocation that creates the chimeric BCR::ABL gene, from portions of the BCR gene on chromosome 22 and the ABL gene on chromosome 9. It is present in more than 90% of cases of chronic myeloid leukaemia.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 566
    A8

    Importance of the Philadelphia chromosome.

    A8Q8
    • It is the hallmark of chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), which is distinguished from other myeloproliferative neoplasms by the chimeric BCR::ABL gene.
    • BCR::ABL directs the synthesis of a constitutively active BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase, usually 210 kDa in size. The BCR part has a dimerisation domain that self-associates and activates the ABL kinase.
    • The kinase drives the RAS and JAK/STAT pathways, the same progrowth and prosurvival pathways turned on by haematopoietic growth factors. It preferentially drives proliferation of granulocytic and megakaryocytic progenitors and causes abnormal release of immature granulocytes from the marrow.
    • It shows that the cell of origin is a pluripotent haematopoietic stem cell.
    • Diagnosis: BCR::ABL detected by chromosomal analysis or PCR-based tests. In the remaining cases, where the fusion gene is formed by complex or cryptic rearrangements, it is detected by fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) or PCR.
    • Treatment: BCR-ABL inhibitors give sustained haematological remissions in more than 90% of patients. Sensitive molecular tests monitor for recurrence.
    • BCR::ABL1 is also found in a subset of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 566p. 561p. 560
    A8

    What do you mean by blast crisis / blastic transformation?

    A8Q8, Q12
    • Blast crisis is the terminal event in CML, a picture resembling acute leukaemia.
    • About 50% of patients first enter an accelerated phase after a variable period averaging 3 years, with increasing anaemia and thrombocytopenia, sometimes a rise in basophils, and new cytogenetic abnormalities such as trisomy 8, isochromosome 17q or duplication of the Ph chromosome. Within 6 to 12 months this ends in blast crisis.
    • In the other 50%, blast crisis occurs abruptly without an accelerated phase.
    • In 70% of crises the blasts are myeloid (myeloid blast crisis)
      in most of the remainder they are of pre-B cell origin (lymphoid blast crisis). This is evidence that CML originates from a pluripotent stem cell with both myeloid and lymphoid potential.
    • In lymphoid blast crisis, 85% of cases have mutations that interfere with Ikaros, a transcription factor encoded by IKZF1.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 560p. 567
    A8

    Laboratory diagnosis of CGL/CML.

    A8Q12

    1. Peripheral blood - Leucocytosis, often exceeding 100,000 per microlitre, of neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils and basophils. - Blasts usually less than 10% of circulating cells. - Platelets usually increased, sometimes markedly. - Mild to moderate anaemia. 2. Bone marrow - Markedly hypercellular, with massively increased maturing granulocytic precursors, usually with a raised proportion of eosinophils and basophils. - Megakaryocytes increased, usually small and dysplastic. - Erythroid progenitors normal or mildly decreased. - Scattered sea-blue histiocytes (macrophages with abundant wrinkled green-blue cytoplasm). - Increased reticulin. Overt fibrosis is rare. 3. Molecular and cytogenetic tests: the BCR::ABL fusion gene, with the Philadelphia chromosome [t(9;22) producing the BCR-ABL1 fusion] t(9;22), detected by chromosomal analysis, FISH or PCR-based tests. This differentiates CML from other myeloproliferative neoplasms.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 531p. 560
    A8

    Why is the prognosis of blast crisis worse than classical CGL?

    A8Q17
    • Untreated classical CML progresses slowly, with a median survival of about 3 years.
    • Blast crisis is the greatest threat to the patient.
    • It resembles acute leukaemia.
    • The accelerated phase brings additional clonal cytogenetic abnormalities: trisomy 8, isochromosome 17q, duplication of the Ph chromosome.
    • Lymphoid blast crisis has mutations in Ikaros in 85% of cases.
    • BCR-ABL inhibitors control blood counts and decrease the risk of transformation to the accelerated phase and blast crisis.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 560p. 567p. 533

    Define chronic leukaemia.

    DU03Ja

    Leukaemias are neoplasms that present with widespread involvement of the bone marrow and, usually but not always, the peripheral blood. The chronic leukaemias are chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, a B-cell neoplasm, and chronic myeloid leukaemia, a myeloproliferative neoplasm distinguished by the BCR::ABL gene.

    Give the clinical manifestations of chronic granulocytic leukaemia.

    DU07Ju
    • Insidious onset, mainly in adults, with peak incidence in the fifth and sixth decades.
    • Mild to moderate anaemia and hypermetabolism from increased cell turnover cause fatigability, weakness, weight loss and anorexia.
    • Dragging sensation in the abdomen from splenomegaly, or sudden left upper quadrant pain from splenic infarction.
    • Mild hepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy from extramedullary haematopoiesis.
    • Slow progression
      Untreated median survival about 3 years.
    • Accelerated phase in about 50%, after an average of 3 years: increasing anaemia and thrombocytopenia, sometimes more basophils, and new cytogenetic abnormalities.
    • Blast crisis within 6 to 12 months, resembling acute leukaemia
      in the other 50% it occurs abruptly.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 531p. 560

    Give the laboratory diagnosis (blood/bone marrow) of chronic myeloid leukaemia.

    9DU26MDU24NDU21MDU20NDU20JuDU19MDU18MDU17MDU14Ju

    1. Peripheral blood - Leucocytosis, often exceeding 100,000 per microlitre, of neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils and basophils. - Blasts usually less than 10% of circulating cells. - Platelets usually increased, sometimes markedly. - Mild to moderate anaemia. 2. Bone marrow - Markedly hypercellular, with massively increased maturing granulocytic precursors, usually with a raised proportion of eosinophils and basophils. - Megakaryocytes increased, usually small and dysplastic. - Erythroid progenitors normal or mildly decreased. - Scattered sea-blue histiocytes (macrophages with abundant wrinkled green-blue cytoplasm). - Increased reticulin. Overt fibrosis is rare. 3. Molecular and cytogenetic tests: the BCR::ABL fusion gene, with the Philadelphia chromosome [t(9;22) producing the BCR-ABL1 fusion] t(9;22), detected by chromosomal analysis, FISH or PCR-based tests.     Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia

    A8

    Laboratory diagnosis of CLL.

    A8Q17

    1. Peripheral blood - Absolute lymphocyte count more than 5000 per cubic millimetre (the diagnostic requirement for CLL). - Variable numbers of small round lymphocytes with scant cytoplasm and condensed chromatin. - Smudge cells, tumour cells disrupted in making smears. - Leucocyte count highly variable. Counts above 200,000 per cubic millimetre are sometimes seen. - With autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, spherocytes. with marrow infiltration, nucleated red cells. 2. Lymph node: diffuse effacement by small lymphocytes 6 to 12 mm in diameter with round to slightly irregular nuclei, condensed chromatin and scant cytoplasm. Proliferation centres of larger activated lymphocytes are pathognomonic. The bone marrow, spleen and liver are also involved. 3. Immunophenotype: CD19, CD20, CD23 and CD5. low-level surface immunoglobulin, usually IgM, or IgM and IgD. high-level BCL2. 4. Cytogenetics: deletions of 13q14.3, 11q and 17p, and trisomy 12. NOTCH1 mutations in 10% to 18%. 5. Prognostic markers: deletions of 11q and 17p (involving TP53), lack of somatic hypermutation, ZAP-70 expression and NOTCH1 mutations indicate a worse outcome. 6. A small monoclonal immunoglobulin spike is present in some patients. Hypogammaglobulinaemia is common.

    A8

    What do you know about Reed-Sternberg cells?

    A8Q38
    • Reed-Sternberg cells [binucleate owl-eye giant cell] are the neoplastic giant cells that are the distinctive feature of Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells].
    • Origin: germinal centre or post-germinal centre B cells, shown by clonal IGH gene rearrangements and somatic hypermutation. In classic Hodgkin lymphoma they fail to express most B-cell-specific genes, including immunoglobulin genes.
    • Diagnostic Reed-Sternberg cell: a large cell (about 45 micrometres) with multiple nuclei or a nucleus with multiple lobes, each with a large inclusion-like nucleolus about the size of a small lymphocyte, and abundant cytoplasm.
    • Variants: mononuclear, lacunar and lymphohistiocytic (L&H, popcorn) cells.
    • Immunophenotype (classic types): positive for PAX5, CD15 and CD30
      Negative for other B-cell markers, T-cell markers and CD45.
    • NF-κB activation promotes their growth and survival, through EBV latent membrane protein 1 or loss-of-function mutations in IκB or TNF-induced protein 3.
    • They secrete cytokines and chemokines (interleukin-5, interleukin-10, M-CSF, eotaxin) that attract reactive cells. PD-L1 and PD-L2 on them blunt cytotoxic T-cell responses.
    • In classic forms they die by shrinking and becoming pyknotic, called mummification.
    • Similar cells may be seen in infectious mononucleosis, solid tissue cancers and certain non-Hodgkin lymphomas.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 556p. 557
    A8

    Classification of Hodgkin's lymphoma.

    A8Q39

    Classic Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells]

    1. Nodular sclerosis.
    2. Mixed cellularity.
    3. Lymphocyte-rich.
    4. Lymphocyte-depleted.

    Nonclassic

    1. Nodular lymphocyte predominant.

    In the first four the Reed-Sternberg cells [binucleate owl-eye giant cell] have a similar distinctive immunophenotype. In nodular lymphocyte predominant, the Reed-Sternberg cells have a B-cell immunophenotype different from the classic types.

    A8

    How will you proceed to diagnose a case of lymphoma?

    A8Q39
    1. Suspicion is clinical: most lymphoid neoplasms present as enlarged nontender lymph nodes, often more than 2 cm.
    2. Histological examination of a lymph node or other involved tissue is required for diagnosis.
    3. Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells]: diagnosis rests on identifying Reed-Sternberg cells [binucleate owl-eye giant cell] in a background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells, confirmed by their immunohistochemical profile.
    4. Markers: antibodies to lineage-specific proteins characterise the tumour. Analysis of genetic alterations complements the morphology.
    5. Antigen receptor gene rearrangement studies separate monoclonal (malignant) from polyclonal (reactive) proliferations.
    6. Staging: physical examination, radiological imaging of the abdomen, pelvis and chest, and bone marrow biopsy.

    A 20y male has multiple painless cervical/axillary lymph nodes. What is your provisional diagnosis?

    DUno yr

    Provisional diagnosis: lymphoma, most probably Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells].

    • Lymphomas most commonly present as painless lymphadenopathy.
    • Hodgkin lymphoma has a peak in young adults and arises in a single node or chain of nodes. Cervical and axillary nodes are commonly involved.

    Same: what tests can you do on the lymph nodes?

    DUno yr
    1. Excision biopsy with histological examination of a node: the diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells] depends on Reed-Sternberg cells [binucleate owl-eye giant cell] in a background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells.
    2. Immunohistochemistry: Reed-Sternberg cells of classic types are positive for PAX5, CD15 and CD30 and negative for CD45.
    3. Antigen receptor gene rearrangement studies, to separate monoclonal from polyclonal proliferations.
    4. Staging: imaging of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, and bone marrow biopsy.

    Describe in brief the morphological features of Hodgkin's disease.

    DU05M
    • Reed-Sternberg cells [binucleate owl-eye giant cell] and variants (mononuclear, lacunar, lymphohistiocytic) in a background of nonneoplastic cells: reactive lymphocytes, macrophages and granulocytes, which make up more than 90% of the tumour cellularity.
    • Diagnostic Reed-Sternberg cells: large, with multiple nuclei or a multilobed nucleus, each lobe with a large inclusion-like nucleolus, and abundant cytoplasm.
    • Nodular sclerosis: lacunar cells
      Bands of collagen dividing the node into nodules.
    • Mixed cellularity: node diffusely effaced by T cells, eosinophils, plasma cells and macrophages, with plentiful Reed-Sternberg cells.
    • Lymphocyte-rich: reactive lymphocytes predominate
      Node diffusely effaced.
    • Lymphocyte-depleted: few lymphocytes, many Reed-Sternberg cells or pleomorphic variants.
    • Nodular lymphocyte predominant: nodules of small lymphocytes and macrophages
      L&H (popcorn) cells
      Classic Reed-Sternberg cells usually absent.
    • Involvement of spleen, liver, bone marrow and other organs appears as irregular tumour nodules resembling those in the nodes.
