    Write a short note on Hodgkin's lymphoma.

    DU19Nov

    Definition: a group of lymphoid neoplasms that differ from non-Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells]. It arises in a single node or chain of nodes and spreads first to contiguous lymphoid tissues. The distinctive feature is the Reed-Sternberg cell [binucleate owl-eye giant cell], which induces reactive lymphocytes, macrophages and granulocytes that make up more than 90% of the tumour. Average age at diagnosis is 39, with a bimodal distribution, peaks in young adults and in adults older than 55.

    Pathogenesis

    • Reed-Sternberg cells derive from germinal centre or post-germinal centre B cells.
    • NF-κB activation, through EBV latent membrane protein 1 or loss-of-function mutations in IκB or TNF-induced protein 3.
    • EBV in a subset of classic cases.
    • Gains of REL on chromosome 2p and of PD-L1 and PD-L2 genes on chromosome 9p.
    • Reed-Sternberg cells secrete cytokines (interleukin-5, interleukin-10, M-CSF) and chemokines that attract reactive cells. PD-L1 and PD-L2 make the host immune response ineffective.

    Morphology: Reed-Sternberg cells and variants in a reactive background. WHO subtypes: nodular sclerosis (65% to 70%), mixed cellularity (20% to 25%), lymphocyte-rich, lymphocyte-depleted (less than 5%), and nodular lymphocyte predominant (about 5%).

    Clinical features

    • Painless lymphadenopathy.
    • Fever, night sweats and weight loss in stage III and IV disease, mixed cellularity and lymphocyte-depleted subtypes.
    • Cutaneous anergy from depressed cell-mediated immunity, from interleukin-10 suppressing Th1 responses.
    • Stereotyped spread: nodes, then spleen, then liver, then marrow and other tissues.
    • Stage is the most important prognostic variable
      Cure rate close to 90% in stages I and IIA.

    Complications of treatment: second cancers after radiotherapy (lung cancer, melanoma, breast cancer) and acute myeloid leukaemia after alkylating agent chemotherapy.

    Write a short note on nodular sclerosis variety of Hodgkin's disease.

    DU09Ju
    • Most common form of Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells], 65% to 70% of cases.
    • Lacunar variant Reed-Sternberg cells [binucleate owl-eye giant cell], with collagen deposited in bands that divide the node into circumscribed nodules
      Fibrosis may be scant or abundant.
    • Polymorphous background of T cells, eosinophils, plasma cells and macrophages. Diagnostic Reed-Sternberg cells are usually uncommon.
    • Reed-Sternberg cells are positive for PAX5, CD15 and CD30, and negative for other B-cell markers, T-cell markers and CD45.
    • Uncommonly associated with EBV.
    • Equal in males and females
      Involves lower cervical, supraclavicular and mediastinal nodes of adolescents or young adults.
    • Prognosis is excellent.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 557

    Plasma Cell Disorders

    A8

    What is paraproteinaemia?

    4A8Q28DU23NDU13JuDU10Ja

    Paraproteinaemia (monoclonal gammopathy) is the term used for the abnormal immunoglobulins associated with plasma cell neoplasms. Neoplastic plasma cells virtually always secrete monoclonal immunoglobulin or immunoglobulin fragments. A monoclonal immunoglobulin identified in the blood is called an M component.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 552
    A8

    Give 4 common causes of paraproteinaemia.

    A8Q28DU10Ja

    Also asked as: Common causes of paraproteinaemia.

    1. Multiple myeloma (plasma cell myeloma), with its variants solitary plasmacytoma and smouldering myeloma.
    2. Waldenström macroglobulinaemia [lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with IgM paraprotein], in which high levels of IgM cause hyperviscosity.
    3. Heavy-chain disease, with free heavy-chain fragments.
    4. Immunoglobulin-related (AL) amyloidosis, from monoclonal plasma cells secreting light chains.
    5. Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS).
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 553
    A8

    What is myeloma?

    A8Q29

    Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm commonly associated with lytic bone lesions, hypercalcaemia, renal failure and acquired immune abnormalities.

    A8

    Pathophysiological and biochemical features of myeloma.

    A8Q29

    Pathophysiology

    • Rearrangements of the IGH locus on chromosome 14q32 with proto-oncogenes, including cyclin D1 and cyclin D3
      Deletion of 17p (the TP53 locus) gives a poor outcome
      Rearrangement of MYC in aggressive forms such as plasma cell leukaemia. Mutations in the NF-κB pathway.
    • Interleukin-6 is the main growth factor, made by the tumour cells and by marrow stromal cells.
    • Bone destruction: myeloma-derived MIP1a (CCL3) increases osteoclast formation, and Wnt pathway modulators inhibit osteoblasts. The net result is increased bone resorption, with hypercalcaemia and pathological fractures.
    • Excess immunoglobulin of a single type with abnormal physicochemical properties: hyperviscosity in about 7% (usually IgA or IgG3 subtype), and AL amyloidosis from certain light chains (lambda 6 and lambda 3 families).
    • Suppression of normal humoral immunity leads to recurrent bacterial infections
      Cellular immunity is relatively unaffected.
    • Renal failure in up to 50%
      The most important factor is Bence Jones [free monoclonal light chains in the urine] proteinuria, as light chains are toxic to renal tubular epithelial cells.

    Biochemical features

    • M protein in the serum, usually more than 3 g/dL
      IgG in about 55% and IgA in about 25%.
    • Bence Jones protein in the urine, usually more than 6 mg/dL.
    • Free light chains alone in about 20%
      About 1% are nonsecretory.
    • Hypercalcaemia.
    • Decreased levels of normal polyclonal immunoglobulins.
    A8

    Laboratory diagnosis of myeloma.

    A8Q30
    1. Serum and urine electrophoresis: a sharp abnormal protein spike (M protein) in place of the broad polyclonal band. Confirmed and typed by immunofixation.
    2. Immunoglobulins: increased in the blood in 99% of patients, and/or light chains (Bence Jones proteins [free monoclonal light chains in the urine]) in the urine. Most myelomas have more than 3 g/dL of serum immunoglobulin and/or more than 6 mg/dL of urine Bence Jones protein. Free light chains alone are present in about 20%, and about 1% are nonsecretory.
    3. Bone marrow examination: clonal plasma cells, usually more than 30% of the cellularity
      Positive for CD138 and often CD56, with cytoplasmic kappa or lambda light chain.
    4. CRAB criteria: hypercalcaemia, renal dysfunction, anaemia and bone lesions, assessed by calcium levels, renal function and blood counts.
    5. Radiography: punched-out lytic defects, usually 1 to 4 cm in diameter
      Sometimes diffuse osteopenia.
    6. Peripheral blood smear: rouleaux formation
      Rarely plasma cell leukaemia.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 553p. 554p. 555
    A8

    What is Bence-Jones protein?

    A8Q30

    Free light chains, made in excess by neoplastic plasma cells, are small and are excreted in the urine, where they are called Bence Jones proteins [free monoclonal light chains in the urine].

    A8

    Classify immunoproliferative disorders.

    A8Q32
    DisorderFeatures
    Multiple myeloma (plasma cell myeloma)Tumour masses scattered through the skeletal system
    Variants are solitary plasmacytoma (single mass in bone or soft tissue) and smouldering myeloma (no symptoms, high plasma M component)
    Waldenström macroglobulinaemia [lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with IgM paraprotein]High IgM levels cause hyperviscosity
    Usually with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma
    Heavy-chain diseaseSynthesis and secretion of free heavy-chain fragments
    Seen with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma and small bowel marginal zone lymphoma (Mediterranean lymphoma)
    Immunoglobulin-related (AL) amyloidosisMonoclonal plasma cells secrete light chains, usually lambda, that are deposited as amyloid
    Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS)No symptoms
    Small to moderately large M component
    May transform to multiple myeloma or another symptomatic plasma cell neoplasm
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 553
    A8

    Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia (in short).

    A8Q32

    Definition: a syndrome in which high levels of IgM lead to symptoms from hyperviscosity of the blood. It occurs in older adults, most commonly with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, a B-cell neoplasm of the sixth or seventh decade in which many tumour cells differentiate into plasma cells that secrete monoclonal IgM.

    Pathogenesis: virtually all cases have acquired mutations in MYD88, which activates NF-κB and may promote tumour cell growth and survival.

    Morphology

    • Marrow infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells and plasmacytoid lymphocytes, often with mast cell hyperplasia.
    • Periodic acid–Schiff positive inclusions of immunoglobulin in the cytoplasm (Russell bodies [eosinophilic immunoglobulin inclusions in plasma cells]) or nucleus (Dutcher bodies [intranuclear immunoglobulin inclusions in plasma cells]) of some plasma cells.
    • At diagnosis the tumour has usually spread to lymph nodes, spleen and liver.

    Clinical features

    • Weakness, fatigue and weight loss
      About half have lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Anaemia from marrow infiltration.
    • About 10% have autoimmune haemolysis from cold agglutinins (IgM antibodies that bind red cells below 37°C).
    • Hyperviscosity syndrome: visual impairment with venous congestion, retinal haemorrhages and exudates. Headache, dizziness, deafness and stupor
      Bleeding, from IgM complexes with clotting factors and interference with platelet function.
    • Cryoglobulinaemia: precipitation of IgM in the cold, with Raynaud phenomenon [episodic digital vasospasm] and cold urticaria.
    • Renal failure and amyloidosis from free light chains are rare, and bone destruction does not occur.

    Course: indolent
    Plasmapheresis relieves the symptoms of high IgM
    Median survival is greater than 10 years.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 553p. 555p. 556

    How will you diagnose a case of multiple myeloma?

    7DU25NDU23NDU21MDU19MDU16JuDU12JuDU06S
    1. Serum and urine electrophoresis: a sharp abnormal protein spike (M protein) in place of the broad polyclonal band. Confirmed and typed by immunofixation.
    2. Immunoglobulins: increased in the blood in 99% of patients, and/or light chains (Bence Jones proteins [free monoclonal light chains in the urine]) in the urine. Most myelomas have more than 3 g/dL of serum immunoglobulin and/or more than 6 mg/dL of urine Bence Jones protein. Free light chains alone are present in about 20%, and about 1% are nonsecretory.
    3. Bone marrow examination: clonal plasma cells, usually more than 30% of the cellularity
      Positive for CD138 and often CD56, with cytoplasmic kappa or lambda light chain.
    4. CRAB criteria: hypercalcaemia, renal dysfunction, anaemia and bone lesions, assessed by calcium levels, renal function and blood counts.
    5. Radiography: punched-out lytic defects, usually 1 to 4 cm in diameter
      Sometimes diffuse osteopenia.
    6. Peripheral blood smear: rouleaux formation
      Rarely plasma cell leukaemia.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 553p. 554p. 555

    Give the bone marrow findings of multiple myeloma.

    DU10Ja
    • Plasma cells increased, usually more than 30% of the cellularity
      They may infiltrate subtly or completely replace the normal marrow elements.
    • Malignant plasma cells have a perinuclear clearing from a prominent Golgi apparatus and an eccentrically placed nucleus.
    • Cytological forms range from relatively normal-looking plasma cells, plasmablasts with vesicular chromatin and a prominent single nucleolus, to bizarre multinucleated cells.
    • Cytoplasmic immunoglobulin accumulates in variants: flame cells with fiery red cytoplasm, Mott cells [plasma cells filled with Russell bodies] with grape-like cytoplasmic droplets, and cells with fibrils, crystalline rods and globules.
    • Globular inclusions are Russell bodies [eosinophilic immunoglobulin inclusions in plasma cells] if cytoplasmic and Dutcher bodies [intranuclear immunoglobulin inclusions in plasma cells] if nuclear.
    • Immunophenotype: positive for CD138 and often CD56, with cytoplasmic kappa or lambda light chain.

    Why is ESR sky-high in multiple myeloma?

    DU23N
    • High levels of M protein in the blood cause red cells to stick to one another in linear arrays on smears, called rouleaux formation.
    • Rouleaux formation is characteristic but not specific. it is also seen in other conditions with high immunoglobulin levels, such as lupus erythematosus and early HIV infection.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 553

    An elderly patient has low back/bone pain, punched-out lesions, sky-high ESR. What is your probable diagnosis?

    6DU25NDU21MDU19MDU16JuDU15JaDU12Ju

    Probable diagnosis: multiple myeloma

    • Bone pain and pathological fractures, from plasma cell tumours that erode bone. The radiographic defects are punched-out and 1 to 4 cm across.
    • The high ESR fits the M protein in the blood, which makes red cells stick together in rouleaux.
    • Confirmed by bone marrow examination and by serum and urine M protein studies.

    Write a short note on Bence-Jones protein and its detection in urine.

    DU14JuDU13JaDU10Ju

    Definition: free light chains made in excess by neoplastic plasma cells are small enough to be excreted in the urine, where they are called Bence Jones proteins [free monoclonal light chains in the urine].

    Detection

    • Light chains in the urine are found as an abnormal protein spike on urine electrophoresis, then characterised by immunofixation.
    • Most myelomas have more than 6 mg/dL of urine Bence Jones protein
      Light chains in the urine and/or increased immunoglobulin in the blood are found in 99% of patients.
    • About 20% of patients have only free light chains.

    Significance

    • Bence Jones proteins are excreted by the kidney and contribute to myeloma kidney.
    • They are the most important factor in the renal failure seen in up to 50% of patients, being toxic to renal tubular epithelial cells.
    • Certain light chains (lambda 6 and lambda 3 families) cause AL amyloidosis.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 553p. 556p. 554

    Myeloproliferative and Myelodysplastic Disorders

    A8

    What do you know about myelodysplastic syndrome?

    A8Q19

    Definition: myelodysplastic neoplasms (MDS, formerly myelodysplastic syndromes) are clonal stem cell disorders characterised by maturation defects that cause ineffective haematopoiesis and carry a high risk of transformation to AML. The marrow is partly or wholly replaced by the clonal progeny of a neoplastic multipotent stem cell that differentiates in an ineffective and disordered fashion, so patients have peripheral blood cytopenias. MDS may be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to previous genotoxic drug or radiation therapy (t-MDS), which usually appears 2 to 8 years after exposure.

    Pathogenesis

    • Driver mutations overlap partly with those of AML: epigenetic factors (DNA methylation, histone modifications, chromatin looping), RNA splicing factors, and transcription factors such as RUNX1 (mostly loss of function).
    • About 10% have loss-of-function TP53 mutations, with a complex karyotype and poor outcome.
    • Recurrent chromosomal abnormalities: monosomies 5 and 7, deletions of 5q, 7q and 20q, and trisomy 8. The region lost on 5q contains RPS14
      Loss of one copy produces ineffective erythropoiesis.

    Morphology

    • Marrow usually hypercellular
      Dysplastic differentiation of the erythroid, granulocytic, monocytic and megakaryocytic lineages.
    • Erythroid: ring sideroblasts, megaloblastoid maturation, nuclear budding.
    • Neutrophils: decreased secondary granules, toxic granulations, Döhle bodies [pale blue cytoplasmic inclusions in neutrophils], and pseudo-Pelger-Hüet cells (neutrophils with only two nuclear lobes).
    • Megakaryocytes with single nuclear lobes or multiple separate nuclei (pawn ball megakaryocytes).
    • Marrow blasts increased but less than 20%
      Blood blasts usually less than 10%.
    • Blood: pseudo-Pelger-Hüet cells, giant platelets, macrocytes, poikilocytes and relative or absolute monocytosis.

    Clinical features and complications

    • Mainly a disease of older adults
      Mean age of onset is 70 years
      up to half are found incidentally on routine blood tests.
    • Symptoms are weakness, infections and haemorrhages from pancytopenia.
    • All forms can transform to AML, most frequently and rapidly in t-MDS.
    • Median survival in primary MDS ranges from less than 6 months to more than 5 years
      in t-MDS it is only 4 to 8 months.
    • Worse outcomes are predicted by a higher blast count, more severe cytopenias and complex cytogenetics.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 564p. 565p. 566
    A8

    What are myeloproliferative disorders?

    4A8Q20DU05JaDU04MDU03S

    Also asked as: Define myeloproliferative disorder.

    Myeloproliferative neoplasms are myeloid neoplasms in which there is usually increased production of one or more types of blood cells. Their common pathogenic feature is mutated, constitutively activated tyrosine kinases, or other acquired aberrations in signalling pathways, that lead to growth factor independence. Differentiation is not impaired, so the usual result is an increase in mature blood elements.

    Common features:

    • Increased proliferative drive in the bone marrow.
    • Variable homing of neoplastic stem cells to secondary haematopoietic organs, producing extramedullary haematopoiesis.
    • Variable transformation to a spent phase with marrow fibrosis and peripheral blood cytopenias.
    • Variable transformation to acute leukaemia.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 560p. 566
    A8

    Classify myeloproliferative disorder.

    A8Q20
    DisorderMutation (frequency)
    Chronic myeloid leukaemiaBCR::ABL fusion gene (100%)
    Polycythaemia veraJAK2 mutations (more than 95%)
    Essential thrombocythaemiaJAK2 (50% to 60%), CALR (25% to 35%), MPL (5% to 10%)
    Primary myelofibrosisJAK2 (50% to 60%), CALR (25% to 35%), MPL (5% to 10%)
    Systemic mastocytosisKIT mutations (more than 90%)
    Chronic eosinophilic leukaemiaFIP1L1::PDGFRA fusion gene (common)
    PDE4DIP::PDGFRB fusion gene (rare)
    Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene mutationsFusion genes involving FGFR1, PDGFRA, PDGFRB or JAK2 (100%)
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 568
    A8

    What do you mean by polycythaemia?

    A8Q21

    Polycythaemia denotes an abnormally high number of circulating red cells, usually with a corresponding increase in the haemoglobin level. It may be relative (when there is haemoconcentration due to decreased plasma volume) or absolute (when there is an increase in the total red cell mass).

    A8

    Clinical features of polycythaemia.

    A8Q21

    Clinical features of polycythaemia vera:

    • Insidious onset, usually in adults of late middle age.
    • Increased red cell mass, haematocrit and total blood volume cause abnormal blood flow, with distension of the low-pressure venous side.
    • Patients are plethoric and cyanotic, from stagnation and deoxygenation of blood in peripheral vessels.
    • Headache, dizziness, hypertension and gastrointestinal symptoms.
    • Intense pruritus and peptic ulceration, both possibly from histamine release by basophils.
    • Hyperuricaemia from high cell turnover
      Symptomatic secondary gout in 5% to 10%.
    • Thrombosis: about 25% first come to attention with deep venous thrombosis, myocardial infarction or stroke. Hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd-Chiari syndrome [hepatic vein thrombosis], thrombosis of the hepatic veins) and portal or mesenteric vein thrombosis with bowel infarction.
    • Bleeding: minor haemorrhages (epistaxis, bleeding gums) are common. life-threatening haemorrhages occur in 5% to 10%.
    • Mild organomegaly, caused early in the course largely by congestion.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 568p. 569
    A8

    Differences between polycythaemia vera and secondary polycythaemia.

    A8Q22
    FeaturePolycythaemia veraSecondary polycythaemia
    NaturePrimary
    Myeloproliferative neoplasm with an intrinsic abnormality of haematopoietic precursors    		Absolute polycythaemia from a response of red cell progenitors to raised erythropoietin
    CauseActivating mutations in the tyrosine kinase JAK2 (more than 97% with a valine-to-phenylalanine change at residue 617)Compensatory or pathologic increase in erythropoietin secretion: erythropoietin-secreting tumours (renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, cerebellar haemangioblastoma), high oxygen affinity haemoglobin mutants, inherited defects that stabilise HIF-1α
    Serum erythropoietinLowHigh
    Erythropoietin dependenceProgenitors have markedly decreased requirements for erythropoietin and other growth factorsRed cell progenitors respond to erythropoietin
    Cell linesIncreased red cells, granulocytes and platelets (panmyelosis)Red cells
    A8

    Laboratory diagnosis of polycythaemia.

    A8Q22
    1. Red cell parameters: haemoglobin typically more than 16 g/dL
      Haematocrit often 55% or more. Chronic bleeding may cause iron deficiency, which can lower the haematocrit into the normal range.
    2. White cell count 12,000 to 50,000 per cubic millimetre
      Platelet count often more than 500,000 per cubic millimetre, with giant forms and defective aggregation on functional tests.
    3. Peripheral blood: increased basophils and abnormally large platelets.
    4. Serum erythropoietin: low in polycythaemia vera, high in secondary forms.
    5. JAK2 mutation: more than 97% have the valine-to-phenylalanine substitution at residue 617. Other JAK2 mutations are found in most of the rest.
    6. Bone marrow: hypercellular with some residual fat
      a subtle increase in red cell progenitors, usually with increased granulocytic precursors and megakaryocytes. a moderate to marked increase in reticulin fibres in about 10%.
    A8

    Non-CML myeloproliferative disorders.

    A8Q23
    DisorderMutationsFeatures
    Polycythaemia veraJAK2 in more than 95% (more than 97% at residue 617)Increased red cells, granulocytes and platelets
    Plethora, pruritus, thrombosis and bleeding
    Low serum erythropoietin
    Spent phase in 15% to 20% and transformation to AML in about 1% to 2%
    Essential thrombocythaemiaJAK2 (50% to 60%), CALR (about 30%), MPL (5% to 10%)Raised platelet count with thrombosis or bleeding
    no polycythaemia and no marrow fibrosis
    Erythromelalgia
    Primary myelofibrosisJAK2, CALR or MPL in about 90%Obliterative marrow fibrosis, leukoerythroblastosis, teardrop red cells, splenomegaly from extramedullary haematopoiesis
    A8

    WHO diagnostic criteria for polycythaemia vera.

    A8Q23

    The WHO 2016 criteria. The diagnosis requires either all three major criteria, or the first two major criteria and the minor criterion.

    Major criteria

    1. Haemoglobin more than 16.5 g/dL in men or more than 16.0 g/dL in women, or haematocrit more than 49% in men or more than 48% in women, or red cell mass more than 25% above the mean normal predicted value.
    2. Bone marrow biopsy showing hypercellularity for age with trilineage growth (panmyelosis), including prominent erythroid, granulocytic and megakaryocytic proliferation with pleomorphic mature megakaryocytes.
    3. Presence of a JAK2 V617F or JAK2 exon 12 mutation.

    Minor criterion

    • Subnormal serum erythropoietin level.

    Bone marrow biopsy may not be required in cases with sustained absolute erythrocytosis, with haemoglobin more than 18.5 g/dL in men (haematocrit more than 55.5%) or more than 16.5 g/dL in women (haematocrit more than 49.5%), if the third major criterion and the minor criterion are present.

    A8

    Define myelofibrosis.

    A8Q24

    The hallmark of primary myelofibrosis is the development of obliterative marrow fibrosis. The replacement of the marrow by fibrous tissue reduces bone marrow haematopoiesis, leading to cytopenias and extensive extramedullary haematopoiesis.

    A8

    Laboratory diagnosis of myelofibrosis.

    A8Q24

    1. Peripheral blood - Moderate to severe normochromic normocytic anaemia. - Leukoerythroblastosis: premature release of nucleated erythroid and early granulocyte progenitors. - Teardrop-shaped red cells (dacryocytes). - White cell count usually normal or mildly reduced, but may be markedly elevated (80,000 to 100,000 per microlitre) early in the course. - Platelet count usually normal or elevated at diagnosis. Thrombocytopenia may supervene as the disease progresses. - Abnormally large platelets and basophilia, which are nonspecific. 2. Bone marrow biopsy is essential for diagnosis, because the blood findings are not specific. - Early: hypercellular, with increases in maturing cells of all lineages. Large megakaryocytes with bulbous, hyperchromatic or cloud-like nuclei, abnormally clustered. Minimal fibrosis. - Later: hypocellular and diffusely fibrotic. Clusters of atypical megakaryocytes
    Haematopoietic elements within dilated sinusoids
    Very late, conversion of the marrow space to bone (osteosclerosis). 3. Mutations: about 90% have activating mutations of JAK2, CALR or MPL.

    A8

    Types of myelofibrosis.

    A8Q25
    1. Primary myelofibrosis: a myeloproliferative neoplasm whose hallmark is obliterative marrow fibrosis, with activating mutations of JAK2, CALR or MPL in about 90%.
    2. Secondary myelofibrosis (spent phase): the marrow fibrosis that develops late in other myeloproliferative neoplasms, such as polycythaemia vera and essential thrombocythaemia. The histological appearance is identical to primary myelofibrosis.
    A8

    Conditions associated with secondary myelofibrosis.

    A8Q25
    • Polycythaemia vera: the disease passes into a spent phase of obliterative marrow fibrosis with extensive extramedullary haematopoiesis, mainly in the spleen, in about 15% to 20% of patients after an average period of 10 years. Patients with two mutated copies of JAK2 progress at a greater rate.
    • Essential thrombocythaemia: a spent phase of marrow fibrosis supervenes uncommonly.
    • Other myeloproliferative neoplasms: variable transformation to a spent phase with marrow fibrosis and peripheral blood cytopenias. in chronic myeloid leukaemia overt marrow fibrosis is rare.
    A8

    Essential thrombocythaemia (in short).

    A8Q26

    Definition: a myeloproliferative neoplasm with an elevated platelet count, separated from polycythaemia vera and primary myelofibrosis by the absence of polycythaemia and marrow fibrosis respectively.

    Pathogenesis

    • Over 90% have activating mutations in JAK2 (50% to 60%), MPL (5% to 10%) or CALR (about 30%).
    • Constitutive JAK2 or MPL signalling makes the progenitors thrombopoietin independent and leads to hyperproliferation.
    • Mutated CALR is secreted and binds and activates the thrombopoietin receptor, an oncogenic autocrine feedback loop.
    • In cases without a mutation, causes of reactive thrombocytosis, such as inflammatory disorders and iron deficiency, must be excluded.

    Morphology

    • Marrow cellularity usually only mildly increased
      Megakaryocytes markedly increased, including abnormally large forms. Delicate reticulin fibrils, without overt fibrosis.
    • Blood: abnormally large platelets, often with mild leucocytosis.
    • Mild organomegaly in about 50% from extramedullary haematopoiesis.

    Clinical features and complications

    • Incidence 1 to 3 per 100,000 per year
      Usually past the age of 60 years.
    • Thrombosis and haemorrhage from platelet dysfunction: deep venous thrombosis, portal and hepatic vein thrombosis, myocardial infarction and abnormal bleeding.
    • Up to one-third have acquired von Willebrand disease [inherited bleeding disorder from deficient or defective von Willebrand factor].
    • Erythromelalgia, a throbbing and burning of hands and feet from occlusion of small arterioles by platelet aggregates.
    • Indolent
      Median survival 12 to 15 years
      Uncommonly a spent phase of marrow fibrosis or transformation to AML.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 569

    What do you mean by sub-leukaemic leukaemia (marrow picture)?

    DU11JuDU09JuDU08Ju

    Subleukaemic leukaemia is a leukaemia with abnormal white cells in the peripheral blood in which the total white cell count is normal.

    In aleukaemic leukaemia blasts are entirely absent from the blood, so a bone marrow examination is essential to exclude acute leukaemia in pancytopenic patients.

    How will you differentiate sub-leukaemic leukaemia from aplastic anemia?

    DU13JuDU12Ju
    FeatureSubleukaemic or aleukaemic leukaemiaAplastic anaemia
    Bone marrowHypercellular, packed with blasts, generally 20% or moreMarkedly hypocellular, largely devoid of haematopoietic cells
    Fat cells, fibrous stroma and scattered lymphocytes and plasma cells remain
    Marrow aspirateCells yielded, showing blastsOften yields little material (dry tap)
    Aplasia best seen on biopsy
    BloodAbnormal white cells present with a normal total count
    in aleukaemic leukaemia blasts are absent
    Pancytopenia may be present    		Pancytopenia inevitably
    Reticulocytopenia
    Red cells usually slightly macrocytic and normochromic
    DiagnosisBone marrow examination is essential to exclude acute leukaemia in pancytopenic patientsRests on bone marrow biopsy

    Write a short note on polycythaemia rubra vera.

    DU06MDU04M

    Definition: polycythaemia vera (PCV) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm with increased marrow production of red cells, granulocytes and platelets (panmyelosis). The increase in red cells causes most of the symptoms.

    Pathogenesis

    • Activating mutations of the tyrosine kinase JAK2
      More than 97% have the valine-to-phenylalanine substitution at residue 617.
    • Progenitors have markedly decreased requirements for erythropoietin, so serum erythropoietin is low
      in secondary polycythaemia it is high.
    • Raised haematocrit increases blood viscosity and sludging. with thrombocytosis and abnormal platelet function this predisposes to thrombosis and bleeding.

    Morphology

    • Hypercellular marrow with some residual fat
      Subtle increase in red cell progenitors, with more granulocytic precursors and megakaryocytes. Increased reticulin in about 10%.
    • Blood: increased basophils and abnormally large platelets.
    • Mild organomegaly from congestion.

    Clinical features and complications

    • Insidious onset in late middle age
      Plethora and cyanosis
      Headache, dizziness, hypertension.
    • Intense pruritus and peptic ulceration, possibly from histamine released by basophils.
    • Hyperuricaemia, with secondary gout in 5% to 10%.
    • Thrombosis and bleeding.
    • Spent phase with marrow fibrosis and extramedullary haematopoiesis in the spleen and liver. Transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia in about 1%.
    • Untreated, death from bleeding or thrombosis occurs within months of diagnosis.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 561p. 568p. 569

    Spleen and Hypersplenism

    A8

    Causes of hypersplenism.

    A8Q26

    Hypersplenism is a syndrome of splenomegaly with anaemia, leucopenia and/or thrombocytopenia. The probable cause of the cytopenias is increased sequestration of formed elements and the consequent enhanced phagocytosis by splenic macrophages.

    Causes are the disorders associated with splenomegaly:

    • Congestive splenomegaly from portal or splenic vein hypertension: cirrhosis (the main cause of massive congestive splenomegaly), the pipestem hepatic fibrosis of schistosomiasis, portal vein thrombosis, splenic vein thrombosis from tumours of the stomach or pancreas, and right-sided heart failure. In congestive splenomegaly, slowing of blood flow from the cords to the sinusoids prolongs exposure of blood cells to macrophages, resulting in excessive destruction.
    • Infections: blood-borne infections, particularly infective endocarditis, and infectious mononucleosis.
    • Haematological: non-Hodgkin [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells] lymphomas, lymphocytic leukaemias, multiple myeloma, myeloproliferative neoplasms and haemolytic anaemias.
    • Infiltrative disorders: sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, glycogen storage and lipid storage diseases, and metastases.
    A8

    Causes of splenomegaly.

    A8Q27

    1. Infections: nonspecific splenitis of any blood-borne infection, particularly infective endocarditis. Infectious mononucleosis
    Malaria
    Typhoid fever. 2. Haematological disorders: non-Hodgkin [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells] lymphomas and lymphocytic leukaemias. Multiple myeloma
    Myeloproliferative neoplasms, such as chronic myeloid leukaemia and primary myelofibrosis, through extramedullary haematopoiesis. Haemolytic anaemias and thalassaemia, through compensatory extramedullary haematopoiesis in severe chronic anaemia. 3. Congestion from venous outflow obstruction - Intrahepatic disorders retarding portal drainage: cirrhosis (the main cause of massive splenomegaly), schistosomiasis. - Extrahepatic obstruction of the portal or splenic vein: portal vein thrombosis, pyelophlebitis (inflammation of the portal vein), thrombosis from tumours of the stomach or pancreas. - Systemic venous congestion from right-sided heart failure, as in tricuspid or pulmonic valve disease and chronic cor pulmonale. The spleen rarely exceeds 500 g. 4. Infiltrative disorders: sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, glycogen storage diseases, lipid storage diseases and metastases.

    A8

    Diagnostic criteria of hypersplenism.

    A8Q27
    • Splenomegaly.
    • Anaemia, leucopenia and/or thrombocytopenia, singly or together.
    • Increased sequestration of formed elements in the spleen, with enhanced phagocytosis by splenic macrophages, is the probable cause of the cytopenias.
    • Bone marrow: with excessive peripheral destruction of cells the marrow is usually hypercellular, from a compensatory increase in precursors.

    Clinical Scenarios

    A10

    Elderly man (55 or 65 years) with bone/back pain, punched-out skull lesions or osteolytic lesions, high ESR, vertebral fracture — Most probable diagnosis? How will you establish / confirm the diagnosis?

    A10Q7, Q19

    Most probable diagnosis: multiple myeloma

    Confirmation

    1. Serum and urine electrophoresis for an M protein spike, characterised by immunofixation. Bence Jones protein [free monoclonal light chains in the urine] in the urine.
    2. Bone marrow examination showing clonal plasma cells, usually more than 30% of the cellularity.
    3. CRAB criteria: hypercalcaemia, renal dysfunction, anaemia and bone lesions.
    4. Radiography showing punched-out lytic lesions.
    A10

    40-year-old man with massive splenomegaly and total WBC count 2,50,000/cu.mm — Diagnosis?

    A10Q11

    Diagnosis: chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML)

    • Massive splenomegaly from extramedullary haematopoiesis, with a white cell count above 100,000 per microlitre, in an adult.
    • Blood: neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils and basophils. Blasts usually less than 10%
      Platelets often increased.
    • Confirmed by detection of the BCR::ABL fusion gene (Philadelphia chromosome [t(9;22) producing the BCR-ABL1 fusion], t(9;22)) by chromosomal analysis or PCR-based tests. This separates CML from other myeloproliferative neoplasms.
    A10

    10-year-old boy with weakness, fever, joint pain and gum bleeding — Clinical diagnosis? Expected PBF findings?

    A10Q15

    Clinical diagnosis: acute leukaemia, most probably acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL), the most common cancer of children.

    • Weakness from anaemia
      Fever from infections secondary to neutropenia
      Gum bleeding from thrombocytopenia
      Joint and bone pain from marrow expansion and infiltration of the subperiosteum.

    Expected peripheral blood film findings

    • Anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia.
    • Blast count highly variable
      Blasts may be absent from the blood (aleukaemic leukaemia).
    • Lymphoblasts have condensed chromatin, small nucleoli and scant agranular cytoplasm.

    Bone marrow examination is essential to confirm the diagnosis.

    Haemopoiesis and Laboratory Assessment

    Haemopoiesis

    A6

    What is haemopoiesis?

    A6

    All formed elements of blood (red cells, granulocytes, monocytes, platelets and lymphocytes) have a common origin from haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), pluripotent cells at the apex of a hierarchy of bone marrow progenitors.

    • HSCs have pluripotency (generating all mature blood cells) and self-renewal.
    • Progressive commitment gives early progenitors, then colony-forming units, then morphologically recognisable precursors such as myeloblasts, proerythroblasts and megakaryoblasts.
    • Short-term needs are regulated by colony-stimulating factors (erythropoietin, GM-CSF, G-CSF, thrombopoietin) acting on committed progenitors.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 531p. 532
    A6

    Sites of normal haemopoiesis.

    A6
    PeriodSite
    Third week of embryonic lifeYolk sac
    Transient, mainly embryonic red cells
    Several weeks laterDefinitive HSCs arise in the mesoderm of the intraembryonic aorta/gonad/mesonephros region
    Third monthLiver, the chief site until shortly before birth
    HSCs also in the foetal placenta
    Fourth month onwardsBone marrow
    BirthMarrow throughout the skeleton is active
    Hepatic haematopoiesis dwindles
    After pubertyRestricted to the axial skeleton
    in adults only about half of the marrow space is active
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 531
    A6

    Where does extramedullary haemopoiesis occur?

    A6

    Extramedullary haematopoiesis occurs in the spleen, liver and lymph nodes, when circulating neoplastic or stressed stem cells settle there.

    • Chronic myeloid leukaemia: spleen greatly enlarged from extramedullary haematopoiesis. Mild hepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy.
    • Polycythaemia vera, spent phase: spleen and liver, with prominent organomegaly.
    • Primary myelofibrosis: spleen, liver and lymph nodes, as marrow fibrosis displaces haematopoiesis.
    • Severe beta-thalassaemia: liver, spleen and lymph nodes
      in extreme cases extraosseous masses in the thorax, abdomen and pelvis.

    Write the developmental stages of RBC.

    DU14Ju
    1. Haemopoietic stem cell: pluripotent cell at the apex of the marrow hierarchy.
    2. Committed erythroid progenitor (CFU-E, colony-forming unit erythroid): proliferates under erythropoietin.
    3. Proerythroblast: the first morphologically recognisable red cell precursor.
    4. Basophilic erythroblast.
    5. Polychromatic erythroblast.
    6. Orthochromatic erythroblast (normoblast): enucleates to form the reticulocyte.
    7. Reticulocyte: released into the peripheral blood
      Larger than a mature red cell, with blue-red polychromatophilic cytoplasm due to RNA.
    8. Mature red cell (erythrocyte).

    What are the essential nutrients for haemopoiesis?

    DU14JuDU08Ju
    1. Iron: needed for haemoglobin synthesis
      Deficiency leads to inadequate haemoglobin production and hypochromic microcytic anaemia.
    2. Vitamin B12: needed for DNA synthesis
      Deficiency leads to megaloblastic anaemia.
    3. Folic acid: needed for DNA synthesis
      Deficiency leads to megaloblastic anaemia.

    What is reticulocyte?

    DU09Ja

    Reticulocytes are the newly released red cell precursors in the peripheral blood. They are larger than normal red cells and have blue-red polychromatophilic cytoplasm due to the presence of RNA, a feature that allows them to be identified in the clinical laboratory.

    Mention the cells in the steps of granulopoiesis.

    DU19Nov
    1. Myeloblast
    2. Promyelocyte: coarse primary (azurophilic) granules.
    3. Myelocyte: specific (secondary) granules appear
      Neutrophilic, eosinophilic or basophilic.
    4. Metamyelocyte: indented nucleus.
    5. Band form: band-shaped nucleus.
    6. Segmented granulocyte: mature cell with a lobed nucleus.

    Peripheral film, red cell indices and haemoglobin

    A10

    Information you can get from a stained peripheral blood film.

    A10Q4
    • Red cell size, colour and shape: normocytic, microcytic or macrocytic
      Normochromic or hypochromic
      Red cell shape is assessed by visual inspection of the smear.
    • Examples of shape: spherocytes in hereditary spherocytosis, sickled cells in sickle cell anaemia, macro-ovalocytes in megaloblastic anaemia, hypochromic microcytic cells in iron deficiency.
    • Reticulocytes: larger, with blue-red polychromatophilic cytoplasm from RNA.
    • Rouleaux formation: red cells stuck in linear arrays, from high M protein.
    • White cells: toxic granulation, Döhle bodies [pale blue cytoplasmic inclusions in neutrophils] and vacuoles in sepsis. Immature granulocytes (leukaemoid reaction, chronic myeloid leukaemia). Blasts in acute leukaemia
      Increased basophils.
    • Platelets: abnormally large platelets in polycythaemia vera.
    A6

    What are red cell indices?

    A6

    Red cell indices describe the red cells measured by special instrumentation.

    IndexMeaningAdult reference range
    Mean cell volume (MCV)Average volume of a red cell, in femtolitres82 to 96 fL
    Mean cell haemoglobin (MCH)Average haemoglobin content (mass) per red cell, in picograms27 to 33 pg
    Mean cell haemoglobin concentration (MCHC)Average concentration of haemoglobin in a given volume of packed red cells, in g/dL33 to 37 g/dL
    Red cell distribution width (RDW)Coefficient of variation of red cell volume11.5 to 14.5

    Importance of red cell indices.

    A6
    • They are the most useful measurements in the morphological classification of anaemia, giving clues to the cause.
    • MCV classifies red cells as normocytic, microcytic or macrocytic. MCH and MCHC reflect haemoglobinisation, normochromic or hypochromic.
    • Microcytic hypochromic anaemias are caused by disorders of haemoglobin synthesis, for example iron deficiency and thalassaemia.
    • Macrocytic anaemias often stem from abnormalities that impair maturation of erythroid precursors in the marrow, for example megaloblastic anaemia.
    • Normochromic normocytic anaemias have diverse causes.
    • RDW reflects variation in red cell size (anisocytosis).

    A6
    GroupHaemoglobin (g/dL)
    Adult male13.6 to 17.2
    Adult female12.0 to 15.0
    • Anaemia is usually diagnosed from reductions in haematocrit and haemoglobin concentration below the normal range.
    • Haemoglobin correlates with red cell mass except when plasma volume changes, as in fluid retention or dehydration.

    What information can you get from a stained PBF?

    DU25N

    Red cells

    • Size: normocytic, microcytic or macrocytic
      Variation in size (anisocytosis).
    • Haemoglobinisation: normochromic or hypochromic
      The zone of central pallor is enlarged in iron deficiency.
    • Shape (poikilocytosis): pencil cells in iron deficiency
      Target cells, basophilic stippling and fragmented cells in thalassaemia. macro-ovalocytes in megaloblastic anaemia
      Sickled cells
      spherocytes.
    • Reticulocytes: larger, with blue-red polychromatophilic cytoplasm because of RNA.
    • Nucleated red cell precursors (normoblasts), in severe anaemia and thalassaemia.

    White cells: hypersegmented neutrophils with five or more nuclear lobules in megaloblastic anaemia.

    Platelets: large platelets (megathrombocytes) in immune thrombocytopenic purpura. Confirms a low count, since clumping of platelets during automated counting can cause spurious thrombocytopenia.

    Define ESR / write a short note on ESR.

    6DU24MDU21MDU17JaDU16JaDU14JaDU10Ju

    Definition: the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is the rate at which red cells settle in a vertical tube of anticoagulated blood over one hour, measured in millimetres in the first hour.

    Methods: Westergren [most commonly used], modified Westergren, Wintrobe [ESR method using a 100 mm tube] and micro-ESR.

    Principle

    • Red cells normally repel each other because of the negative charge on their surfaces and settle slowly.
    • Fibrinogen and immunoglobulins neutralise this repulsion and make the red cells aggregate into stacks called rouleaux, which are heavier and sediment faster.
    • ESR depends on the balance between factors that promote and factors that resist sedimentation.

    Phases of sedimentation: rouleaux formation, rapid sedimentation at a constant rate, and packing of the rouleaux with slow sedimentation.

    Technical requirements: the tube must be held upright
    Tilting and higher temperature increase the rate
    The sample should be set up within two hours of collection.

    Clinical significance

    • A nonspecific test, a general index of disease activity, interpreted with the clinical findings.
    • Raised in infectious, inflammatory and malignant conditions that change plasma proteins. Also raised in anaemia and pregnancy.
    • Low in polycythaemia, sickle cell anaemia and hereditary spherocytosis.
    • A normal or mildly raised ESR does not exclude significant disease.

    Mention the major physiological factors affecting ESR.

    DU08Ja
    1. Age: values increase slightly with age.
    2. Sex.
    3. Pregnancy: values rise, because of haemodilution and an increased fibrinogen to albumin ratio, which increases rouleaux formation.
    4. Lifestyle: obesity, smoking and physical activity.

    How do changes in blood components influence ESR?

    DU10Ju

    Plasma proteins

    • Increased fibrinogen and immunoglobulins promote rouleaux formation and increase ESR.
    • Albumin retards sedimentation
      Hypoalbuminaemia permits faster sedimentation.
    • Removal of fibrinogen by defibrination decreases ESR.

    Red cells

    • Anaemia increases ESR.
    • Polycythaemia decreases ESR.
    • Sickle cells and spherocytes cannot form rouleaux, so ESR is low in sickle cell anaemia and hereditary spherocytosis.
    • Macrocytes settle faster
      Microcytes settle more slowly.

    DU19MDU17Ja
    TestFinding in iron deficiency
    Serum ironLow
    Serum ferritinLow
    Below 12 µg/L
    Total iron-binding capacity (reflects transferrin)High
    Transferrin saturationBelow 15%
    Serum hepcidinLow, because reduced iron stores inhibit its synthesis

    In health transferrin is about one-third saturated. Serum iron averages 120 µg/dL in males and 100 µg/dL in females.

    Enumerate the laboratory methods of assessing iron stores.

    DU07Ja
    1. Serum ferritin: plasma ferritin generally correlates with body iron stores. Below 12 µg/L in iron deficiency
      Values approaching 5000 µg/L in iron overload.
    2. Bone marrow iron: Prussian blue stain on smears of aspirated marrow. Absence of stainable iron in macrophages is diagnostic of iron deficiency, and increased storage iron is seen in anaemia of chronic inflammation.
    3. Serum iron and transferrin saturation: fall as the storage pool is depleted, before anaemia appears.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 596p. 598

    Define PCV.

    DU10Ju

    The packed cell volume (haematocrit) is the ratio of packed red cells to total blood volume.

    Write a short note on MCV.

    DU05M

    Definition: the mean cell volume is the average volume of a red cell, expressed in femtolitres (fL).

    Reference range: 82 to 96 fL.

    Use: it classifies anaemia by red cell size.

    • Microcytic (low MCV): microcytic hypochromic anaemias are caused by disorders of haemoglobin synthesis, such as iron deficiency anaemia and thalassaemia.
    • Normocytic: for example acute blood loss.
    • Macrocytic (high MCV): macrocytic anaemias often stem from abnormalities that impair the maturation of erythroid precursors in the bone marrow, such as megaloblastic anaemia of vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

    Bone marrow examination

    A6A10

    Indications of bone marrow biopsy / aspiration / examination.

    4A6A10Q2, Q20, Q25
    • Leukaemias: acute leukaemias in adults
      Essential to exclude acute leukaemia, aleukaemic leukaemia and myelodysplastic neoplasm in pancytopenic patients.
    • Multiple myeloma and Waldenström macroglobulinaemia [lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with IgM paraprotein]: definitive diagnosis of myeloma requires bone marrow examination.
    • Bone marrow metastases and some storage diseases.
    • Aplastic anaemia: diagnosis rests on bone marrow biopsy.
    • Agranulocytosis, immune thrombocytopenic purpura and hypersplenism.
    • Staging of Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells] (bone marrow biopsy).
    • Trephine biopsy is added when no marrow is aspirated despite repeated attempts (dry tap or blood tap), in bone marrow necrosis, metabolic bone disease and when looking for metastases.
    A6A10

    How is trephine biopsy done?

    A6A10Q2
    • Trephine biopsy takes a core of bone marrow with a long hollow needle. a guidewire pushes the specimen out from the sharp end, which avoids crushing the marrow.
    • The usual site in adults is the posterior iliac crest
      Aspiration is usually from the sternum or iliac crest.
    • Aspiration and trephine biopsy are complementary and together give a higher diagnostic yield.
    • It is used when aspiration fails (dry tap or blood tap). Aplasia, for example, is best appreciated in marrow biopsies.
    A10

    What do you mean by blood tap and dry tap?

    A10Q25

    Dry tap or blood tap: failure to obtain marrow particles on bone marrow aspiration. Reported in 2.7% to 10% of aspirates.

    • It is a red flag for underlying marrow pathology rather than only a failed procedure. in one series 93.7% had an underlying bone marrow pathology and 6.3% a faulty technique.
    • Causes include acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (commonest in children), non-Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells] and metastatic tumours (commonest in the elderly), marrow fibrosis, and aplastic anaemia.
    • The trephine biopsy must always be studied in such cases.

    How can bone marrow be examined?

    DU24NDU08Ju

    Bone marrow is examined by two procedures, usually done together:

    1. Bone marrow aspiration: a sample of semi-liquid marrow is withdrawn through a needle.
    2. Trephine biopsy: a core of bone with solid marrow is removed with a different, wider needle (Jamshidi needle), usually from the posterior iliac crest.

    What are the indications of bone marrow examination/aspiration?

    • Leukaemias: acute leukaemias in adults
      to exclude acute leukaemia, aleukaemic leukaemia and myelodysplastic neoplasm in pancytopenic patients.
    • Multiple myeloma and Waldenström macroglobulinaemia [lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with IgM paraprotein]: definitive diagnosis of myeloma requires bone marrow examination.
    • Bone marrow metastases and some storage diseases.
    • Aplastic anaemia: diagnosis rests on bone marrow biopsy.
    • Agranulocytosis, immune thrombocytopenic purpura and hypersplenism.
    • Staging of Hodgkin lymphoma [lymphoma defined by Reed-Sternberg cells] (bone marrow biopsy).
    • Trephine biopsy is added when no marrow is aspirated despite repeated attempts (dry tap or blood tap), in bone marrow necrosis, metabolic bone disease and when looking for metastases.

    Name the white cell disorders for which bone marrow aspiration is done.

    DU09Ju
    1. Acute leukaemias.
    2. Aleukaemic leukaemia.
    3. Myelodysplastic neoplasm.
    4. Multiple myeloma and Waldenström macroglobulinaemia [lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with IgM paraprotein].
    5. Agranulocytosis.

    Mention the site of marrow puncture in a child below 2 years.

    DU09Ja

    The anteromedial face of the tibia (upper end of the shinbone). In children younger than 18 months it is the preferred site for marrow aspiration.

    What is trephine biopsy?

    4DU19NovDU16JuDU11JaDU09Ja

    Trephine biopsy is a procedure in which a core of bone marrow is taken with a trephine needle (Jamshidi needle), usually from the posterior superior iliac crest. The core is processed to evaluate marrow cellularity and to rule out marrow involvement by solid tumours, lymphomas or other processes.

    Indications:

    • Inadequate or failed marrow aspiration.
    • Suspected bone marrow fibrosis.

    What is dry tap?

    DU26MDU19M

    Dry tap is the failure to obtain marrow particles on bone marrow aspiration.

    • It is a red flag for underlying marrow pathology and not only a failed procedure.
    • The trephine biopsy must always be studied in such cases.

    What is blood tap?

    DU18Nov

    A blood tap is an aspirate that yields blood without marrow particles. It is grouped with dry tap as a failed aspiration, and the trephine biopsy must be studied.

    Mention 4 conditions where dry tap is frequent.

    DU11JaDU09Ja
    1. Marrow fibrosis (myelofibrosis).
    2. Aplastic anaemia.
    3. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (commonest in children).
    4. Metastatic tumours (commonest in the elderly).
    5. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

    Anaemia: General

    A6A7

    What is anemia?

    5A6A7Q13DU07JuDU06M

    Also asked as: Define anaemia.

    Anaemia is a reduction of the total circulating red cell mass below normal limits.

    A6

    Morphological types of anaemia.

    A6
    1. Microcytic hypochromic: red cells small and with reduced haemoglobin.
    2. Normocytic normochromic.
    3. Macrocytic: red cells large.

    Classification rests on red cell size (normocytic, microcytic, macrocytic), degree of haemoglobinisation shown by colour (normochromic, hypochromic), and shape.

    A6

    Examples of each morphological type.

    A6

    Microcytic hypochromicIron deficiency anaemia
    Thalassaemia
    MacrocyticMegaloblastic anaemia from vitamin B12 and folate deficiency
    Normocytic normochromicAcute blood loss
    Anaemia of chronic inflammation, whose cells may be normocytic and normochromic or slightly hypochromic and microcytic
    A6

    Pathophysiological categories of anaemia.

    A6

    1. Blood loss - Acute: trauma. - Chronic: gastrointestinal lesions, gynaecological disturbances. 2. Increased red cell destruction (haemolysis) - Inherited: membrane disorders, enzyme deficiencies, haemoglobin abnormalities. - Acquired: paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, antibody-mediated, mechanical trauma, infections of red cells, toxic injury, membrane lipid abnormalities, sequestration (hypersplenism). 3. Decreased red cell production - Inherited defects, nutritional deficiencies, erythropoietin deficiency, immune-mediated injury of progenitors, inflammation-mediated iron sequestration, primary haematopoietic neoplasms, space-occupying marrow lesions, infections of red cell progenitors, unknown mechanisms.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 579

    How will you investigate a case of anaemia?

    A6
    1. Haemoglobin and haematocrit: anaemia is usually diagnosed from reductions in these below the normal range (male 13.6 to 17.2 g/dL, female 12.0 to 15.0 g/dL).
    2. Red cell indices: mean cell volume, mean cell haemoglobin, mean cell haemoglobin concentration and red cell distribution width, to classify the anaemia as microcytic, normocytic or macrocytic, and hypochromic or normochromic.
    3. Peripheral blood smear: red cell shape, and other findings that point to a cause.
    4. Reticulocyte count: raised after blood loss, reaching 10% to 15% after 7 days
      Reticulocytopenia in aplastic anaemia.
    5. Iron studies in suspected iron deficiency: serum iron and ferritin low, total iron-binding capacity high, transferrin saturation below 15%.
    6. Bone marrow examination: aspirate with Prussian blue stain for iron
      Biopsy for aplasia.
    7. Search for the underlying cause, for example gastrointestinal blood loss in adult males and postmenopausal women.

    Write the morphological/red-cell-indices classification of anemia with examples.

    12DU26MDU24NDU23NDU22NDU21MDU18NovDU17NovDU17MDU16JaDU15JaDU13JaDU08Ju

    Anaemia is classified by red cell size (normocytic, microcytic, macrocytic), degree of haemoglobinisation shown by colour (normochromic, hypochromic) and shape.

    TypeExamples
    Microcytic hypochromic (disorders of haemoglobin synthesis)Iron deficiency anaemia
    Thalassaemia syndromes
    Normocytic normochromic (diverse aetiologies)Acute blood loss
    Mild anaemia of hypothyroidism
    Anaemia of chronic inflammation (may also be slightly hypochromic and microcytic)
    Macrocytic (impaired maturation of erythroid precursors)Megaloblastic anaemia of vitamin B12 or folate deficiency
    Aplastic anaemia (slightly macrocytic and normochromic)

    Write a short note on investigations for morphological classification of anemia.

    DU14Ju
    1. Haemoglobin concentration and haematocrit: reductions below the normal range establish anaemia.
    2. Red cell indices: mean cell volume, mean cell haemoglobin, mean cell haemoglobin concentration and red cell distribution width, determined by instrumentation. They classify size and haemoglobinisation.
    3. Peripheral blood smear: visual inspection for red cell shape and other morphology that points to specific causes.
    4. Reticulocyte count: reference range 0.5% to 1.5%.

    Define polycythemia.

    DU13Ju

    Polycythaemia denotes an abnormally high number of circulating red cells, usually with a corresponding increase in the haemoglobin level. It may be relative (haemoconcentration from decreased plasma volume) or absolute (an increase in the total red cell mass).

    Iron Deficiency and Microcytic Anaemia

    A6

    Causes of iron deficiency anaemia.

    A6

    Iron deficiency can result from:

    1. Dietary lack, in infants, the impoverished, older adults and vegans.
    2. Impaired absorption: sprue, other causes of fat malabsorption (steatorrhoea), chronic diarrhoea, and gastrectomy.
    3. Increased requirement: growing infants, children and adolescents, and premenopausal females, particularly during pregnancy.
    4. Chronic blood loss: external haemorrhage, or bleeding into the gastrointestinal, urinary or genital tracts. The most common cause in developed societies.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 598
    A6

    Causes of IDA in relation to different age groups.

    A6
    GroupCauses
    InfantsDietary lack, as milk contains very little iron
    Increased requirement for growth
    Children and adolescentsIncreased requirement for growth
    Premenopausal femalesIncreased requirement, particularly during pregnancy
    Chronic blood loss from the genital tract
    Multiple, closely spaced pregnancies in low-resource countries carry exceptional risk
    Adult malesChronic blood loss, attributed to gastrointestinal bleeding until proven otherwise
    Postmenopausal femalesChronic blood loss, attributed to gastrointestinal bleeding until proven otherwise
    Older adultsRestricted diets with little meat, from limited income or poor dentition
    Any agePoor diet from poverty
    Vegan diet
    Malabsorption
    Gastrectomy
    A6

    Causes of IDA in adult males.

    A6
    • Chronic gastrointestinal blood loss. Iron deficiency in adult males in high-income countries must be attributed to gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise.
    • Ascribing it prematurely to another cause risks missing a gastrointestinal cancer or other bleeding lesion.
    • Other causes: bleeding into the urinary tract, malabsorption, and a restricted or vegan diet.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 598
    A6

    Causes of IDA in post-menopausal women.

    A6
    • Chronic gastrointestinal blood loss. Iron deficiency in postmenopausal females in high-income countries must be attributed to gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise.
    • Ascribing it prematurely to another cause risks missing a gastrointestinal cancer or other bleeding lesion.
    • Other causes: malabsorption, and a restricted diet with little meat in older adults.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 598
    A6

    Causes of IDA in infants and children.

    A6
    • Dietary lack: infants are at high risk because milk contains very little iron. Human breast milk provides only about 0.3 mg/L
      cow's milk contains about twice as much, but its bioavailability is poor.
    • Increased requirement in growing infants, children and adolescents.
    • Impaired absorption: sprue, other causes of fat malabsorption (steatorrhoea) and chronic diarrhoea.
    • Chronic blood loss: external haemorrhage, or bleeding into the gastrointestinal, urinary or genital tracts.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 598
    A6

    Important laboratory findings in IDA.

    A6
    • Haemoglobin and haematocrit depressed, usually to a moderate degree.
    • Blood film: hypochromia, microcytosis and modest poikilocytosis. Small elongated "pencil" cells
      Enlarged central pallor, with haemoglobin only in a narrow peripheral rim.
    • Serum iron and ferritin low.
    • Total plasma iron-binding capacity high, reflecting elevated transferrin.
    • Transferrin saturation below 15%.
    • Hepcidin serum levels fall.
    • Bone marrow: mild to moderate increase in erythroid progenitors. Absence of stainable iron in macrophages on Prussian blue stain of aspirate.
    • Response to iron: oral iron raises reticulocytes in about 5 to 7 days, followed by a steady rise in counts and normalisation of red cell indices.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 598p. 599
    A6

    Biochemical tests done for IDA.

    A6
    • Serum iron: low.
    • Serum ferritin: low.
    • Total iron-binding capacity: high.
    • Transferrin saturation: below 15%.
    • Serum hepcidin: low, as reduced iron stores inhibit its synthesis.
    • Stainable marrow iron (Prussian blue stain of aspirated marrow): absent in macrophages.
    • Progressive depletion of stores first lowers serum iron and transferrin saturation without anaemia. Anaemia appears only when stores are completely depleted, with low serum iron and ferritin.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 598p. 599
    A6

    Who are more susceptible to IDA, and why?

    A6
    • Infants: very little iron in milk, and growing requirement.
    • Children and adolescents: increased requirement for growth.
    • Premenopausal females: increased requirement, particularly in pregnancy. Females in low-resource countries with multiple, closely spaced pregnancies are at exceptional risk. Many females consume only marginal amounts of iron, while most males ingest more than adequate amounts.
    • The impoverished: suboptimal diets at any age.
    • Older adults: restricted diets with little meat, from limited income or poor dentition.
    • Vegans: no haem iron in the diet.
    • Patients with malabsorption or gastrectomy: gastrectomy lowers duodenal acidity and speeds transit through the duodenum.
    • Adult males and postmenopausal females: chronic gastrointestinal blood loss.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 598
    A6

    A6

    Pancytopenia inevitably appears    		Inadequate haemoglobin production from lack of iron

    Symptoms often those of the underlying cause
    TreatmentStem cell transplantation, with 5-year survival of more than 75% where a donor exists
    Immunosuppressive therapy for older patients or those without a donor    		Oral iron produces a reticulocyte rise in 5 to 7 days and normalisation of red cell indices
    PrognosisVariableCorrectable once the cause is treated

    Iron deficiency anaemia gives a microcytic hypochromic anaemia:

    1. Mean cell volume: reduced.
    2. Mean cell haemoglobin: reduced.
    3. Mean cell haemoglobin concentration: reduced.

    Haemoglobin and haematocrit are depressed. Oral iron normalises the red cell indices.

    What are the causes of microcytic hypochromic anemia?

    4DU19MDU17JaDU12JaDU10Ja

    Microcytic hypochromic anaemias are caused by disorders of haemoglobin synthesis.

    1. Iron deficiency anaemia, the commonest cause.
    2. Thalassaemia syndromes.
    3. Anaemia of chronic inflammation: the red cells may be normocytic and normochromic, or slightly hypochromic and microcytic.
    4. TMPRSS6 mutations (rare): high hepcidin, reduced iron absorption and failure to respond to iron therapy.

    Enumerate the causes of iron deficiency anemia.

    DU21M
    1. Dietary lack: infants, the impoverished, older adults and vegans (lack of haem iron).
    2. Impaired absorption: sprue, other causes of fat malabsorption (steatorrhoea), chronic diarrhoea, and gastrectomy (decreased acidity of the proximal duodenum and faster passage of gut contents).
    3. Increased requirement: growing infants, children and adolescents, and premenopausal females, particularly during pregnancy. Multiple, closely spaced pregnancies carry exceptionally high risk.
    4. Chronic blood loss: external haemorrhage or bleeding into the gastrointestinal, urinary or genital tracts. The commonest cause in developed societies. In adult males and postmenopausal females, gastrointestinal blood loss must be assumed until proven otherwise.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 598

    Why is iron deficiency the most common anemia in infancy and childhood?

    DU07Ja
    1. Very little iron in milk: human breast milk provides only about 0.3 mg/L
      cow's milk contains about twice as much, but its bioavailability is poor.
    2. Increased requirement in growing infants, children and adolescents.

    Give the changes in iron deficiency anemia.

    DU17Ja

    Stages

    1. Progressive depletion of iron stores first lowers serum iron and transferrin saturation without anaemia. Marrow erythroid activity is increased.
    2. Anaemia appears only when stores are completely depleted, with low serum iron and ferritin and low transferrin saturation.

    Bone marrow: mild to moderate increase in erythroid progenitors. Absence of stainable iron in macrophages.

    Peripheral blood: small (microcytic) and pale (hypochromic) red cells. Enlarged zone of central pallor
    Pencil cells.

    Tissue changes in severe, long-standing deficiency: koilonychia, alopecia, atrophic changes in the tongue and gastric mucosa, and intestinal malabsorption. Pica, a craving for non-foodstuffs such as clay, or for ice (pagophagia). Oesophageal web with microcytic hypochromic anaemia and atrophic glossitis forms the triad of Plummer-Vinson syndrome [oesophageal web with iron deficiency anaemia].

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 598

    Give the laboratory diagnosis/blood picture of iron deficiency anemia.

    10DU26MDU25MDU24NDU23NDU22NDU21MDU17NovDU16JaDU15JaDU08Ju

    Blood picture

    • Haemoglobin and haematocrit depressed, usually to a moderate degree.
    • Hypochromia, microcytosis and modest poikilocytosis. Pencil cells.

    Iron studies

    • Serum iron low.
    • Serum ferritin low.
    • Total iron-binding capacity high.
    • Transferrin saturation below 15%.
    • Serum hepcidin low.

    Bone marrow: mild to moderate increase in erythroid progenitors. Absence of stainable iron in macrophages on Prussian blue stain of aspirated marrow.

    Response to iron: oral iron produces a rise in reticulocytes in about 5 to 7 days, followed by a steady increase in blood counts and normalisation of red cell indices.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 598p. 599

    A pregnant lady has weakness, exertional dyspnoea, pale conjunctivae, smooth tongue. What is your probable diagnosis?

    DU25M

    Probable diagnosis: iron deficiency anaemia.

    • Increased requirement in pregnancy.
    • Weakness, malaise and dyspnoea on mild exertion are the general symptoms of anaemia.
    • Smooth tongue: atrophic changes in the tongue from depletion of iron-containing enzymes.

    A 50y male with bleeding peptic ulcer has Hb 9 g%. What morphological type of anemia do you expect on blood film?

    DU13Ja

    Microcytic hypochromic anaemia of iron deficiency.

    • Chronic blood loss, here gastrointestinal, depletes iron reserves and leads to iron deficiency anaemia.
    • Red cells are small and pale, with an enlarged zone of central pallor and pencil cells.

    1. Serum iron low.
    2. Serum ferritin low.
