    Megaloblastic and Macrocytic Anaemia

    A6

    Define macrocytic anemia.

    A6DU24M

    Also asked as: What is macrocytic anaemia?

    Macrocytic anaemia is an anaemia in which the red cells are larger than normal, the adult reference range for mean cell volume being 82 to 96 fL.

    A6

    Classify macrocytic anemia with example.

    A6DU24M

    Also asked as: Classify macrocytic anaemia.

    TypeExample
    MegaloblasticDeficiency of vitamin B12 or folate, leading to inadequate thymidine synthesis and defective DNA replication
    Enlarged abnormal precursors (megaloblasts), ineffective haematopoiesis, macro-ovalocytes and, in most cases, pancytopenia
    NonmegaloblasticAnaemia of hepatocellular disease, slightly macrocytic from lipid abnormalities that add phospholipid and cholesterol to red cell membranes
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 601
    A6

    Causes of normoblastic macrocytic anaemia.

    A6
    • Hepatocellular disease, toxic, infectious or cirrhotic: the anaemia is often slightly macrocytic because lipid abnormalities of liver failure make red cell membranes acquire phospholipid and cholesterol, increasing cell size.
    • Aplastic anaemia: red cells usually slightly macrocytic and normochromic.
    • Reticulocytosis, as after bleeding, since reticulocytes are larger than normal red cells.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 579p. 603p. 601
    A6

    Write a short note on megaloblastic anemia.

    A6DU04S

    Also asked as: What is megaloblastic anaemia?

    Definition

    The common theme among the various causes of megaloblastic anaemia is an impairment of DNA synthesis that leads to ineffective haematopoiesis and distinctive morphological changes, including abnormally large erythroid precursors and red cells.

    Aetiology and pathogenesis

    • Vitamin B12 and folic acid are cofactors required for the synthesis of thymidine, one of the four bases found in DNA.
    • A deficiency of these vitamins, or impairment of their metabolism, results in defective nuclear maturation due to deranged or inadequate DNA synthesis, with a delay or block in cell division.
    • The two principal subtypes are pernicious anaemia (the major form of vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia) and folate deficiency anaemia.
    • Other causes: ileal resection or disease, fish tapeworm infestation, bacterial overgrowth in blind loops, and metabolic inhibitors of DNA synthesis or folate metabolism such as methotrexate.
    • The derangement in DNA synthesis causes most precursors to undergo apoptosis in the marrow (ineffective haematopoiesis) and leads to pancytopenia. A mild degree of red cell haemolysis of uncertain aetiology adds to the anaemia.

    Morphology

    • Blood: macro-ovalocytes (macrocytic and oval red cells) are highly characteristic. Most lack central pallor and appear hyperchromic, but the mean cell haemoglobin concentration is not raised.
    • Marked anisocytosis and poikilocytosis
      Low reticulocyte count
      Nucleated red cell progenitors occasionally appear when anaemia is severe.
    • Neutrophils are larger than normal with nuclear hypersegmentation, five or more lobules instead of the normal three to four.
    • Marrow: markedly hypercellular, with megaloblastic changes at all stages of erythroid development.
    • Promegaloblasts are large, with deeply basophilic cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli and fine nuclear chromatin. The nucleus keeps its fine chromatin instead of developing the clumped pyknotic chromatin of normoblasts, while cytoplasmic maturation proceeds normally (nuclear-to-cytoplasmic asynchrony).
    • Granulocytic precursors show giant metamyelocytes and band forms
      Megakaryocytes may be abnormally large with bizarre multilobate nuclei.

    Clinical features and complications

    • Pernicious anaemia is insidious and the anaemia is often quite severe by the time it comes to medical attention.
    • Vitamin B12 deficiency produces central nervous system lesions: demyelination of the dorsal and lateral spinal tracts, giving spastic paraparesis, sensory ataxia and severe paraesthesias of the lower limbs. Folate deficiency does not cause neurological changes.
    • Folate given to a patient with vitamin B12 deficiency corrects the anaemia but does not prevent, and may worsen, the neurological deficit.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 591p. 592p. 595
    A6

    How can you differentiate megaloblastic anaemia from other macrocytic anaemias?

    A6
    FeatureMegaloblastic anaemiaAplastic anaemia (slightly macrocytic)
    Red cellsMacro-ovalocytes
    Marked anisocytosis and poikilocytosis    		Usually slightly macrocytic and normochromic
    NeutrophilsLarger than normal, with five or more nuclear lobules (hypersegmentation)Neutropenia
    ReticulocytesLowReticulocytopenia is the rule
    Marrow cellularityMarkedly hypercellularMarkedly hypocellular, largely fat cells
    Marrow cellsMegaloblasts with nuclear-to-cytoplasmic asynchrony
    Giant metamyelocytes
    Large megakaryocytes    		Largely devoid of haematopoietic cells
    "dry tap" on aspiration
    CauseImpaired DNA synthesis from vitamin B12 or folate deficiencyChronic primary haematopoietic failure
    A6

    How can you diagnose a case of megaloblastic anaemia?

    A6

    1. Peripheral blood: macro-ovalocytes, marked anisocytosis and poikilocytosis, low reticulocyte count, and neutrophils with five or more nuclear lobules. 2. Bone marrow: markedly hypercellular, with megaloblasts at all stages, nuclear-to-cytoplasmic asynchrony, giant metamyelocytes and band forms, and large megakaryocytes with bizarre nuclei. 3. Find the cause by the vitamin level: - Vitamin B12 deficiency: low serum vitamin B12
    Raised serum homocysteine and methylmalonic acid
    Serum antibodies to intrinsic factor, which are highly specific for pernicious anaemia. - Folate deficiency: decreased serum or red cell folate. Homocysteine raised but methylmalonate normal
    no neurological changes. 4. Response to treatment: an outpouring of reticulocytes and a rise in haematocrit beginning about 5 days after parenteral vitamin B12 confirms vitamin B12 deficiency. 5. Vitamin B12 deficiency must be excluded before starting folate, because folate does not prevent the neurological deficit.

    A6

    Causes of folate deficiency.

    A6

    The three major causes are decreased intake, increased requirements and impaired utilisation.

    1. Decreased intake - Nutritionally inadequate diet, most frequently in chronic alcohol use disorder, the indigent and the very old. in alcohol use disorder with cirrhosis, trapping of folate in the liver, excessive urinary loss and disordered folate metabolism are also implicated. - Impaired intestinal absorption: malabsorption syndromes such as sprue, and infiltrative diseases of the small intestine such as lymphoma. - Drugs that interfere with absorption: the anticonvulsant phenytoin and oral contraceptives. 2. Increased requirements: pregnancy, infancy, hyperactive haematopoiesis (for example chronic haemolytic anaemia) and disseminated cancer. 3. Impaired utilisation: folic acid antagonists such as methotrexate inhibit dihydrofolate reductase and lead to a deficiency of tetrahydrofolic acid. Many chemotherapeutic drugs that damage DNA or inhibit DNA synthesis also cause megaloblastic changes.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 595
    A6

    Why is folate deficiency more common than vitamin B12 deficiency?

    A6

    Folate

    • The body's reserves of folate are relatively modest, and a deficiency can arise within weeks to months if intake is inadequate.
    • Folic acid in food is largely folylpolyglutamates, which are sensitive to heat. Boiling, steaming or frying for 5 to 10 minutes destroys up to 95% of the folate content.
    • Requirements rise in pregnancy, infancy, hyperactive haematopoiesis and disseminated cancer, so normal intake becomes inadequate.
    • Alcohol use disorder, malabsorption, and drugs such as phenytoin, oral contraceptives and methotrexate all cause deficiency.

    Vitamin B12

    • The daily requirement is only 2 to 3 µg.
    • A diet that includes animal products contains significantly more than the minimal daily requirement and builds intrahepatic stores sufficient to last several years.
    • Only strictly vegetarian or macrobiotic diets, which contain little cobalamin, fail to provide enough.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 593p. 595
    A6

    Causes of vitamin B12 deficiency.

    A6

    1. Decreased intake: strictly vegetarian or macrobiotic diets, because plants and vegetables contain little cobalamin. 2. Impaired absorption - Pernicious anaemia: autoimmune gastritis impairing the production of intrinsic factor. - Gastrectomy: intrinsic factor is lost. - Achlorhydria and loss of pepsin secretion, in some older adults: vitamin B12 is not readily released from food proteins. - Insufficiency of the exocrine pancreas: vitamin B12 cannot be released from haptocorrin-vitamin B12 complexes. - Ileal resection, ileitis or diffuse ileal disease, including diffuse intestinal disease such as lymphoma and systemic sclerosis. - Competitive parasitic uptake: fish tapeworm, acquired by eating raw fish. - Bacterial overgrowth in blind loops and diverticula of the bowel. 3. Increased requirement: pregnancy, hyperthyroidism, disseminated cancer and chronic infection produce a relative deficiency even with normal absorption. 4. Recreational use of nitrous oxide oxidises and inactivates vitamin B12.

    A6

    Cardinal manifestations of vitamin B12 deficiency.

    A6

    1. Megaloblastic anaemia: moderate to severe, insidious, with leucopenia and hypersegmented granulocytes. The anaemia is often quite severe when the patient presents. 2. Neurological lesions: found in about three-quarters of cases of florid pernicious anaemia, and can occur without overt haematological findings. - Demyelination of the dorsal and lateral spinal tracts, sometimes followed by loss of axons. - Spastic paraparesis, sensory ataxia and severe paraesthesias in the lower limbs. - Less frequently, degenerative changes in the ganglia of the posterior roots and in peripheral nerves. 3. Gastrointestinal changes in pernicious anaemia: atrophic glossitis (a shiny, glazed, "beefy" tongue) and chronic atrophic gastritis, with an increased risk of gastric carcinoma. 4. Raised plasma and urine methylmalonic acid and raised serum homocysteine.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 595
    A6

    What is pernicious anemia?

    A6DU12Ju

    Also asked as: What is pernicious anaemia?

    Pernicious anaemia is a specific form of megaloblastic anaemia caused by an autoimmune gastritis that impairs the production of intrinsic factor, which is required for vitamin B12 uptake from the gut.

    A6

    Main pathogenesis of pernicious anaemia.

    A6
    • Pernicious anaemia is believed to result from an autoimmune attack on the gastric mucosa, producing chronic atrophic gastritis with loss of parietal cells, a prominent infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells, and megaloblastic changes in mucosal cells.
    • Three types of autoantibody are present in many, but not all, patients:
    • Type I (about 75%): blocks the binding of vitamin B12 to intrinsic factor.
    • Type II: blocks binding of the intrinsic factor-vitamin B12 complex to cubilin, preventing intestinal absorption.
    • Type III (85% to 90%): recognises the alpha and beta subunits of the gastric proton pump. it is not specific, being found in as many as 50% of older adults with idiopathic chronic gastritis.
    • Type I and type II antibodies are found in plasma and gastric juice.
    • Autoantibodies are of diagnostic use but are not thought to be the primary cause of the gastric pathology. an autoreactive T-cell response initiates the gastric mucosal injury and triggers the formation of autoantibodies.
    • When the mass of intrinsic factor-secreting cells falls below a threshold and stored vitamin B12 is depleted, anaemia develops.
    • It is associated with other autoimmune disorders, particularly autoimmune thyroiditis and adrenalitis.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 594
    A6

    How can you diagnose a case of pernicious anaemia?

    A6

    The diagnosis is based on:

    1. A moderate to severe megaloblastic anaemia.
    2. Leucopenia with hypersegmented granulocytes.
    3. Low serum vitamin B12.
    4. Raised serum levels of homocysteine and methylmalonic acid.
    5. Serum antibodies to intrinsic factor, which are highly specific for pernicious anaemia.

    The diagnosis is confirmed by an outpouring of reticulocytes and a rise in haematocrit beginning about 5 days after parenteral administration of vitamin B12.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 595

    Mention the causes of macrocytosis/macrocytic anemia.

    DU18NovDU11Ja

    Megaloblastic

    1. Vitamin B12 deficiency: pernicious anaemia
    Gastrectomy (loss of intrinsic factor)
    Achlorhydria
    Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency
    Ileal resection or disease
    Fish tapeworm
    Bacterial overgrowth in blind loops
    Increased demand (pregnancy, hyperthyroidism, disseminated cancer, chronic infection). 2. Folate deficiency: - Decreased intake: poor diet (alcohol use disorder, the indigent, the very old). Malabsorption (sprue, lymphoma)
    Drugs such as phenytoin and oral contraceptives. - Increased requirement: pregnancy, infancy, chronic haemolytic anaemia, disseminated cancer. - Impaired utilisation: folic acid antagonists such as methotrexate. 3. Drugs inhibiting DNA synthesis: many chemotherapeutic drugs.

    Nonmegaloblastic

    • Anaemia of hepatocellular disease, from lipid abnormalities that add phospholipid and cholesterol to red cell membranes.

    Write the laboratory investigation/blood picture of megaloblastic anemia.

    4DU25MDU24MDU18NovDU12Ju

    Blood

    • Macrocytic, oval red cells (macro-ovalocytes), highly characteristic. Mean cell haemoglobin concentration not raised.
    • Marked anisocytosis and poikilocytosis.
    • Low reticulocyte count.
    • Hypersegmented neutrophils, with five or more nuclear lobules.
    • Nucleated red cell progenitors occasionally, in severe anaemia.
    • Leucopenia and pancytopenia from ineffective haemopoiesis.

    Bone marrow

    • Markedly hypercellular.
    • Megaloblastic change at all stages of erythroid development. Large promegaloblasts with deeply basophilic cytoplasm and fine nuclear chromatin. Nuclear to cytoplasmic asynchrony.
    • Giant metamyelocytes and band forms
      Large megakaryocytes with bizarre multilobate nuclei.

    Biochemical

    • Vitamin B12 deficiency: low serum vitamin B12
      Raised serum homocysteine and methylmalonic acid
      Antibodies to intrinsic factor in pernicious anaemia.
    • Folate deficiency: decreased serum or red cell folate
      Raised homocysteine
      Normal methylmalonate.

    What is megaloblast?

    DU25M

    Megaloblasts are the enlarged, abnormal haemopoietic precursors of megaloblastic anaemia. The most primitive (promegaloblasts) are large, with deeply basophilic cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli and a fine nuclear chromatin. as they differentiate, the nucleus keeps its fine chromatin while haemoglobin accumulates normally in the cytoplasm, producing nuclear to cytoplasmic asynchrony.

    Write a short note on Schilling test.

    DU11Ja

    The Schilling test [vitamin B12 absorption test] finds the cause of vitamin B12 deficiency by measuring absorption of an oral dose of radiolabelled vitamin B12 as excretion in the urine.

    Stage 1: radiolabelled (cobalt) vitamin B12 is given by mouth, after an intramuscular dose of unlabelled vitamin B12 to saturate body stores. Urine is collected for 24 hours. Less than 10% excreted indicates malabsorption.

    Stage 2: the test is repeated with oral intrinsic factor.

    • Normal excretion: lack of intrinsic factor, that is pernicious anaemia.
    • Persistently low excretion: malabsorption from another cause, for example ileal disease.

    Many laboratories no longer perform it, because the radiolabelled test substances are no longer produced.

    A patient after partial gastrectomy has pallor, weakness, neuropathy/paresthesia. What is your provisional diagnosis?

    DU16JaDU14JuDU13Ju

    Provisional diagnosis: megaloblastic anaemia from vitamin B12 deficiency.

    • Pallor and weakness: anaemia.
    • Neuropathy and paraesthesia: demyelination of the dorsal and lateral spinal tracts, producing severe paraesthesiae in the lower limbs, sensory ataxia and spastic paraparesis. Also peripheral nerve change.

    Same: what is the cause?

    DU13Ju

    With gastrectomy, intrinsic factor is lost, so vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed. Once stored vitamin B12 is depleted, anaemia develops.

    Same: what is the hematological profile / how will you confirm?

    DU16JaDU14Ju
    1. Blood: macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils, low reticulocyte count, leucopenia.
    2. Marrow: hypercellular, with megaloblastic change.
    3. Serum vitamin B12: low.
    4. Homocysteine and methylmalonic acid: raised.
    5. Therapeutic response: reticulocyte outpouring and rise in haematocrit about 5 days after parenteral vitamin B12.

    Haemolytic Anaemias

    A7

    Define haemolytic anaemia.

    A7Q12, Q13

    Haemolytic anaemias are the result of extravascular or intravascular haemolysis. They share the following features:

    • A shortened red cell life span below the normal 120 days.
    • Elevated erythropoietin levels and a compensatory increase in erythropoiesis.
    • Accumulation of haemoglobin degradation products created during the process of red cell haemolysis.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 579
    A7

    What do you mean by premature destruction of RBC?

    A7Q12

    Premature destruction of red cells is the removal of red cells before the normal life span of 120 days. It occurs in two ways:

    • Extravascular haemolysis: in the great majority of haemolytic anaemias the premature destruction occurs within phagocytes. It is usually caused by alterations that make red cells less deformable, so that they are sequestered and phagocytosed by macrophages in the splenic cords. If persistent, it leads to hyperplasia of phagocytes and splenomegaly.
    • Intravascular haemolysis: less common
      Caused by mechanical injury, complement fixation, intracellular parasites (for example falciparum malaria) or exogenous toxic factors.
    A7

    Outline classification of haemolytic anaemia.

    A7Q13
    MechanismExamples
    Inherited genetic defects
    Red cell membrane disordersHereditary spherocytosis, hereditary elliptocytosis
    Hexose monophosphate shunt enzyme deficienciesG6PD deficiency, glutathione synthetase deficiency
    Glycolytic enzyme deficienciesPyruvate kinase deficiency, hexokinase deficiency
    Deficient globin synthesisThalassaemia syndromes
    Structurally abnormal globins (haemoglobinopathies)Sickle cell disease, unstable haemoglobins
    Acquired genetic defect
    Deficiency of phosphatidylinositol-linked glycoproteinsParoxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria
    Antibody-mediated destructionHaemolytic disease of the newborn (Rh disease), transfusion reactions, drug-induced, autoimmune disorders
    Mechanical trauma
    Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemiasHaemolytic uraemic syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
    Cardiac traumatic haemolysisDefective cardiac valves
    Repetitive physical traumaBongo drumming, marathon running, karate chopping
    Infections of red cellsMalaria, babesiosis
    Toxic or chemical injuryClostridial sepsis, snake venom, lead poisoning
    Membrane lipid abnormalitiesAbetalipoproteinaemia, severe hepatocellular liver disease
    SequestrationHypersplenism
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 579p. 591
    A7

    Common examples of congenital haemolytic anaemias.

    A7Q12
    1. Red cell membrane disorders: hereditary spherocytosis, hereditary elliptocytosis.
    2. Red cell enzyme deficiencies: G6PD deficiency and glutathione synthetase deficiency (hexose monophosphate shunt). Pyruvate kinase deficiency and hexokinase deficiency (glycolytic enzymes).
    3. Haemoglobin abnormalities: thalassaemia syndromes (deficient globin synthesis). Sickle cell disease and unstable haemoglobins (structurally abnormal globins).
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 579
    A7

    Haemolytic anaemias due to extracorpuscular defect.

    A7Q14

    Causes that act on the red cell from outside:

    1. Antibody-mediated destruction (immunohaemolytic anaemia): warm antibody type (IgG), cold agglutinin type (IgM) and cold haemolysin type (IgG). Also haemolytic disease of the newborn (Rh disease), transfusion reactions and drug-induced haemolysis.
    2. Mechanical trauma: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (disseminated intravascular coagulation, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, haemolytic uraemic syndrome), cardiac valve prostheses, and repetitive physical trauma.
    3. Infections of red cells: malaria, babesiosis.
    4. Toxic or chemical injury: clostridial sepsis, snake venom, lead poisoning.
    5. Membrane lipid abnormalities: abetalipoproteinaemia, severe hepatocellular liver disease.
    6. Sequestration: hypersplenism.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 579
    A7

    Why does jaundice occur in haemolytic anaemia?

    A7Q11
    • Haem groups derived from haemoglobin are metabolised to bilirubin within mononuclear phagocytes, leading to jaundice.
    • In all types of uncomplicated haemolytic anaemia the excess serum bilirubin is unconjugated.
    • The level of hyperbilirubinaemia depends on the functional capacity of the liver and the rate of haemolysis. When the liver is normal, jaundice is rarely severe.
    • Excessive bilirubin excreted by the liver into the biliary tract often leads to the formation of pigment gallstones derived from haem.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 579
    A7

    Evidence of increased haemoglobin breakdown.

    A7Q15

    1. Extravascular haemolysis - Jaundice from unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. - Variable decrease in plasma haptoglobin, because some haemoglobin escapes from phagocytes. - Haemosiderosis: accumulation of haemosiderin in the spleen, liver and bone marrow. - Pigment gallstones (cholelithiasis) with chronic haemolysis. 2. Intravascular haemolysis - Haemoglobinaemia and haemoglobinuria. - Haemosiderinuria
    Iron released from haemoglobin accumulates within renal tubular cells, giving renal haemosiderosis. - Free haemoglobin is bound by haptoglobin. as serum haptoglobin is depleted, free haemoglobin oxidises to brown methaemoglobin, which gives the urine a red-brown colour. - Jaundice, as bilirubin is formed in mononuclear phagocytes from the haemoglobin-haptoglobin complexes.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 579
    A7

    Evidence of compensatory erythroid hyperplasia.

    A7Q16
    • Anaemia and lowered tissue oxygen tension trigger the production of erythropoietin, which stimulates erythroid differentiation.
    • Bone marrow shows increased numbers of erythroid precursors (normoblasts).
    • Peripheral blood shows a prominent reticulocytosis.
    • If the anaemia is severe, extramedullary haematopoiesis appears in the liver, spleen and lymph nodes.
    • In sickle cell disease and thalassaemia major, marked marrow expansion leads to bone resorption and secondary new bone formation, giving prominent cheekbones and a "crewcut" appearance of the skull on radiographs.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 579
    A7

    Evidence of haemolysis in PBF.

    4A7Q11, Q15, Q16, Q17

    1. Reticulocytosis, with larger red cells that show blue-red polychromatophilic cytoplasm. 2. Anisocytosis and poikilocytosis, with changes specific to the cause: - Spherocytes: small, dark-staining red cells lacking central pallor, in hereditary spherocytosis and autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. - Heinz bodies [denatured haemoglobin inclusions in red cells] and bite cells, in G6PD deficiency. - Irreversibly sickled cells and target cells, in sickle cell disease. - Target cells, basophilic stippling and fragmented red cells, in thalassaemia. - Schistocytes (fragmented red cells), burr cells, helmet cells and triangle cells, in microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and with defective cardiac valves. 3. Howell-Jolly bodies [nuclear remnants in red cells, seen after splenectomy] (small nuclear remnants) when the spleen is absent or nonfunctional.

    A7

    Conditions where nucleated RBCs are seen in PBF.

    A7Q17
    1. Severe megaloblastic anaemia: nucleated red cell progenitors occasionally appear in the circulating blood when the anaemia is severe.
    2. Thalassaemia major: poorly haemoglobinised normoblasts, from "stress" erythropoiesis and abnormal release of red cell precursors from sites of extramedullary haematopoiesis.
    3. Myelophthisic anaemia: marrow replaced by metastatic cancer, granulomatous disease or the fibrosis of the spent phase of myeloproliferative neoplasms. Nucleated erythroid precursors and immature granulocytic forms are released prematurely (leukoerythroblastosis), with teardrop-shaped red cells.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 585p. 592p. 601
    A7

    What is autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA)?

    A7Q18

    Immunohaemolytic anaemia is caused by antibodies that recognise red cells and cause their premature destruction. Although these disorders are commonly referred to as autoimmune haemolytic anaemias, the designation immunohaemolytic anaemia is preferred because the immune reaction is initiated in some instances by an ingested drug.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 590
    A7

    Causes of AIHA.

    A7Q18
    TypeAntibodyCauses
    Warm antibody type (about 80% of cases)IgG (less commonly IgA), active at 37°CAbout 50% idiopathic (primary). Secondary: autoimmune disorders (particularly systemic lupus erythematosus), drugs, lymphoid neoplasms
    Cold agglutinin type (15% to 20% of cases)IgM, active below 37°C (binds at 0°C to 4°C)Acute: mycoplasmal infection, infectious mononucleosis (also cytomegalovirus, influenza and HIV). Chronic: B-cell neoplasms or idiopathic
    Cold haemolysin typeIgG, active below 37°C (binds the P blood group antigen)Rare
    Mainly in children following viral infections

    Drug-induced warm antibody type acts by two mechanisms:

    • Antigenic drugs, for example penicillin and cephalosporins: the drug binds to the red cell membrane and creates a new antigenic determinant. Haemolysis follows large intravenous doses, 1 to 2 weeks after therapy starts.
    • Tolerance-breaking drugs, of which alpha-methyldopa is the prototype: they lead to antibodies against red cell antigens, particularly Rh antigens. About 10% of patients develop autoantibodies and roughly 1% develop clinically significant haemolysis.

    Narrate the features of haemolysis found in PBF.

    DU12Ju
    • Reticulocytosis, which is prominent, from the compensatory increase in erythropoiesis.
    • Spherocytes in warm antibody immunohaemolytic anaemia, as in hereditary spherocytosis, from loss of red cell membrane.
    • Red cell fragments (schistocytes), burr cells, helmet cells and triangle cells in haemolysis due to red cell trauma, such as cardiac valve prostheses and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 579p. 590p. 591

    Write down the general evidence/laboratory features of haemolysis.

    DU12JuDU09Ja
    1. Shortened red cell life span, below the normal 120 days.
    2. Anaemia, with raised erythropoietin levels.
    3. Reticulocytosis in the peripheral blood.
    4. Increased erythroid precursors (normoblasts) in the bone marrow.
    5. Hyperbilirubinaemia, in which the excess serum bilirubin is unconjugated
      Jaundice follows.
    6. Raised lactate dehydrogenase and low plasma haptoglobin.
    7. Haemosiderosis, with haemosiderin in the spleen, liver and bone marrow.
    8. Extramedullary haematopoiesis in the liver, spleen and lymph nodes if the anaemia is severe.
    9. Pigment gallstones in chronic haemolysis.
    10. Extravascular haemolysis: splenomegaly, from hyperplasia of phagocytes.
    11. Intravascular haemolysis: haemoglobinaemia, haemoglobinuria and haemosiderinuria. no splenomegaly.
    12. Positive direct Coombs test [antiglobulin test for antibody-coated red cells] in immunohaemolytic anaemia.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 579

    Write down the evidence of intravascular haemolysis.

    DU21M
    1. Anaemia.
    2. Haemoglobinaemia: free haemoglobin from lysed red cells in the plasma.
    3. Haemoglobinuria: some filtered haemoglobin and methaemoglobin passes out in the urine, giving a red-brown colour.
    4. Haemosiderinuria and renal haemosiderosis: iron released from haemoglobin accumulates in renal tubular cells.
    5. Jaundice: haem from haemoglobin-haptoglobin complexes is metabolised to bilirubin in mononuclear phagocytes.
    6. Serum haptoglobin is depleted
      Free haemoglobin then oxidises to methaemoglobin, which is brown.
    7. Splenomegaly is not seen.
    8. In chronic haemolysis, iron loss in the urine may lead to iron deficiency.

    Causes: mechanical injury, complement fixation, intracellular parasites (falciparum malaria) and toxic factors such as clostridial sepsis.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 579

    Write a short note on Coombs' test (direct).

    7DU23NDU20NDU20JuDU19MDU12JaDU08JaDU05Ja

    Principle. The direct Coombs [antiglobulin test for antibody-coated red cells] antiglobulin test detects antibodies or complement on the surface of the patient's red cells. The patient's red cells are mixed with sera containing antibodies specific for human immunoglobulin or complement. If either is present on the red cells, the antibodies cause agglutination, seen as clumping.

    Uses - Diagnosis of immunohaemolytic anaemia, which requires detection of antibodies or complement on the patient's red cells. - Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction: typically positive, unless all the donor red cells have lysed. - Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction: positive. - About 10% of patients taking alpha-methyldopa develop autoantibodies detected by the direct Coombs test
    Roughly 1% develop clinically significant haemolysis.

    Indirect Coombs test. The patient's serum is tested for its ability to agglutinate commercially available red cells bearing known antigens. It characterises the target antigen and the temperature dependence of the antibody.

    What do you mean by haemolytic disease of newborn?

    DU18M

    Immune hydrops is a haemolytic disease caused by blood group antigen incompatibility between mother and foetus.

    A7

    Define haemoglobinopathies.

    A7Q21, Q23

    Haemoglobinopathies are disorders caused by mutations in globin genes that produce structurally abnormal globins. Several hundred are known.

    A7

    A7Q21, Q23, Q27

    2. HbSC disease: the compound heterozygous state for HbS and HbC.
    3. HbC: a variant haemoglobin common in regions where HbS is found.
    4. Unstable haemoglobins.

    5DU22MDU20NDU20JuDU12JuDU11Ju

    Write a short note on hemoglobinopathy.

    DU25MDU18NovDU17Ja

    Definition: inherited disorders caused by mutations in globin genes that produce structurally abnormal haemoglobin. Several hundred are known. Sickle cell disease is the commonest and the one considered here.

    Pathogenesis of sickle cell disease

    1. A missense mutation in the β-globin gene replaces glutamate with valine, producing HbS.
    2. Deoxygenated HbS stacks into polymers, turning the red cell cytosol into a viscous gel and then into needle-like fibres, which distort the cell into a sickle or holly-leaf shape.
    3. Repeated sickling damages the membrane
      Cells become dehydrated, dense and rigid, and finally irreversibly sickled. These are removed by mononuclear phagocytes (extravascular haemolysis), and fragile cells cause some intravascular haemolysis.
    4. Sickled cells are sticky, with increased adhesion molecules
      Microvascular occlusion is helped by inflammation and vasoconstriction, which slow the passage of red cells.
    5. Sickling is affected by HbS with other haemoglobins (HbA and HbF inhibit polymerisation), mean cell haemoglobin concentration, intracellular pH and transit time through microvascular beds.

    Morphology

    • Blood: irreversibly sickled cells, reticulocytosis, target cells. Howell-Jolly bodies [nuclear remnants in red cells, seen after splenectomy] from asplenia.
    • Hyperplastic marrow, with bone resorption and a "crewcut" skull on X-ray. Extramedullary haemopoiesis.
    • Hyperbilirubinaemia and pigment gallstones.
    • Spleen: autoinfarcted remnant.

    Clinical features

    • Chronic haemolytic anaemia, microvascular occlusions and ischaemic tissue damage.
    • Chronic hypoxia: impaired growth and development
      Damage to spleen, heart, kidneys and lungs
      hyposthenuria.
    • Increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms (Pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae, meningococcus), because of impaired splenic function.
    • Infants become symptomatic at 5 or 6 months, when HbF falls.
    • Diagnosis: irreversibly sickled cells and tests for sickle haemoglobin. Treatment with hydroxyurea, which raises HbF.

    Thalassaemia

    A7

    Define thalassemia.

    9A7Q22, Q23, Q28, Q30DU25NDU20NDU20JuDU17JaDU07Ja

    Also asked as: Define thalassaemia.

    Thalassaemia is a genetically heterogeneous disorder caused by germline mutations that decrease the synthesis of either alpha-globin or beta-globin, leading to anaemia, tissue hypoxia, and red cell haemolysis related to the imbalance in globin chain synthesis.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 585
    A7

    How is thalassemia classified?

    5A7Q28, Q29DU20NDU20JuDU07Ja

    Also asked as: Classify thalassaemia.

    Thalassaemia is classified by the globin chain that is deficient, and then by clinical severity.

    SyndromeGenetic basisClinical features
    Beta-thalassaemia majorTwo beta-thalassaemia alleles (beta-zero or beta-plus)Severe
    Requires blood transfusions
    Beta-thalassaemia intermediaMilder variants of two defective alleles, and unusual heterozygous formsSevere, but does not require regular blood transfusions
    Beta-thalassaemia minor (trait)One beta-thalassaemia allele and one normalAsymptomatic, with mild or absent anaemia
    Red cell abnormalities seen
    Silent carrier (alpha)Deletion of one alpha-globin geneAsymptomatic
    no red cell abnormality
    Alpha-thalassaemia traitDeletion of two alpha-globin genesAsymptomatic, like beta-thalassaemia minor
    Haemoglobin H diseaseDeletion of three alpha-globin genesSevere
    Resembles beta-thalassaemia intermedia
    Alpha-thalassaemia major (hydrops fetalis)Deletion of all four alpha-globin genesLethal in utero without transfusions
    A7

    Clinical features of thalassaemia.

    A7Q22, Q28

    Beta-thalassaemia major

    • The anaemia manifests 6 to 9 months after birth, as haemoglobin synthesis switches from HbF to HbA. in untransfused patients haemoglobin is 3 to 6 g/dL.
    • Untreated children have growth retardation and die early from the effects of anaemia. Severe cachexia occurs in untreated patients.
    • Hepatosplenomegaly from extramedullary haematopoiesis. The spleen may weigh as much as 1500 g.
    • Skeletal changes: expanding marrow erodes cortical bone, giving a "crewcut" skull on radiographs. in survivors the cheekbones and other bony prominences are enlarged and distorted.
    • Iron overload (haemosiderosis and secondary haemochromatosis) from increased gut absorption and repeated transfusions damages the heart, liver and pancreas. Cardiac disease is an important cause of death.
    • With transfusions and iron chelation, survival into the third decade is possible.

    Beta-thalassaemia minor

    • Usually asymptomatic
      Anaemia, if present, is mild.

    Alpha-thalassaemia

    • Silent carrier: asymptomatic, with slight microcytosis. Trait: small red cells, minimal or no anaemia, no abnormal physical signs.
    • Haemoglobin H disease: moderately severe anaemia
      HbH has very high oxygen affinity, so tissue hypoxia is out of proportion to the haemoglobin level.
    • Hydrops fetalis: foetal distress by the third trimester, severe pallor, generalised oedema and massive hepatosplenomegaly. Lifelong transfusion dependence in survivors.
    A7

    Type of mutation in beta thalassaemia.

    A7Q29

    Beta-thalassaemia is caused by more than 100 different mutations, mostly point mutations, of two kinds:

    • Beta-zero mutations: absent beta-globin synthesis.
    • Beta-plus mutations: reduced but detectable beta-globin synthesis.

    They fall into three major classes:

    1. Splicing mutations: the most common cause of beta-plus thalassaemia. Some destroy normal RNA splice junctions and prevent production of normal beta-globin mRNA (beta-zero). Others create an ectopic splice site within an intron, so that some normal mRNA is still made (beta-plus).
    2. Promoter region mutations: reduce transcription by 75% to 80%
      Associated with beta-plus thalassaemia.
    3. Chain terminator mutations: the most common cause of beta-zero thalassaemia
      Nonsense mutations that introduce a premature stop codon, or small insertions or deletions that shift the reading frame (frameshift mutations).
    A7

    Laboratory diagnosis of thalassaemia.

    A7Q29

    1. Peripheral blood: anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, microcytosis and hypochromia. Target cells, basophilic stippling and fragmented red cells. Reticulocyte count elevated. 2. Haemoglobin electrophoresis - Beta-thalassaemia major: HbF markedly elevated. HbA completely absent (beta-zero/beta-zero) or present in small amounts. - Beta-thalassaemia minor: HbA2 increased to 4% to 8% of total haemoglobin (normal 2.5% plus or minus 0.3%). HbF normal or occasionally slightly increased. - Alpha-thalassaemia trait: HbA2 normal or low. 3. Exclude iron deficiency, the most common cause of microcytic anaemia, by serum iron, total iron-binding capacity and serum ferritin. The raised HbA2 is useful in females of childbearing age, who are at high risk of iron deficiency. 4. Bone marrow: mild erythroid hyperplasia in the minor form. Striking expansion of haematopoietically active marrow in the major form. 5. Prenatal diagnosis is possible by molecular analysis of DNA.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 585
    A7

    PBF findings of thalassaemia major.

    A7Q30
    • Marked variation in red cell size (anisocytosis) and shape (poikilocytosis).
    • Microcytosis and hypochromia.
    • Target cells (haemoglobin collects in the centre of the cell), basophilic stippling and fragmented red cells.
    • Reticulocyte count elevated, but lower than expected for the severity of the anaemia because of ineffective erythropoiesis.
    • Variable numbers of poorly haemoglobinised nucleated red cell precursors (normoblasts).
    • Inclusions of aggregated alpha chains are efficiently removed by the spleen and are not easily seen.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 585p. 592
    A7

    Confirmatory test for thalassaemia.

    A7Q30

    Diagnostic tests:

    • Haemoglobin electrophoresis: in beta-thalassaemia major the major haemoglobin is HbF, markedly elevated, with HbA absent or small. in beta-thalassaemia minor HbA2 is increased to 4% to 8%.
    • Molecular analysis of DNA for prenatal diagnosis.

    Write the genetic basis of β-thalassemia major.

    DU19M

    - The β-globin chains are encoded by a single β-globin gene on chromosome 11. - β-Thalassaemia major results from two β-thalassaemia alleles: β+/β+, β+/β0 or β0/β0. - β0 mutations: absent β-globin synthesis. β+ mutations: reduced but detectable β-globin synthesis. - More than 100 causative mutations are known, mostly point mutations, in three classes: 1. Splicing mutations: the commonest cause of β+-thalassaemia
    Those destroying normal splice junctions cause β0-thalassaemia. 2. Promoter region mutations: reduce transcription by 75% to 80%. β+-thalassaemia. 3. Chain terminator mutations: the commonest cause of β0-thalassaemia
    Nonsense mutations with a premature stop codon, or frameshift insertions or deletions. - Consequence: unpaired α chains precipitate in red cell precursors, causing membrane damage and apoptosis (70% to 85% of precursors in severe disease), ineffective erythropoiesis and haemolysis.

    Give the laboratory diagnosis of thalassemia/β-thalassemia major.

    15DU25NDU22MDU20NDU20JuDU19MDU17MDU17JaDU16JuDU14JuDU13JuDU12JaDU11JuDU10JuDU08JuDU06S

    Blood

    • Haemoglobin 3 to 6 g/dL in untransfused patients.
    • Smear: anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, microcytosis and hypochromia. Target cells, basophilic stippling and fragmented red cells. Nucleated red cell precursors (normoblasts).
    • Reticulocyte count raised, but lower than expected for the degree of anaemia, because of ineffective erythropoiesis.

    Haemoglobin analysis

    • HbA absent (β0/β0) or present in small amounts (β+/β+ or β0/β+).
    • HbF markedly elevated and the major haemoglobin.
    • In β-thalassaemia trait (minor): HbA2 increased to 4% to 8% (normal 2.5% plus or minus 0.3%)
      HbF normal or slightly increased.

    Other findings: striking marrow expansion
    "crewcut" appearance of the skull on X-ray
    Splenomegaly up to 1500 g
    Iron overload.

    A child has severe anemia, mongoloid face, hepatosplenomegaly, repeated transfusions, target cells. What is your probable diagnosis?

    9DU24NDU23NDU22NDU19NovDU18NovDU17NovDU11JaDU10JaDU08Ju

    Probable diagnosis: β-thalassaemia major.

    • Anaemia appears 6 to 9 months after birth, as haemoglobin synthesis switches from HbF to HbA.
    • Marrow expansion in facial bones and skull alters the face.
    • Hepatosplenomegaly from extramedullary haemopoiesis.
    • Target cells on the blood smear.
    • Repeated transfusions are required, with the risk of iron overload.

    Same child: how will you confirm the diagnosis?

    9DU24NDU23NDU22NDU19NovDU18NovDU17NovDU11JaDU10JaDU08Ju
    1. Blood smear: microcytosis, hypochromia, anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, target cells, basophilic stippling, fragmented cells and normoblasts.
    2. Haemoglobin analysis: HbA absent or reduced
      HbF markedly elevated.
    3. Reticulocyte count: raised, but lower than expected.
    4. X-ray of skull: "crewcut" appearance.
    5. Iron studies: iron overload.

    Sickle cell anaemia

    A7

    Which type of abnormal haemoglobin is found in sickle cell anaemia?

    A7Q25

    Sickle haemoglobin (HbS). A missense mutation in the beta-globin gene replaces a charged glutamate residue with a hydrophobic valine residue. In affected individuals almost all the haemoglobin in the red cell is HbS (two alpha chains and two sickle beta chains).

    A7

    Clinical features of sickle cell anaemia.

    A7Q25, Q26
    • Infants become symptomatic only at 5 or 6 months of age, when the level of HbF normally falls.
    • Chronic haemolytic anaemia with jaundice and pigment gallstones
      Chronic tissue hypoxia impairs growth and development and damages the spleen, heart, kidneys and lungs.
    • The course is punctuated by crises:
    • Vaso-occlusive (pain) crises: hypoxic injury and infarction causing severe pain, most often in the bones, lungs, liver, brain, spleen and penis. in children, bone crises and the hand-foot syndrome (dactylitis).
    • Acute chest syndrome: fever, cough, chest pain and pulmonary infiltrates. May be fatal.
    • Sequestration crisis in children with an intact spleen: massive entrapment of sickled cells, rapid splenic enlargement, hypovolaemia and sometimes shock.
    • Aplastic crisis: parvovirus B19 infection of red cell progenitors causes a sudden worsening of the anaemia.
    • Priapism in up to 45% of males after puberty
      Stroke and retinopathy with loss of vision.
    • Autosplenectomy: the spleen is enlarged in early childhood, then infarcted and fibrosed to a small nubbin by adolescence or early adulthood.
    • Increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms (Pneumococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, meningococcus), from impaired splenic function and defects in the alternative complement pathway.
    • Hyposthenuria (inability to concentrate urine) from sickling in the renal medulla.
    • Leg ulcers in adults from vascular stagnation in subcutaneous tissues.
    • Marrow expansion gives prominent cheekbones and a "crewcut" skull. Cor pulmonale may follow pulmonary vessel infarcts.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 583p. 584p. 585
    A7

    How does leg ulcer occur in sickle cell anaemia?

    A7Q26

    In adult patients, vascular stagnation in subcutaneous tissues often leads to leg ulcers
    The complication is rare in children.

    The stagnation reflects the microvascular occlusion that underlies the disease:

    • Sickling occurs within microvascular beds with slow transit times.
    • Sickle red cells express increased amounts of adhesion molecules and are sticky, and inflammation slows or arrests their movement through the microvasculature.
    • Stagnation prolongs exposure to low oxygen tension, so more cells sickle and obstruct the vessel: a vicious cycle of sickling, obstruction, hypoxia and more sickling.
    • Free haemoglobin from lysed sickle cells binds and inactivates nitric oxide, which raises vascular tone and enhances platelet aggregation.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 583p. 584
    A7

    Laboratory diagnosis of sickle cell anaemia.

    A7Q27
    1. Peripheral blood: variable numbers of irreversibly sickled cells, reticulocytosis and target cells (from red cell dehydration). Howell-Jolly bodies [nuclear remnants in red cells, seen after splenectomy] from asplenia. Anisocytosis and poikilocytosis.
    2. Bone marrow: hyperplastic from compensatory erythroid hyperplasia.
    3. Hyperbilirubinaemia from the increased breakdown of haemoglobin.
    4. Confirmation: the diagnosis is suggested by the clinical findings and the presence of irreversibly sickled red cells, and is confirmed by various tests for sickle haemoglobin.
    5. Prenatal diagnosis by analysis of foetal DNA obtained by amniocentesis or chorionic biopsy.
    6. Newborn screening for sickle haemoglobin, using heel-stick samples obtained at birth.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 583p. 585

    Aplastic Anaemia and Pancytopenia

    A6A7

    What is pancytopenia?

    13A6A7Q19DU25NDU24MDU22MDU20NDU20JuDU19NovDU18MDU16JaDU14JaDU12JaDU10Ja

    Also asked as: Define pancytopenia.

    Pancytopenia is the combination of anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia.

    A6A7A10

    Write down the important causes of pancytopenia.

    14A6A7Q19, Q20A10Q9DU25NDU20NDU20JuDU19NovDU18MDU16JaDU14JaDU12JaDU10Ja

    Also asked as: Causes of pancytopenia.

    1. Aplastic anaemia: chronic primary haematopoietic failure, from: - Chemicals and drugs: dose-related marrow suppression (many cancer chemotherapy drugs, benzene) or idiosyncratic reactions (chloramphenicol, gold salts). - Viral infections, most commonly viral hepatitis (about 5% of cases). - Whole-body irradiation. - Inherited defects: Fanconi anaemia [autosomal recessive defect in DNA repair] and telomerase defects. - Idiopathic in about 65% of cases. 2. Megaloblastic anaemia: impaired DNA synthesis causes most precursors to undergo apoptosis in the marrow (ineffective haematopoiesis). 3. Bone marrow replacement: leukaemia, disseminated cancer and granulomatous disease (myelophthisic marrow failure). 4. Ineffective haematopoiesis: myelodysplastic neoplasm. 5. Acute myeloid leukaemia: replacement of the marrow with blasts. 6. Hypersplenism: sequestration of blood cells in an enlarged spleen. 7. Hairy cell leukaemia: pancytopenia from marrow involvement and sequestration of cells in the enlarged spleen, in more than one-half of cases.

    A6A7

    How will you diagnose/investigate a case of pancytopenia?

    6A6A7Q19DU10JuDU07JuDU07JaDU05M

    Also asked as: How will you investigate a case of pancytopenia?

    1. Clinical examination for splenomegaly: characteristically absent in aplastic anaemia
    if present, the diagnosis of aplastic anaemia should be questioned. 2. Blood count and film: in aplastic anaemia the red cells are usually slightly macrocytic and normochromic, with reticulocytopenia. in megaloblastic anaemia look for macro-ovalocytes and neutrophils with five or more lobes. 3. Bone marrow biopsy: the diagnosis of aplastic anaemia rests on it. Aspirates often give little material (a "dry tap"), so aplasia is best seen in the biopsy. - Aplastic anaemia: markedly hypocellular marrow. - "Aleukaemic" leukaemia and myelodysplastic neoplasm: usually a hypercellular marrow filled with neoplastic progenitors. - Megaloblastic anaemia: markedly hypercellular marrow with megaloblasts. 4. Look for the cause: serum vitamin B12 and folate levels if the picture is megaloblastic. History of drug, chemical, viral or radiation exposure for aplastic anaemia.

    A6A7

    Blood and bone marrow picture of aplastic anaemia.

    A6A7Q20

    Blood

    • Pancytopenia: anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia.
    • Red cells usually slightly macrocytic and normochromic.
    • Reticulocytopenia is the rule.

    Bone marrow

    • Markedly hypocellular, largely devoid of haematopoietic cells.
    • Often only fat cells, fibrous stroma, and scattered lymphocytes and plasma cells remain.
    • Aspirates often yield little material (a "dry tap"). Aplasia is best appreciated in marrow biopsies.
    • If multiple transfusions are needed, systemic haemosiderosis can appear.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 599p. 603
    A6

    Why does pancytopenia occur in acute leukaemia?

    A6
    • In acute myeloid leukaemia, the replacement of the marrow with blasts produces marrow failure, with anaemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia.
    • In acute lymphoblastic leukaemia with a leukaemic presentation, the marrow is hypercellular and packed with lymphoblasts, which replace normal marrow elements.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 541p. 562
    A6

    Why does pancytopenia occur in some cases of splenomegaly?

    A6
    • Splenomegaly can cause hypersplenism, characterised by anaemia, leucopenia and/or thrombocytopenia.
    • The probable cause of the cytopenias is increased sequestration of formed elements and the consequent enhanced phagocytosis by the splenic macrophages.
    • The spleen normally sequesters 30% to 35% of the body's platelets, which can rise to 80% to 90% when the spleen is enlarged.
    • In congestive splenomegaly, slowing of blood flow from the cords to the sinusoids prolongs the exposure of blood cells to macrophages, resulting in excessive destruction.
    • In hairy cell leukaemia, pancytopenia results from marrow involvement and sequestration of cells in the enlarged spleen.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 13)p. 549p. 573
    A8

    How will you differentiate aplastic anaemia from subleukaemic acute leukaemia in the laboratory?

    A8Q16

    Aplastic anaemia must be distinguished from "aleukaemic" leukaemia and myelodysplastic neoplasm, which may have identical clinical manifestations. The diagnosis rests on examination of a bone marrow biopsy.

    FeatureAplastic anaemiaAleukaemic acute leukaemia
    Bone marrow cellularityHypocellular, usually markedly soHypercellular
    Bone marrow cellsLargely fat cells, fibrous stroma, scattered lymphocytes and plasma cellsPacked with neoplastic blasts, which replace normal marrow elements
    Marrow aspirateOften a "dry tap"Not stated
    SpleenSplenomegaly characteristically absentNot stated

    Write down the causes of marrow aplasia.

    DU11Ju

    1. Chemicals and drugs (most cases of known aetiology) - Dose-related and reversible marrow suppression: many cancer chemotherapy drugs and the organic solvent benzene. - Idiosyncratic and unpredictable: chloramphenicol and gold salts. 2. Viral infections: viral hepatitis (about 5% of cases), cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus [herpesvirus that causes infectious mononucleosis] and herpes zoster (varicella zoster). 3. Whole-body irradiation: therapeutic irradiation or nuclear accidents, which destroy haemopoietic stem cells in a dose-dependent fashion. 4. Fanconi anaemia [inherited DNA-repair defect causing marrow failure]: autosomal recessive defect of a multiprotein complex required for DNA repair, with congenital anomalies such as kidney and spleen hypoplasia and thumb or radial anomalies. 5. Telomerase defects: found in 5% to 10% of adult-onset aplastic anaemia
    Abnormally short telomeres are found in the marrow cells of as many as half of those affected. 6. Idiopathic: about 65% of cases.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 599p. 600

    What are the clinical presentations of pancytopenia?

    DU07Ju

    Pancytopenia, as seen in aplastic anaemia, presents according to the cell line affected:

    1. Anaemia: progressive weakness, pallor and dyspnoea.
    2. Thrombocytopenia: petechiae and ecchymoses.
    3. Neutropenia: frequent and persistent infections, or sudden chills, fever and prostration.

    Splenomegaly is characteristically absent
    if present, the diagnosis of aplastic anaemia should be questioned.

    Give the laboratory diagnosis of aplastic anemia (PBF and bone marrow findings).

    8DU20NDU20JuDU19NovDU18MDU16JaDU14JaDU12JaDU11Ju

    Peripheral blood

    • Pancytopenia.
    • Red cells usually slightly macrocytic and normochromic.
    • Reticulocytopenia.

    Bone marrow

    • Markedly hypocellular, largely devoid of haemopoietic cells. Only fat cells, fibrous stroma and scattered lymphocytes and plasma cells remain.
    • Aspirates often yield little material (dry tap), so aplasia is best appreciated in marrow biopsies.

    The diagnosis rests on bone marrow biopsy. It distinguishes aplastic anaemia from aleukaemic leukaemia and myelodysplastic neoplasm, which have hypercellular marrows filled with neoplastic progenitors.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 603

    A boy of 11y has Hb 2 g, WBC 500/cmm, platelets 12000/cmm. What is the probable diagnosis?

    DU12Ja

    Probable diagnosis: aplastic anaemia, with pancytopenia affecting all three cell lines.

    Confirmation: bone marrow biopsy showing a markedly hypocellular marrow. Other causes of pancytopenia, such as aleukaemic leukaemia and myelodysplastic neoplasm, have hypercellular marrows.

    Bleeding and Coagulation Disorders

    Bleeding disorders

    A9

    Define hemorrhagic disorders with example.

    A9Q21DU24N

    Also asked as: Define haemorrhagic disorder.

    Haemorrhagic diatheses (bleeding disorders) are conditions in which excessive bleeding results from (1) increased fragility of vessels, (2) platelet deficiency or dysfunction, and (3) derangement of coagulation, alone or in combination.

    Examples:

    • Vessel wall: hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia.
    • Platelets: immune thrombocytopenic purpura.
    • Coagulation: haemophilia A.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 602p. 603p. 604
    A9

    Classify haemorrhagic disorder.

    A9Q21
    GroupExamples
    Vessel wall abnormalitiesInfections (meningococcaemia, septicaemia, infective endocarditis, rickettsioses)
    Drug reactions
    Scurvy and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome [inherited collagen disorder with hyperextensible skin and joints]
    Cushing syndrome [glucocorticoid excess] and ageing
    Henoch-Schönlein purpura [IgA vasculitis]
    Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia
    Perivascular amyloidosis
    Platelet disordersThrombocytopenia (decreased production, decreased survival, sequestration, dilution)
    Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
    Thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP and HUS)
    Coagulation disordersInherited: haemophilia A, haemophilia B, von Willebrand disease [inherited bleeding disorder from deficient or defective von Willebrand factor]. Acquired: vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, disseminated intravascular coagulation
    A9

    Approach to diagnosing a patient with a bleeding disorder.

    A9Q21

    Excessive bleeding results from vessel fragility, platelet deficiency or dysfunction, or derangement of coagulation. The clinical pattern is matched with laboratory tests.

    PatternClinical pictureLaboratory findings
    Vessel wallSmall haemorrhages (petechiae and purpura) in skin and mucous membranes, particularly the gingivae
    Occasionally joints, muscles, menorrhagia, nosebleeds, gastrointestinal bleeding, haematuria    		Platelet count, PT and PTT usually normal, pointing by exclusion to the vessel wall
    ThrombocytopeniaBleeding from small vessels into skin and the mucous membranes of the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts
    Intracranial bleeding is most feared    		Platelet count below 150,000 per µL
    PT and PTT normal when thrombocytopenia is isolated
    Coagulation factor deficiencyLarge post-traumatic ecchymoses or haematomas
    Prolonged bleeding from a laceration or after surgery
    Bleeding into the gastrointestinal and urinary tracts and weight-bearing joints (haemarthrosis)    		Prolonged PT and/or PTT
    Specific factor assays

    Tests used:

    • Prothrombin time (PT): assesses the extrinsic and common pathways
      Prolonged by deficiency or dysfunction of factor V, factor VII, factor X, prothrombin or fibrinogen.
    • Partial thromboplastin time (PTT): assesses the intrinsic and common pathways
      Prolonged by deficiency or dysfunction of factors V, VIII, IX, X, XI or XII, prothrombin or fibrinogen, or by interfering antiphospholipid antibodies.
    • Platelet count: reference range 150,000 to 350,000 per µL
      Confirm abnormal counts on a peripheral blood film, as clumping can cause spurious thrombocytopenia.
    • Tests of platelet function: platelet aggregation, and quantitative and qualitative tests of von Willebrand factor [platelet-adhesion glycoprotein that carries factor VIII].
    • Specific tests: levels of specific clotting factors, fibrinogen, fibrin split products and circulating anticoagulants.
    A9

    What are the causes of haemorrhagic disorders?

    A9Q19DU03M

    Also asked as: Causes of haemorrhagic disorders.

    1. Vessel wall abnormalities - Infections (meningococcaemia, other septicaemias, infective endocarditis, rickettsioses): microbial damage to the microvasculature (vasculitis) and disseminated intravascular coagulation. - Drug reactions: drug-induced immune complexes in vessel walls (hypersensitivity vasculitis). - Scurvy and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome [inherited collagen disorder with hyperextensible skin and joints]: collagen defects that weaken vessel walls. - Acquired vascular fragility in older adults. Cushing syndrome [glucocorticoid excess]. - Henoch-Schönlein purpura [IgA vasculitis]: immune complex deposition in vessels. - Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia: autosomal dominant
    Dilated, thin-walled vessels. - Perivascular amyloidosis, most common with AL amyloidosis. 2. Platelet deficiency or dysfunction - Decreased production: aplastic anaemia, leukaemia, certain drugs and alcohol, HIV, myelodysplastic neoplasm. - Decreased survival: immune (immune thrombocytopenic purpura, alloimmune, drug-induced) or nonimmune (DIC, thrombotic microangiopathies, mechanical injury from prosthetic heart valves). - Sequestration in an enlarged spleen. - Dilution after massive transfusion. - Platelet function defects from von Willebrand factor [platelet-adhesion glycoprotein that carries factor VIII] deficiency. 3. Derangement of coagulation - Inherited: haemophilia A, haemophilia B, von Willebrand disease [inherited bleeding disorder from deficient or defective von Willebrand factor]. - Acquired: vitamin K deficiency, severe parenchymal liver disease, DIC, and inhibitory autoantibodies.

    A9

    What do you mean by coagulation disorders?

    A9Q1DU08Ju

    Also asked as: What do you mean by coagulation disorder?

    Coagulation disorders are bleeding disorders caused by inherited or acquired deficiencies of coagulation factors. Deficiencies of virtually every coagulation factor have been reported as causes of abnormal bleeding.

    Bleeding commonly manifests as large post-traumatic ecchymoses or haematomas, or prolonged bleeding from a laceration or after a surgical procedure. Unlike bleeding with thrombocytopenia, it often occurs in the gastrointestinal and urinary tracts and in weight-bearing joints (haemarthrosis).

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 606
    A9

    Classify coagulation disorders.

    4A9Q1DU22NDU15JaDU11Ju
    TypeFeaturesExamples
    InheritedTypically affect a single clotting factorFactor VIII deficiency (haemophilia A)
    Factor IX deficiency (haemophilia B)
    Von Willebrand factor [platelet-adhesion glycoprotein that carries factor VIII] deficiency (von Willebrand disease [inherited bleeding disorder from deficient or defective von Willebrand factor])
    AcquiredUsually involve multiple factors, from decreased protein synthesis or a shortened protein half-lifeVitamin K deficiency (factors II, VII, IX, X and protein C)
    Severe parenchymal liver disease
    DIC, in which multiple factors are consumed
    Acquired, single factorRare
    Caused by inhibitory autoantibodies    		Autoantibody to a single clotting factor
    A9

    What is bleeding time?

    A9Q22

    Bleeding time is a test of platelet function in which a standardised incision is made and the time taken for the bleeding to stop is measured.

    • Ivy method [bleeding time using a blood-pressure cuff and a standard skin incision]: the most common
      a cuff on the arm is inflated to 40 mm of mercury, a standardised device makes a small cut on the inner forearm, and the blood is blotted every 2 minutes until bleeding stops.
    • Duke method [bleeding time from a lancet puncture of the earlobe or fingertip]: a lancet stab wound is made in a cleaned finger or earlobe, and timed in the same way.

    It is an older test, time-consuming and difficult to standardise, which has been discarded.

    A9

    What is clotting time?

    A9Q22

    Clotting time is the time taken for blood to clot in a glass tube, the clotting being triggered by contact with the glass surface. It reflects the integrity of the intrinsic clotting pathway.

    A9

    Normal limits of bleeding time and clotting time.

    A9Q22
    TestNormal limitConcerning (prolonged)
    Bleeding time, Duke method [bleeding time from a lancet puncture of the earlobe or fingertip]Under 3 minutesAbove 5 minutes
    Bleeding time, Ivy method [bleeding time using a blood-pressure cuff and a standard skin incision]Under 8 minutesAbove 10 minutes
    Clotting time (whole blood, glass tube)9 to 15 minutesAny defect in the intrinsic pathway prolongs it
    A9

    Tests / screening tests / investigations for bleeding (haemorrhagic) disorders.

    A9Q15, Q22, Q23
    1. Prothrombin time (PT): assesses the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways. Clotting of plasma after addition of tissue thromboplastin and calcium is measured in seconds. Prolonged by deficiency or dysfunction of factor V, factor VII, factor X, prothrombin or fibrinogen.
    2. Partial thromboplastin time (PTT): assesses the intrinsic and common pathways. Clotting of plasma after addition of kaolin, cephalin and calcium is measured in seconds. Prolonged by deficiency or dysfunction of factors V, VIII, IX, X, XI or XII, prothrombin or fibrinogen, or by interfering antiphospholipid antibodies.
    3. Platelet count: reference range 150,000 to 350,000 per µL, by an electronic particle counter. Confirm abnormal counts on a peripheral blood film, as clumping can cause spurious thrombocytopenia.
    4. Tests of platelet function: platelet aggregation tests, and quantitative and qualitative tests of von Willebrand factor [platelet-adhesion glycoprotein that carries factor VIII], including the ristocetin agglutination test.
    5. Specific tests: levels of specific clotting factors, fibrinogen, fibrin split products (particularly D-dimers) and circulating anticoagulants.
    6. Bleeding time: an older test, time-consuming and difficult to standardise, which has been discarded.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 602
    A9

    Two causes of raised prothrombin time.

    A9Q23
    1. Vitamin K deficiency: impairs the synthesis of factors II, VII, IX and X.
    2. Severe parenchymal liver disease: inadequate synthesis of coagulation factors.

    The prothrombin time is prolonged by deficiency or dysfunction of factor V, factor VII, factor X, prothrombin or fibrinogen.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 602p. 606
    A9

    Normal findings in ITP, haemophilia and DIC in haemorrhagic screening tests.

    A9Q24
    DisorderNormalAbnormal
    Immune thrombocytopenic purpuraPT and PTTLow platelet count (isolated thrombocytopenia)
    Haemophilia A and BPTPTT prolonged
    Disseminated intravascular coagulationNone statedConsumption of platelets, fibrin and coagulation factors, with fibrin degradation products from fibrinolysis
    A9

    What is von Willebrand factor?

    A9Q2

    Von Willebrand factor is a large protein that promotes the adhesion of platelets to subendothelial collagen and stabilises factor VIII.

    • It is made by endothelial cells and by megakaryocytes, which are the source of the vWF in platelet alpha-granules.
    • It is secreted as multimers containing as many as 100 subunits, which can exceed 20 million daltons in molecular mass.
    • Some of the secreted vWF is deposited in the subendothelial matrix, ready to promote platelet adhesion if the endothelial lining is disrupted.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 606p. 610
    A9

    Functions of von Willebrand factor.

    A9Q2
    1. Promotes adhesion of platelets to the subendothelial matrix: the most important haemostatic function
      Bridging interactions between platelet glycoprotein Ib/IX, vWF and matrix components such as collagen.
    2. Promotes platelet aggregation by binding to activated glycoprotein IIb/IIIa integrins, of particular importance under high shear stress, such as in small vessels.
    3. Carries and stabilises factor VIII in the circulation
      The half-life of factor VIII rises from about 2.4 hours to about 12 hours.
    4. Interacts with other proteins involved in haemostasis, including collagen and heparin.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 606
    A9

    Why are both bleeding time and clotting time prolonged in von Willebrand disease?

    A9Q18
    • Bleeding time (platelet function): vWF promotes the adhesion of platelets to the subendothelial matrix, so patients with von Willebrand disease [inherited bleeding disorder from deficient or defective von Willebrand factor] have defects in platelet function despite normal platelet counts. The level of active vWF, measured as ristocetin cofactor activity, is reduced.
    • Clotting time (intrinsic pathway): vWF stabilises factor VIII in the circulation, so a deficiency of vWF lowers factor VIII. Type 1 and type 3 disease are associated with a prolonged PTT.
    A9

    What is haemophilia?

    A9Q25

    Haemophilia A is the most common hereditary disease associated with life-threatening bleeding. It is caused by mutations in the gene encoding factor VIII, an essential cofactor for factor IX in the coagulation cascade, and is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait.

    Haemophilia B (Christmas disease [haemophilia B, factor IX deficiency]) is an X-linked disorder caused by mutations in coagulation factor IX. it is clinically identical to haemophilia A.

    A9

    Classify haemophilia.

    A9Q25
    TypeDeficient factorInheritance
    Haemophilia AFactor VIIIX-linked recessive
    Haemophilia B (Christmas disease [haemophilia B, factor IX deficiency])Factor IXX-linked recessive

    Haemophilia A is graded by the level of factor VIII activity:

    SeverityFactor VIII activity
    SevereLess than 1% of normal
    Moderately severe2% to 5% of normal
    Mild6% to 50% of normal
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 607p. 608
    A9

    Give the laboratory diagnosis/findings of hemophilia.

    12A9Q2, Q25DU26MDU24MDU22MDU19NovDU17JaDU16JaDU14JaDU11JaDU09JaDU08Ja

    Also asked as: Laboratory diagnosis of haemophilia.

    1. Prolonged PTT and normal PT, pointing to an abnormality of the intrinsic coagulation pathway.
    2. Haemophilia A: factor VIII-specific assays are required for diagnosis. Factor VIII function is measured by coagulation assays with mixtures of patient plasma and factor VIII-deficient plasma.
    3. In severe haemophilia A from point mutations that impair function, factor VIII protein levels may be normal by immunoassay.
    4. Haemophilia B: diagnosis is made by assay of factor IX levels
      in about 15% of patients factor IX protein is present but nonfunctional.
    5. About 15% of patients with severe haemophilia A develop antibodies that bind and inhibit factor VIII after treatment with recombinant factor VIII.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 606p. 608
    A9

    What do you mean by DIC?

    A9Q3

    Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is an acute, subacute or chronic thrombohaemorrhagic disorder characterised by excessive activation of coagulation factors and the formation of thrombi in the microvasculature. It occurs as a secondary complication of many disorders.

    The thrombotic diathesis leads to the consumption of platelets, fibrin and coagulation factors and, secondarily, activation of fibrinolysis.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 608
    A9

    Give the laboratory diagnosis of DIC.

    A9Q3DU24N

    Also asked as: Laboratory diagnosis of DIC.

    Diagnosis is based on clinical observation and laboratory studies:

    1. Fibrinogen level, platelet count, PT and PTT: reflect the consumption of fibrinogen, platelets and clotting factors.
    2. Fibrin degradation products, particularly D-dimers: produced when plasmin cleaves fibrin during fibrinolysis.
    3. Peripheral blood film: fragmented red cells, from microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia.
    A9

    Write a short note on ITP.

    4A9Q17DU13JaDU09JaDU08Ja

    Also asked as: What do you mean by ITP?

    Definition

    Chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura is caused by autoantibody-mediated destruction of platelets. It is secondary when it occurs with predisposing conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus, HIV infection and B-cell neoplasms like chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, and primary (idiopathic) when no risk factor is known. Primary ITP is diagnosed only after secondary causes are excluded.

    Aetiology and pathogenesis

    • Autoantibodies, most often against platelet membrane glycoproteins IIb/IIIa or Ib/IX, are found in the plasma and bound to platelets in about 80% of patients
      Most are IgG.
    • The antibodies act as opsonins, recognised by IgG Fc receptors on phagocytes, so platelets are destroyed. The spleen is the major site, and splenectomy markedly improves the thrombocytopenia.
    • Autoantibodies may also damage megakaryocytes, decreasing platelet production.

    Morphology

    • Spleen of normal size, with congested sinusoids, enlarged follicles with prominent reactive germinal centres, and scattered megakaryocytes in the sinuses.
    • Marrow: modestly increased megakaryocytes, some immature with large, nonlobulated single nuclei.
    • Blood: unusually large platelets (megathrombocytes).
    • Petechial bleeds into skin and mucous membranes.

    Clinical features and complications

    • Most common in adult females younger than 40 years
      Female to male ratio 3 to 1
      Insidious onset.
    • Bleeding into skin and mucosal surfaces: petechiae in dependent areas, ecchymoses, easy bruising, nosebleeds, gingival bleeding, soft tissue haemorrhage, melaena, haematuria and excessive menstrual flow.
    • Subarachnoid and intracerebral haemorrhage are serious and sometimes fatal but rare in treated patients.
    • No splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy in primary disease.
    • Laboratory: low platelet count, normal or increased megakaryocytes, large platelets, normal PT and PTT.
    • Treatment: glucocorticoids, splenectomy (normalises the count in about two-thirds), intravenous immunoglobulin, rituximab and thrombopoietin mimetics.
    • Acute ITP is mainly a childhood disease, appearing abruptly 1 to 2 weeks after a viral illness and usually resolving spontaneously within 6 months.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 604
    A9

    How are platelets destroyed in peripheral blood in ITP?

    A9Q16
    • Autoantibodies, most often against platelet membrane glycoproteins IIb/IIIa or Ib/IX, are bound to the platelet surface. in most cases they are of the IgG class.
    • As in autoimmune haemolytic anaemias, the antiplatelet antibodies act as opsonins, recognised by IgG Fc receptors expressed on phagocytes, leading to increased platelet destruction.
    • The spleen is the major site of removal of opsonised platelets, as shown by the marked improvement in thrombocytopenia after splenectomy.
    • The splenic red pulp is also rich in plasma cells, a source of autoantibodies.
    • The autoantibodies may also bind to and damage megakaryocytes, decreasing platelet production.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 604
    A9

    How is ITP diagnosed in the laboratory?

    14A9Q17DU24MDU22MDU20NDU20JuDU18MDU17NovDU16JuDU15JaDU14JaDU12JaDU11JaDU09JuDU07Ju

    Also asked as: How will you diagnose a case of ITP in the laboratory?

    1. Platelet count low, with normal or increased megakaryocytes in the bone marrow and large platelets (megathrombocytes) in the peripheral blood. These are presumptive evidence of accelerated platelet destruction.
    2. PT and PTT normal.
    3. Bone marrow examination is done to rule out thrombocytopenia due to marrow failure or other primary marrow disorders.
    4. Tests for platelet autoantibodies have low sensitivity and specificity and are not clinically useful.
    5. The diagnosis is one of exclusion: it is made only after other causes of thrombocytopenia have been ruled out, including secondary causes such as systemic lupus erythematosus, HIV infection and B-cell neoplasms.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 604
    A9

    What are the causes of thrombocytopenia?

    5A9Q19, Q20DU26MDU25MDU11Ja

    Also asked as: Causes of thrombocytopenia (incl. 3 important causes).

    A platelet count below 150,000 per µL is thrombocytopenia. The causes fall into four categories.

    1. Decreased platelet production - Conditions that depress marrow output generally: aplastic anaemia, leukaemia, disseminated cancer, granulomatous disease, megaloblastic anaemia from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. - Conditions that affect megakaryocytes selectively: drugs (thiazides, cytotoxic drugs) and alcohol. Infections such as measles and HIV
    Myelodysplastic neoplasm, which occasionally presents with isolated thrombocytopenia. 2. Decreased platelet survival - Immunologic: autoimmune (immune thrombocytopenic purpura, systemic lupus erythematosus, B-cell lymphoid neoplasms). Alloimmune (post-transfusion and neonatal)
    drug-associated (quinidine, heparin, sulfa compounds). Infections (HIV, infectious mononucleosis, dengue fever). - Nonimmunologic: disseminated intravascular coagulation and the thrombotic microangiopathies, in which platelet consumption reduces life span. Mechanical injury, as with prosthetic heart valves. 3. Sequestration: the spleen normally sequesters 30% to 35% of the body's platelets, which can rise to 80% to 90% when the spleen is enlarged. 4. Dilution: massive transfusions.
