    What are the causes of gum bleeding?

    DU23N
    1. Vessel wall abnormalities: small haemorrhages in the skin or mucous membranes, particularly the gingivae. Causes include infections (meningococcaemia, septicaemia, infective endocarditis), drug reactions, scurvy, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome [inherited collagen disorder with hyperextensible skin and joints], Henoch-Schönlein purpura [IgA vasculitis], hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia and perivascular amyloidosis.
    2. Chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura: easy bruising, nosebleeds and gingival bleeding from minor trauma.
    3. Thrombocytopenia: spontaneous bleeding from small vessels, in the skin and mucous membranes.
    4. Coagulation factor deficiencies: prolonged bleeding after a tooth extraction.

    Platelet disorders and ITP

    Define thrombocytopenia.

    DU26MDU25M

    Reduction in platelet number is called thrombocytopenia. A count less than 150,000 platelets per µL is generally considered to constitute thrombocytopenia.

    Discuss in short the pathogenesis of ITP.

    DU24M

    Chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura is caused by autoantibody-mediated destruction of platelets.

    1. Autoantibodies, most often against platelet membrane glycoproteins IIb/IIIa or Ib/IX, are found in the plasma and bound to platelets in about 80% of patients.
    2. They are mostly of the IgG class.
    3. As in autoimmune haemolytic anaemias, the antibodies act as opsonins, recognised by IgG Fc receptors on phagocytes, which leads to increased platelet destruction.
    4. The spleen is the major site of removal of opsonised platelets, so splenectomy markedly improves the thrombocytopenia.
    5. The splenic red pulp is rich in plasma cells, so splenectomy may also remove a source of autoantibodies.
    6. The autoantibodies may also bind and damage megakaryocytes, which decreases platelet production.

    Chronic ITP may be secondary (systemic lupus erythematosus, HIV infection, B-cell neoplasms such as chronic lymphocytic leukaemia) or primary (idiopathic). In acute ITP the autoantibodies appear 1 to 2 weeks after a self-limited viral illness, by uncertain mechanisms.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 604

    Give the blood and bone marrow picture of ITP.

    DU25MDU19MDU18Nov

    Blood - Low platelet count (isolated thrombocytopenia). - Unusually large platelets (megathrombocytes), a sign of accelerated thrombopoiesis. - PT and PTT normal.

    Bone marrow - Modestly increased number of megakaryocytes
    Some are immature, with large nonlobulated single nuclei. - These findings reflect accelerated thrombopoiesis and are not specific. - Marrow examination is important to rule out thrombocytopenia due to marrow failure or other primary marrow disorders.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 604

    A child has purpuric rash/gum bleeding, thrombocytopenia, normocellular marrow with active megakaryopoiesis. What is the likely diagnosis?

    4DU20NDU20JuDU18MDU09Ju

    Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). - Purpura and gingival bleeding point to bleeding from a low platelet count. - A low platelet count with normal or increased megakaryocytes in the marrow is taken as presumptive evidence of accelerated platelet destruction. - Acute ITP is mainly a disease of childhood, with abrupt onset, often 1 to 2 weeks after a viral illness, and it is self-limited, usually resolving within 6 months. - Diagnosis is one of exclusion, after other causes of thrombocytopenia are ruled out.

    Coagulation disorders and haemophilia

    Why is APTT prolonged in hemophilia?

    DU23N
    • Haemophilia A is caused by mutations in the gene for factor VIII, an essential cofactor for factor IX in the coagulation cascade.
    • The factor VIIIa and factor IXa complex has the preeminent role in activation of factor X.
    • Factor VIII deficiency therefore causes an abnormality of the intrinsic coagulation pathway.
    • The PTT assesses the intrinsic and common pathways, so it is prolonged
      The PT, which assesses the extrinsic and common pathways, is normal.

    Write a short note on von Willebrand disease.

    DU10Ju

    Definition. Autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in von Willebrand factor [platelet-adhesion glycoprotein that carries factor VIII] (vWF), a large protein that promotes the adhesion of platelets to subendothelial collagen and stabilises factor VIII.

    Factor VIII and vWF - Factor VIII is a cofactor of factor IX
    vWF is made by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes. - vWF binds and stabilises factor VIII, raising its half-life from about 2.4 hours to about 12 hours. - vWF promotes platelet adhesion to the subendothelial matrix, by bridging platelet glycoprotein Ib/IX and collagen.

    Types 1. Type 1: autosomal dominant
    Mild to moderate quantitative deficiency of vWF
    About 70% of cases
    Incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity
    Generally mild. 2. Type 2: autosomal dominant
    Qualitative defect with missense mutations that cause defective multimer assembly, so large and intermediate multimers are missing. 25% of cases
    Type 2A is commonest
    Mild to moderate bleeding. 3. Type 3: autosomal recessive
    Deletions or frameshift mutations of both alleles, with little or no vWF. Factor VIII is also reduced
    Severe bleeding.

    Clinical and laboratory features - Mild to moderate bleeding disorder resembling that of thrombocytopenia. - Defective platelet function with a normal platelet count. - Reduced ristocetin cofactor activity. - Prolonged PTT in types 1 and 3.

    Treatment. Desmopressin, which stimulates vWF release, or plasma concentrates containing factor VIII and vWF, or recombinant vWF, for types 1 and 2. Prophylactic plasma concentrates for type 3.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 606p. 607p. 610

    Write a short note on hemophilia (A) / its characteristic features.

    5DU24NDU22NDU12JuDU10JaDU07Ja

    Definition and aetiology - The most common hereditary disease associated with life-threatening bleeding. - Caused by mutations in the gene encoding factor VIII, an essential cofactor for factor IX. - Inherited as an X-linked recessive trait
    Affects mainly males and homozygous females. - About 30% of patients have no family history and have new mutations.

    Severity, by factor VIII activity - Less than 1% of normal: severe. - 2% to 5%: moderately severe. - 6% to 50%: mild. - The most severe deficiencies result from an inversion involving the X chromosome that abolishes synthesis of factor VIII.

    Clinical features - Easy bruising and massive haemorrhage after trauma or surgery. - Spontaneous haemorrhage into joints (haemarthroses) and other regions susceptible to trauma
    Recurrent bleeding causes progressive disabling deformities. - Petechiae are characteristically absent.

    Laboratory - Prolonged PTT and normal PT. - Factor VIII-specific assays are required for diagnosis.

    Treatment - Recombinant factor VIII, or a bispecific antibody linking factor IXa and factor Xa. - About 15% of patients with severe disease develop antibodies that inhibit factor VIII.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 607p. 608

    Why is hemophilia called an X-linked recessive disorder?

    DU19Nov
    • Haemophilia A is caused by mutations in the gene encoding factor VIII, which is carried on the X chromosome.
    • It is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait.
    • It therefore affects mainly males and homozygous females.
    • Rarely, heterozygous females bleed excessively, presumably because the X chromosome bearing the normal factor VIII allele is inactivated by chance in most cells (unfavourable lyonisation).
    • About 30% of patients have no family history
      The disease is caused by new mutations.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 607

    A boy has hemarthrosis after a small fall
    Maternal uncle bled after tooth extraction. What is your provisional diagnosis?

    5DU26MDU24MDU22MDU17JaDU14Ja

    Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency), an X-linked recessive disorder.

    • Haemarthrosis after minor stress to a joint and prolonged bleeding after a tooth extraction are typical of bleeding due to coagulation factor deficiency.
    • The affected maternal uncle fits X-linked recessive inheritance, which affects mainly males.
    • Haemophilia B (factor IX deficiency) is clinically indistinguishable, so factor VIII and factor IX assays are needed to confirm.
    • PTT is prolonged and PT is normal.

    Same: what type of disease is it?

    DU26M
    • An inherited bleeding disorder due to deficiency of a coagulation factor, factor VIII in haemophilia A.
    • X-linked recessive: it affects mainly males and homozygous females.

    Disseminated intravascular coagulation

    Describe the pathogenesis of DIC.

    DU25NDU18MDU09Ju

    DIC is not a primary disease but an acquired coagulopathy that occurs in the course of many clinical conditions. It results from pathological activation of coagulation or impairment of clot-inhibiting mechanisms.

    Two major triggers 1. Release of tissue factor or other procoagulants into the circulation. - Sources: placenta in obstetric complications. Tissues injured by trauma or burns. - Mucus from certain adenocarcinomas can activate factor X directly. 2. Widespread endothelial injury. - Endothelial cell necrosis exposes the subendothelial matrix, which activates platelets and the coagulation pathway. - TNF in sepsis makes endothelial cells express tissue factor and reduces thrombomodulin, and increases adhesion molecules, so leucocytes release reactive oxygen species and proteases. - Other causes: antigen-antibody complexes (systemic lupus erythematosus), temperature extremes (heat stroke, burns), and microorganisms (meningococci, rickettsiae).

    Associated conditions. Obstetric complications, malignant neoplasms, sepsis and major trauma. Among cancers, acute promyelocytic leukaemia and adenocarcinomas of the lung, pancreas, colon and stomach.

    Consequences 1. Widespread deposition of fibrin in the microcirculation, causing ischaemia of organs and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. 2. Consumption of platelets and clotting factors and activation of plasminogen, causing a haemorrhagic diathesis.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 608p. 609

    Explain why bleeding occurs in DIC.

    DU09Ja
    1. The thrombotic diathesis consumes platelets, fibrin and coagulation factors.
    2. Fibrinolysis is activated: plasmin cleaves fibrin and also digests factors V and VIII, reducing their concentration further.
    3. Fibrin degradation products inhibit platelet aggregation, fibrin polymerisation and thrombin.
    4. This depletion of the factors required for haemostasis, with activated fibrinolysis, causes bleeding.

    Acute DIC, for example with obstetric complications or major trauma, is dominated by a bleeding diathesis.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 608p. 609

    Blood Groups, Transfusion and Anticoagulants

    A9

    Classify blood groups.

    A9Q4

    Blood groups are classified by the red cell antigens that define them. The two systems of main clinical importance are:

    SystemGroupsBasis
    ABOA, B, AB and OPresence of antigen A, antigen B, both, or neither on the red cells
    RhRh positive and Rh negativePresence or absence of the D antigen on the red cells

    Other red cell antigens, such as Kell [red cell blood group system] and Kidd [red cell blood group system], can cause delayed haemolytic transfusion reactions.

    A9

    Name the ABO and Rh blood groups with their agglutinins.

    A9Q4
    Blood groupAntigen on red cellsAgglutinin (antibody) in serum
    AAAnti-B
    BBAnti-A
    ABA and BNeither anti-A nor anti-B
    ONeither A nor BAnti-A and anti-B
    Rh positiveD antigen presentNo naturally occurring anti-D
    Rh negativeD antigen absentAnti-D formed only after exposure to D-positive red cells, by transfusion or foetal red cells in pregnancy

    The anti-A and anti-B antibodies occur naturally, mainly IgM and IgG. anti-D is an immune antibody, mainly IgG.

    A9

    What do you mean by cross matching?

    A9Q5

    Cross matching is the final check that a specific donor unit is compatible with a specific recipient. It tests ABO compatibility and whether the recipient has an unexpected antibody that reacts with donor red cells.

    A9

    How is cross matching performed?

    A9Q5

    1. Major crossmatch (standard test): donor red cells are mixed with recipient serum or plasma. 2. Immediate spin phase: donor red cells in saline are added to the patient serum, mixed and centrifuged for 15 to 30 seconds. Agglutination or haemolysis is read (detects ABO incompatibility only
    Misses most IgG antibodies such as anti-D, anti-K, anti-Jka, anti-Fya). 3. 37°C incubation phase: donor red cells in a potentiating agent are added to the patient serum and incubated at 37°C. 4. Antiglobulin phase: the cells are washed, antihuman globulin (Coombs [antiglobulin test for antibody-coated red cells] reagent) is added, the mixture is centrifuged for 15 to 30 seconds and read for agglutination. Agglutination means patient IgG is bound to the donor antigen. 5. Minor crossmatch: donor plasma with recipient cells. Largely obsolete for packed red cells because little donor plasma remains. 6. Electronic crossmatch is allowed only if all four conditions are met: - Two ABO determinations, one on the current specimen - Current antibody screen negative - No history of a clinically significant unexpected antibody - A validated on-site computer system that blocks release of ABO-incompatible units 7. Specimen is collected within 3 days of transfusion, or within the last 3 months if the patient is pregnant.

    A9

    Why is cross matching essential for blood transfusion?

    A9Q7DU08Ja
    • Confirms serologically that the donor unit is ABO compatible with the recipient.
    • Detects unexpected red cell antibodies in the recipient that react with the donor cells.
    • Prevents acute haemolytic reaction, caused by preformed IgM antibodies against donor red cells that fix complement. it usually results from an ABO-incompatible unit given through an error in patient identification or tube labelling.
    • The immediate spin detects ABO incompatibility only. The antiglobulin phase is needed to detect IgG antibodies.
    A9

    Mention 4 important hematological changes of stored blood.

    A9Q6DU08Ja

    Also asked as: Important haematological changes of stored blood.

    1. Fall in pH: lactate accumulates
      pH falls from 7.2 on day 0 to 6.54 on day 35 (CPDA-1 blood).
    2. Rise in plasma potassium: about eight-fold rise
      4.33 mmol/L on day 0 to 33.05 mmol/L on day 35 (CPDA-1 blood).
    3. Depletion of 2,3-DPG: falls to zero in about 2 weeks
      The oxygen dissociation curve shifts to the left
      it is regenerated within 24 hours of transfusion.
    4. Fall in ATP: rises over days 1 to 7, then falls from day 7 onwards.
    5. Increased haemolysis: 0.09% on day 0 to 0.68% on day 35 (CPDA-1 blood)
      Plasma haemoglobin increases and sodium decreases.
    6. Loss of platelets and labile factors: platelets lose viability and function very quickly. Factor VIII deteriorates rapidly, especially after the first 24 hours. Factor V is labile.
    7. At expiry, at least 75% of transfused red cells must remain in circulation 24 hours after transfusion.

    Screening tests for safe blood transfusion / diseases for which blood must be screened.

    A9Q8, Q9
    1. HIV-1 and HIV-2: anti-HIV-1/2 immunoassay, or preferably a combined p24 antigen and antibody immunoassay.
    2. Hepatitis B: HBsAg immunoassay.
    3. Hepatitis C: anti-HCV immunoassay, or preferably a combined antigen and antibody assay.
    4. Syphilis: treponemal antibody test (TPHA or EIA).
    5. Malaria: thick film or antigen EIA in endemic areas (selective).
    6. Chagas disease [Trypanosoma cruzi infection], HTLV-I/II and CMV: antibody tests where indicated (selective).
    7. ABO and RhD grouping is done on all donations
      Only units non-reactive on all tests are released.
    A9

    Contraindications of blood transfusion.

    A9Q9
    • Absolute: patient refusal, such as religious objection.
    • Transfusion should be avoided in a stable patient with haemoglobin 7 to 8 g/dL, who is not expected to benefit.
    • Iron deficiency without haemodynamic instability calls for iron therapy first.
    • Plasma is not given for a mildly raised INR (below 1.8) or routine non-emergent warfarin reversal. Vitamin K is preferred.
    • Severe IgA deficiency needs washed cells or platelets, or plasma from IgA-deficient donors.
    • Patients at risk of circulatory overload need slow infusion of red cells with prophylactic diuretics.
    • Post-transfusion purpura: avoid further platelet or red cell transfusion.
    A9

    Mention the diseases transmitted by blood transfusion.

    A9Q10DU18MDU17Ja

    Also asked as: Diseases that can be transmitted by blood transfusion.

    1. Viruses: HIV, hepatitis C and hepatitis B
      Estimated rates are 1 in 1.5 million, 1 in 1.2 million and 1 in 1 million units respectively. Also West Nile virus, HTLV-I/II and CMV.
    2. Bacteria: mostly skin flora contaminating the unit at collection. Symptomatic contamination is much more common with platelets (as high as 1 in 5000) than with red cells, because platelets are stored at room temperature.
    3. Syphilis
    4. Protozoa: malaria, Chagas disease [Trypanosoma cruzi infection] (trypanosomes) and babesia.
    5. Emerging agents: variant CJD, dengue, chikungunya.

    Write a short note on Rh-incompatibility.

    5A9Q11DU13JuDU11JuDU04JaDU03Ja

    Also asked as: What is Rh incompatibility?

    Definition. Immune hydrops is a haemolytic disease caused by blood group antigen incompatibility between mother and foetus. it occurs in second and subsequent pregnancies of an Rh-negative mother with an Rh-positive father.

    Aetiology and pathogenesis - The foetus inherits red cell antigens from the father that are foreign to the mother. - Foetal red cells reach the maternal circulation in the last trimester or during childbirth, and the mother becomes sensitised. - The first exposure evokes IgM antibodies, which do not cross the placenta. so Rh disease is uncommon in the first pregnancy. - Exposure in a later pregnancy gives a brisk IgG response. The antibodies cross the placenta and lyse foetal red cells. - Of the Rh antigens, only the D antigen is a major cause. - Haemolytic disease develops only after a significant transplacental bleed (more than 1 mL of Rh-positive foetal red cells). - Concurrent ABO incompatibility protects the mother, because foetal red cells are promptly coated and removed by anti-A or anti-B IgM antibodies.

    Morphology - Foetus and placenta are pale
    Liver and spleen are enlarged. - Bone marrow shows compensatory hyperplasia of erythroid precursors, and extramedullary haematopoiesis is present in liver, spleen and lymph nodes. - Many immature red cells (reticulocytes and erythroblasts) circulate, called erythroblastosis fetalis. - Kernicterus: brain is enlarged, oedematous and bright yellow from bilirubin, especially in the basal ganglia, thalamus, cerebellum, cerebral grey matter and spinal cord. Usually needs bilirubin above 20 mg/dL in term infants.

    Clinical features and complications - Anaemia, with hypoxic injury to the heart and liver. Cardiac failure and fall in plasma proteins lead to generalised oedema and anasarca (hydrops fetalis). - Unconjugated bilirubin passes through the infant's poorly developed blood-brain barrier and causes jaundice and kernicterus. - Mild cases show pallor, with hepatosplenomegaly. Severe cases show intense jaundice, generalised oedema and neurological injury. - Infants may be stillborn, die in the first days, or recover completely. - Treatment: phototherapy, exchange transfusion. Foetal intravascular transfusion and early delivery in severe intrauterine haemolysis. - Prevention: Rhesus immune globulin (anti-D) to Rh-negative mothers at 28 weeks and within 72 hours of delivery, and after abortions.

    A9

    Complications of mismatched blood transfusion.

    A9Q12
    • Cause: preformed IgM antibodies against donor red cells fix complement. Most commonly an ABO-incompatible unit given through an error in patient identification or tube labelling.
    • Intravascular haemolysis and haemoglobinuria.
    • Fever, shaking chills and flank pain appear rapidly. Direct Coombs test [antiglobulin test for antibody-coated red cells] is typically positive.
    • Signs and symptoms are due to complement activation rather than intravascular haemolysis itself.
    • Free haemoglobin causes acute kidney injury with reduced urine output.
    • DIC, with diffuse bleeding.
    • Shock and acute renal failure.
    • Death in severe cases.
    A9

    What is an anticoagulant?

    A9Q13

    An anticoagulant is a chemical substance that prevents blood from clotting. In the laboratory it is added to blood in a fixed proportion and used only in vitro.

    A9

    Enumerate anticoagulants used in the laboratory.

    A9Q13
    1. EDTA (purple cap): chelates calcium.
    2. Trisodium citrate (light blue cap): binds calcium reversibly.
    3. Heparin (green cap): binds antithrombin, which inactivates thrombin and other clotting factors.
    4. Oxalates: double oxalate (potassium and ammonium oxalate in the ratio 2 to 3, at 2 mg/mL) or potassium oxalate. Precipitate calcium as insoluble calcium oxalate.
    5. Sodium fluoride: used with oxalate for glucose estimation.
    6. ACD, CPD and CPDA-1: used for blood storage.

    Write a short note on mismatched blood transfusion (adverse effects).

    DU21MDU19NovDU18Nov

    Cause. An error in patient identification or tube labelling that allows a patient to receive an ABO-incompatible unit of blood.

    Pathogenesis - Preformed high-affinity natural IgM antibodies, usually against the polysaccharide blood group antigens A or B, bind the donor red cells. - They fix complement and rapidly induce complement-mediated lysis, intravascular haemolysis and haemoglobinuria. - The signs and symptoms are due to complement activation rather than intravascular haemolysis itself.

    Adverse effects 1. Fever, shaking chills and flank pain, appearing rapidly. 2. Haemoglobinuria. 3. The direct Coombs test [antiglobulin test for antibody-coated red cells] is typically positive, unless all the donor red cells have lysed. 4. In severe cases the process rapidly progresses to DIC, shock, acute renal failure and occasionally death.

    Delayed haemolytic reactions - Caused by IgG antibodies to red cell antigens to which the recipient was sensitised earlier, for example by a prior transfusion. - Extravascular haemolysis, with a positive direct Coombs test, low haptoglobin and raised lactate dehydrogenase. - Antibodies to Rh, Kell [red cell blood group system] and Kidd [red cell blood group system] antigens may cause severe and potentially fatal reactions.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 610

    Name the immediate blood transfusion reactions.

    DU14Ja
    1. Febrile nonhaemolytic reaction: fever and chills, sometimes with mild dyspnoea, within 6 hours.
    2. Allergic reactions: urticarial, or severe in IgA-deficient recipients.
    3. Acute haemolytic reaction: fever, shaking chills and flank pain.
    4. Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI): sudden respiratory failure during or soon after transfusion.
    5. Bacterial infection: fever, chills and hypotension.
    6. Circulatory overload: respiratory distress or hypertension within 12 hours.

    What is hemolytic transfusion reaction?

    DU07Ju
    • Acute haemolytic reaction: preformed IgM antibodies against donor red cells fix complement. Usually after an ABO-incompatible unit is given through an error in patient identification or labelling. Intravascular haemolysis, haemoglobinuria, fever, shaking chills and flank pain.
    • Delayed haemolytic reaction: IgG antibodies against red cell antigens to which the recipient was sensitised previously. Extravascular haemolysis with a positive direct Coombs test [antiglobulin test for antibody-coated red cells], low haptoglobin and raised lactate dehydrogenase.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 610

    Write a short note on preservation of blood.

    DU10Ju

    Collection - About 450 mL of blood is collected into a bag containing 63 mL of anticoagulant-preservative solution, usually citrate phosphate dextrose adenine (CPDA-1). - Citrate chelates calcium and prevents clotting. - Phosphate maintains the pH and the 2,3-DPG level. - Dextrose is the energy source for red cell metabolism. - Adenine is the substrate for ATP synthesis, and extends the shelf life.

    Storage - Whole blood and red cells are kept at 1°C to 6°C. - Shelf life is 21 days in ACD and CPD, 35 days in CPDA-1 and 42 days with additive solutions. - Platelet concentrates are kept at 20°C to 24°C with constant agitation, for 5 days. - Fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate are kept at or below minus 18°C, for 12 months and 1 year.

    Changes during storage (storage lesion) 1. Fall in pH. 2. Rise in plasma potassium. 3. Depletion of 2,3-DPG, which shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the left. it is regenerated within 24 hours of transfusion. 4. Fall in ATP after day 7. 5. Increased haemolysis. 6. Loss of platelets and of the labile factors V and VIII. 7. At expiry, at least 75% of transfused red cells must remain in circulation 24 hours after transfusion.

    Inhibits platelet clumping
    Suits PCR
    Trisodium citrateBinding of calcium is reversible, so factors V and VIII are preserved
    HeparinDoes not alter red cell size
    Reduces lysis
    Double oxalateUsed for chemistry tests, PCV, ESR and total leucocyte count
    Sodium fluoridePreserves glucose

    For blood bags

    SolutionAdvantages
    ACD (acid citrate dextrose)Citrate prevents clotting
    Dextrose supplies energy
    Storage for 21 days
    CPD (citrate phosphate dextrose)Phosphate maintains pH and 2,3-DPG
    Storage for 21 days
    CPDA-1Adenine supports ATP synthesis
    Storage for 35 days
    Additive solutionsRed cells stored for 42 days

    Clinical Scenarios

    A10

    DIC picture after delivery or induced abortion — Probable diagnosis? Tests / laboratory investigations to establish it (with results)?

    A10Q1, Q14, Q22

    Probable diagnosis: disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), an acquired coagulopathy and not a primary disease. Obstetric conditions are among the commonest triggers
    Procoagulants derived from the placenta, dead retained foetus or amniotic fluid enter the circulation.

    Investigations

    Diagnosis is based on clinical observation and laboratory studies:

    TestResult
    Platelet countReduced, from consumption of platelets
    FibrinogenReduced, from consumption of fibrin and clotting factors
    Prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time (PTT)Prolonged, from depletion of clotting factors
    Plasmin also digests factors V and VIII
    Fibrin degradation products, particularly D-dimersRaised, from activation of fibrinolysis
    Peripheral blood filmFragmented red cells of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia
    A10

    Child with severe anaemia, mongoloid facies, splenomegaly/hepatosplenomegaly ± jaundice, short stature, microcytic hypochromic picture with target cells/normoblasts/fragmented cells — Probable / provisional diagnosis? How will you confirm it?

    4A10Q3, Q6, Q17, Q21

    Probable diagnosis: β-thalassaemia major.

    Basis

    • Anaemia manifests 6 to 9 months after birth as haemoglobin synthesis switches from HbF to HbA. Untransfused haemoglobin is 3 to 6 g/dL.
    • Marrow expansion in facial bones and skull gives the facial change.
    • Hepatosplenomegaly from phagocyte hyperplasia and extramedullary haematopoiesis. The spleen may weigh up to 1500 g.
    • Growth retardation in untreated children.

    Confirmation

    1. Blood smear: anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, microcytosis and hypochromia. Target cells, basophilic stippling and fragmented red cells. Nucleated red cell precursors (normoblasts).
    2. Reticulocyte count: raised, but lower than expected for the severity of the anaemia, because of ineffective erythropoiesis.
    3. Haemoglobin analysis: HbA absent (β0/β0) or present in small amounts (β+/β+ or β0/β+). HbF is the major haemoglobin and is markedly elevated.
    4. Marrow: striking expansion of haematopoietically active marrow. "crewcut" appearance of the skull on X-ray.
    5. Iron studies: to separate from iron deficiency
      Iron overload (haemosiderosis) occurs in transfused patients.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 585
    A10

    9-year-old / 7-year-old girl with sudden purpuric rash, thrombocytopenia, normocellular marrow with active megakaryopoiesis — Likely diagnosis? Further investigations for confirmation?

    A10Q5, Q18, Q24

    Likely diagnosis: acute immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

    Basis

    • Acute ITP is mainly a disease of childhood.
    • Symptoms appear abruptly, often 1 to 2 weeks after a self-limited viral illness.
    • It is caused by autoantibodies to platelets.
    • It is self-limited, usually resolving within 6 months.

    Further investigations

    1. Platelet count: low, with large platelets (megathrombocytes) in the peripheral blood.
    2. Coagulation tests: PT and PTT normal.
    3. Bone marrow: normal or increased megakaryocytes, some immature. Its importance is to rule out marrow failure or other primary marrow disorders.
    4. Exclusion of secondary causes: systemic lupus erythematosus, HIV infection and B-cell neoplasms.
    5. Tests for platelet autoantibodies have low sensitivity and specificity and are not clinically useful.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 604
    A10

    10-year-old boy with history of gum bleeding — Probable causes?

    A10Q24

    Excessive bleeding can result from increased fragility of vessels, platelet deficiency or dysfunction, or derangement of coagulation.

    1. Vessel wall abnormalities: small haemorrhages, particularly of the gingivae
      Platelet count, PT and PTT normal. Examples are scurvy and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome [collagen defects].
    2. Thrombocytopenia: immune thrombocytopenic purpura (gingival bleeding and easy bruising). Aplastic anaemia
      Marrow replacement by leukaemia.
    3. Defective platelet function: von Willebrand disease [inherited bleeding disorder from deficient or defective von Willebrand factor]
      Inherited disorders of platelet function.
    4. Clotting factor deficiency: haemophilia A and B.
    5. Acute leukaemia: mucosal haemorrhages into the gingivae
      Monocytic leukaemias infiltrate the gingiva.
    6. Disseminated intravascular coagulation.
    A10

    Boy with haemarthrosis, family history through maternal uncle (or excessive bleeding after tooth extraction / spontaneous bleeding) — Provisional diagnosis? How to confirm / which test helps?

    A10Q8, Q16, Q23

    Provisional diagnosis: haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency).

    Basis

    • X-linked recessive trait, affecting mainly males
      Transmitted through carrier females, hence the affected maternal uncle.
    • Easy bruising and massive haemorrhage after trauma or surgery.
    • "Spontaneous" haemorrhages in regions susceptible to trauma, particularly the joints (haemarthroses). Recurrent bleeding leads to progressive disabling deformities.
    • Petechiae are characteristically absent.

    Confirmation

    1. PTT: prolonged.
    2. PT: normal, pointing to an abnormality of the intrinsic pathway.
    3. Factor VIII assay: required for diagnosis. Severity: less than 1% of normal is severe, 2% to 5% moderately severe, 6% to 50% mild.
    4. Factor IX assay, to exclude haemophilia B (Christmas disease [haemophilia B, factor IX deficiency]), which is clinically indistinguishable and also shows prolonged PTT and normal PT.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 14)p. 608
    A10

    25-year-old woman, 7 months pregnant, with anaemia — Probable causes? How will you confirm the case?

    A10Q10

    Probable causes

    1. Iron deficiency anaemia: increased requirement in pregnancy
      The commonest cause.
    2. Folate deficiency (megaloblastic anaemia): increased requirement in pregnancy from increased DNA synthesis.
    3. Vitamin B12 deficiency: relative deficiency from increased demand in pregnancy.

    Confirmation of iron deficiency

    1. Haemoglobin and haematocrit depressed, with hypochromia, microcytosis and modest poikilocytosis. Pencil cells.
    2. Serum iron and ferritin low.
    3. Total iron-binding capacity high.
    4. Transferrin saturation below 15%.
    5. Absent stainable iron in marrow macrophages, on Prussian blue stain of marrow aspirate.
    6. Reticulocyte rise in 5 to 7 days after oral iron.

    Confirmation of folate deficiency

    1. Macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils and low reticulocyte count on the blood film.
    2. Decreased serum or red cell folate.
    3. Raised serum homocysteine
      Methylmalonate normal.
    4. Vitamin B12 deficiency must be excluded before folate is given.
    A10

    Ataxic gait, glossitis/weakness, anaemia/palpitation with history of partial gastrectomy — Most probable haematological diagnosis?

    A10Q12, Q13

    Most probable diagnosis: megaloblastic anaemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency.

    Basis

    • With gastrectomy, intrinsic factor is lost, so vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed.
    • Ataxic gait: demyelination of the dorsal and lateral spinal tracts, giving sensory ataxia and paraesthesiae.
    • Weakness and palpitation: symptoms of anaemia.

    Other cause after gastrectomy: iron deficiency, because gastrectomy diminishes iron absorption, giving a microcytic hypochromic picture.

    Confirmation: macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils
    Hypercellular marrow with megaloblasts
    Low serum vitamin B12
    Raised homocysteine and methylmalonic acid
    Reticulocyte rise about 5 days after parenteral vitamin B12.

    All topics / Ch 23

    The Breast

    16 questions · viva and written, in Robbins order.

    Inflammatory and Benign Lesions

    Inflammatory lesions

    Name inflammatory lesions of breast.

    DU26M

    Inflammatory disease of the breast is rare (less than 1% of breast symptoms) and is caused by infection, autoimmune disease, or foreign body-type reactions to keratin or secretions.

    1. Acute mastitis: lactational, usually in the first month of breastfeeding, through cracks and fissures in the nipple. Staphylococcus aureus (abscesses) or streptococci (cellulitis) 2. Squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts (recurrent subareolar abscess, periductal mastitis, Zuska disease [recurrent periareolar abscess with squamous metaplasia of ducts]): keratinising squamous metaplasia plugs ducts. More than 90% are smokers
    Fistula and nipple inversion 3. Duct ectasia: periareolar mass with thick white nipple secretion in multiparous females in the fifth or sixth decade. Not related to smoking 4. Fat necrosis: painless mass mimicking cancer. About half have a history of trauma or surgery 5. Lymphocytic mastopathy (diabetic mastopathy): hard masses with dense collagenised stroma and lymphocytic infiltrate. Type 1 diabetes and Hashimoto thyroiditis [autoimmune thyroiditis causing hypothyroidism] 6. Granulomatous mastitis: granulomatous lobular mastitis (parous females, often idiopathic), cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis (lipophilic Corynebacteria), and systemic or infective causes such as sarcoidosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, tuberculosis - Inflammatory carcinoma mimics inflammation and must always be considered in an erythematous swollen breast

    Causes of breast lump

    What are the causes of breast lump?

    DU26MDU08Ju

    Most palpable breast masses (more than 95%) are benign.

    Benign

    • Fibroadenoma and cysts (the commonest)
    • Fibrocystic changes
    • Fat necrosis, which may mimic cancer
    • Duct ectasia
    • Lactational adenoma
    • Abscess from infection, during lactation
    • Granulomatous mastitis

    Tumours

    • Phyllodes tumour
    • Invasive carcinoma, which is usually an irregular mass
    • Angiosarcoma and lymphoma (rare)

    Fibroadenoma

    Give the morphology of fibroadenoma of breast.

    DU03M
    • Size varies from less than 1 cm to large tumours that replace most of the breast
    • Well-circumscribed, rubbery, grey-white nodules that bulge above the surrounding tissue
    • Often contain slit-like spaces lined by epithelium
    • On radiography a well-circumscribed mass
      The absence of adipose tissue accounts for its radiodensity
    • Microscopy: proliferation of delicate, often myxoid intralobular stroma, which surrounds, pushes and distorts the epithelium. The border is sharply delimited
    • Two patterns: pericanalicular (stroma surrounds patent ducts) and intracanalicular (stroma compresses ducts into cleft-like spaces)
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 23)p. 967p. 968

    Carcinoma of the Breast

    Classification

    Classify breast tumour/carcinoma.

    5DU25MDU23NDU19NovDU14JuDU07Ju
    GroupTypes
    In situ carcinomaDuctal carcinoma in situ (DCIS)
    Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS)
    Invasive carcinomaInvasive carcinoma of no special type (about 75%)
    Invasive lobular carcinoma (up to 15%)
    Special types: mucinous, tubular, cribriform, papillary, apocrine, micropapillary, metaplastic
    Stromal tumoursFibroadenoma, phyllodes tumour (intralobular stroma)
    Angiosarcoma (interlobular stroma)
    OtherLymphoma, metastases from other sites (less than 5% of malignant tumours)
    • Paget disease of the nipple [DCIS extending into the nipple epidermis] is DCIS extending into the skin of the nipple
    • Inflammatory carcinoma is not a histological type
      it is a clinical presentation

    Write down the molecular classification of breast cancer.

    DU25N

    Breast cancers fall into three major molecular groups: luminal (ER-positive), HER2 and triple negative.

    GroupFeatures
    Luminal AER-positive, HER2-negative
    50% to 65% of cancers are luminal
    Strongly ER and PR positive
    Well differentiated
    Low proliferation
    Gain of 1q, loss of 16q, PIK3CA mutations
    Luminal BER-positive, HER2-negative
    High proliferation
    Lower ER and PR expression
    Poorly differentiated
    More aggressive than luminal A
    HER2-positiveAmplification of the HER2 gene on chromosome 17q
    About 20% of cancers
    ER-positive or ER-negative
    Respond well to HER2 inhibitors
    Triple negative (TNBC)Negative for ER, PR and HER2
    About 15% of cancers
    basal-like gene expression
    TP53 mutation
    Defective DNA repair, often from BRCA1 defects
    High grade
    Relatively poor prognosis

    Risk factors

    What are the risk factors of breast carcinoma?

    DU08Ju

    Breast cancer is multifactorial.

    1. Sex: 99% of those affected are female 2. Increasing age 3. Lifetime exposure to oestrogen: postmenopausal hormone therapy increases the incidence of luminal cancers 4. Genetic inheritance: - 25% to 35% of cases are due to inherited susceptibility variants - BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations account for 80% to 90% of single gene familial breast cancers and 3% to 6% of all breast cancers 5. Family history: breast cancer in a first-degree relative, in multiple relatives, or at an early age 6. Environmental and lifestyle factors, such as low physical activity

    Factors that decrease risk are early pregnancy (before 20 years of age) and prolonged breastfeeding.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 23)p. 955p. 956p. 958

    Prognostic and predictive factors

    What are the prognostic (and predictive) factors of breast cancer?

    5DU25MDU23NDU19NovDU16JuDU14Ju

    Prognostic factors

    1. Distant metastases: the most important
    2. Lymph node metastases: the most important in the absence of distant metastases. 10-year disease-free survival is 70% to 80% with no nodes involved, 35% to 40% with one to three positive nodes and 10% to 15% with more than 10 positive nodes
    3. Tumour size: node-negative carcinoma less than 1 cm has a 10-year survival of more than 90%, falling to 77% above 2 cm
    4. Locally advanced disease: invasion of skin or skeletal muscle
    5. Histologic grade: high-grade tumours do worse
    6. Histologic subtype: tubular and cribriform carcinomas have a good prognosis
    7. Lymphovascular invasion
    8. Inflammatory carcinoma: 3-year survival of only 3% to 10%

    Prognostic and predictive biomarkers

    • ER and PR
    • HER2
    • Gene expression profiling, which identifies slow-growing ER-positive cancers that can be spared chemotherapy
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 23)p. 964p. 965

    What is the role of ER, PR and HER-2 neu in breast cancer?

    DU23N
    • ER: both prognostic and predictive
      ER-positive tumours (1% or more of cells with nuclear staining) respond to endocrine therapy, which reduces recurrence and improves survival
      "low positive" tumours (1% to 10% staining) have a worse prognosis
    • PR: ER-positive tumours are usually PR-positive
      ER-positive tumours with low PR expression have worse outcomes than those with high ER and PR
    • HER2: both prognostic and predictive
      Positivity indicates aggressive behaviour and response to HER2-targeting agents
    • HER2 is detected by immunohistochemistry for protein overexpression or by in situ hybridisation for gene amplification
    • Cancers negative for ER, PR and HER2 are triple negative
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 23)p. 957p. 961p. 965

    Paget disease of the nipple

    Short note on Paget's disease of nipple.

    DU04S

    Definition and pathogenesis. Ductal carcinoma in situ arising within the ductal system extends up the lactiferous ducts into the skin of the nipple without crossing the basement membrane. The malignant cells disrupt the squamous epithelial barrier, so fluid seeps out and forms an oozing, scaly crust.

    Features

    • Most females without a palpable mass have DCIS and are staged as such
    • About one-half have a palpable breast mass, which usually proves to be invasive carcinoma

    Prognosis. It depends on the features of the invasive carcinoma, if present, and is not affected by the presence or absence of Paget disease [disordered bone remodelling].

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 23)p. 953p. 954

    Breast Lumps

    A5

    20-year-old woman with a free, movable breast lump — Probable diagnosis? Investigations to diagnose the case?

    A5

    Probable diagnosis: fibroadenoma, the most common benign stromal tumour of the female breast.

    • Most occur in females in their 20s and 30s
      Frequently multiple and bilateral
    • Usually presents as a palpable mass in young females
    • Hormonally responsive: may grow during pregnancy and regress after menopause

    Investigations - Imaging: radiograph shows a characteristically well-circumscribed mass. The absence of adipose tissue accounts for its radiodensity - Histology: proliferation of intralobular stroma that surrounds, pushes and distorts the associated epithelium, with a sharply delimited border - Gross: rubbery, white, well-circumscribed mass

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 23)p. 967p. 968

    A woman has a hard, firm breast lump fixed to tissue (± skin dimpling). What is your likely diagnosis?

    DU13JaDU11Ju

    Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type

    • It most commonly presents as a hard, irregular, radiodense mass with a desmoplastic stromal reaction
    • Malignant tumours invade across tissue planes, so they are irregular, unlike the round, rubbery, mobile benign masses
    • The cut surface produces a grating sound from chalky-white desmoplastic stroma
    • Skin dimpling, with peau d'orange, is seen in inflammatory carcinoma, where dermal lymphovascular channels are plugged by tumour cells and the skin is tethered by Cooper ligaments [suspensory ligaments of the breast]

    Same: what investigations would you perform?

    DU13JaDU11Ju
    1. Mammography: densities, architectural distortions and calcifications. The average invasive carcinoma detected is about 1 cm
    2. Ultrasonography, digital breast tomosynthesis or MRI when the carcinoma is not visible on standard mammograms (about 10%)
    3. Histology to confirm invasive carcinoma and grade it by the Nottingham score
    4. Biomarkers: ER, PR and HER2
    5. Axillary lymph nodes: histological examination, since clinical assessment is unreliable. Sentinel node biopsy
